descs.en: The boy next door followed her to university and stayed “unofficial” for years. She loves him. She just doesn’t know how to go from friends to forever.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Eliana Lin and Wang Yu Chen grew up next door to each other in the Walled City, with a knee-high wall between their front steps. On the night she finishes school she can’t sleep, and goes to sit on her step at two in the morning. He comes out with a blanket and sits down beside her, and somewhere before dawn he realises he’s in love with her. In the morning he turns down the better medical school in the north and follows her up the hill. He tells everyone it was the course.

She works it out in a fortnight. At Mid-Autumn she climbs onto his roof to tell him to stop hovering, and he kisses her before she’s finished the sentence. After that they’re together in secret, because that’s how she wants it.

She’s the youngest Lin, born the night her mother died, and her father can barely look at her. At night, on five screens, she cleans the family’s name out of places it shouldn’t be. Yu Chen never asks her to stop. He brings tea.

Friends to lovers · Boy next door · Secret relationship · He waits · Complete in four volumes, plus twenty-two side stories

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Eliana has been in the corner of every Lin book: asleep under a ladder, filming everyone’s kisses, opening a phone in under four minutes. I kept wondering who was waiting for her on the kerb when she got home.

Yu Chen looks like the clean one, and mostly he is. But he reads her food orders every night because they’re on his card, he chose his medical school because of her, and once he lied to the cousin who raised him. The book doesn’t tell him off. In seven years he never once asks her to be someone else. He makes more tea.

Nobody cheats, and nothing hangs on a misunderstanding. They get together early, and their first times are shy and funny, because he researches everything and she wrecks the plan.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers.

A gentle, funny friends-to-lovers romance, with some hard moments:

• Love scenes on the page

• A mother who died giving birth, and a father’s coldness towards the daughter she left

• The heroine’s secret work for a crime syndicate

• A sister abducted; trafficking referred to but not shown

• A nineteen-year-old’s death in an emergency department

• Threatening messages and photographs from strangers

• A cyber-attack, a crowd crush and a crushed leg

• An attack with a broken bottle

• A partner who reads her food orders to know when she hasn’t eaten, shown without judgement

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Yu-er — Eliana's family name. Her sisters use it when they want something. Yu Chen uses it all the time, and it's the only time it comes without a favour attached.
The tall house — the Lin family house in the Walled City: old, narrow, too many stairs, a red door, and three front steps under a small tiled roof.
The porch — those three steps, with the crack in the third one, where everything that matters between them happens at two in the morning. From 2026 it runs the width of both houses.
The old Song house — next door to the Lins. Yu Chen's uncle's house, which he bought from Wei Long; later rebuilt with one long room and two desks facing each other.
The persimmon tree — in the Song garden. Its best branch hangs over the Lin side, so by old neighbourly rule its fruit are Lin persimmons. Ripe every October.
The jar — a plum-jam jar of Nainai's, kept behind a loose brick in the garden wall under the persimmon branch. Notes go in it. You don't read one until the writer has gone inside.
The Eraser — what the Syndicate calls Eliana, because she erases the Lin family's footprints. She hates the name.
The fence — what she built in October 2022, after her sister was taken: a watch on the family's names, faces and addresses that wakes her wherever she is. Two short buzzes mean family.
FENCE — her own security firm, from March 2026, in two rooms above a dumpling shop on Terrace Road. For the first month the sign was a sticky note: FENCE. Legal. Mostly.
The Spreadsheet — Eliana's record of every family secret, kept for years. "You're on a spreadsheet" is a warning.
DRAW (OFFICIAL) — Eliana's caption on the video of the paper twins' birthday party at Fig Tree Lane. Raiden contests it every year.
Red egg — a boiled egg dyed red, a traditional birthday gift. One is left at Eliana's door before dawn every 18 February. She thinks for years she knows who leaves it.
Study room 4B — the quiet room at the end of the library's fourth floor, booked to "Wang Y.C." every weekday morning since March 2022. Nobody has ever found out how.
Graduate-entry medicine — a four-year medical degree for students who already have a first degree. Yu Chen's, at the university on the hill, 2021 to 2025.
OSCE — the practical part of medical finals: timed stations with examiners and actors playing patients.
Mid-Autumn — the harvest festival at the full moon of the eighth lunar month: mooncakes, family dinners and lanterns. Every year Yu Chen puts a white rabbit lantern on his roof.
PLAN — Yu Chen's plans, in capitals, on small squares of paper. PLAN, PLAN B, PLAN C. She wrecks every one.
Nainai — grandmother on the father's side. Yu Chen's lives in the north and has had a letter from him every month for years.
The Lins, the Wangs and the Songs — Yu Chen's father was a Wang from the north, the younger brother of Xing Yue's father. His mother was a Song, Wei Long's aunt, which is how he came to live in the old Song house next door to the Lins.

chapters.title: The Boy Next Door Who Never Left
chapters.desc: The night she finishes school, Eliana can’t sleep and goes to sit on her front step at two in the morning. Yu Chen brings his blanket out and sits with her, and before it gets light he works out that he’s in love with her.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to talk. I’ll just sit here. That’s allowed.”
chapters.content:
The night Eliana Lin finished school, nobody congratulated her.

Her father came home at eight, glanced at the certificate on the dining table, and asked whether she had submitted her university documents. She said yes. He nodded once, poured himself a glass of water, and went into his study. That was the celebration. No dinner, no photographs, no question about the last paper. Not even a well done.

At eleven she tried sleeping. At midnight she checked the admissions portal for the fourth time. At one she watched three videos of people surprising their families with their results and regretted every one of them. At two she gave up, pulled a cardigan over her sleep shirt, put on her rabbit slippers and let herself out of the front door of the tall house.

The Walled City was as quiet as it ever got. Three stone steps under a little tiled roof, a crack in the third one, and a knee-high wall dividing her steps from the steps next door. On the other side of the wall, one window was lit on the second floor.

Wang Yu Chen’s room. Of course.

She sat on the middle step, pulled her knees up and put her chin on them. She had decided she wasn’t going to cry tonight. There was something especially embarrassing about crying over a missing congratulations. She was eighteen. She had survived twelve years of school and the general misery of being a teenager. She was surely old enough not to care.

A moth went round the porch light. A door opened.

“Eliana?”

Yu Chen was on his own step in a grey T-shirt and black lounge trousers, hair flattened on one side as if he’d been reading on his elbow. He looked at her, and then at the empty bit of step beside her.

“Why are you sitting outside?”

“Enjoying the scenery.”

He looked round. There was a bin, two parked cars and a shrub that had given up.

“At two in the morning.”

“It’s a beautiful neighbourhood.”

He went back inside without a word. Eliana stared at his door, mildly offended.

Thirty seconds later it opened again, and he came out with two cups and a folded blanket over his arm: cream, old, with little flowers embroidered along the hem. She knew that blanket. It lived on the end of his bed and never went anywhere.

“That’s your mother’s.”

“It’s warm.” He stepped over the wall the way he’d been stepping over it since he was six, put a cup down by her slippers, and shook the blanket out over both their knees. “You don’t have to talk. I’ll just sit here. That’s allowed.”

She looked into the cup. Honey and lemon. Her favourite, which he knew, because he knew everything.

“Thank you.”

He leaned his back against her doorframe and didn’t ask why she was outside. He had known her almost thirteen years; asking only sent her further in. So he waited. Waiting was the thing he did best.

“Do you know what’s funny?” she said eventually. “Today was supposed to be important. I finished school. Twelve years. That’s longer than I’ve known some people.”

“Congratulations.”

She turned her head.

“Well done, Eliana.”

Her fingers tightened round the cup. It took her a moment. “Oh. Thanks.” She looked at the road. “Nobody said that today.”

“Who didn’t?”

“Nobody. Baba came home and asked about my university forms. He didn’t ask how the paper went. I thought maybe he’d be pleased I’d finished, but it’s not as if I expected anything.”

It was a sentence he’d heard about birthdays, school concerts and every set of results she’d ever brought home. Yu Chen had been around long enough to know she always expected something. She had only learned to pretend she didn’t.

“Your results were good,” he said. “You made me work out your average three times because you didn’t believe the first one.”

“You could have made a mistake.”

“Eliana. I came second in the year in maths.”

She considered it. “That’s true.”

“Thank you for acknowledging my qualifications.”

A laugh got out of her, small and real, and he reached over and took the cup before she tipped it on his mother’s blanket.

“Will you miss it?” he asked. “School.”

“The uniform? No. The teachers? Depends on the teacher. My friends are all leaving. Overseas, the north, or here but somewhere else. I’ll probably go to the hill university, which is nearly an hour away.”

“Forty minutes without traffic.”

“I’ll be all alone. What if everyone’s mean?”

“Then don’t make friends with them.”

“What if they don’t want to be friends with me?”

“Then they’re stupid.”

“You’re biased.”

“I’m aware.”

She smiled into her tea. He had been easy to be around since she was five and had climbed over this exact wall because she thought his family’s golden retriever looked lonely. The dog had been asleep. Yu Chen, six and grave, had asked what she was doing in his garden. She’d said she was making friends. He had looked at her for a while and then moved over so she could sit down.

“Do you think everyone leaves in the end?” she said. “People grow up. They get lives. Then one day the people who used to know everything about you don’t know what you’re doing any more.”

“Some people stay.”

“How do you know?”

“Because they choose to.”

“That sounds like a film.”

“Then the film’s right.” He let her laugh at him. Then she went still.

“Are you going north?”

He had the best offer in the country from the northern medical school, the one he’d wanted since he was fourteen. She knew that. She also knew there was a second offer, from the hill.

“No,” he said.

“What?”

“I’m not going.”

“Why? You wanted it.”

“I changed my mind.”

She frowned at him, eyebrows pulled together, the rabbit ears on her slippers pointing in opposite directions. “You shouldn’t change your plans because of me.”

He went still. She’d said it so easily, as if the idea of him doing anything for her sake had never once crossed her mind. She had no idea that he’d learned her chosen faculty before she’d sent her application, that he’d spent a month comparing bus routes and campus maps, or that he had declined the north that afternoon, because four years somewhere she wasn’t had made the letter feel like nothing much.

“I can make my own decisions,” he said. “And I’m not going somewhere just because it’s famous.”

“But you worked so hard. I don’t want you to regret it.”

He pulled the blanket up round her shoulders. “I won’t.”

By three the tea was cold. By half past she was complaining about the possibility of a roommate who snored, and by a quarter to four she’d explained why she would never wake up for a nine o’clock lecture.

“Set three alarms. Put the phone across the room.”

“What if I don’t hear it?”

“Then you’re beyond help.”

“You’re supposed to encourage me.”

“I’m encouraging you to become a functioning adult.”

Somewhere in there she shifted closer, because it had got cold, and her shoulder settled against his arm.

“Chen. Will we still see each other? When you’re busy?”

“I’ll be busy. I’ll still see you.”

“Promise?”

He held out his little finger. She stared at it.

“Seriously?”

“Do you want the promise or not?”

She laughed and hooked hers round it. His hand was warm, hers was cold, and he held on a second longer than a promise needed.

That was when he realised he was in trouble.

It didn’t arrive with thunder. It arrived while she was telling him, hands going under the blanket, about a girl in her class who had a crush on the maths teacher purely because he was tall. Yu Chen stopped listening. He was watching her nose scrunch when she couldn’t find a word, and the way she laughed at her own jokes before anyone else had a chance to. He knew the scar on her left knee was from falling off her bicycle at nine. He knew she hated coriander, couldn’t have coffee after six, bought strawberry milk when she was upset and slept with the curtains a little open because the full dark frightened her. He knew she’d tell him everything eventually: a photo with no caption, a knock on his window, her face at his gate asking if he was free.

He’d spent thirteen years making room for her and never asked himself why.

Oh, he thought, and looked at the street so she wouldn’t see his face. I’m in love with her.

He nearly laughed. He’d been in love with her for years. He’d just been comfortable calling it something else.

“You’re not listening.”

“I am.”

“What did I just say?”

“Something about the tall part.”

“You’re lying.”

“Probably.”

She leaned her head on his shoulder. “You’re so annoying.” A minute later: “I’m sleepy.”

“Then go in. Your bed has a blanket.”

“This one’s warmer.”

“Because it’s my mother’s.”

“Exactly.”

Her eyes closed. Her head slid from his shoulder into the crook of his arm, and her fingers caught in the hem of his T-shirt and stayed there. He checked the time on his phone. Three fifty-two. He should wake her. He tucked the blanket round her shoulders instead and rested his head on the doorframe.

“Congratulations, Eliana,” he whispered. “You’re going to do well. And when you don’t, I’ll still be here.”

He didn’t know if he was promising her or himself.

✦ ✦ ✦

By five the sky had gone grey and his arm was dead from the shoulder down. He didn’t move it. A delivery van went past the end of the lane.

Then the front door behind them opened, and Elowen stood there in a long cardigan over her nightdress. She had come in after midnight from the shop and slept in her old room, meaning to take her sister out for breakfast. She looked at Eliana, then at the blanket, then at him, and her face changed.

“She fell asleep?”

“She was tired.”

Elowen came down one step and brushed the hair off Eliana’s cheek. She didn’t ask why her sister was outside, or what they’d talked about, or how long he’d been sitting there. “She hasn’t been sleeping.”

“I know.”

Elowen looked at him properly then, because of the way he’d said it. Not like a neighbour. Like someone who’d been paying attention.

“Go home and sleep,” she said. “I’ve got her.”

He eased his arm out. Eliana’s fingers tightened on his shirt and he stopped, and for a second he looked helpless. Elowen put her hand over her sister’s. “It’s all right, sweetheart. Go to sleep.” The fingers let go.

He stood and his shoulder cracked.

“Your arm?”

“It’s fine.”

“You’re a terrible liar.” She glanced down at Eliana. “She was lucky you were awake.”

“No,” he said. “I’m lucky she came outside.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Back in his room he stood at the window and watched Elowen help her sister in, the blanket over her arm, the two cups collected. The front door shut. His phone buzzed: the hill university’s portal. Your acceptance has been recorded. The northern letter was still in his inbox. He opened it once more and closed it.

The phone buzzed again.

Eliana: are you awake

He laughed out loud in an empty room.

Yu Chen: No. I’m asleep.

Eliana: then why are you replying

Yu Chen: Sleepwalking.

Eliana: idiot. thank you for tonight. and for saying congratulations

Yu Chen: You deserved it.

Eliana: chen? i’m glad you’re next door

He read it three times and stood against his desk grinning at the screen like a fool.

Yu Chen: Me too.

He could have said more. Something that would change the shape of everything. But she was tired, and he had thirteen years of patience behind him, and he could wait. He would go to the hill. He would work hard and build a life that was his. He wouldn’t tell her she was part of the reason. He’d let her find the university at her own pace, make friends, become whoever she wanted. He wouldn’t ask her to stay beside him. He’d just make sure she always knew where to find him.

It wasn’t a noble decision. There was something selfish in wanting to stay in the middle of someone’s ordinary life, and he knew it.

At nine sixteen her phone buzzed beside her pillow.

Yu Chen: Don’t forget breakfast.

Eliana: good morning to you too

Yu Chen: It’s nearly ten. Good morning, idiot.

She laughed into the pillow. Across the wall, on three hours’ sleep, he was smiling too.

She didn’t know he was in love with her. She didn’t know about the north. And she didn’t know that years later, when someone asked Yu Chen when he’d first fallen for her, he would say a cold front step, two cups of honey lemon, his mother’s blanket, and a girl asleep on his arm at three fifty-two in the morning, the night nobody congratulated her except him.

chapters.title: Two Gowns, Eventually
chapters.desc: First day on the hill. Eliana starts computer science and would like to be invisible, and Yu Chen has somehow started medicine at the same university and swears it’s about the course.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s the best medical course in the country. You being here is a coincidence.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Eliana Lin learned about university was that the campus was unnecessarily large. The second was that nobody on the hill had considered the possibility of a student with no sense of direction whatsoever.

It was the first Monday in September and she had been walking for nearly half an hour. Her registration email said the computer science building was ten minutes from the main gate. She had followed the signs, crossed a courtyard, passed something called the School of Business and arrived, somehow, outside a sports hall.

She checked her phone. Then the map. A group of second years went past looking terribly sure of themselves, which she found offensive, and she decided against asking them anything.

Yu Chen: Where are you?

Eliana: university

Yu Chen: Very informative.

Eliana: i’m exploring

Yu Chen: You’re lost. Send me your location.

Eliana: no. i can find it myself

Yu Chen: Of course.

She put the phone away. She was eighteen, an incoming computer scientist and perfectly capable of finding a building. She took three steps, turned round, and read the sign over the door behind her. SPORTS SCIENCE AND ATHLETICS CENTRE.

She shut her eyes.

A minute later he received a photograph of a campus directory taken at an angle so tragic that half the names were upside down.

Eliana: hypothetically. if someone were at the sports centre. how would they get to computer science

Yu Chen: Turn around.

Eliana: why

Yu Chen: I’m behind you.

He was fifteen metres away with two takeaway cups and his black backpack on one shoulder, white shirt, dark trousers, hair neat apart from the two strands that never were. He looked annoyingly put together. He also looked pleased with himself, which was worse.

“You’re supposed to be at registration.”

“I was. Then someone sent me a photograph of the sports centre.” He handed her a cup. Iced milk tea, less sugar, no pearls. “Impressive. You managed the exact opposite direction.”

“I was looking around.”

“Of course.”

“Stop saying it like that.”

“I believe you,” he said, and didn’t, and they both knew it.

As they walked back he took a folded sheet out of his bag. It was a map of the campus, drawn by hand: the roads, the faculties, the libraries, the canteens and the shuttle stops, in his small neat printing with arrows between the places that mattered. Some places were circled. A courtyard behind engineering. A corner of the library. A bench by the east garden. A café wedged between two lecture halls. Beside the circles, notes.

Quiet. Good for reading.

Usually empty after three.

Cheap. Don’t buy the chicken rice.

Good place to hide if it’s too much.

“Why did you write that?”

“Because you like quiet places.”

“I don’t hide.”

He looked at her.

“Sometimes,” she said.

“Last month you hid behind the curtains when the delivery man knocked.”

“I was in my pyjamas.”

“You were fully dressed.”

“I wasn’t emotionally prepared.”

He laughed. At the bottom corner of the map he had written If you get lost, ring me. She ran her thumb over it and asked when he’d done all this, and he said last week, because her orientation email had implied she’d struggle, and she said it had implied no such thing, and he said it had implied it to him.

He had spent two evenings on that map. He’d walked the routes with a stopwatch and found the corners where she could sit without having to talk to anybody. He’d also marked the shortest way from her building to the medical school, and he didn’t mention that part.

She stopped dead in the middle of the path. She was looking at the card on his lanyard.

“Medicine?”

“That’s what it says.”

“Here?”

“Unless they’ve made a mistake.”

All summer, when she’d asked him where he was going, he’d said he was still deciding. She stared at him. “You had the north. The north is the best.”

“It’s the best medical course in the country. You being here is a coincidence.”

“That isn’t even true. When did you decide?”

“Recently.”

“How recently?”

“You’re demanding this morning.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“You didn’t ask the right question.”

She opened her mouth and shut it again. And then, quite without meaning to, she smiled, the kind of smile that made her eyes go narrow and that she never noticed she was giving. “So you’re going to be here. Six years.”

“Possibly longer.”

“That’s nice. At least I’ll know someone.”

He looked away before his face did anything. “Unfortunately you’ll have to know me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The registration hall was full of students carrying folders and parents standing behind them looking anxious, and Eliana regretted coming in at once. Too many voices. Too many chances to do something stupid. She stood behind him with her documents against her chest.

“Computer science, counter six,” he said. “Documents?”

“Yes.”

“Student number?”

“Yes. Why are you talking like Baba?”

“Someone has to make sure you don’t forget your own name.”

She elbowed him. The queue moved. Seven people, then three, then none, and the woman at the counter looked up.

“Name?”

Eliana opened her mouth and nothing came out. Obviously she knew her name. It was on the papers in her hands. She’d written it ten thousand times. But with the woman looking straight at her and a line of people behind, the simplest question in the world had become impossible.

“El—“ Her ears went hot. “Sorry.”

She stepped backwards, and before he could say anything she was behind the nearest pillar.

He looked at the space where she’d been, then at the pillar.

“Don’t laugh,” it said.

“I’m not.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m allowed to smile.”

He went round. She was flat against the stone with the folder up like a shield, pink to the neck. He took it out of her hands, gently, and held it.

“I can’t. I forgot how to speak.”

“That happens.”

“Does it happen to you?”

“No. Look at me.” She did. “You tell her your name. Eliana Lin. Nothing else. I’ll stand beside you.”

He didn’t hold her hand. He stood close enough that she could feel him there, and when the woman smiled and asked again Eliana said, “Eliana Lin,” and then her student number and her faculty, and the whole thing took less than a minute. When she turned round he was looking at her with a face that was far too pleased.

“Well done.”

“Shut up.”

Before he went to his own induction he straightened the lanyard round her neck. His fingers touched the side of her throat and she went still.

“Have lunch,” he said. “And don’t hide behind any more pillars.”

“Go away.”

He went, and she watched him into the crowd, and felt odd for a minute. Not lonely. Just aware that the person who’d been with her all morning was somewhere else.

✦ ✦ ✦

The frisbee came at a quarter to twelve.

She was walking towards the library with her eyes on the map, looking for the east garden, which she was reasonably confident about, and so she didn’t see the bright orange disc coming at her face from the lawn.

“Eliana!”

A hand appeared beside her head. The frisbee landed in his palm about an arm’s length from her nose.

“Are you all right?” He looked past her at the lawn. “Watch where you’re throwing.” A boy lifted a hand and shouted sorry, and Yu Chen sent it back without looking at it and steered her off the path with his hand flat on her back. “You’re supposed to look where you’re walking.”

“I was looking at the map.”

“Then stop walking.”

“That’s what I was doing.”

He looked at the map in her hands. It was upside down. He rotated it without a word.

“Don’t say anything.”

“I’m thinking many things.”

The library had four floors, long windows over the east garden and the hush of a church, and she loved it immediately. He knew her books were on the second floor because he’d checked, he said, because she was always going to come here. He put his flask on the table, a dark blue thing scratched round the lid that he’d carried since he was fourteen.

“That’s ugly.”

“It’s functional.”

They spent twenty minutes on their timetables. Every few minutes she said “Chen?” and asked what a tutorial group was, or the difference between a lecture and a seminar, and once she said “Chen?” and then “nothing, just checking,” and he gave her a look over the top of his screen.

They left at half past one. He’d gone ahead down the stairs to return a book, and she came after him holding his flask.

“Is this yours? Why did you leave it?”

“I thought you were carrying it.”

“Why would I—“

Her foot slipped. The flask went. It hit one step, then the next, then the next, and the clang went up the whole stairwell, and it came to rest on the landing with a long dent down its side.

“Oh my God.” She came down at a run. “I’m sorry. I’m so sorry.”

He turned it over and pressed the dent with his thumb. “It’s fine.”

“It’s dented. You’ve had it for years.”

“Are you going to cry?”

“No!”

“Your face says otherwise.” He unscrewed the lid, checked it, closed it. No leak. “Now it has character.”

“That’s what people say when things are broken.”

“Then it’s broken. I’m keeping it.”

“Why?”

He shrugged. “It reminds me of today.”

She didn’t understand why that made her feel so warm. She just stood there on the landing and let it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They had lunch outside the student centre, a sandwich for her and water for him, out of the newly dented flask, which she kept looking at.

“You’ve looked at it six times.”

“It’s ugly.”

“You did that.”

A breeze came through the trees and her hair blew across her face, and he reached over and tucked it behind her ear. He had done it a thousand times. When she was small and couldn’t see her book. At fifteen, crying over a failed maths test. At seventeen, when her hair kept getting into a photograph. It had never meant anything. Or nothing they’d said.

But now there was a table of students right next to them, and someone laughing nearby, and all at once she was aware of his fingers.

“Chen. Not here.”

His hand stopped. “Not here?”

“People can see.”

“See what?”

“You know what.”

“All right.” He lowered his hand. She went back to her sandwich. A few seconds passed. “Where, then?”

She nearly choked.

“Where can I do it?” he said, perfectly innocent.

“Wang Yu Chen.”

“Eat your lunch.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past four she was alone on the bench by the east garden, waiting for him to finish his faculty welcome, when her other phone buzzed.

Qian: Did you bring the folder?

Eliana: yes

Qian: All of it? The shipping records too?

Under her laptop, under the registration forms, was a slim folder of copies: shipping manifests, transfer summaries, internal notes a clerk had been selling to anybody who asked. Names, dates, company accounts. One name came up far too often.

Lin Jian.

She’d spent weeks finding every copy. Qian, who worked for Chen Si and asked for things in short sentences, had come to her last winter because something in her father’s business was leaking, and someone had to make it stop existing. She hadn’t asked what would happen to the clerk. She had learned not to ask things in her father’s house a long time ago. Her mother had died the night she was born, and Lin Jian had never once let her forget it. He never said it. He didn’t have to. It was in the way he spoke about her mother and the way the whole house went silent when she asked a question.

Qian: Don’t keep the originals. Don’t mention this to anyone.

She locked the phone. A shadow fell over her shoes.

“Ready?” He had changed into a dark jacket. He looked at her face. “What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Heavy?” He reached for her bag. “I’ll carry it.”

She snatched it up before his hand arrived. “No. It’s fine. I’ve got it.”

He looked at her for a second longer than usual, and nodded, and didn’t push. But all the way down to the gates he noticed that she kept one hand on the front pocket, as if she were checking something was still there.

At the bus stop she asked to see his timetable, just curious, and studied it while he looked at the road.

“Eight o’clock lectures on Mondays? That’s horrible.”

“You start at nine.”

“Exactly. Much better.”

She gave the phone back. Neither of them noticed that she’d memorised his Monday building, or that she’d already saved a photo of the whole week.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she pinned his map above her desk beside her calendar, the circles still showing. On her phone she had a picture of him outside the medical school holding two coffees, which he hadn’t known she’d taken, and one of him laughing in the library, and one of them both in the east garden with his face half turned away. She put that one in her favourites.

Then she opened her notes. There was a heading, Wang Yu Chen — University, and under it:

Medicine. Monday, 8 a.m., Building C.

Likes the coffee at the café by the east gate.

Keeps carrying that ugly flask.

Waits even when he says he won’t.

She looked at the last line and added another. Get him something before his birthday.

Yu Chen: Home? Ate dinner?

Eliana: yes, mother

Yu Chen: Show me.

She sent him a photo of an empty bowl and a pair of chopsticks laid neatly across it, and then buried her face in her pillow for no reason.

Yu Chen: Good first day?

She thought about the wrong building, the frisbee, the flask, and him standing beside her when she couldn’t say her own name.

Eliana: maybe a little good. i’m glad we’re at the same university

Across the wall he read it at his desk. He’d spent the whole day pretending it was a coincidence. He’d drawn her a map, learned her faculty’s timetable and chosen his welcome sessions so he’d be free at her lunchtime. And she was glad.

Yu Chen: Me too.

Eliana: don’t get busy and forget me

He looked at that one for some time.

Yu Chen: I don’t think that’s possible.

He sent it before he could change his mind, and then opened her timetable, which he knew nearly as well as his own, and wrote three lines in his notes. Check she’s had lunch. Don’t let her walk alone past the sports field. Umbrella: she never checks the weather. He laughed at himself, and didn’t delete any of them.

Eliana fell asleep with her phone by her pillow. Her student card was on the desk. In a folder on her laptop, under a pile of university forms, was a scanned shipping record with her father’s name on it.

She had two lives now. One had lectures and milk tea and a boy next door who’d somehow followed her up a hill. The other was quieter, and far more dangerous. If he ever found it, he’d ask questions, and she wasn’t ready to answer them.

Not when she was still learning how to be eighteen, and the boy next door had just made her first day a little less frightening.

chapters.title: The Flask, the Headphones, the Tea
chapters.desc: Ten days in, Yu Chen has her new timetable memorised and a box of the headphones she destroys every fortnight. Eliana has found out she can’t concentrate when he turns pages, which is new and annoying.
chapters.epigraph: “I bought ten pairs. Don’t argue. You go through them like socks.”
chapters.content:
By the tenth day of term Wang Yu Chen had three new habits. He checked the weather before he left the house. He carried an umbrella when the sky was perfectly clear. And he knew exactly where Eliana Lin was supposed to be at any hour of the week.

He considered the third one practical. Eliana had a gift for disappearing. Not on purpose, mostly. She had no sense of direction, a poor relationship with her phone battery, and a way of falling so far into whatever she was doing that the rest of the world went out like a light.

So he’d learned her timetable. Monday, programming at nine and maths at eleven. Tuesday, discrete maths and a lab. Wednesday, a free morning in the library. Thursday, the tutorial she complained about every week. Friday, three classes and an afternoon she said was for assignments and spent on videos. He knew the table by the east windows, the café where she bought strawberry milk, the courtyard she liked because nobody went there, and the bench outside computer science where she sat when she was waiting for him.

He also knew what time her bedroom light usually went off. That was less practical. He knew it anyway.

At twenty to eight on Thursday she opened her front door and found him on her step with a paper bag.

“Why are you here? It isn’t even eight.”

“Excellent observation.” He held it out. An egg sandwich, still warm, and a carton of strawberry milk. “You didn’t eat yesterday.”

“How do you know?”

“You told me.” At half past eleven the night before she’d sent him a photograph of her terrible code, two paragraphs about her lecturer, and somewhere in the middle, forgot dinner lol. She hadn’t expected him to remember.

“You’re nosy.”

“You’re easy to monitor.”

“That’s creepy.” She took the sandwich. “Don’t you have class?”

“Half eight. I’ll walk you to your building first.”

“My building’s on the other side of the hill.”

“It’s on the way.”

“It isn’t.”

He looked at her until she laughed and went to get her bag. She came back with her hair in a loose knot and a pair of headphones with one cup hanging at an unfortunate angle.

“Again?”

“They still work.”

“On one side.”

“That’s enough.”

The headphones were a recurring problem. Her first summer pair had lasted three weeks. The second, twelve days. This lot had made it almost exactly two weeks before the left side died. He’d assumed she was careless until he found out she carried them loose in her bag wrapped round her charger, slept in them, and had once tried to fix a loose wire with a paper clip. He had banned the paper clip. She had accused him of suppressing innovation.

“How long have you had those?”

“Two weeks.”

“Eliana.”

“Thirteen days.”

“You’ll destroy the next pair too.”

“Then I’ll buy another.”

“With what money?”

She thought about it. “Yours?” And then, when he looked at her, “Joking!”

He shook his head. He was already thinking about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunchtime she found she couldn’t concentrate.

She had an assignment due on Monday and a programming exercise she’d been looking at for forty minutes. It wasn’t hard. She understood it. She just couldn’t make herself finish it, because across the table Yu Chen was reading an anatomy textbook thick enough to stun a burglar, and every so often he turned a page.

The sound wasn’t even loud. A perfectly ordinary page, turning. She stared at him. He turned another.

“Chen. Can you stop that?”

“Reading?”

“Turning pages.”

“Would you prefer I read without turning them?”

“Don’t be sarcastic.”

He put his finger between the pages and stopped. She managed about thirty seconds of excellent progress. When she looked up, he was watching her.

“You’ve been on the same paragraph for fifteen minutes,” he said. “And you’ve blinked four times in the last thirty seconds. Your eyes are dry.”

“You’re counting my blinks now?”

“Apparently.” He unscrewed the dented flask. Tea, chrysanthemum and dried pear with a lump of rock sugar, the way Auntie Tsoi made it for him when he was ten and the way he’d made it for Eliana ever since, too sweet. He poured some into the lid and pushed it across. “Drink.”

“I drank this morning.”

He raised an eyebrow. She drank. He watched until the lid was empty, and she narrowed her eyes at him.

“You’re treating me like a child.”

“Then stop behaving like one.”

She kicked his shoe under the table. He caught her foot against his shin and kept it there. She tried to move it. He didn’t let her.

“Your leg’s in my way.”

“Then move yours.”

She gave him an offended look and went back to her laptop, and her foot stayed exactly where it was, against his shin, and neither of them mentioned it again.

The real problem, she decided, was that he was distracting. He wasn’t doing anything. He was just there, sleeves rolled to the elbow, watch loose on his wrist, hair falling forward when he looked down, writing in the margins in handwriting that was annoyingly neat. Calm. Untroubled. Sixty centimetres away from a girl having a crisis about a for-loop.

“Chen. Can you go somewhere else?”

“Why?”

“I can’t concentrate.”

“Because I’m here?”

“Maybe.”

The corner of his mouth went up. “Interesting.”

“Don’t make it weird.”

“Would you like me to leave?”

She looked at his book, his flask, the chair beside him. “No.”

He laughed under his breath. He didn’t turn another page for twenty minutes.

At two she fell asleep on her folded arms with the assignment still open. He noticed after a few minutes. A strand of hair had fallen across her cheek and he moved it. Then he took his grey hoodie out of his bag, warm from being folded there all morning, and put it round her shoulders. He didn’t move for forty minutes.

She woke and the first thing she noticed was the hoodie. The second was that he wasn’t reading. He was looking at her.

“How long?”

“Forty minutes.”

“Why didn’t you wake me? My assignment!”

“Still there. It autosaved.” He watched her pull the sleeves down over her hands. “No, I stole it from a passing student.”

“I didn’t ask.”

“You were going to.”

It smelled of his washing powder. She didn’t give it back. He noticed, and said nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening his cousin rang while he was walking home from the bus.

Wang Xing Yue was ten years older, a surgical registrar at City Hospital, and the kind of man who could make a room uncomfortable by looking at it. The faculty gave every first year a mentor from the hospitals, and Nainai had made sure Yu Chen’s was family. Xing Yue didn’t waste words. He seemed to have a limited supply and to resent spending them.

“You’re alive.”

“Unfortunately.”

“Eaten?”

“Yes.”

“And the girl?”

Yu Chen stopped walking. “What girl?”

There was a pause. “Nainai says you turned down the north for someone. She read it in your last letter.”

“I didn’t mention anyone in my letter.”

“Exactly. She noticed what you left out. Three pages and you said ‘the library’ eleven times.” Xing Yue let that sit. “Have you told her?”

“There’s nothing to tell.”

“Be careful, Chen. Being someone’s whole world before she’s had a chance to build one of her own. You have a habit of deciding things and then calling them inevitable.”

“You’re one to talk.”

“That’s why I’m qualified. Bring her to dinner one day. I’d like to meet the reason you’re on the hill.” He rang off before Yu Chen could say she wasn’t.

On Saturday Xing Yue came to the house for dinner and found his cousin in the kitchen fitting dumplings into a lunch box with the care of a man setting a fracture. Auntie Tsoi had made them. She had kept the house for the Songs since before Yu Chen was born, and after his parents died, when Wei Long, at fifteen, had more or less decided to raise his small cousin himself, she’d been the one who cooked, so nobody had ever thought of her as staff. When Yu Chen asked her for an extra batch she didn’t need to be told who they were for.

“The little girl next door still likes the prawn and chive?”

“She hasn’t been eating.”

“That child.” Auntie Tsoi folded another. “You’ve become attentive.”

“I’ve always been attentive.”

“Not like this,” she said, and smiled at her board.

Xing Yue leaned in the kitchen doorway with his gold-rimmed glasses catching the light, and watched, and asked three questions. Does she eat. Does she sleep. Does she study too much. Yu Chen answered all three without thinking. Not always. Not enough. Yes. Xing Yue said, “Hm,” which from him was a paragraph.

Yu Chen: Are you home? Come outside.

Eliana: why

Yu Chen: I have something. Come outside, Lin.

She came out to find him at the gap in the wall with a container. “Unless you know someone else who likes prawn and chive.”

Her face lit up. She reached for it and he didn’t let go.

“Did you have dinner?”

“I was going to.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“I had biscuits.”

“Biscuits.”

“Two.”

“That’s worse.” He let go. “Eat those first.”

The dumplings were lined up in neat rows with a tiny pot of vinegar and ginger beside them. “Tell Auntie Tsoi thank you,” she said. Then, when he was halfway back across his garden, she shouted after him, “Chen! Tell her they’re really pretty!”

He turned round. “Pretty?”

“The dumplings!”

An hour later he got a photograph of the empty box.

Eliana: finished! also. why do you always know when i haven’t eaten

Yu Chen: Because you tell me. More often than you realise.

Eliana: oh. that’s embarrassing. now you know everything

He looked at that for a while. Not everything.

She sent a confused face. He put the phone down. There were things she didn’t tell him. Her father. The folder she wouldn’t let him carry. The nights her light stayed on until four. He knew her timetable and her food and the way she slept, but he didn’t know everything, and he thought perhaps that was right. For now.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday she arrived at the library with a problem. Her headphones had stopped working. Both sides. She laid them on the table like a small body.

“Did you drop them?”

“No.”

“Sit on them?”

“No.”

“Wash them?”

“Why would I wash my headphones?”

He tested them. Dead. “You’ve had them thirteen days.”

“Fourteen. Almost.”

He reached into his bag and put a box on the table. Black, over-ear, with a proper braided wire, a great deal nicer than anything she’d ever bought herself.

“These are expensive.”

“Not particularly.”

“Why did you buy me headphones?”

He put down a second box. Then a third. A fourth. Then he kept going, while she stared, until there were ten identical boxes in a wall between them.

“Chen. Why are there ten?”

“I bought ten pairs. Don’t argue. You go through them like socks.”

“Ten?”

“Would you prefer twenty?”

She hit his arm, and then she started laughing so hard the girl at the next table looked over, and he sat back and watched her. He liked making her laugh. He liked knowing she’d be wearing something he’d chosen. He liked, most of all, that she’d think of him every time she put them on, which was an embarrassingly selfish thought, and he didn’t mind it.

“I can’t take ten. I’ll take two.”

“Ten.”

“Three.”

“Ten.”

“Two.”

“Fine,” he said, and pushed all ten at her.

“Chen!”

Then she went pink and reached into her own bag. “I’ve got something for you.” A soft parcel. Inside was a dark green jumper, slightly too big, with a tiny stitched detail on the cuff. “Your birthday’s in April, but I saw it last week. It was on sale and I thought the colour would suit you and you always say the library’s cold and you never bring enough clothes, so—“

She stopped, because he was looking at her.

“Do you like it?”

“Yes.”

“Really?”

“Really.”

That evening he went home wearing it. He knew the green suited him because she’d told him so, and he knew she had stood in the shop for ten minutes choosing between two colours, because she’d sent him a photo of both by accident.

Eliana: did you try it on? let me see properly

He stood in front of the mirror and sent her one.

Eliana: SEE. i told you the colour suits you

Yu Chen: You were right. I’ll wear it often.

She sent a small heart. He looked at it far too long.

At half past eleven she was cross-legged on her bed with the assignment finally done. Two headphone boxes were stacked on her desk and the other eight had somehow ended up in her wardrobe. She was wearing his grey hoodie, which she had forgotten to give back, or hadn’t. The sleeves covered her hands. She’d sent him a mirror selfie in it before she’d really thought about it.

Yu Chen: Keep it tonight.

Eliana: what if i forget to return it

Yu Chen: Then I’ll buy another.

Eliana: you have too many clothes

Yu Chen: Apparently you have too many headphones.

She sent an angry sticker. Across the wall his desk lamp was the only light in his room, and the green jumper’s spare button sat in his palm, the one she’d left in the parcel. He put it in his drawer. Then he opened a folder on his phone. Her in the library with her cheek on her hand, not knowing he was there. Her laughing in the east garden. Her hand on the map. Her asleep on his shoulder on the bus. He had a folder. He didn’t like admitting it. It was getting full.

Xing Yue rang just after midnight.

“Did you buy her something?”

Yu Chen looked at the ten empty boxes on his floor. “Headphones.”

“How many.”

“Ten.”

There was a silence on the line and then a sound he had never once heard his cousin make, which was a laugh.

“She took two,” Yu Chen said.

“You like her.”

“Yes.”

“Does she know?”

He thought about her foot against his shin, her eyes when she saw the dumplings, i’m glad we’re at the same university. “I think she likes me too.”

“Then what’s the problem?”

The problem was that he liked things the way they were. He liked being the one she rang when she couldn’t find a building, the one who knew when she hadn’t eaten, the one she never had to be nervous with. He wanted to stay her first choice. He wanted, if he was honest, to be the only person she needed, and he knew exactly how unpleasant a thought that was. She deserved a life that wasn’t him. Friends. People who’d make her laugh when he wasn’t there. He didn’t want to take any of that from her. But the idea of someone else mattering to her the way he did made something tighten in his chest, and he couldn’t pretend it didn’t.

“You’re thinking too loudly,” said Xing Yue. “Loving someone doesn’t mean you have to be her whole world. Goodnight.”

Across the garden her light went off.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning there was a paper bag on her step. Inside was an eleventh pair of headphones and a box of Auntie Tsoi’s dumplings.

Eliana: CHEN. YOU GAVE ME ELEVEN

Yu Chen: The first one’s a replacement.

Eliana: for what

Yu Chen: Your ability to look after things. Eat breakfast.

She sat on her bedroom floor with the box open on her knees and laughed, and then she typed something before she could think better of it.

Eliana: i think i like you

He was halfway across his garden. He stopped. He read it twice, and his heart did something that had nothing to do with anatomy. The dots appeared on his screen and disappeared and appeared again.

Yu Chen: You think?

Eliana: maybe

He smiled at the phone, slowly, helplessly.

Yu Chen: I’ll take that.

He put the phone away and went for the bus in the green jumper he’d sworn to wear often. And Eliana, who had no idea what she had just done to his morning, was already eating the first dumpling.

chapters.title: Mid-Autumn, on the Roof
chapters.desc: Eliana climbs onto his roof at Mid-Autumn to pick a fight, because she’s worked out he didn’t end up at her university by accident. He doesn’t deny it. He kisses her in the middle of her sentence instead.
chapters.epigraph: “Stop. You’ve been circling me since September. I’m not blind. Say it.”
chapters.content:
Eliana Lin had a problem. Several, in fact. She had found something she wasn’t meant to know. The person responsible was Wang Yu Chen. And Wang Yu Chen was at this moment sitting on his roof enjoying the Mid-Autumn moon, as if he hadn’t rearranged his entire university life around her.

She was going to kill him. Probably not literally.

Dinner in the tall house was meant to start at seven. At a quarter past, the big round table was still half empty. At twenty past, Elowen arrived from the hill with three boxes of mooncakes and no husband. At half past, Baba began talking to Evangeline about a warehouse lease. And by twenty-five to eight Eliana had noticed that nobody had asked her a single question since she came downstairs.

It wasn’t unusual. Mid-Autumn had never been warm in that house. There was expensive food and porcelain and lanterns in the garden, and a table built for twelve that was never full. This year Raiden had told Ah Sim he wasn’t coming, without a reason, and Elara was on a ward somewhere. Evangeline sat opposite, peeling a pear in one long ribbon without a word.

“Her term’s started?” Baba asked Evangeline.

Eliana stopped with her chopsticks in the air.

“Two weeks ago,” said Evangeline.

“Computer science.” Baba nodded. “At least it’s practical. She should concentrate on her studies. There’s no reason to waste time on people.”

“Baba,” said Elowen, “she’s allowed to have friends.”

“Friends won’t get her a degree.”

“Neither will sitting alone in a library every day.”

Baba reached for his tea and didn’t answer that. Instead he said, “Your mother wouldn’t have wanted her distracted.”

The table went quiet. There it was. Her mother. Never in photographs or stories, never as anyone Eliana might have known. Only as a sentence you could use to end a conversation.

She put her chopsticks down. “I’ve finished.”

“You’ve hardly eaten.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“Then you should have eaten earlier.”

“Take some mooncakes up,” said Elowen gently. “The salted egg yolk ones are yours.”

Nobody stopped her leaving.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside, the moon sat over the rooftops of the Walled City, round and white, with thin cloud going over it now and then. She stood by the garden wall with the little box in her hands. Next door the lanterns were lit and someone had hung paper rabbits along the veranda, and through the kitchen window she could see Auntie Tsoi moving about. Upstairs, a familiar light.

She had found the spreadsheet that afternoon.

It hadn’t been snooping. Mostly. She had borrowed his laptop in the library to check a room number, and a folder had been sitting on his desktop, open, with his university applications in it. His offers. His acceptance. And a spreadsheet called University Planning — Final.

The north had offered him a place months before the hill decided. He had accepted it. He’d even applied for a room there. Then everything changed. The spreadsheet compared the two medical schools on teaching, clinical placements, rankings, living costs and the bus. Which was all perfectly ordinary, until the last column.

Distance from Eliana’s faculty.

Underneath were notes in his tidy hand. Computer science six minutes’ walk from the medical school. Library central, easy meeting point. East gate closer to her usual route. Check whether her mornings overlap. There was a list of dates, and she knew them. The day she’d sent her application. The day her offer came. The day he’d told her he was still thinking. The day he’d turned down the north.

She’d shut the laptop. Opened it again. Checked everything twice, in case there was some innocent reason for a medical student to know the walking time to her building to the minute. There wasn’t. The universe hadn’t written a note beside her favourite library chair saying Quiet. Good for her.

He had.

At nine she climbed the tree.

It was the persimmon in the Song garden, the one whose best branch hung over the Lin side, and from that branch a sufficiently determined person could get onto his roof. She had done it at twelve, and at fourteen, and once at sixteen when he refused to give her the answer to a maths problem. Tonight she was eighteen, in a cream cardigan and a long skirt, with a mooncake box held to her chest, and she was absolutely determined.

He was sitting near the edge of the flat part of the roof in a dark T-shirt, with a cup of tea on the tiles beside him. He looked up and smiled.

“You’re late.”

“Excuse me?”

“You’ve been glaring at my window for twenty minutes. I thought you’d rather climb up than have me come down.” He held out his hand for the box. “Happy Mid-Autumn.”

She pulled it out of his reach. “These are for you. You don’t get them yet.” She put the box down on the tiles and folded her arms. “We need to talk.”

“That sounds serious. Should I sit up?”

“Yu Chen.”

He sat up. She held out her phone with the spreadsheet on it. He looked at it for a while.

“Where did you find that?”

“That’s your first question?”

“It’s a reasonable question.”

“You left it open!”

“Ah.” He looked at the screen again. “Which part?”

She nearly threw the phone at him. “THE DISTANCE FROM MY FACULTY.”

He laughed. Not loudly, just a small helpless laugh that made her want to push him off the roof. She hated that laugh. She especially hated that she liked it.

She lowered the phone. “Stop. You’ve been circling me since September. I’m not blind. Say it.”

The laugh went out of his face. He moved the tea out of the way. “Come and sit down. You’re too near the edge.”

She looked behind her, took two steps towards the middle, and didn’t sit.

“I came because you came,” he said.

There was no joke in it, and no attempt to make it smaller than it was.

“You wanted the north. You worked so hard for it.”

“I know. I didn’t come here because I couldn’t get in there. I came here because I wanted to be here.”

“Because of me.”

“Yes.”

He said it again without hesitating, and that was somehow worse. She sat down, not because he’d asked but because her knees had gone unreliable. “You’re ridiculous. You can’t make decisions like that without telling me.”

“Why not?”

She opened her mouth and found she had no answer. He didn’t need her permission. He was allowed to choose his own university. But knowing he’d made a choice that size because of her felt too big to hold. It frightened her and warmed her at the same time.

“What if you regret it?”

“I won’t. I thought about it for months. I looked at both. I talked to both faculties. You were part of the decision.” He looked at her steadily. “I didn’t come here so you’d owe me anything. I didn’t do it so you’d have to stay with me. I just wanted to be close.”

The moon was bright enough to show the shadows under his eyes. He’d been busy. The reading was already burying him, and he still came to the library with her, still brought her food, still walked her to the bus. She’d thought it was because they were neighbours. Because he’d known her since she was five. Because he was Yu Chen. She hadn’t seen how carefully he’d arranged his whole life to stay next to hers.

“Do you do this for everyone? The maps and the food and the timetables?”

He considered it. “No. They’re not you.”

She stopped breathing for about two seconds. “That’s unreasonable. You can’t just say things like that.”

“Why not?”

“Because I don’t know what to do when you say them!”

His smile widened, slowly, and there it was: the tilt of his head and the look she’d started to recognise and couldn’t hold against.

“Chen,” she said. “Are you in love with me?”

For once he didn’t have an answer ready. He’d imagined telling her a dozen ways. Somewhere quiet. After an exam. When she wasn’t already furious with him. He hadn’t imagined a roof and a mooncake box and a girl holding a spreadsheet like evidence at a trial.

“Do you want me to answer honestly?”

“Obviously.”

“Then yes. Very much.”

“Since when?”

“Since the night you finished school, at least.” He watched her remember: the step, the blanket, his arm. “I think I knew before that. I’m still trying to work out how I didn’t notice.”

“How could you not know?”

“That’s what I’m asking myself.”

She should have gone. She’d come to confront him and she’d had her answer. There was no reason to sit beside him under the Mid-Autumn moon feeling as if the world had been rearranged. No reason at all to keep looking at his mouth.

“You’re still my neighbour,” she said. “And my best friend.”

“Yes.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

“You’ve been looking at my mouth for thirty seconds.”

“I have not!”

His face changed, went gentler. “Can I kiss you?”

She stared at him. He didn’t move closer. He was waiting for her to decide.

“I don’t know,” she whispered.

“All right.” He began to lean back, and that made her panic more than anything else had.

“Wait. I didn’t say no.” She swallowed. “I just think you’re being completely—“

He kissed her.

Not carelessly, and not hard. Just quickly enough to stop the sentence she’d been struggling to build. His hand came up to her jaw, warm fingers against her cheek, and for one second she forgot how breathing worked. Her eyes went wide and then shut, and before she’d decided anything her fingers had caught the front of his T-shirt and she was kissing him back.

He made a low sound against her mouth. His other hand came down on the tiles beside her as he leaned in. It was careful at first, nearly uncertain, and then she pulled on his collar and felt him smile against her lips. He was smiling. While kissing her. She drew back half an inch to complain about it and he kissed her again, and she made a small indignant noise, and he laughed, and she kissed him again anyway, because she had apparently lost the ability to make sensible decisions.

Somewhere below them a door shut. Neither of them heard it.

When they came apart she was flushed to the ears with her lips parted and her hand still fisted in his collar. He looked down at the hand, then at her.

“Hi.”

“Hi?” She let go of his shirt as if it had caught fire. “What was that?”

“A kiss.”

“I know that!” She covered her face. “Oh my God.”

He waited until she lowered her hands, and then he took a mooncake out of the box and held it out. “Salted egg yolk?”

“You’re asking me that now?”

“Would you rather I asked something else?”

She took it so she wouldn’t have to answer. Their fingers touched and she looked down at once, and he was enjoying himself so much she could hardly stand it. She took a bite. He reached over and brushed a crumb from the corner of her mouth with his thumb, and she froze, and he smiled, and she said “Don’t,” and he said “All right.”

The panic came afterwards. Not during the kiss, or when his hand had been on her jaw, or when she’d kissed him back. It came when she remembered everything else. The spreadsheet. The north. The fact that he loved her, and that she might love him too.

He was folding the mooncake wrapper into a small neat square, calm, comfortable, as if he’d always known this would happen and knew exactly what came next. All at once she felt about twelve.

“What happens now?”

“We don’t have to decide anything tonight.”

He wasn’t asking her to call him anything. He wasn’t asking for a single promise. And somehow that made it worse, because she wanted to give him an answer, and she didn’t have one. She’d never imagined anyone could want her this much without being disappointed eventually.

She stood up. “I should go.”

“Do you want me to walk you?”

“No.”

“Your cardigan—“

“I know!”

It came out sharper than she meant. He held the cardigan out without a word and she took it.

“Sorry.”

“It’s all right. Go slowly. The branch is slippery.”

She didn’t go slowly. She went down that tree like someone leaving a crime scene. The cardigan caught on a twig and she yanked it free. Her slipper skidded on the bark. And on the last drop her foot came down on a root and turned, and something sharp went across her knee.

“Ah!”

She caught the trunk and stood there breathing. There was a thin line of blood just below her kneecap. Of course. Of course she’d hurt herself running away from a boy who’d kissed her. She was going to die of embarrassment. She pulled her skirt down and limped towards her gate.

On the roof he’d heard the sound and was on his feet. “Eliana?” She looked up, considered going back, and walked faster instead. He made himself stay where he was. She needed room. He knew that, even with every bit of him wanting to climb down after her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came in through the back door. Evangeline was in the small sitting room with a book, and looked up, and looked at Eliana’s knee.

“Come here.”

“It’s nothing.”

Evangeline put the book down and took the first-aid box off the side table. She didn’t ask where Eliana had been, or why her hair was a mess, or why there was a leaf caught by her temple. She cleaned the cut, which stung, and murmured “Sorry” when Eliana winced, and put a plaster on it. Then she reached up and took the green leaf out of her sister’s hair and laid it on the table between them, a little piece of the tree. She didn’t ask about that either.

Not every silence needed filling. Being allowed to keep a secret was its own kind of comfort, and in this house Evangeline was the only person who’d ever given it to her.

“Thank you.” Eliana got up, and stopped. “Can people change their minds? About something important?”

“Yes.”

“Even after they’ve decided?”

Evangeline turned a page. “Especially then.”

Eliana carried that upstairs with her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen: Are you home?

The message sat there showing read for a minute, then two. He put the phone down. He wasn’t going to chase her tonight. When she was overwhelmed she needed to sort her thoughts without someone standing over her asking for answers. He could give her that. He’d been waiting for years.

At eleven she was in bed with the plaster on her knee and the cardigan over her chair, and she had opened their conversation six times.

Eliana: yes

Yu Chen: Is your knee all right? You were limping. Did you clean it?

Eliana: evangeline did. chen

Yu Chen: Hm?

She looked at the keyboard. Why did you kiss me. Do you really love me. What if I don’t know how to love you properly. What if this changes everything.

Eliana: goodnight

Yu Chen: Goodnight. Happy Mid-Autumn.

Eliana: happy mid-autumn :) chen? i don’t regret it

Across the garden he sat down on the edge of his bed and read it, and smiled, not the teasing smile but a quieter one, almost disbelieving.

Yu Chen: Me neither. Sleep well, sweetheart.

She looked at the word for a long while and then pulled the duvet over her head and smiled into her pillow for ten minutes.

Eliana: and chen? don’t tell anyone

Yu Chen: About what?

Eliana: YOU KNOW WHAT

Yu Chen: My lips are sealed.

Yu Chen: Literally.

Eliana: GOODNIGHT

He opened his window. Her room was dark. He touched his lower lip and remembered her hand twisting his collar, and laughed at himself. He’d imagined their first kiss being careful and romantic and possibly a little clever. Instead he’d interrupted an argument on a roof, and she’d fled down a tree and cut her knee. As first-kiss stories went, it was terrible. He loved it.

On the table by her bed there was a mooncake she hadn’t finished. On his desk was the green jumper. And somewhere between the two houses, under the persimmon tree they’d climbed as children, a secret had started that neither of them had named yet.

chapters.title: Not Official, She Says
chapters.desc: The morning after the roof, Eliana turns up with a typed list of rules: nobody knows, and it doesn’t get a name. Yu Chen agrees to every one of them and adds one of his own.
chapters.epigraph: “Fine. No name. But I’m not going to lie and say it isn’t the best thing that’s ever happened to me.”
chapters.content:
At seven forty-three the next morning Eliana stood on his step holding one sheet of paper, neatly typed.

He opened the door with wet hair and the face of a man who had been awake for twelve minutes, and looked at her, and at the paper.

“Good morning.”

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face is saying something.”

She walked past him into the kitchen. She had spent the whole night thinking about the roof and had achieved nothing else. She’d replayed the exact angle of his face when he said very much. She’d replayed the kiss until her cheeks burned under the duvet. She’d checked three times whether he’d sent anything after sweetheart. He hadn’t, which was worse, because she had wanted him to. And because she’d wanted him to, she had decided something needed doing. Something organised, with rules.

She put the paper on his counter. TERMS AND CONDITIONS, centred, bold, underlined.

“Should I be worried?”

“Yes.”

There were six of them, numbered, generously spaced, as if she were presenting a business case rather than the terms of whatever it was with the boy who’d kissed her twelve hours ago.

1. Nobody knows.

2. We don’t talk about the roof.

“In public,” she said.

3. This doesn’t change anything. 4. No expectations. 5. No telling people.

“That’s the same as one.”

“It’s more specific.”

6. We don’t give it a name.

He laid the paper down carefully, like an important document. “You typed this.”

“Yes.”

“At what time?”

“That’s irrelevant.”

“Before or after you decided to pretend you weren’t thinking about kissing me?”

“That’s not in the document.”

His smile came slowly. “Fine. No name. But I’m not going to lie and say it isn’t the best thing that’s ever happened to me.”

She blinked. “You’re agreeing? All of it?”

“All of it. One addition.” He took a pen off the windowsill, turned the page over and wrote under her sixth rule in his neat slanting hand, and underlined it once.

7. THIS IS REAL.

“That’s not a rule.”

“It is now. You brought me a contract.”

“It’s not a contract.”

“It has numbered clauses.”

“I said no names.”

“I haven’t given it one. It’s a reminder that you don’t have to call it anything for it to mean something.”

She forgot to be defensive for a second. He wasn’t pushing. He was just standing barefoot in his kitchen with her ridiculous paper between them. She didn’t know how to say that it scared her, how easily he agreed to everything and still found a way to make her feel seen. So she folded the page in half.

“Fine. You can have seven. But it doesn’t mean we’re together. You can’t call me your girlfriend. And no acting strange around me.”

“Define strange.”

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

She gave up. He reached past her for the kettle. “Have you eaten?”

“That’s not relevant.”

“Then I’ll make you something irrelevant.”

She ate half of it. He didn’t mention the other half. At the door she put her hand on the latch and said, “Nobody knows. No name,” and he said, “Nobody knows. No name,” and then she leaned up and kissed his cheek, so quickly it was nearly a mistake.

“That’s not breaking any rules.”

“I didn’t say it was.”

“Have a nice day.”

“You too, sweetheart.”

When she’d gone he smoothed the crease out of the paper with his thumb, read his own line again, and put it in the drawer beside his bed. Obviously.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble with her rules was that she’d written them as if she could control what happened when he was standing within reach. By Friday she knew she couldn’t.

The second-floor study area was packed with first years panicking about their first assessments. She had spent forty minutes on the same page while he annotated pharmacology beside her. He wasn’t doing anything. That was the trouble. His sleeve brushed hers. His pen moved. Every so often he turned a page and she heard it.

“You’re not reading,” he murmured.

“It’s a difficult paragraph.”

“It’s database normalisation.”

“Exactly.”

She lasted thirty seconds and shut her laptop. “I’m finished.”

“With your work?”

“With you.” She heard herself. “I mean—“

“I know,” he said, and closed his book.

On the stairs he was a step below her with his books in one hand, and at the landing he stopped to let a group go by, and she was standing one step up, which made them exactly the same height. Rule one, she thought. Nobody knows. Rule six, no name. Rule seven, THIS IS REAL, which was no help at all.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

She leaned down and kissed him. Fast, warm, there and gone.

For one extraordinary second he looked completely surprised. Then his face went soft, and hers went scarlet.

“Bye.”

“Eliana.”

She was already down the stairs.

“Have a good day,” he called after her, warm with laughter, and she nearly fell off the bottom step.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the next week she had a system. It wasn’t a good one. It involved booking study rooms under his name and getting there first and pretending the room was for studying.

Eliana: 4B. now

Yu Chen: Is something wrong?

Eliana: just come

When he arrived she was at the table with her laptop open on a real assignment. He sat down beside her and waited, and she stared at him until he asked what.

“Come here.”

“I’m here.”

“No. Here.” She pointed at him and then at herself.

A small smile at the corner of his mouth. “Are you sure?”

“You’re so annoying.”

She caught his shirt and pulled him down. It wasn’t graceful. Her chair scraped, his hand slapped onto the edge of the table, her fingers gripped the cotton as if he might get away. He kissed her back slowly, slowly enough that she forgot why she’d been impatient, and when they parted she stayed close.

“Was that why you booked the room?”

“I also have an assignment.”

“Of course.”

They managed about four seconds of pretending to study before he tucked her hair behind her ear, and she said don’t, and he stopped, and a minute later she put her head on his shoulder. The assignment was still unfinished when they left.

The gap beside the bins was not romantic. She was clear about that. It was a narrow space between the back wall of the student centre and a row of wheelie bins, smelling of detergent and wet concrete, used only as a short cut. They were walking past when she saw a crowd of her classmates coming the other way, grabbed his sleeve and pulled him in.

“What are we hiding from?”

“People.”

“You are aware we’re next to the bins.”

“I didn’t say it was romantic.”

He looked down at her. Then he took her hand and laced his fingers through hers. “Are you in a hurry?”

“No.”

“Good.”

This time he didn’t wait to be pulled. He put his hand to her cheek with his thumb under her cheekbone and bent and kissed her, unhurried, as if he had all afternoon. When he drew back she followed him without thinking.

“Again?”

She nodded. He did it again. When footsteps passed on the other side of the wall she hid her face in his chest to hide the smile, and he put his chin on the top of her head and didn’t laugh. He was learning that some things made her shy even when she’d started them. He liked that far too much.

✦ ✦ ✦

His kitchen became a dangerous place. Her hair clips appeared by his sink. Her laptop charger moved in beside his sofa. And she found out he could cook. Not brilliantly, but well enough, and he always knew what she’d eat.

On a Sunday evening with Auntie Tsoi at her sister’s, he was making rice and she was supervising.

“That’s too much water.”

“It’s what the cooker says.”

“The cooker’s wrong.”

“Have you ever made rice?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“Before.”

“That’s not a date.”

“Are you questioning my qualifications?”

“I’m trying to establish them.”

She reached for the measuring cup. He moved it out of reach. She said she hated him. Then she hiccupped. And again. And she tried to sneak the cup back while he was rinsing, and knocked it, and a fan of raw rice went across the counter. They both looked at it. She burst out laughing and hiccupped in the middle of the laugh and tried to apologise and hiccupped through that too.

He fetched a cloth and wiped the counter while she stood there giggling. Then he took her chin in his fingers and kissed her in the middle of a hiccup.

She stared at him. He looked pleased with himself. “Better?”

She hiccupped.

He laughed properly, low and warm, and she hit his arm. “That didn’t work!”

“Apparently not. Sit down, sweetheart.”

She sat. She spent the rest of the evening smiling into her bowl.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana was not jealous. She had explained this to herself several times in the canteen while a girl from his year asked him an anatomy question, laughed at his answer, and moved her chair closer. Eliana was simply observing. Observation was practically her degree.

He came over with his tray. The girl followed as far as the table. “Are you coming to the review session? I’ll send you my notes.”

“Thank you.”

The girl left. Eliana held her fork.

“You haven’t eaten.”

“I’m thinking.”

“About?”

“She’s pretty. Your friend.”

“She’s in my year.”

“That’s nice.”

He drank some water, slowly, and she narrowed her eyes at him. “Are you jealous?” he asked.

“No.”

“I believe you.”

“You don’t.”

She pushed her chair back and said she had work, and made it halfway down the corridor before she heard him behind her. He caught her near the quiet end of the building and stepped in front of her, and when she tried to go round him he moved with her.

“Sweetheart.”

“Don’t call me that.”

“Look at me.”

She did, cross and embarrassed, and found the amusement had gone out of his face entirely. He took her wrist, loosely enough that she could have pulled away, and drew her into the shallow recess by the wall, out of sight of the people at the other end.

“I don’t look at her the way I look at you. I don’t wait for her messages. I don’t know what she eats. I don’t know what makes her laugh when she’s trying not to. And I don’t think about kissing her when she’s standing in front of me.”

“You’re only saying that because you know I’m jealous.”

“I’m saying it because it’s true. Can I?”

Her answer was to grab his shirt. He kissed her as if he’d been waiting for her to stop pretending she didn’t want to be reassured, his hand moving from the wall to her waist, her fingers curling against his chest, until she was breathing fast.

“I still don’t like her,” she whispered against his forehead.

“You don’t have to.”

“You’re not allowed to like her either.”

“Is that another rule? Should I expect a revised document?”

She kissed him to shut him up.

✦ ✦ ✦

The boy who pulled her hood down did it on a rainy Tuesday. She was crossing the quad with her hood up and her phone in one hand and her tote bag sliding off the other shoulder, and somebody yanked the hood back so hard her head jerked and strands of hair came with it.

“Hey, Lin. Can’t see your face under there.”

She knew him vaguely from a lecture. He was grinning. “Don’t do that,” she said. “Don’t touch my clothes.”

He reached for the hood again, and another hand closed round his wrist.

Yu Chen had come from the medical school with his umbrella still furled. He’d gone past anger into something worse: complete stillness.

“Put it back,” he said.

“What?”

“Her hood. You pulled it down. Put it back.”

“You’re making a big deal out of nothing.”

Yu Chen tightened his grip just enough that the boy stopped trying to pull free. His voice didn’t rise. He looked at him as if the conversation had already ended and the boy hadn’t noticed. “She told you not to touch her. Now put it back.”

The boy looked at his face and changed his mind. He reached towards the hood.

“Don’t,” said Eliana, and he froze.

“Apologise,” said Yu Chen.

“Sorry.”

He went. Yu Chen let his breath out and looked at her hair. “Did he hurt you?” He lifted the hood over her head himself and arranged it so it wouldn’t catch, and his fingers brushed her temple.

“I don’t need you to fight people for me.”

“I’m not fighting anyone.”

“You looked like you wanted to.”

“I wanted him to understand.” There was something in his face she couldn’t name. Colder than anger, and more controlled. It frightened her a little. It also made her chest go warm. He opened the umbrella over both of them and walked her all the way to her building, and didn’t mention the boy again.

She did. That night.

His university account wasn’t difficult. She didn’t need anything clever. She knew how the university’s systems were put together and how carelessly people left themselves lying around online. She told herself it was research, to see if he’d done it to anyone else. None of that explained why she ended up inside his drafts.

There was a document for the compulsory first-year reflective writing module. The prompt was a moment you would do differently. He’d written three sentences. His title was I Pulled A Girl’s Hood Down.

She laughed out loud, a small delighted laugh, and took a screenshot. She didn’t change anything. She didn’t send anything. She saved it in a folder that would make no sense to anyone else, called miscellaneous.

Eliana: guess what. i found something funny

Yu Chen: Should I be concerned?

Eliana: probably not. goodnight ♡

He rang. She rejected the call.

Eliana: GOODNIGHT

Yu Chen: Goodnight, sweetheart.

✦ ✦ ✦

In October she failed to make a friend.

There was no fight. Bai Qing sat beside her in two lectures and was friendly and talkative and had asked her to lunch twice. The first time Eliana said she had work. The second time she said she was waiting for someone. Both were true. Neither was the whole truth.

“We’re doing the assignment at the café,” Bai Qing said the third time. “Come.”

Eliana looked at her phone. Yu Chen: Have you eaten? She hadn’t.

“I might have to go somewhere.”

“Another time, then.” Bai Qing smiled and went.

Eliana felt an unfamiliar pinch of guilt. She’d wanted friends. She thought she had. But working out when to speak at a table of strangers, and how much to say, seemed exhausting, and it was easier to go where he was. He knew when she was uncomfortable. He knew her real smile from the one she used to make people leave.

He was outside the medical school with two cups.

“Your classmate asked you to lunch?” he said, when she told him. “Did she make you uncomfortable?”

“No. She’s nice.”

“Then maybe go next time.”

“Do you want me to?”

He hesitated, and in the hesitation was a selfish relief he didn’t like. She’d said no to someone else and come to him instead. She had already settled against his arm and started telling him about a lecture, her voice going softer as her shoulders came down. He liked being where she came back to. He liked it far too much.

“Only if you want to,” he said.

“I think I’d rather stay with you.”

“All right.”
