He had promised himself he would never make her world smaller, and here he was, grateful she hadn’t let anyone else into it that afternoon. He knew that liking her need for him wasn’t the same as loving her well. He held her hand a little tighter anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of October the rules were mostly decorative. Nobody knew. They didn’t hold hands in crowds; he didn’t call her sweetheart where anyone could hear. They had never said boyfriend or girlfriend. But his spare charger lived in her bag and her clips lived in his bathroom. He knew her footsteps outside his door. She’d started leaving drawings on sticky notes in his textbooks. And every night before she slept she checked whether he’d written.

One evening she was cross-legged on his sofa with her laptop when she said, “Do you think we’re strange?”

“Probably.”

“You’re meant to say no.”

“Would you believe me?”

She nudged his thigh with her foot. He caught her ankle and kept it. She shut the laptop. “Rule seven. Do you still mean it?”

He put his notes down and turned to face her. “Yes.”

“Even with no name? Even though nobody knows? Even though I keep making rules?”

“Especially then.”

She leaned in and kissed the corner of his mouth, and he kissed her properly, and she climbed closer with one hand on his shoulder until he gathered her into his lap as if there had never been a question about where she went.

“Still not official,” she whispered against his forehead.

“I know.”

“Don’t look so happy.”

He did anyway. She hid her face in his neck, and he held her there and thought that he’d agree to every rule she ever wrote, for as long as she needed them, and that one day, when she stopped being afraid of the word, she’d understand he had never been waiting for permission to love her.

chapters.title: The Drawing in His Pharmacology Notes
chapters.desc: Eliana can say anything with a keyboard and nothing out loud, so she hides a drawing in his notes and tells him not to look until he’s in the library. He looks in the library and has to walk out into the rain.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t look at it till you’re in the library. If you look on the bus I’ll know, because you go red on buses.”
chapters.content:
Eliana Lin was brilliant at saying things, as long as nobody could hear her.

Give her a keyboard and she could write a paragraph explaining exactly why someone was wrong. Give her a comment box and she could take an argument apart so neatly that its owner reconsidered his life. Give her Yu Chen, sitting in front of her, looking at her with those patient eyes, and she couldn’t remember a single word.

It was inconvenient, because she had something to tell him, and she’d been trying for three days.

On the first Friday in November, at the bus stop at the end of their lane, she took a folded square of paper out of her pocket and slid it between the pages of his pharmacology notes while he was looking at the timetable.

“Don’t look at it till you’re in the library. If you look on the bus I’ll know, because you go red on buses.”

“I don’t go red on buses.”

“You do. And not your usual table. Somewhere else in the library. And don’t show anyone.”

“Is this a puzzle?”

“No.”

“Should I be worried?”

“No.”

He looked at her, the way he did when he could hear the whole conversation she was having inside her head. “I’ll read it when you want me to.”

He didn’t look on the bus, and he didn’t go red. He waited until his last lecture of the morning was over and he’d found a table alone on the top floor, where hardly anyone went before exams. Then he opened his notes.

It was a drawing in her slightly wobbly lines. Two figures on a bench under a tree. One had long hair and a small frown. The other was taller, with a book on his knee and one arm stretched along the bench behind her, as if he were keeping her there. Tiny flowers round their feet. Their shoulders touching. Above them, in her handwriting, three words.

don’t go anywhere.

At the bottom, a tiny heart.

He stopped breathing, which he knew was ridiculous. He was a medical student. He could have told you exactly what his heart was doing and why his chest felt tight. It was still ridiculous. Not I like you, and not I love you, and not even stay. Just three words, written as if she’d been trying to say them for years. He thought about the roof, and her typed rules, and the way she always left before he could answer anything too directly, and how lately she’d started leaning against him whenever she was tired.

He put the textbook in his bag, kept the drawing in his hand, and walked out of the library.

It had started to rain. Not hard. The fine, steady autumn kind that turned the paths dark and made the trees look as though they were holding their breath. He stood under the awning and took out his phone.

Yu Chen: Yes.

It was too short and didn’t say enough, but he couldn’t trust himself with anything longer.

Eliana: yes what

Yu Chen: I won’t go anywhere.

Eliana: oh. okay. it was just a drawing

Yu Chen: Of course.

Eliana: don’t be smug

Yu Chen: Come outside. It’s raining. I want to walk with you.

A minute went by.

Eliana: wait for me

He put the drawing inside his coat, where it couldn’t get wet, and waited.

She came out under the awning ten minutes later with her hood up and her face pink, and didn’t say a word about the drawing, and neither did he. He held the umbrella over her all the way down the hill.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shoebox had lived under her bed for months. It had once held a pair of shoes she’d bought and immediately disliked. Now it held dead headphones. Some had broken wires, some had split cushions, one had a cracked headband, and one pair was so knotted that even she had given up on it.

He found it on Saturday. He’d gone down to Ah Sim’s kitchen for two glasses of barley water, and when he came back up the stairs she was sitting on her bedroom floor staring into the box with the face of someone defusing a bomb.

“Are those all broken?”

“Not all. That one works sometimes. Depending on the angle. That one’s left side only. That one’s complicated.”

He crouched beside her and counted. “You have nine pairs of dead headphones under your bed and eight new ones in your wardrobe.”

“The new ones are for best.”

“Why keep these?”

“They were expensive.”

He didn’t argue. He picked up the worst knot and started working it loose, and she watched his fingers go through it, patient and careful. He separated the cables, checked the plugs, and put the good parts in one pile and the hopeless ones in another. Then he went next door and came back with a small label maker.

“Why do you own that?”

“For organising things.”

“You’re strange.”

“Probably.”

WORKING: LEFT SIDE ONLY. DAMAGED CABLE. NEEDS NEW CUSHIONS. SPARE PARTS. He cleaned the cushions and coiled every cable and set aside one pair that a new plug would save, and the box stopped being a box of broken things and turned into a box of things that had been sorted out and given a place.

“You don’t have to fix everything,” she said, chin on her knees.

“I’m not fixing. I’m organising.”

“That’s worse. Now you’ll label my whole life.”

“Would you like me to?”

“No.”

She moved closer and leaned her head on his shoulder. He kept working one-handed. His other hand rested on her knee. When he’d finished he put the box beside her bag.

“Why did you do all of it?”

“Because you kept them. I thought there might be a reason.”

There was. She just didn’t know how to explain it. She hated waste. She hated spending money. And sometimes it was easier to keep a broken thing than to admit it was time for a new one. He hadn’t asked her to explain. He’d just sat down on her floor and untangled them.

“Thank you,” she said, and reached for his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Monday he’d discovered that she would do almost anything for a kiss, and argue about the terms of all of it.

They were in his room, him on pharmacology, her on a maths sheet she’d been staring at for an hour.

“How many have you done?”

“Three.”

“There are twelve. You keep stopping halfway through each question.”

“You’re supposed to encourage me.”

He took her pencil and turned the sheet towards himself. “One page. You finish one page and I’ll kiss you.”

“That’s bribery.”

“Motivation.”

“That’s not how academic motivation works.”

“Would you rather have a lecture?”

She snatched the pencil back. For fifteen minutes she worked with a ferocity he’d rarely seen, checking every line twice, and then she pushed the page at him and held out her hand.

“My kiss.”

He laughed and leaned over and kissed her. Once. Briefly.

“That’s it?”

“That’s the agreement.”

“You’re stingy. Two per page.”

“That’s not what we agreed.”

“Inflation.”

He laughed again, and touched her cheek, and gave her the second. The second page came quickly, and the third, and by the fourth she was going so fast she made mistakes, and he pointed them out, and she groaned.

“Do I still get the kiss?”

“If the page is right.”

“You’re so strict.”

“You want the answer to be right.”

“I want you to kiss me.”

He stopped. His face changed. “That’s different.”

He pushed his book away and opened one arm, and she left her chair so fast it rolled, and settled onto his lap as if she’d been planning it all afternoon. His hand came to her waist.

“Is this part of the arrangement?”

“Yes.”

“Which page?”

“All of them.”

“That’s a generous reading.”

She put her arms round his neck and kissed him, one hand in his hair. When they parted their noses were nearly touching. “Eight pages left,” he said. “Get back to work.”

“Can I do them here?”

“How will you write?”

She considered the problem and reached for the paper. He laughed and shifted the notebook on the desk so she could sit sideways across his knees, which was a terrible arrangement. She finished all eight anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday night Baba came home early.

She knew before she heard his voice. His key in the lock, a pause, and the front door shut harder than it needed to. Yu Chen was on her bedroom floor with his notes all over her rug and she was at the desk with her laptop, and her hands stopped.

“Eliana?”

Yu Chen closed his book. “Do you want me to go?”

She shook her head, and then whispered, “You can’t.”

His footsteps were on the stairs. Her face had gone white. Yu Chen moved without a sound: notes under the bed, bag over his shoulder, a glance at the wardrobe. She nodded. He folded himself in among her coats, and she pulled the door to and left a gap for air, and sat down at the desk.

Baba knocked once. “Why is your light on?”

“I’m studying.”

“At this hour?”

It was nine. “Yes.”

The door opened. He looked at the laptop, the books, the rumpled duvet. His eyes stayed on the second cup on the desk.

“Who were you with?”

“Nobody.”

“Then why are there two cups?”

“I made one earlier.”

“For whom?”

“Me.”

He didn’t say anything, and the silence was worse than a question. He picked up a printout from her desk. “Still doing these useless things?”

“It’s an assignment.”

“Then finish it.” He put it down and turned to go, and stopped in the doorway. “Your mother used to stay awake all night too. She never knew when to stop.”

He went. The door shut.

Eliana sat absolutely still with the laptop humming in front of her. After a while the wardrobe door opened behind her and Yu Chen stepped out, and put his bag down, and pulled the other chair up beside hers.

“He’s tired,” she said. “He didn’t mean anything.”

He didn’t argue with her.

“Can you sit here for a bit?”

“Of course.”

She held his hand until the house went quiet. Later, still dressed, they ended up on her bed, him sitting up against the headboard so he wouldn’t take too much room, her curled against his side with his arm round her shoulders. At eleven she was awake. At half past she’d stopped answering him. At one, just as he thought she’d finally gone, her phone rang.

She was up before the second ring. “Sorry,” she whispered, and looked at the screen, and her face changed. Qian.

She took it to the far side of the room. He could hear her half and nothing of the other.

“Yes, I’m awake. Send me the details.” She opened the laptop. Her shoulders went square, and the sleepy girl who’d been hiding her face in his shirt was gone. Someone else sat there, precise and quick, reading fast. “No, that’s not the problem. Your first approach was too obvious. I can fix it, but I need the right access. I’m not going to guess.” A pause, and her voice went cold. “Qian. Don’t do that again.”

It went on for nearly forty minutes. She didn’t explain. He didn’t ask. He looked at the ceiling. He had heard the name before, never with anyone else in the room, and he knew enough to understand that whoever rang at one in the morning wasn’t asking about coursework.

When she shut the laptop she sat with her hands on the lid.

“Come back,” he said, and lifted the duvet.

“You’re still awake?”

“So are you.”

She came, and lay down against him, and was quiet for a while. “Sorry. About the call.”

“You don’t have to apologise.”

He looked exhausted. He’d hidden in her wardrobe because she’d asked him not to leave, and listened to her father, and stayed while she fell asleep, and then waited through a phone call she couldn’t explain to him. Her chest went tight. She leaned up and kissed him, barely more than a touch.

“What was that for?”

“Thank you for staying.”

“You don’t have to thank me for that.”

“I want to.”

She kissed him again and stayed longer, and his hand came round the back of her head and held her there, and when they parted he put his forehead against hers.

“You’re welcome, sweetheart.”

She closed her eyes, and for the first time that night let herself believe she didn’t have to stay awake to stop someone leaving.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke first. Baba’s car had gone at seven; he’d heard Uncle Mok start the engine under the window. She was asleep against him with one hand fisted in his shirt and a crease on her cheek from the pillow, taking up most of the bed despite being half his size.

His phone had two messages.

Xing Yue: Alive?

Xing Yue: Nainai asks if you’re coming to lunch.

Yu Chen: Later.

Xing Yue: You’re at Lin’s again.

He didn’t reply to that. She stirred, and her fingers tightened on his shirt.

“Yu Chen? What time is it?”

“Eight. Go back to sleep.”

“Are you leaving?”

“Not yet.”

She relaxed. Then, almost asleep, she murmured into his shirt, “Don’t go anywhere.”

He thought of the drawing inside his coat. Two people on a bench, and three words she’d had to write down because she couldn’t say them. He kissed her hair.

“I won’t.”

She smiled against him. And Yu Chen, who had turned down a university because the other one was closer to her and spent an evening folded among her coats rather than leave her alone, held her a little closer, and stayed exactly where he was.

chapters.title: He Researched This Part Too
chapters.desc: Their first night together goes nothing like his plan: it’s clumsy and shy, they keep laughing, and they start over twice. Afterwards, in the dark, he says the thing she’s most scared of so that she doesn’t have to.
chapters.epigraph: “I love you. You don’t have to say it back. I just didn’t want to be the only one who knew.”
chapters.content:
The man made one mistake. He thought the woman was alone.

Eliana had been in the corner of the private lounge for forty minutes, one leg crossed over the other, a glass of water untouched by her laptop. It was on the ninth floor of an office building on Harbour Road that belonged, on paper, to a shipping agency, and in fact to Chen Si’s people: dark wood, polished stone, low lamps, chairs nobody was meant to relax in. Qian had sent her to look at a discrepancy in some internal records. A payment trail, an employee who’d been opening files she shouldn’t. Routine.

The man’s name had come up three times. The woman’s had come up much more often. And the messages Eliana had found while tracing the payments had made the situation rather less ambiguous.

“You’re not listening to me,” he said.

The woman across the room kept her eyes on the carpet. “I’m listening.”

“Then you understand what happens if you refuse.”

“I told you. I can’t.”

“You can. You just don’t want to.”

He’d used his position on this floor to make her understand he could take her access, her work, her future. He’d asked to see her alone, over and over. When she said no, he’d started suggesting that certain private things about her could stop being private. Eliana had read every message twice. Then she’d stopped working on what Qian had sent her for.

“Look at me when I’m talking to you.”

The woman flinched. Eliana shut her laptop. It was a small sound. They both turned round.

“She said she can’t.”

He took a second to place her: young, plainly dressed, quiet in the corner all evening. “This is a private conversation.”

“Then you should have picked a private room.” She stood up. She wasn’t tall. She didn’t need to be. “I’ve been trying to finish my work. I was. Until I found your messages.”

Something moved in his face. “What messages?”

“The ones you sent her. The ones you thought were private.” She’d already copied them, with enough around them to show they weren’t a misunderstanding or a bad day, and sent the lot to the people whose names were on the building. She wasn’t going to negotiate with him, and she wasn’t going to warn him. “You’ve been using your access to frighten someone who works here. It’s documented. It’s gone to the people above you.”

He laughed, without any confidence at all. “You think anyone will believe you?”

“That isn’t something you get to decide.” She turned to the woman. “Come with me. You don’t have to explain anything to him.”

He moved to follow. Eliana said “Don’t,” and held his eyes until he stopped, and walked out with the woman and didn’t look back.

By the time she was on the street her hands were shaking. Not enough for anyone to see. Enough that she missed the zip on her bag twice, and couldn’t unlock her phone at the first try. The job was done. The woman was with a supervisor who’d looked at the messages and gone grey. Eliana should have felt satisfied. She felt like a wire with current still in it. She knew it was the adrenaline. She also knew what she wanted to do with it.

Yu Chen: Still awake?

Eliana: yes

Yu Chen: Have you eaten? What did you eat?

Eliana: food

Yu Chen: Try again.

She laughed in the empty street, a small tired sound, and typed and deleted and typed.

Eliana: can i come over

Yu Chen: Of course. Are you all right?

Eliana: i think so

Yu Chen: I’ll leave the door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

He heard the front door just after midnight. He had been reading the same paragraph for an hour. He knew she’d been working; he hadn’t asked where or for whom. He’d learned that she told him what she could when she could, and that pushing only made her go further away.

“Yu Chen?”

She was in his doorway wrapped in a blanket. Not wearing it. Wrapped in it, the end of it trailing on the floor, her hair loose. She had gone home first, and taken the blanket off her own bed, and come over the wall in it.

“Are you cold?”

“No.”

“Then why—“

“I wanted to.”

“Come here,” he said, and she went, and he put his arms round her, blanket and all. She pushed her face into his chest.

“Long night?”

“Mm. Not bad. Can I stay? Even though it’s late?”

He held her away far enough to see her face. “You never have to ask me that.”

“Do you want tea?” he said after a while. “Water? Food?”

She shook her head each time.

“Then what do you want?”

She looked at him, and her cheeks were already going pink. “You.”

He went completely still. She looked away at once. “I mean—“

“I know what you mean.”

“No, you don’t.”

“All right.”

“Stop being so calm.”

“Would you rather I panicked?”

“Maybe.”

He kissed her forehead. “Come and sit down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the paper by accident. Mostly. He’d gone to wash his hands and she was on the edge of his bed in the blanket when she saw a folder on the desk, half open, with a sheet sliding out of it and her own name across the top.

ELIANA — PLAN (IF)

Her first thought was that it was a revision timetable. Her second was that he was even stranger than she’d suspected. Her third was that she shouldn’t read it. She looked at the bathroom door. “Just checking,” she whispered, and pulled it out.

If she ever says she wants to:

Don’t assume she means now. Ask if she’s sure. Make sure she isn’t saying yes because she thinks she should. Don’t rush. Room warm. Water by the bed. Phone away. Condoms in the drawer (checked the date). Somewhere comfortable for her to sleep after.

Things to remember: She gets nervous when she feels watched. She laughs when she’s embarrassed. Don’t make her feel silly. If she changes her mind, stop. No questions. She sets the pace. Ask before anything new. Don’t make it a big thing.

After: Water. Blanket. Stay close unless she wants space. Don’t ask her to say anything. Tell her what she means to me.

She read the last line again and put the page down on her knee. She hadn’t expected this. She’d expected him to be confident, because he always was with her, so patient she sometimes forgot he could be nervous at all. It had never crossed her mind that he might have thought about this. Planned for it. Not the way she’d been afraid of, with an expectation she’d have to live up to. The way he planned everything that mattered. Carefully, and without telling anyone, as if he were getting ready to look after something precious.

The bathroom door opened. He stopped. His eyes went from her face to the paper and back, and for the first time that evening he looked caught.

“Oh.”

“What is this?”

“Something you weren’t meant to read.” He shut the door behind him. “I hadn’t decided whether to show you.”

“Why did you write it?”

“Because I wanted to be ready.”

“You researched this?”

“Some of it. I read a few things.”

“How many?”

“Eliana.”

“How many?”

He looked almost embarrassed. “Enough.”

The handwriting was neat but not perfect. Words crossed out and rewritten. Things added in the margins. It had taken him time. “You noticed I laugh when I’m embarrassed.”

“Yes.”

“And this. Feeling watched.”

“You don’t like being the centre of anything.”

“When did you write it?”

“Before tonight. A while ago.”

That made her face burn worse. She folded the page and put it back on his desk. “You planned everything.”

“Not everything. I wanted to know how to make it good for you.”

She was quiet. Then she looked up. “Did you plan step two?”

He blinked. “What?”

“Step two.” She pointed at the paper.

He glanced at it and back at her, and his face changed slowly into a smile. “I don’t remember numbering the steps.”

“You did.”

“Did I?”

He was teasing her, and she knew it, and knowing it made her more flustered than ever. She took a step towards him. Then another. She caught the front of his T-shirt and pushed him backwards, and he went down onto the bed with a startled laugh, one hand catching the mattress. She climbed onto the edge and leaned over him.

“Before step two.”

He didn’t move. Then his hand came, light, to her waist. “Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“Tell me if you want to stop. Any time.”

“I know.”

She bent down to kiss him and her forehead hit his.

“Ow.”

“Sorry! Are you all right?”

He touched his forehead and looked at her. “Are you laughing?”

“No.”

She was. So was he. She hid her face in his shoulder and said “don’t laugh,” and he said “I’m not laughing at you, you head-butted me,” and she lifted her head and found a pink mark over his eyebrow and kissed it.

“Better?”

“Much.”

He kissed her cheek, and then her mouth, and for a while it was easy. They knew how to kiss. They knew where each other’s hands went. But when his fingers found the hem of her jumper under the blanket, she went rigid, and he felt it at once and stopped.

“Hey. What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. I don’t know.” She looked down. “I thought I’d be less nervous. Because it’s you.”

“Does it being me mean you’re not allowed to be nervous?” He moved her hair off her face. There was no disappointment in him, no impatience, nothing to suggest she’d spoiled anything. He was just waiting.

“Can we stop for a minute?”

“Of course.”

He sat up and gave her room, and reached for the glass of water on the bedside table, which was there because he’d written it down, and handed it to her. She drank half and said sorry, and he said don’t, and she said she’d made him—

“Eliana. I want you comfortable. I don’t want you finishing something because we started it. Shall we just stay here?”

So they stayed. They lay on top of his duvet and talked about nothing: the pharmacology mnemonic he couldn’t remember, the lecturer who talked too fast, the staircase in the engineering building that seemed to have been designed by someone who’d heard of stairs but never used one. At some point she started laughing again, and the stiffness went out of her shoulders, and he kissed the top of her head.

She was the one who lifted her face.

“Can I kiss you?”

“Always.”

This time their foreheads didn’t meet. His hand came to her cheek, and she kissed him, and when she drew back she stayed close.

“I want to try again. Because I want to.”

“All right.”

She sat up and pulled the jumper over her head herself, and the T-shirt under it, and then she didn’t know what to do with her arms. He didn’t stare. He looked at her face first, and then down, slowly, as if he were reading something he wanted to remember, and said her name, and she covered his mouth with her hand because it was too much. He kissed her palm. Then he took his own T-shirt off one-handed, and she put both hands flat on his chest because she’d wanted to for months and hadn’t known it, and felt his heart going as fast as hers.

“You’re nervous too.”

“Terrified,” he said, and she laughed against his collarbone.

He undressed her the rest of the way the way he’d untangled her headphones, without hurrying, asking with his eyes before every button. He kissed the scar on her knee from when she was nine and the new one under it from the tree, and her hipbone, and the soft inside of her wrist, and she pulled the blanket over both of them because the lamp was still on and she couldn’t bear him looking at her and couldn’t bear him stopping. His hand moved down her stomach. He asked. She nodded into his neck, and his fingers slid between her legs and stroked, careful, learning her, and when she made a sound she’d never heard herself make he went still and asked again, and she said “Don’t you dare stop,” and he didn’t.

She came apart against his hand with her face hidden in his shoulder and her nails in his back, shocked, laughing a little afterwards because she couldn’t help it. He was smiling at her as if she’d done something brilliant.

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“I’m going to look at you like that for the rest of my life.”

She pulled the drawer open herself, because she’d read his list. He put the condom on with hands that weren’t quite steady, and she watched, and he said “Stop watching me, it’s harder,” and she laughed again and he kissed the laugh off her mouth. Then he was over her, with his weight on his elbows, and their foreheads together.

“You decide,” he said.

She hooked a leg round his and drew him down. It hurt, a little, and then it hurt less, and he stayed perfectly still inside her and shook with keeping still and asked if she was all right, and she said yes, and he didn’t believe her, and kissed her eyelids until she moved first. Then it was slow. Then it was less slow, because she wanted it to be, and he let her set it, her hips finding the rhythm before her head did. The blanket slid half onto the floor and they laughed at that too. When he came he said her name into her hair as if it hurt, and she held onto him with her arms and her legs and every part of her and didn’t let him go anywhere.

Afterwards the lamp was off and the blanket was mostly on the floor and she lay with her cheek on his shoulder and her hand curled on his chest. He’d brought water, and pulled the duvet up, and was doing everything on his list in the right order, and she knew it, and she was smiling into his skin about it.

“Are you comfortable?”

“Very.”

“Good.”

A pause. “Was it okay?”

“More than okay.”

“You’re just saying that.”

“I’m not. I liked being with you.”

“Don’t say it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you mean it.”

“I do mean it.” Then, into the dark, he said the thing he’d been wanting to say for years. “I love you. You don’t have to say it back. I just didn’t want to be the only one who knew.”

She stopped moving. He didn’t. He kept his hand in her hair and his voice even.

She had heard those words in songs and films and in other people’s messages. Hearing them from him was nothing like that. He wasn’t saying them because the night had been beautiful, or because she’d finally let him close. He was saying them as if they were simply true, and had been since before the roof and the rules and the university, and would go on being true whether or not she ever found the nerve to answer.

She wanted to say it. She wanted to so much that it hurt. Her mouth wouldn’t open. She was afraid. Not of him. Of what the words would do once they were out in the room, how much they’d give him, how badly he could hurt her if she let herself believe he’d never go.

He seemed to understand. He didn’t repeat it or ask. He just reached down and pulled up the blanket that had fallen at the foot of the bed.

She watched him. Then she took the other side and spread it over both of them, herself, and tucked it round his shoulder.

It was a small thing. It was the only answer she had. He looked at her, and she tucked herself under his arm without speaking, and he kissed her forehead.

“Sleep, sweetheart.”

She slept. He didn’t, not for a while. He counted her breathing without meaning to, one, two, three, a habit he’d had since they were small and she used to doze off in the back of other people’s cars. Through his window, across the little gap between the houses, he could see the dark square of her bedroom curtains.

He had chosen this room for a reason. The bed faced her window. From here he could see when her light came on and when it went off and when she was still awake long after midnight. He had never told her. He didn’t know if he ever would.

She shifted, and her fingers tightened on him.

“Still here,” he whispered.

He thought of the drawing, the two figures under the tree, and the three words over their heads. He’d answered her once already. He’d go on answering. He wasn’t going anywhere.

chapters.title: He Already Knew
chapters.desc: After a bad job, Eliana finally tells him what she does at night, and finds out he’s known the outline since the summer: the nights she doesn’t eat, the light still on at four. She’s furious, and then she isn’t. He never once asks her to stop.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going to ask you to stop. I’m going to keep feeding you. That’s all.”
chapters.content:
At a quarter to midnight on the last Friday in November, Eliana ordered three things. A bottle of water. A packet of crackers. An iced coffee. She didn’t order dinner. She hadn’t ordered dinner the night before either, or the night before that.

Yu Chen: Have you eaten?

She was sitting on the floor of a flat that wasn’t hers, back against a kitchen cupboard, one sleeve pushed up, a thin line of dried blood at her wrist. The place smelled of dust and old cigarettes and something metallic she didn’t want to put a name to. On her laptop a file was still open. A photograph of a man. A name. Two lines from Qian. The clerk has been dealt with. Do not pursue.

Eliana: yes

Yu Chen: What did you eat?

Eliana: food

Yu Chen: That’s not an answer.

Eliana: you’re not my mother

The dots came and went and came.

Yu Chen: I know.

Something about those two words stopped her. She locked the phone. Then, because she was tired and her head hurt and the night had gone badly wrong, and she had spent forty minutes trying not to see a pair of hands that would never hold anything properly again, she did something she’d never done before. She rang him.

He answered on the first ring. He didn’t sound sleepy. He sounded as though he’d been waiting.

“Yu Chen. I did something bad.”

He didn’t ask what. He didn’t ask where. “Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“Not badly.”

“Where are you?”

“I’ll come home.”

“Which home?”

The flat wasn’t anybody’s. Qian kept it as somewhere to work until things settled: a nearly empty building, covered windows, new locks. She’d been there six hours. “I don’t know,” she whispered.

“Send me the address.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was there in twenty minutes. He didn’t knock. She heard him in the corridor and then the door, and he stood in the doorway in a dark jumper and his university trousers with his phone in his hand and his hair a mess. His eyes went over her. Her face, her sleeve, the blood, the laptop. He didn’t look surprised. That was the first thing she noticed. The second was the paper bag.

“What’s that?”

“Food.”

“It’s midnight.”

“It’s nearly midnight.”

He put the bag on the counter and crouched in front of her. “Let me see your wrist.”

A shallow cut, not deep enough for stitches, and bruises round it where somebody had grabbed her. He cleaned it from the little kit he carried in his bag, with the same care he gave to practising sutures on a pad, only gentler.

“Thank you, Doctor Wang.”

“Not a doctor yet.”

“Still bossy.”

“Still bleeding.”

He was looking at her face now, and something in it made her uncomfortable. Not anger, because he wasn’t angry. Worry, which she’d seen on him before, when she fell asleep at her desk or came home at hours when normal people were asleep. But underneath it tonight was something else. Something that looked like recognition.

She pulled her arm back. “Don’t look at me like that. Like you know.”

He didn’t answer. He sat down beside her on the floor with a little space between them. “Tell me,” he said.

Maybe it was because he hadn’t demanded it. Maybe because he’d come all this way without asking her a single question she couldn’t answer. Or maybe she’d simply run out of strength to keep it in.

“I work for the Syndicate.”

She waited for shock, for questions, for him to say he’d misunderstood, for him to get up and leave. He looked at her.

“That’s it. That’s what I do at night. I clean my family’s name out of places it shouldn’t be.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

“I think I do.”

“You think—“

“I know you work for them.”

She looked almost blank for a second. Then she laughed once, a disbelieving sound. “How long?”

“Since summer.”

“That’s impossible.”

“I didn’t know the details.” He glanced at the laptop and away. “Your window. You’d leave your desk lamp on till four or five. Sit there for hours without moving. Then you’d vanish for a couple of nights, and when you came back you wouldn’t eat. You’d order coffee. Crackers. Sometimes nothing. When you did order food you left half of it.”

She stared at him. “How long have you been watching me?”

“Not every minute.”

“That’s not what I asked. Every night you were awake?”

He didn’t answer fast enough.

“Oh my God.” She was on her feet. “You watched my window.”

“I can see your light from my room.”

“So you watched it.”

“I noticed when it was on.”

“And when it went off?”

His jaw tightened. “I noticed that too.”

She looked at him as if he’d turned into someone she’d never met. “You counted me. When I ate. When I slept. When I came back.”

“I wanted to know you were home.”

“You could have asked!”

“I knew you wouldn’t tell me.”

It came too fast and too honestly. Her face twisted. “And you thought that gave you the right?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“Because I couldn’t make myself stop worrying about you.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“I know.”

She turned away and put both hands flat on the counter. “You were supposed to be the one person I didn’t have to hide from.”

He stood. He took a step and stopped. “I’m sorry. I should have told you.”

“You should have asked. You should have let me decide.” She swung round. Her eyes were bright and her voice was sharp. “Are you going to tell me to stop?”

“No. I’m not going to ask you to stop. I’m going to keep feeding you. That’s all.”

“Do you know what they ask me to erase? Whose names I’ve taken out?”

“No.”

“Then how can you say you know?”

“I don’t know the details. I know you.”

It was the wrong thing to say. It was also the only thing that could have made her cry. “You don’t.”

“I know you won’t eat when you’re upset. I know you forget to drink when you’re concentrating. I know you keep the paper sleeves from your headphones because throwing them away is wasteful. I know you sleep better when it rains. I know you say you don’t like Auntie Tsoi’s dumplings and you always take the last one. I know you hate being asked where you’re going when you don’t have an answer—“

“Stop!”

Her voice cracked. He stopped at once.

She wanted to hit him. She wanted to hug him. She wanted to know how many nights he’d sat in his room looking across that small distance between the houses waiting for a light to go out. Most of all she wanted to know why he’d never left.

“You’re frightening,” she whispered.

His face went still. “I know. I know it isn’t normal. I won’t pretend I didn’t do it. I wasn’t trying to find out what you were doing. I was trying to make sure you came home.” He kept his voice level. “It wasn’t fair to you.”

“You don’t get to keep me safe without asking.”

“I know.”

“You don’t get to—“

Her breath caught. He didn’t move. He waited, and somehow the waiting was what finished her. The first sob got out before she could swallow it, and then another. She hated it. She’d kept her hands steady all evening. She’d looked at things she didn’t want to remember and done what she’d been asked. She had been composed and useful and good, so good, at being someone who didn’t cry, and now she was crying because the boy next door had watched her window.

He moved only when she reached for him. She caught the front of his jumper and dragged him in.

“I’m angry with you.”

“I know.”

She kissed him hard. It wasn’t the shy kiss she gave him when she wanted something and couldn’t ask. It was angry, nearly a challenge, her fists twisting in his jumper as if she could hold him in place by force. He held her waist and didn’t kiss back at first. He let her push all of it into him until her mouth faltered. Then he kissed her, slowly, with his hand in her hair, and didn’t try to stop her crying, and held her while the anger turned into something that hurt more.

“I don’t know what to do with you,” she said into his chest.

“You don’t have to decide tonight.”

“I don’t know if I can forgive you.”

“You don’t have to do that tonight either. Do you want me to leave?”

She shook her head, and then held his jumper tighter. “No.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d brought congee. Chicken, from Auntie Tsoi, wrapped in a thick cloth so it would stay warm, and pickles in a little jar, and a bottle of warm soy milk.

“Does she know?”

“She knows I was taking food to someone who hasn’t been eating.”

“She’s going to know.”

“She already knows you like her congee. You had three bowls in one sitting.”

“That was a different situation.”

She sat at the little table and he put a bowl in front of her and sat opposite. “Are you going to watch me eat?”

“Yes.”

“That’s creepy.”

“Would you prefer I lied?”

She ate. Once she started she realised how hungry she was. He pushed the soy milk across and said nothing, and warmed the second half when she’d finished the first, and covered what she couldn’t manage and washed the bowl. Then she looked at him with her cheek on her hand.

“Do you track my food orders?”

He went still. Only a little. She saw it.

“Some of your orders go on my card,” he said.

Her eyes narrowed. “Because you linked it. Because you said it was easier when I forgot my wallet. And you’ve been reading them?”

He didn’t answer.

“Did you see the iced coffee? The crackers? The time I ordered two desserts?”

“Yes.”

“That was none of your business. Did you judge me?”

“I was relieved you’d ordered something.”

She had nothing to say to that. She looked at the white dressing on her wrist instead. “You’re really strange.”

“You’ve known that for years.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, she told him about the clerk. Not the files or the names. Just him.

He’d been a junior, the kind who copied documents and passed things between people who preferred not to be seen. The leak from her first week at the university had been his. A trail of records led her to his desk tonight to collect the last copies. He was frightened. Not of her. Of the people who’d come before her.

“He said he didn’t have them any more. He kept apologising. I thought he was lying.” She looked at the table. “Then I saw his hands. They’d broken both of them. He couldn’t hold a glass. He kept trying to open the drawer where he said they were and I kept asking him to stop because I thought he was making it worse. He said he didn’t want anyone else involved.”

Yu Chen’s fingers closed round hers.

“Qian says he’s been dealt with. I don’t know what that means. I found the records anyway.”

“I’m sorry you had to see that.” He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles. “I’m sorry someone did it to him. And I’m sorry you had to bring it home.”

That was worse. She pulled her hand away and covered her eyes. “I didn’t do it.”

“I know.”

“I didn’t break his hands.”

“I know, sweetheart.”

“I keep seeing them.”

“Then don’t look at them on your own.”

She leaned against him. Outside the city had gone quiet. A motorbike, far off. A pipe knocking once somewhere in the building.

“I don’t want you involved. You can’t come with me. You can’t ask where I’m going.”

“All right.”

“You’re agreeing too easily.”

“Would you rather I argued?”

“Yes.”

“No, you wouldn’t.”

She held up two fingers. “Two rules. One: you never ask what I find. Two: you never touch my computers. Not my laptop, not my drives, not my accounts. Not when I’m out. Not because you’re worried.”

“I’ll never touch your work.”

She studied him, as if checking for a lie. Then, lower, “You can ask if I’m safe. You can ask if I’m hurt. You can ask if I’ve eaten. And don’t pretend you don’t worry.”

“I wouldn’t know how.”

“I’m still angry.”

“You can be.”

“I might be angry tomorrow. And next week.”

“I’ll be here.” He looked tired for the first time that night, not medical-student tired, something heavier. “I don’t need to know everything to care about you. If you come home at four in the morning I won’t ask what happened. I’ll ask if you’re hurt. If you don’t want to answer, I’ll leave it.”

“And if I don’t come home?”

“Then I’ll worry. I won’t lie to you.”

She kissed him again, gently this time, just a press of her mouth and away. “I’m sorry I kissed you because I was angry. I was trying to punish you.”

“Did it work?”

A reluctant smile. “A little.”

They took a taxi to the mouth of the Walled City and walked the rest, because cars didn’t fit down their lane. She put her hands up her sleeves against the cold, and he didn’t take her hand until she reached for his. At her step she stopped and caught his sleeve.

“Don’t stop watching.”

His face changed. She looked away, embarrassed. “Not my work. Not the computers. Not what I’m doing. My window. If the light’s on you can know I’m there. If it goes off you can know I’ve gone to sleep, or gone out, or whatever. I don’t mind that part.”

“Are you sure?”

“I’m sure.”

He kissed her fingertips. “I won’t use it for anything else. And if you ever want me to stop—“

“I’ll tell you.”

She went in. He crossed to his own step, went up to his room and turned his lamp off. Across the gap her light came on. He lay down and didn’t check the time and didn’t count. He just watched the small square of light until it went out, and for the first time since the summer, she had asked him to.

chapters.title: The Second Winter
chapters.desc: The heating in the tall house breaks, and Eliana is sent to Zhao’s for the weekend after her father turns down Yu Chen’s offer of a warm room next door. They get through the weekend by text, and on Sunday night they meet at the garden wall.
chapters.epigraph: “He said no to my house. He didn’t say anything about the wall.”
chapters.content:
The boiler in the tall house died on a Thursday night in the middle of January, without warning and without dignity, and by Friday morning Eliana could see her breath on the landing.

She stood in Yu Chen’s grey hoodie looking at the thermostat. Eighteen degrees. Seventeen. She pressed the button. Nothing happened. Downstairs Baba was shouting at the pipes in the voice he usually saved for men who owed him money.

“They can’t come till the weekend,” she said, coming into the kitchen.

“Then wear another layer.”

“I am.”

“Then wear two.”

He was at the table in his coat with his tablet and an untouched cup of tea. Her phone buzzed against the counter.

Yu Chen: Heating still off? Come next door. The spare room’s warm. Stay till it’s fixed.

It was such a Yu Chen answer. Immediate, practical, and already arranged in his head before she’d decided whether she wanted it.

“Yu Chen says I can have their spare room until it’s fixed.”

“No.”

“I haven’t finished.”

“I heard you.” Baba didn’t look up. “Not in the policeman’s old house.”

The house next door had belonged to Yu Chen’s grandfather, Old Song, who’d walked the Walled City beat as a police sergeant for thirty years. His photograph still hung inside the front door. His grandson Wei Long was a detective now. Baba had never liked the house, and he liked the people in it even less.

“It’s not a police station. It’s a spare room. I’m eighteen.”

“And you live here.”

She didn’t argue. She went upstairs and typed no to Yu Chen, and he typed I’m sorry, and she typed not your fault, and he typed I know, and she could hear exactly how he’d said it.

That evening Evangeline, in two cardigans, rang Elowen from the hall. Eliana heard her end of it from the stairs. “Can Eliana come to you for the weekend? Just till it’s fixed. The Wang boy next door offered his spare room and Baba said no.” A pause. “Baba wants to know if your husband would mind.”

Her husband didn’t mind.

✦ ✦ ✦

Uncle Mok drove her up the hill at eight with one suitcase, a laptop, three chargers and a bag of shrimp crackers. Her glasses steamed up the moment she walked into the warm hall. She looked round and said the first thing in her head.

“Your house has too many cameras.”

Zhao took her suitcase. “Hello to you too.”

“Hello, Brother-in-law.”

At the bottom of the stairs she stopped and looked through the glass into the courtyard. “That one’s pointed too far left. It’s missing the path past the lemon tree. And whoever put the one in over the garage didn’t think about the glass. At night it’ll show you the inside of your own garage door.”

He turned and looked at her. She was already looking at the next one.

“Show me,” he said.

It took her thirty-eight minutes, at the kitchen island with a glass of juice, while Zhao wrote down five things in a notebook and Elowen dried her hands and said “Has she started?” and was told her husband had a security problem. The east camera. The lemon-tree blind spot. The garage glass. A delay on the side-door sensor long enough for someone quick. And the backup line to the guardhouse, running through the same box as everything else, so one cut would take the lot.

“That’s without going in the garage.”

“Do the garage tomorrow.” Zhao gave her the Wi-Fi password when she held her hand out for it, and she typed it and looked up at him in real pain.

“That’s your birthday.”

“Yes.”

“Change it.”

“You change it,” he said, and she smiled for the first time since the boiler died.

At dinner there was fish, because the cook had been told there was a Lin in the house and Lins ate fish. She pushed a bone around her plate, and Zhao reached over without a word and took the plate and took the whole fish apart with his chopsticks and gave it back, every piece checked. She ate all of it. Then she took her laptop into the study, and he followed with two cups of tea and listened to her talk about segmenting his network the way he listened to almost nobody, asking one question every few minutes.

At one in the morning her phone lit up on the study sofa.

Yu Chen: Your light’s on.

He’d sent a photograph taken from his window. Her curtains, closed, and behind them the small yellow glow of her desk lamp.

Eliana: i didn’t leave it on

Yu Chen: Someone did.

Eliana: ah sim probably. why are you photographing my window

Yu Chen: Habit. I’m only looking at the light. Not the curtains.

Eliana: good. and don’t stand outside in the cold

Yu Chen: I’m in bed. Did you eat?

Eliana: fish. my brother-in-law took all the bones out for me like i’m four

Yu Chen: I like him already.

She smiled at the phone in a way she didn’t know she was doing, curled up on the sofa with her knees up, typing and smiling and typing for twenty minutes, the firewall forgotten.

“Brother-in-law?” she said eventually, without looking up. “Are you listening?”

“Yes.”

“What did I just say?”

“The guest network goes on its own line. The garage doesn’t share credentials with the house.”

She blinked. “Right.” She put the phone face down on her knee. “Carry on, then.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday she did the garage and found a sixth thing, and by lunch she’d redrawn the guardhouse line and written new permissions and made a list of equipment that ought to go in the harbour. Zhao read it and rang Bao. “Split the guardhouse box. Eliana will send you how. And change the garage code.”

“To what?” she asked.

“Your birthday backwards.”

“That’s not secure.”

“No,” said Zhao. “But you’ll never be locked out.”

She looked at him with her mouth slightly open. Then she went pink, pushed her glasses up her nose, and went back to her list without another word.

That evening she found Zhao in the courtyard by the lemon tree, looking up at the camera on the east wall.

“I’ll have it moved tomorrow.”

“Don’t.” She pointed at the gravel under the tree. “That’s where you and Jiejie stand. Sometimes she’s out here watering and you come and stand next to her. You talk, or you just look at the tree. You don’t need a camera pointed at that. Don’t fix it.”

“All right.”

She turned round to go in, and then turned back and hugged him round the middle, quickly and hard, with her face in his jumper. He went still. Then he put one arm round her shoulders.

“Come whenever you want.”

At a quarter to eleven she was on the edge of the guest bed with her laptop shut.

Yu Chen: Awake?

Eliana: no

Yu Chen: I see.

Eliana: you texted me. say something

Yu Chen: I miss you.

She typed and deleted and typed. it’s been two days. you’re dramatic.

Yu Chen: Probably.

She held the phone against her chest for a minute. i miss you too

Yu Chen: I know.

Eliana: stop knowing things

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday the Walled City rang to say the boiler was mended. Zhao carried her suitcase out to Uncle Mok’s car and gave her a card with the new Wi-Fi password on it in his handwriting.

“So you don’t have to ask.”

“I chose it. I know what it is.”

“Then you’ve got it twice,” he said, and she laughed and hugged him again.

It had started to rain by the time Uncle Mok turned into the end of their lane. The house was warm again, which felt like an insult. Baba was in his study and didn’t come out. She unpacked, and stood at her window, and then took the thick cream blanket off the end of her bed, the one with the small tear in the corner, and went down through the kitchen into the back garden.

He was already at the wall. He’d seen her light.

It was the low brick wall between the two back gardens, waist-high, wet along the top, with the persimmon’s bare branch reaching over it into her side. There was a little roof over his back step, and he stood under the edge of it in a dark hoodie with a textbook still in his hand.

“Hi.”

“Hi.” She held the blanket up. “I brought you this.”

“Why?”

“Your room’s cold. Your window’s old.”

“It’s been there for years.”

“Exactly.”

He put the book down and took the blanket and laid it along the top of the wall, out of the wet. Then he took both her hands across it. Hers were freezing. He frowned at them, turned them over and rubbed his thumbs slowly over her knuckles.

“You’re doing that thing again. Looking after me without asking.”

“Would you rather have cold hands?”

“No.”

He breathed warm air onto her fingers, lashes down, frowning a little, as if this were a serious medical procedure.

“Baba said no to your house,” she said.

“He said no to my house. He didn’t say anything about the wall.”

She laughed, and he looked up at the sound. They’d seen each other every day for months. They’d spent nights together. They’d kissed in stairwells and kitchens and study rooms and the gap behind the bins. And after two days apart they were standing on either side of a wall like strangers who’d forgotten how to start.

“Missed you,” he said, and kissed the backs of her hands.

“I know. I missed you too.”

He kept hold of her hands. “Your father. Last night. He came out of the kitchen door and stood by the pots and looked up at your window for about ten minutes. Then he went in.”

She looked at the tall house. Her window was dark now. “He knew I wasn’t there.”

“I think so.”

“Did he look at you?”

“Once.”

She gave a small humourless laugh. “He doesn’t check on me. He never comes upstairs. Even when I’m ill. Even with a fever. He sends someone to leave medicine outside the door. He’s known where my room is for eighteen years.” She stared at the wall. “He was probably wondering whether the boiler man had been.”

He didn’t contradict her. He knew better.

“Yu Chen? Do you know what’s next month?”

“Your birthday’s in five weeks.”

“Baba has never once said happy birthday to me.” She said it as if she were telling him she’d never liked mushrooms. “Not once. He doesn’t forget. It’s on the calendar in the kitchen. He knows the date. He just doesn’t say it. Sometimes Jiejie brings a cake. Sometimes Evangeline sends a message. Sometimes I buy myself something and pretend it’s just because I wanted it. He never says it. Not even when I was little.”

He reached across the wall and put his hand on her cheek. “I’m sorry he doesn’t.”

Her eyes went bright and she turned her face away. When she spoke again her voice was steadier. “There’s something I should tell you. The camera at home. The one facing the garden. I moved it last month. There’s a blind spot now, by the side door. If you stand close to the wall it doesn’t see you.”

“Why?”

“I wanted somewhere I could leave without being seen. Baba doesn’t know. Nobody does.” She looked at him. “I’m good at this.”

“I know.”

“Don’t start.”

He didn’t ask where she went through the blind spot, or what for. He remembered her rules. She saw him remember, and her shoulders came down.

“Thank you for not asking.”

“You don’t have to explain everything. Even when I want to know. Especially then.”

She reached over and took hold of his hoodie strings and tugged. He looked down at her fingers. She tugged again, and he bent, and she pulled him down the rest of the way and kissed him.

It was meant to be quick. But his hand found her waist across the wall, and when she tried to pull back he followed her just far enough to make her laugh against his mouth, and then he put his hands under her arms and lifted her, and she was sitting on the wet brick on top of her own blanket with her knees on either side of him and her hands on his shoulders.

“Hey! You can’t just pick me up.”

“I can.”

“You’re strong.”

“Thank you.”

“That wasn’t a compliment.”

“I’ll take it anyway.” He put his hands flat on the wall either side of her. “Can I?”

She looked at his mouth and nodded. He kissed her properly then, slow and warm, one hand at her waist and the other on her cheek, her fingers in his hair and still holding one string of his hoodie. When they parted she kept her forehead on his.

“Two days,” she said.

“I know.”

“Don’t say you know.”

“Sorry.”

Her phone buzzed in her pocket. She ignored it. Somewhere inside his house a clock struck the hour. The garden lights shone on the wet path, and the rain came down beyond the edge of his roof, and she leaned her head on his shoulder and stayed there.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen: Inside? Warm enough?

Eliana: yes. thank you for today

Yu Chen: You don’t have to thank me.

Eliana: i know. but i want to

Yu Chen: Then you’re welcome. Your blanket’s on my chair.

Eliana: keep it. your room’s cold

Yu Chen: I’m fine.

Eliana: you always say that

Yu Chen: Then I’ll keep it. I’ll see you tomorrow.

She read it twice. Tomorrow. Not someday, not when things were easier. Tomorrow.

Across the gap, in the house that had once belonged to a policeman, Yu Chen put her blanket over the back of his chair. He didn’t need it. It smelled of her room and her washing powder. He looked across at her window. The light was on, and this time he knew who had turned it on, and she was inside, and she was warm.

chapters.title: Nineteen, and Nobody Says It
chapters.desc: On her birthday her father takes the family to the grave at dawn and won’t look at her, and there’s a red egg at her door like every year. That night Yu Chen gives her a whole sky to herself.
chapters.epigraph: “They wouldn’t let me bring a cake in. I asked. So you’ve got the ceiling instead.”
chapters.content:
The red egg was waiting outside her bedroom door when she woke up.

It sat in a small white bowl on the floorboards with a folded tissue under it and a pair of chopsticks beside it, its shell dyed a deep uneven red. Eliana stood in the doorway and looked at it. She thought she knew who’d left it, and she knew why. And she knew that in nineteen years nobody had ever explained it to her. It simply appeared every eighteenth of February, as reliably as the cold grey light: a red egg, a visit to the grave, and a family gathering that never quite felt like a party.

She picked it up. It was still warm.

Down the corridor Baba’s door stood open and he was already dressed. “We leave at six,” he said from inside. She looked at the clock. Twenty to.

“Okay.”

He didn’t say happy birthday. He didn’t look at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six the lane was still dark and the streetlamps were on. Uncle Mok had the long car at the mouth of the Walled City with the engine running. Elowen was there with a small arrangement of white flowers, having come down from the hill in the dark with Zhao, and Raiden had come from his flat with his hood up and his glasses fogging, and Elara and Evangeline came out behind Eliana with their coats buttoned to the chin.

“Morning, sweetheart.” Elowen kissed her cheek and looked at the bowl in her hands. “You found it.” She touched the shell with one finger. “Still warm. It always is.” She tucked a strand of hair behind Eliana’s ear. “Happy—“

She stopped. Her eyes went to Baba, and back.

“It’s okay,” said Eliana.

Elowen squeezed her shoulder instead.

“Come on,” said Zhao, holding the door. “It’ll be cold up there.”

In the back Eliana sat beside Evangeline, with Raiden and Elara on the seat facing them. Elara went straight back to sleep against the window. Raiden was looking at his phone with an expression she had learned to recognise this winter: a man reading something he liked and pretending he wasn’t.

“Do you know someone with a garage?”

He looked up. “What?”

“Someone with a garage. I heard you say it on the phone at New Year.”

His face did something careful. “Why?”

“Just asking.”

“Who told you?”

“Nobody.” She looked at the window.

“I know someone,” he said after a moment.

She didn’t ask who. She didn’t know that the question had landed somewhere more complicated than she’d meant it to, and Raiden watched her reflection in the glass for another second before he looked away. Evangeline glanced between the two of them and, without a word, handed Eliana a packet of tissues.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mama’s grave was under a tree. Eliana had been there every year of her life. She knew the path from the gate, where the paving went uneven, where the grass grew thickest and where the branches threw their shadows over the stones. She knew the flowers her mother liked and the name carved on the stone. And she knew that her father never once looked at her there.

He laid the flowers first. He straightened the stems, picked off a fallen leaf and stood back with his hands folded and his head bowed. Elowen put down a small offering. Zhao stood just behind her shoulder. Elara and Evangeline came next. Raiden stayed at the edge of the path. Nobody spoke.

In the photograph on the stone her mother was smiling, with her hair over one shoulder, looking as if someone outside the frame had just said something funny. People always told Eliana she had her mother’s eyes. Her father never had.

She put the red egg down by the flowers for a minute. It looked small there.

“Happy birthday,” she whispered, and wasn’t sure whether she meant herself or the woman in the photograph.

“Nineteen years today,” said Baba behind her.

Her fingers stopped.

“You should remember what this day means.”

“I do.”

He looked at the flowers, the stone, the photograph. He looked at each of the others when they moved. He didn’t look at her. She stood there until the cold went into her fingers, and stepped back, and Evangeline came and stood beside her and took off one glove and held it out.

“Then you’ll have one cold hand.”

Evangeline lifted one shoulder and kept holding it out. Eliana nearly smiled, and took it. When they turned to go she picked the egg up again. It wasn’t for the dead.

The family stood round the grave together and looked complete, and Eliana had never understood why she felt most alone when they were all in one place.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home Baba went straight to his study. He didn’t mention breakfast. Elowen stayed to put the flowers away and then came upstairs and found her on the floor beside her bed with the red egg on the desk.

“Can I come in?”

She sat down next to her. “Mama liked red eggs, you know. She said they were pretty. She liked the colour.”

“Did she eat them?”

“Usually. She said they were ordinary eggs made special by the day.”

“That sounds like something she’d say.”

Elowen was seven when Mama died, which meant she remembered things nobody else could. She tucked Eliana’s hair behind her ear again. “I’m glad you’re here.”

Eliana’s throat closed. “Thank you.”

At the door Elowen stopped. “Your birthday doesn’t have to belong to the grave, darling. It can belong to you, too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen: Home? How was this morning?

Eliana: normal

Yu Chen: Did you eat?

Eliana: not yet

Yu Chen: Please eat something.

Eliana: you sound old

Yu Chen: I’m the same age I was yesterday.

He sent a photo of a small paper bag on his desk tied with a ribbon. I have something for you. You’ll get it tonight. Properly.

Eliana: is it expensive

Yu Chen: No.

Eliana: is it alive

Yu Chen: No.

Eliana: is it going to explode

Yu Chen: I hope not. I’ll pick you up at seven.

For the first time since she’d opened her door, she was curious about what came next.

She changed twice. The first outfit was too formal. The second looked as if she’d tried to look pretty. The third was a cream jumper, a dark skirt and her coat, which was the point. Then she put the red egg into a paper bag. She didn’t know why. She just wanted to.

Baba was in the sitting room. “Where are you going?”

“Out.”

“With whom?”

“Yu Chen.”

He went back to his tablet. “Don’t be late.”

There was no birthday in it. Not even an accidental one.

Yu Chen was waiting at the gap in the front wall in a dark coat and the scarf she’d given him last winter, with a small bunch of white flowers. His face changed when he saw her.

“For you.” Then, without any fuss at all, “Happy birthday, Eliana.”

She stopped. It was just her name and the one sentence she’d been waiting all day to hear, and her eyes stung.

“Don’t.”

“Don’t?”

“Please don’t say it. I can’t.”

He didn’t ask what she meant. He lowered the flowers. “Okay.”

She took his hand. He let her. They walked to the end of the lane together and he didn’t say it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The planetarium was closed.

“I know,” he said, and showed a card to the man waiting at the side door, who nodded and let them in. The lobby was dim and empty. No school groups, no children, only the hum of the air conditioning and the man’s footsteps going ahead of them towards the dome.

“Did you hire the whole place?”

“For a few hours.”

“Do you know how expensive that is?”

“It’s not important.”

“It’s important.”

“Eliana,” he said, and held out his hand.

The dome was completely dark. For a while she saw nothing. Then the lights began, one at a time and then dozens and then thousands: not the few the city let through between buildings but a whole sky, with the Milky Way laid across it in a pale ribbon and the constellations coming up one after another. He’d asked for the narration to be switched off. No facts, no distances, no voice telling her what to look at. He wanted her somewhere nobody expected her to remember anything, or be useful, or be someone’s daughter.

A single point of light brightened near the top of the dome. Letters formed beside it.

LIN YU

She looked at him. “That’s my name.”

“Your other one. The one on your birth certificate that nobody uses.” He was beside her, looking up. “The planetarium can put a label on a point of light for a private show. It’s yours for tonight. Yu-er.”

Her sisters called her that when they wanted a favour. He had never used it, and it sounded different from him. She looked back at the ceiling, at her name, tiny under all that dark, and the only thing she could see.

“Did you really name a star after me?”

“For tonight. Not officially.”

She laughed. “You’re ridiculous.”

“I’ve been told.”

“By who?”

“You.”

“Good.”

They sat on the floor under the dome. The man had shown him the control panel by the door and left them alone. She leaned back on her hands. “How long did you plan this?”

“A few weeks.”

“You could have just bought me a cake.”

“I did. It’s in the car. They wouldn’t let me bring a cake in. I asked. So you’ve got the ceiling instead.”

“What kind?”

“Strawberry.”

“Good choice.”

The stars turned slowly. The Milky Way brightened. She blinked, and blinked again, and a tear went down her cheek. He moved closer and put his hand down beside hers.

“Sweetheart?”

“I’m fine. I’m always fine.”

He wiped it away with his thumb. “You don’t have to be.”

She looked up at her name. “I don’t remember my mother. Everyone talks about her as if I should. They say I’ve got her eyes and her smile, and she liked flowers and eggs and old songs. I don’t know what her voice sounded like.” Her voice went smaller. “I don’t know if she’d have liked me. Sometimes I think if she were here, Baba would look at me. Maybe he’d have said happy birthday. Just once.”

He didn’t tell her that her father was wrong, or that her mother would have loved her, though he believed it. “I wish someone had said it to you this morning.”

“You did.”

“I wanted to say it earlier. I didn’t know if it would hurt.”

“It did,” she said, and laughed shakily, and leaned in.

He met her halfway. The kiss was gentle, his hand on her cheek, her fingers curled in his sleeve. Then she pulled him closer by the front of his jumper and kissed him harder, as if she needed to make sure he was really there, and drew him down until they were both lying on the floor under the stars.

“You’re not allowed to disappear,” she said against his mouth. “Even if I get difficult.”

“You’re already difficult. I’m still here.”

She shoved him, without much force. He caught her hand and kissed the palm.

“Happy birthday,” he whispered.

Her eyes filled again. She shook her head. But this time she didn’t ask him to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past nine the house lights came up and she blinked at the empty dome. At the exit she remembered the bag in her coat pocket and took out the egg.

“My birthday egg. It’s a family thing. I don’t want to eat it on my own.”

He took it as if it might break. “Are you sure?”

“It’s yours too.”

They sat at a little table in the empty lobby and she peeled it in uneven pieces and gave him half. It was cold now, and ordinary, exactly as it had been every year. Except that this year she wasn’t eating it alone.

“It’s nothing special,” she said.

“It’s special because you brought it.”

“You say things like that too easily.”

“Would you rather I made it complicated?”

“No.” She looked at him. “Can you say it again?”

He knew what she meant. He put his half down. “Happy birthday, Eliana.”

“Again.”

“Happy nineteenth birthday, Yu-er.”

Her smile shook. She leaned across the table and kissed him. “That’s enough.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she sat with the cake box on her knees and the flowers against the door and watched the lights go by.

“Thank you for giving me a sky. Did you choose a star because you couldn’t buy me a real one?”

“Something like that.”

“It’s an expensive substitute.”

“I’ll bear it in mind.”

At the mouth of the Walled City he walked her to her step with the cake. She turned round at the door. “Yu Chen? Today was good. Even though this morning was awful. I think both things can be true.”

“They can.”

“I’m nineteen.”

“I know.”

“Don’t.”

He laughed. She went inside.

Baba was in the sitting room with the television on low. “It’s late.”

“It’s not.”

“It’s nearly ten.”

“Yu Chen brought a cake.”

He glanced at the box and back at the screen. “Put it in the fridge.”

She thought about telling him. About the planetarium and her name and the whole sky somebody had made into hers for one evening. Instead she said, “Okay,” and took the cake upstairs.

Eliana: home. i think this was my favourite birthday

Yu Chen: I’m glad I was part of it. Sleep well, nineteen.

She laughed and put the phone down, and looked at the flowers by the window and the cake on her desk. The egg had still been there this year. The grave had still been there. Her father had still looked away. But somewhere, under a dark dome, a point of light had carried her name, and someone had said happy birthday. Twice.

Across the gap his light was still on. She turned hers off and went to sleep.

chapters.title: She Breaks a System for Fun
chapters.desc: Someone has been inside the wall Eliana built, fixed the one mistake she didn’t know she’d made, and sent a bill for it. Eliana has never been beaten before. She takes it badly, so Yu Chen turns it into a dare.
chapters.epigraph: “She fixed my mistake and sent a bill. A bill. One day I’m going to beat her.”
chapters.content:
Just after two on a Friday in March, Eliana Lin received an invoice for being wrong.

She read it once. Then again, leaning closer to the screen, as if it might be less offensive from a different angle. It wasn’t.

SECURITY AUDIT: REMEDIATION COMPLETED. Client: the Syndicate. Issue: structural weakness in an existing access boundary. Action taken: unauthorised entry prevented; flaw corrected. Amount due: confidential. And at the bottom, a name.

He Si-Mei.

She’d never heard of her. That wasn’t the problem. The problem was the attached report. Somebody had walked into the wall Eliana had built for Chen Si’s people, found a flaw she hadn’t known was there, fixed it, and then sent them a bill. For fixing her work.

The flaw was small. Embarrassingly small. A gap between two permissions she’d assumed were sealed off from each other. It hadn’t exposed anything catastrophic, but it was enough for someone patient and observant to move where they shouldn’t have been able to move. The stranger hadn’t taken anything. She hadn’t changed anything. She had simply strolled in, mended the door and charged the owner.

Qian: Have you seen the report?

Eliana: yes. she’s very pleased with herself

Qian: She is.

Eliana: who is she

Qian: He Si-Mei. Nineteen. Independent. She approached us.

Nineteen. Eliana was nineteen too.

Eliana: tell her not to touch my work again

Qian: She says she’ll consider it after payment.

For the first time in ages Eliana wanted to throw her laptop across the room. She didn’t, because it was expensive, and more importantly, it was hers.

The worst part was that the work was good. Clean notes. A short, clear explanation. Not a single thing left lying about. And at the end, one line she hated more than all the rest put together.

The original structure was clever. The assumption was not.

She highlighted it. Unhighlighted it. Highlighted it again. She had spent months on that wall. She knew its shape and its habits. She knew how to read the silence between an error and a response. She had never been beaten. Not properly. Not by someone who’d got inside her work and understood it and left without asking.

By the time her tutorial started she had done nothing useful at all.

The tutor was going through an access-control problem on the board. She knew the answer. She’d known it before he finished the question. Her hand was halfway up when the line came back to her, the assumption was not, and her hand came down.

“Eliana? Can you explain the difference between the two approaches?”

She could have talked for five minutes without notes. She had argued with tutors in this room. She’d once spent a quarter of an hour explaining why an assignment question was badly worded. Now her throat shut, and the room was too bright, and everyone was waiting. She looked down and typed the answer, and turned the screen towards him.

He read it and nodded. “Exactly right. Would you mind sharing that with everyone?”

She shook her head. He moved on. She sat with her fingers over the keys for the rest of the hour and didn’t put her hand up again. One stranger had found one flaw, and she couldn’t make her voice work. She hated He Si-Mei. She hated the invoice. She hated that the girl was probably having a perfectly lovely afternoon somewhere.

Yu Chen: Finished? I’ll wait outside.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was under the covered walkway with a book under his arm and two takeaway boxes, coat open, hair blown about. She walked straight past him.

“I’m going to kill someone.”

He fell into step. “Hello to you too.”

“She’s nineteen.”

“Who is?”

“The person I’m going to kill.”

“That’s quite young.”

“Don’t be funny.” She stopped. “Someone got into my wall.”

His face changed. “Did they take anything?”

“No.”

“Damage anything?”

“No. She fixed it.” She said it as if he’d asked something completely unreasonable. “And charged us. She fixed my mistake and sent a bill. A bill. One day I’m going to beat her.”

He was quiet for a second. “That’s rude,” he said carefully.

“Thank you.”

“Extremely rude.”

On the bench by the library courtyard he opened a box. Noodles with greens and sliced beef, and a small tub of smashed cucumber, which she pushed at him.

“You like that.”

“Not today.”

He moved it out of the way and gave her the chopsticks. She ate one mouthful and then the whole report came out of her in pieces. A permission boundary. An assumption. A route she’d thought was closed. A stranger who’d found it and written it up with irritating clarity. He listened without interrupting.

“Was she right?”

“That’s what you’re going to ask me?”

“It’s an important question.”

“Yes,” she said through her teeth.

“Then she did good work.”

“I hate her.”

“You’ve never met her.”

“I don’t need to.”

He reached over and wiped a smear of chilli oil from the corner of her mouth with his thumb. She froze. “I can wipe my own face.”

“I know.”

She looked at the oil on his thumb and then at him. “You’re annoying.”

“I’ve been told.” He leaned back. “You’ve never had an equal before. Someone who can do what you do, well enough to see something you missed. You’re used to being the first one to find the hole. This time somebody got there first. Does that mean you’re not good?”

“No.”

“Does it mean she’s better?”

She didn’t answer.

“That’s why it feels so terrible.” He touched her wrist. “Maybe you should find out what it’s like.”

“You’re making it sound like a game.”

“Would that help?”

“No.” A mouthful of noodles. “Maybe.”

“Then break something for fun.”

“That’s irresponsible.”

“I didn’t say university property.”

Her eyes narrowed. Then a small smile came, slowly. “You’re a bad influence.”

“Only on Fridays.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to seven she was still thinking about it. They’d gone up to the library after lunch, him with pharmacology, her with a notebook she hadn’t touched in twenty minutes and the invoice open in another tab. Her fingers were drumming on the table.

He watched for a while. “Do you want to take the dare?”

“What dare?”

“The one you’ve been thinking about. You’ve been reading the same line for twenty minutes.”

“Maybe it’s a difficult line.”

“It’s a heading.”

She shut the laptop. “Fine. Come with me.”

The top floor was nearly empty. The public terminals were still on, with the room-booking page open. She sat down and logged in with her own account, and he stood behind her chair with one hand on the back of it.

“Do you know what I hate? People who book study rooms and don’t turn up. People who take the room I want.”

“Serious problems.”

The booking system was ordinary, almost painfully so. She wasn’t interested in anything private and didn’t go near anyone else’s reservations. She just found the place where the public page decided what it would and wouldn’t accept, and persuaded it to accept one booking it would normally have refused. One persistent booking.

ROOM 4B. USER: WANG Y.C. EVERY FRIDAY. FULL TERM.

She pressed submit. A small green message: BOOKING CONFIRMED.

She sat back and laughed, not elegantly: a delighted, childish laugh, and nothing like the angry silence she’d carried round all afternoon.

“You booked a study room. In my name. For the whole term.”

“Because I can. And it’s the best one.”

He thought about it. “Thank you.”

“That’s it?”

“Would you like me to complain?”

“Yes.”

“I suppose it’s inconvenient that I’ll have to study with you every Friday.”

“Very.”

“I’m devastated.”

His phone buzzed. Your reservation has been confirmed. She grinned at it.

“Don’t tell anyone. Not even Xing Yue.”

“He’ll find out.”

“Then don’t tell him.”

She felt light, packing up. Not because she’d mended the flaw or proved she was better. Because she’d done something for no reason except that it amused her, and she hadn’t known how much she’d missed that.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went up to the library roof. It wasn’t strictly a public area, but students had been using it for years, and the door was usually left open in the evenings. The air had gone cool. She stood at the rail with her hands up her sleeves and he took his scarf off and wound it round her neck.

“Then you’ll be cold.”

“I’ll survive.”

The lights came on across the campus below them, building by building.

“I still hate her.”

“Fair.”

“She probably thinks she’s clever.”

“She might be.”

“Whose side are you on?”

“Yours. You can dislike someone and still admit she’s good. And if she’s better, you learn.”

“What if I can’t?”

“Then you’re still Eliana,” he said, and left it there.

She leaned her elbows on the rail. “I don’t like not being the best at something.”

“I know.”

“You’re supposed to say I am the best.”

“You’re the best I know at this. You’re not the only one any more. Both of those are allowed to be true.” He stood close enough that his sleeve touched hers. “It was never what I liked about you.”

She turned her head. “What, then?”

“You laugh before the end of your own jokes. You keep my hoodies. You booked me a room for a whole term because a stranger was rude to you.” He shrugged. “That’s a start.”
