She was quiet for a bit. “I think I want to meet her. I want to know how she found it.”

“I thought you wanted to kill her.”

“I can do both.”

He laughed. She caught the edge of his collar and pulled.

“Stop smiling. I want to kiss you.”

“Then kiss me.”

He bent his head. Just before their mouths met she started talking again. “Actually, I was thinking maybe I should ask Qian whether—“

He kissed her in the middle of the word. Her sentence disappeared. She made a small surprised noise and then grabbed his coat and pulled him closer.

“You interrupted me.”

“You were talking.”

“I was making a point.”

“I know. Do you want to finish it?”

She looked at his mouth and shook her head, and kissed him again, and this time he didn’t interrupt anything. His hand settled at her waist and hers went into his hair, and it started out playful, her trying to drag him closer and him letting her, and went soft when she leaned into him.

“Thank you,” she said against his chin. “For making me feel less stupid. And for the dare. And for lunch.”

“You were never stupid.”

“I felt stupid.”

She pinched his side. He caught her hand. “Careful, or I’ll book 4B for the whole year.”

“That’s my trick.”

“It’s our room now. Every Friday.”

She looked down so he wouldn’t see her smile. “That’s a lot of Fridays.”

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she didn’t open her coursework. She opened the logs.

People thought breaking into things was fast. It almost never was. It was reading. Thousands of lines of who knocked at which door and when, and what answered, and what didn’t, until a pattern turned up that shouldn’t have been there. She knew that better than anyone. She’d just never been on the receiving end.

It took her two hours to find where He Si-Mei had come in, and when she found it she sat back from the desk and stared. The girl had been inside for eleven days. Eleven days of sitting perfectly still, reading, touching nothing, moving only along the paths Eliana’s own system thought were allowed, so that nothing in it had ever thought to complain. She hadn’t been clever on the first day. She’d been patient on all eleven, and on the twelfth she’d mended the gap and left.

Except for one thing. In a configuration file nobody but Eliana would ever open, on a line by itself, the girl had left a comment.

hi.

Eliana stared at it. No threat, no boast. Worse than either: it was friendly.

She typed a reply underneath it, deleted it, typed it again, and deleted it again. Then she took a photograph of the screen and sent it next door.

Eliana: she said hi. IN MY CONFIG

Yu Chen: The nerve.

Eliana: thank you

Yu Chen: Are you going to say hi back?

Eliana: absolutely not

She left the line exactly where it was. She told herself it was evidence, and that she was keeping it so she’d recognise the girl’s habits next time, and not because nobody had ever said hi to her inside a system before.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before midnight her laptop chimed. A message through Qian.

Qian: He Si-Mei has agreed to speak to you. Her note is attached.

I’m free tomorrow afternoon. If you want to discuss the flaw, bring your own coffee. I don’t work for free.

Her mouth fell open.

Eliana: tell her i don’t pay people who insult my work

Qian: She says she didn’t insult your work. She corrected it.

She wanted to scream into a pillow. She messaged him instead.

Eliana: she’s doing it again. she’s being pleased with herself

Yu Chen: That’s unfortunate. You should meet her.

Eliana: whose side are you on

Yu Chen: Yours. You’re curious.

She looked at the note. She was. She hated that too.

Eliana: maybe

Yu Chen: Goodnight, sweetheart.

The invoice was still unpaid. The flaw was still fixed. And somewhere in the city a nineteen-year-old called He Si-Mei was presumably sleeping soundly. Eliana lay back on her pillows. She’d never been beaten before, and she didn’t know what to do with it yet. But perhaps having an equal wasn’t the same thing as losing. Perhaps it was just the first time she’d had someone worth meeting.

Tomorrow she was going to make He Si-Mei explain herself. And she was absolutely not bringing coffee.

chapters.title: Useless Advice at a Birthday Lunch
chapters.desc: At Raiden and Evangeline’s birthday lunch, Yu Chen asks Raiden how to get on Lin Jian’s good side. The advice is useless, Eliana overhears it, and by the end both men are sworn to silence by a girl with a spreadsheet.
chapters.epigraph: “You want to date my sister. I want to go on living. I think we can help each other.”
chapters.content:
Raiden made one mistake. He let Wang Yu Chen sit next to him.

It was, in hindsight, the decision of a man who had never considered that a quiet medical student might be more dangerous than a whole table of people asking questions.

The twins’ birthday lunch was in the tall house that year, the second Saturday in April, in the long dining room that opened onto the garden. Ah Sim had cooked for twice the number of people at the table and made one cake, as she always did, because Raiden and Evangeline had shared one birthday on paper all their lives and the house had long ago stopped trying to argue with paper. Elowen had brought the flowers. Elowen also invited the boy next door every year, because he’d been coming to this lunch since he was seven and nobody had ever thought to stop him.

Eliana had insisted they arrive separately. She’d told him on the step that he wasn’t allowed to look at her too much. He’d agreed, and then held the gate for her and taken her bag and looked at her as though the afternoon had been arranged round her. She’d elbowed him. Now she was between Elowen and Evangeline, pretending to care about the peonies, and he was across the table next to her brother, and he’d behaved perfectly for twenty minutes, which was suspicious.

Raiden looked like a man who’d been to a gala the night before and then somewhere else entirely. He’d come in at eleven with his glasses on crooked and a smile he couldn’t quite put away, and Eliana, who’d noticed the smile, had filed it.

When Raiden sat back with his tea, Yu Chen turned slightly towards him.

“Can I ask you something? About Mr. Lin.”

Raiden put the cup down. “Oh.”

Across the table Eliana stopped with a piece of steamed fish halfway to her bowl.

“I was wondering how to get on his good side,” said Yu Chen, with a perfectly straight face.

Raiden stared at him and then laughed, a full delighted laugh that made Elara turn round.

“What?”

“Nothing. Our neighbour wants to get on Baba’s good side.” Raiden wiped his eyes. “Why?”

Yu Chen looked across at Eliana, who was now looking straight at him. He gave her a small innocent smile. “Practical reasons.”

“Have you tried bringing him tea? The kind old men like. In a wooden box.”

“Does he drink tea?”

“I’ve no idea.”

“Then that might not help.”

“Flowers. Everybody likes flowers.”

“Raiden,” said Elara. “Jiejie’s a florist. He’s had flowers on this table every week for two years and he’s never once said thank you.”

“See? That’s why you ask people. You learn things.”

Yu Chen nodded slowly, as if this were a valuable lesson. Eliana put her chopsticks down. She could see exactly where it was going. She was going to kill Raiden. Not now, because there were guests. But eventually.

“I could ask him about his work,” Yu Chen said.

“Excellent. Men love talking about their work.”

“He doesn’t talk about his work.”

“Then ask more questions.”

“You’re telling him to interrogate Baba?” said Elara.

“I’m telling him to build a relationship.”

“Does he have hobbies?”

Raiden considered. “Being angry. Disapproving of things. Looking at people as if they’ve personally let him down. You could compliment his garden. The patch by the side door.”

“It’s mostly weeds,” said Eliana.

Everyone looked at her. She picked up her tea.

“You’re not helping,” said Raiden.

“Neither are you.”

Yu Chen lowered his eyes to his plate, but she saw the corner of his mouth go. He was enjoying this. He was taking lessons from her brother on how to impress her father, and he was enjoying it, and she was going to make his afternoon difficult.

By the time the dishes were cleared he’d collected three more suggestions: offer Baba a lift somewhere, ask about his favourite wine, and agree with him whenever possible.

“Don’t agree with him,” said Elara. “He’ll know you’re lying.”

“Then disagree?”

“No. Just don’t say anything.”

“That’s terrible advice,” said Raiden.

“It’s better than yours.”

Yu Chen listened with the patience of a man collecting evidence. Eliana knew that look. He would go home and make a list and sort it into headings and almost certainly a spreadsheet. She leaned towards Evangeline.

“Do you think he knows he’s asking the wrong people?”

Evangeline looked at Raiden. “Neither of them knows.”

Eliana nearly choked on her tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch there were presents. Elowen gave Evangeline a slim watch with a pale blue face. Zhao gave Raiden a leather case for his phone, which Raiden said he didn’t need and put his phone into at once. Somebody wanted a photograph of the birthday pair with Eliana between them.

“Smile,” said Raiden.

“I am.”

“You look like you’re at a funeral.”

“Maybe I am.”

“It’s my birthday.”

“Exactly.”

Yu Chen took it on Raiden’s phone. When she came to look he’d caught the exact second she’d glanced sideways at him.

“Why that one? My mouth’s weird.”

“It’s your mouth,” he said, and then, low enough that nobody else heard, “I like your mouth.”

Her ears went pink. She took the phone off him and walked away.

Raiden followed his look across the room. “You’re in trouble.”

“I know.”

“You really want to marry into this family?”

“I haven’t decided.”

Raiden laughed. Yu Chen’s face didn’t move. “That was the joke,” he said. “The rest isn’t.”

The laugh stopped. Raiden looked at him properly, without the act, the way he looked at buildings when he thought nobody was watching. “Baba won’t make it easy. He doesn’t welcome people. Least of all people close to her.”

“That’s why I’m asking.”

“You know what your problem is? You think if you get enough things right he’ll approve of you.” Raiden turned his glass in his fingers. “He’s not angry with you. He’s angry with himself. He has been for nineteen years. He just doesn’t know where to put it, so it goes where it always goes.”

He didn’t say where. He didn’t need to.

Eliana came back with a plate of cake and stood beside them and ate a forkful. “I’ve been thinking about the garage by the docks,” she said pleasantly.

Raiden said nothing at all.

“Interesting place to spend your evenings. You’re predictable, actually. Same route, same time, and you’re always gone before the house settles.”

“Who told you?”

“Nobody. I’m not going to explain my methods.” Another forkful. “So I suggest we all agree nothing was said today.”

“Are you threatening me?”

“I’m asking nicely.”

“You’re holding a fork.”

“It’s cake, Raiden.”

“That’s not reassuring.”

“Good.”

Yu Chen had gone still. “I didn’t hear anything,” he said. “I was discussing tea. Expensive tea.”

Raiden looked from one to the other and then, slowly, grinned at Yu Chen. “You want to date my sister. I want to go on living. I think we can help each other.” He shook his head at Eliana. “Your girlfriend is terrifying.”

“She isn’t my girlfriend,” said Yu Chen automatically. Eliana’s head turned. He looked at her. “According to her.”

Raiden laughed so hard he had to put his glass down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Baba came in from his study when Ah Sim brought out the fruit. He nodded to Zhao, said a word to the birthday pair, and sat in the chair Elowen had kept for him. He didn’t look at Eliana. He never noticed her come into a room unless she was doing something he disapproved of, and she’d become good at not expecting otherwise.

Yu Chen noticed. He noticed the way she sat up straighter when her father sat down, the way her fingers went still on her cup, the sudden enormous interest she took in the arrangement of the sliced pears. He’d spent years learning her silences.

Baba poured himself tea and spoke to Elowen. “She’s been keeping her light on late again. Past two some nights. She has no routine. All night at that computer, then she sleeps half the morning. It isn’t healthy.”

“She has assignments,” said Elowen.

“Assignments.” He said it as if it were a poor excuse. “She needs discipline.”

“I’ll talk to her.”

“You shouldn’t have to.”

“No,” said Elowen. “I shouldn’t.”

He didn’t hear the difference. Eliana looked down at her cup. The complaint didn’t matter. The shape of it did, because she knew it so well. He could have asked her. He could have said her name. Instead he talked to Elowen as if Eliana weren’t at the table.

Yu Chen put his cup down. “Mr. Lin.”

The table went quiet.

“She’s sitting here.”

Baba looked at him for the first time that afternoon. “I know.”

“Then you can speak to her.”

“I don’t believe this concerns you.”

“No,” said Yu Chen. “It doesn’t. But she said she can hear you.”

Nobody moved. He hadn’t raised his voice. He hadn’t said anything dramatic. That was the thing. He hadn’t said she was sensitive, or tired, or that her father should be kinder. Just that she was there, at the table, and could hear every word.

Baba looked at Eliana. For one second their eyes met. Then he looked away. “I was only talking about her hours.”

“Then perhaps talk to her about them.”

Baba drank his tea. It took the table a minute to remember how conversations went. Yu Chen didn’t look at Eliana again until her foot nudged his under the table and stayed there, small and deliberate, and he looked up and found her staring at her plate with her fingers finally loose.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the cake she went to the pantry for another box of tea, which was not an escape, she told herself. Ah Sim’s pantry was off the kitchen passage, and smelled of dried mushrooms and cedar and rice, with sacks stacked against one wall and jars labelled in Ah Sim’s square hand. She found the box. Behind her the door opened and shut.

“Your advice was useless,” she said without turning round.

“I’ve been told.”

“Tea. Flowers. The garden. You listened to all of it. You were making a spreadsheet in your head.”

“I was.”

She turned. “Why?”

“Because I wanted to know if there was something I hadn’t tried.”

The teasing went out of her face. “He won’t like you because you bring him expensive tea. He might never like you.”

“I know that too.” He came closer. “I thought it might make things easier for you.”

She hated how easily he did that, took an ordinary sentence and put it somewhere tender. “You can’t make everything easier. You can’t keep standing in front of me.”

“Sometimes.”

He took the box out of her hands and put it on a shelf, and touched her wrist. “Are you upset?”

“Embarrassed. You said it in front of everyone.”

“Would you rather I hadn’t?”

She thought about it. “No. I don’t like being defended.”

“Even when you need it?”

“Especially then.”

“I’ll remember.”

She stepped closer, barely at all, and he noticed. He always noticed. His eyes went to her mouth.

“Someone might come in.”

“I know.”

“It’s a pantry.”

“I noticed.”

She caught his shirt and pulled him down. Her back met the rice sacks, which shifted and rustled behind her, and she kissed him again before he could say anything. He smiled against her mouth.

“Don’t.”

“I was going to ask if you’re sure.”

“I’m sure.”

He kissed her slower then, one hand at her waist and the other at her cheek, his thumb under her ear, and she held his shirt and felt him smile when she tipped her face to follow him. For a few seconds there was no lunch, no Baba, no table full of people. Only the cedar shelves and the boy who’d followed her up a hill because wherever she went was where he wanted to be.

The door opened.

“Has anyone seen the—“

They came apart. Not fast enough. Ah Sim stood in the doorway with an empty basket. Her eyes went from Eliana to Yu Chen to the rice sacks to Yu Chen.

“Oh,” said Ah Sim.

“Hello, Ah Sim,” said Yu Chen.

“Hello, Young Wang.” She came in as if nothing at all were happening and took a jar down. “I came for the dried mushrooms.” She put it in her basket. “Shall I come back later?”

“No,” said Eliana, much too fast.

“Of course.” Ah Sim went out and shut the door.

Eliana wanted the floor to open. She wanted to be buried under the rice. She wanted to emigrate.

“I think she knows,” said Yu Chen.

“Don’t.”

“I think she might have noticed.”

“Wang Yu Chen.”

She pushed his chest. He caught her hand and kissed her knuckles, which made it worse.

“You owe me. For being caught. For asking Raiden for advice. For making me blush.”

“That last one I can’t promise,” he said, and kissed her once more, and picked up the tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he opened the notebook on his desk to a page headed LIN JIAN — APPROACH. Tea, possibly. Ask about work. Don’t mention the university. Compliment the garden if appropriate. Avoid wine unless confirmed. Don’t agree with everything. Be polite. Don’t seem too keen.

He crossed out every line, dark and deliberate. Then he sat with the pen.

He’s angry with himself. He could understand that. He could even feel sorry for a man who’d spent nineteen years turning grief into something his daughter had to carry. But understanding it didn’t make it go away, and it didn’t mean she had to keep sitting alone at that table while people talked about her as though she wasn’t there.

At the bottom of the page he wrote two words and underlined them once.

STAND IN THE WAY.

And under that, smaller: She should never have to ask to be seen.

Eliana: did ah sim say anything

Yu Chen: She asked me to pass the dried mushrooms next time.

Eliana: i hate you

Yu Chen: No, you don’t.

Eliana: unfortunately

Across the gap her light came on. He looked at it, and then at his notebook. He wouldn’t try to make Lin Jian like him. He’d be polite and patient, and he wouldn’t turn every family meal into a fight. But he wouldn’t help the man pretend she was invisible either.

Her light stayed on. For once he didn’t count the minutes until it went out. He let it shine.

chapters.title: A Hackathon, Allegedly
chapters.desc: He takes her to his family’s house by the sea for a weekend, and everyone at home thinks it’s a coding retreat. Wei Long, who raised him, rings twice with terrible advice. Nobody does any coding.
chapters.epigraph: “Bring fruit. Don’t talk about her father. Actually, don’t talk at all — you talk too much when you’re nervous.”
chapters.content:
The first lie was Eliana’s idea. The second was Yu Chen’s fault. By the time they left on the last Friday in July the story had become so elaborate that she suspected they could have just said they were going on holiday and saved everyone the effort. But she’d said hackathon, and Yu Chen, who had never been good at refusing her anything, had gone along with it.

Elowen: What’s this hackathon called?

Eliana: it’s not a public one

Elowen: A private hackathon.

Eliana: very private

Elowen: And the Wang boy is going too?

Eliana: he’s going to study

Elowen: Of course. Have fun, darling.

No questions. No address asked for. Which was much worse than being questioned. Elowen knew. Eliana was almost certain Elowen knew, and the fact that she’d let it go meant she’d remember every detail of it later.

She’d imagined a hotel. A small room, a desk, a sea view if they were lucky. Instead he drove up a coast road for two hours, through a private gate and along a narrow drive under the trees, and stopped in front of a house built into the edge of a cliff. Pale stone, wide glass, wooden balconies, a long terrace facing the water. It followed the shape of the rock instead of fighting it. Below it a path went down to a strip of beach that didn’t seem to belong to anyone else.

“What’s that?”

“My house.”

She turned slowly. “Whose?”

“It’s held in my father’s trust. He left a few properties. This is one of them.”

“And you just have a house by the sea.”

“Apparently. I don’t come often.”

“Why?”

“I didn’t have much reason.” He looked at her. “Until now.”

She turned away before he could see how much she liked that, and failed, and he saw it anyway.

It had the clean, looked-after feel of somewhere kept up whether anyone came or not. The windows had been opened before they arrived. There were flowers by the door and food in the kitchen and towels folded upstairs. He showed her round without making a show of it: the long room onto the terrace, the kitchen with its island and its windows full of water, a bedroom at the end of the corridor, and a study with a wide window over the sea, a desk, a big monitor and a neat row of pens.

“Is this yours?”

“It can be. I thought you’d want somewhere to work.”

She inspected the chair and the monitor. “It’s nice.”

“That’s high praise.”

“Don’t get used to it. We should unpack. And check the internet. And make a schedule.”

He was smiling. She pointed at him. “Don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long rang at half past eleven, while Yu Chen was cutting fruit and Eliana had her laptop open at the island.

“Ge.”

She could hear the voice from across the kitchen: level, unhurried, the voice of someone used to asking questions in small rooms. Had they arrived. Was the house all right. Had he checked the water heater, the air conditioning, the locks. Yes, yes, yes, yes.

“You’ve brought her?”

“Yes.”

“Then listen. Bring fruit. Don’t talk about her father. Actually, don’t talk at all — you talk too much when you’re nervous.”

Eliana put her hand over her mouth.

“I’m already here,” said Yu Chen. “I’ve already brought the fruit.”

“Put her on.”

He held the phone out with the expression of a man being led to the gallows. She took it.

“Hello?”

“Eliana.” The voice changed. Not softer, exactly. More careful. She’d known Wei Long all her life, the serious cousin next door who’d done his homework on the step and later came home in a black coat at strange hours. “Have you eaten?”

“Not yet.”

“Make sure you do. He forgets meals when he’s busy. Don’t let him drive tired. He thinks he’s more capable than he is. And don’t let him decide everything. He’ll ask what you want and then arrange things so they happen the way he thinks is best. He’s done it since he was eight. Tell him when he’s being unreasonable.”

“I do. Quite often.”

“Good.”

“Ge,” said Yu Chen.

“I’m only saying be careful with him,” said Wei Long, and hung up.

She gave the phone back. “You talk too much when you’re nervous?”

“He has never once been right about me.”

“You do, though. At two in the morning. You told me the whole circulatory system once because you didn’t want to say goodnight.”

He picked up a small knife and an apple and didn’t answer. He cut two little ears into a slice and rounded them and made two neat nicks for eyes, and then another, and another, until there was a whole crowd of apple rabbits on the plate.

“Why are there so many?”

“You like them.”

“I like them when you make them.”

“That’s the same thing.”

“It isn’t.” She picked one up. Its ears were uneven. “It’s ugly.” She ate it. “It’s cute.”

The second call came before dinner, and this time Eliana answered, because his phone was on the counter and he was out on the terrace.

“Is he behaving?” said Wei Long.

“He made apple rabbits.”

“That’s not what I asked.” A pause. “He isn’t used to having someone here just for him. Be patient with him. But don’t let him make you responsible for everything.”

She looked out at the terrace, where Yu Chen was watching her through the glass. “I understand,” she said.

“He worries,” Yu Chen said afterwards, taking the phone.

“He loves you.”

“That’s what I said.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By Saturday afternoon the hackathon had produced almost nothing. She’d checked the network, opened a few files and written a list of things she meant to do. Then he’d brought her lunch on the terrace, where there was a wide daybed under a canopy, and she’d eaten half of it and shut her eyes.

He found her asleep two hours later. The laptop was still open on the little table with a page of unfinished notes on it. One hand lay by the keyboard and the other on her stomach. Her hair had come out of its clip and a strip of sun had moved across her shoulder. He shut the laptop, moved her water into the shade, angled the canopy so the light wouldn’t reach her face and fetched a thin blanket from inside. When he came back she’d turned towards the empty side of the daybed. He sat down, and her fingers found his wrist almost at once, still asleep.

He stayed where he was.

“Almost four?” she said, when she woke. “I was supposed to work.”

“You were asleep.”

“That’s the problem. Why didn’t you wake me?”

“You needed it.” He turned a page.

“Are you studying? You brought anatomy to the beach?”

“I thought you were going to code.”

She looked at her shut laptop and the sea and him. “Neither of us is any good at this hackathon.” She put her head on his shoulder. “It’s a terrible retreat.”

“I’ll write a complaint.”

That evening, hunting for a charger, she found a folder on the study desk. Product pages. Specifications. A handwritten list of parts. A whole workstation, powerful and expensive and put together for exactly the kind of work she did.

“Why are you looking at computer hardware?”

He put his phone down. “Your set-up’s getting old. I thought you might enjoy something better.”

“How much is this?”

“It’s something I can afford.”

“That isn’t the point.” Her voice came out sharper than she meant. Her laptop was old. One key was worn smooth and one hinge had a hairline crack and she’d meant to replace it for months. But she’d earned it. She’d chosen it. She’d made it work. There were things she could take from him: food, warmth, his hoodies, his time, the occasional ridiculous gift. Not this. “My tools are mine. I don’t want to owe you my work.”

“You don’t owe me anything.”

“I know you think that.”

“I don’t think it. I know it.” He didn’t touch her. “I wanted to give you something useful, not something that made you feel in debt. I should have asked before I started looking. I’ll ask next time.”

She looked at him suspiciously. “That’s it? You’re not going to say it’s already paid for?”

“It isn’t. I’ll put it away.”

She took his hand. “It’s not that I don’t like you doing things for me. I want to know I can still do things myself.”

“You can.” He kissed her knuckles. “Your tools are yours. If you ever want help choosing something, I’ll be here.”

She leaned her forehead on his chest. “I’m not trying to make you need me,” he said into her hair, and held her a little longer than that needed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that night she heard his cousin’s voice again.

He’d gone downstairs to take a call. She was in the study looking for a book. The door was ajar and the balcony doors were open and she could hear the sea, and below it the low sound of his voice, and she wasn’t listening. Then she heard a word.

“Eraser.”

She stopped. It was Wei Long’s voice, on speaker, flat and clear.

“I’m not asking you to investigate. I’m asking whether you’ve heard anything. The Syndicate’s Eraser isn’t an ordinary contractor. People who work under that name don’t leave much behind. They make things disappear, and the people who hire them don’t ask what it costs. If that person is anywhere near you, you need to understand what you’re dealing with. Especially if Eliana’s involved.”

She stopped breathing.

“She knows what she’s doing,” said Yu Chen.

“That isn’t what I said. You can care about her without walking into something you don’t understand.”

“I understand enough.”

“Yu Chen.” Something in Wei Long’s voice that wasn’t anger. Fear, perhaps. “She may be good at what she does. That doesn’t make her safe.”

“She isn’t something I can keep safe by pretending I don’t know her.”

She looked down at the book in her hands. It was upside down. She hadn’t noticed.

When he came up ten minutes later she was sitting on the edge of the bed. He stopped in the doorway.

“Who’s the Eraser?”

He shut the door. “You heard.”

“Is that what they call me?”

He sat down beside her. “It’s a name people use. Because of the work.”

It wasn’t the first time she’d heard people describe what she did as erasing. But hearing a detective say it out loud made it sound like a warning. Like a reputation that had grown up somewhere without asking her whether she wanted it.

“Does he know what I do?”

“He knows enough to worry.”

“Are you afraid of me?”

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“No. I know the difference between what you do and who you are. And you don’t have to explain anything to me tonight.”

She put her forehead against his shoulder. He held her hand, and the sea went on in the dark beyond the windows.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday afternoon they went down to the beach with a book each, a bottle of water, a towel and the blanket off the bed. They settled at the edge of the shade under the low rise of the dunes, where the trees hid them from the path and the sand was warm but not hot. For a while they behaved like people who’d come to a beach to read.

Then she stopped turning pages. She watched the sun on his cheekbone and the line of his mouth and the wind in his hair, and she reached out and touched his wrist.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s usually not true.”

She took hold of the front of his shirt and pulled him down, and he stopped a breath away and searched her face. “Eliana?”

She rubbed her nose against his. “I want to kiss you.”

“Then kiss me.”

It was slow at first, interrupted by the wind and by her laughing when his hair blew into his eyes. He pushed it back. She kissed him again. His hand came to her cheek, and her book slid off the blanket into the sand, and neither of them went after it. She kissed his jaw and the side of his neck where it tasted of salt. She pushed his shirt up with both hands and he pulled it over his head, and she put her palms flat on his chest, warm from the sun, and pushed him onto his back.

“Here?” he said.

“There’s nobody for a mile. You told me.”

“I did tell you that.”

She sat astride him in her sundress and looked down at him, and he looked up at her as if he couldn’t believe his luck, and that made her brave. She reached behind her for the zip. He sat up and did it for her, slowly, his mouth on her shoulder as the dress came down, and then on her breast, and she made a sound that the wind took away and held his head there. His hands moved down her back and over her hips and slid her underwear off, and she lifted to help him, laughing at the sand that got everywhere, and then not laughing at all when his fingers found her and stroked her the way he’d learned she liked, unhurried, until she was moving against his hand and saying his name into his hair.

He’d put the condom in his pocket that morning. She knew because she’d watched him do it and pretended she hadn’t. She took it from him and tore it open herself and rolled it onto him with more concentration than she’d ever given an exam, and he lay back with his forearm over his eyes and said, “You’re going to kill me,” and she said, “Not yet,” and sank down onto him.

The sun was on her back. The sea came in and went out. She rode him slowly, her hands on his chest, finding the angle that made her breath catch and staying there, and he held her hips and let her take it however she wanted it, his eyes on her face the whole time. When she began to shake he sat up and wrapped his arms round her and held her against him and moved with her, and she came with her face in his neck and her heels digging into the blanket, and he followed her a moment later, gasping her name against her ear as if it were the only word he had left.

They lay together afterwards under the open sky with the blanket half over them and sand in places sand should never be. She had her cheek on his chest and his fingers were moving slowly through her hair.

“I think the hackathon’s a failure,” she said. “We haven’t coded. We haven’t opened the project.”

“I opened my anatomy notes.”

“That doesn’t count.”

“Then we’ll have to try again.”

She tipped her face up. “Another weekend?”

“Whenever you want.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She showered first and came down to find food waiting, which of course there was, and a cream envelope on the kitchen table with her name on it. Not in his writing. The hand was neat and slightly old-fashioned.

“It’s from Nainai,” he said from the study door. “She wrote it a while ago. I was waiting to give it to you properly.”

The letter wasn’t long. His grandmother wrote that he’d mentioned her many times: the girl in the library who drew in the margins of his notes and made him smile at his phone. She said she’d been asking when he would bring her home, and that she hoped Eliana would come when she felt comfortable, because she would like to meet the person who’d made her grandson so happy. At the bottom, in slightly darker ink:

I keep asking him to bring you. He keeps telling me to be patient. I am not a patient old woman.

Eliana laughed out loud, surprised, and held the letter against her chest. “What have you told her?”

“That you study computer science. That you draw. That you don’t eat unless someone reminds you. That you pretend not to like sweet things.”

“I don’t pretend.”

“You do. That you’re clever and stubborn and you make me happy.”

“Does she know we’re—“ She stopped.

“Yes.”

“Would she like me?”

“She already does. She’s been waiting for months.”

Eliana looked down at the paper. She wasn’t afraid of meeting his family in the ordinary way. She was afraid of being welcomed. Of being given a place at a table and having someone remember how she took her tea, and ask if she’d eaten, and make room for her without needing a reason. It was a kindness she’d never learned to take without wondering when it would end.

He didn’t ask her to decide. He waited.

“Can I keep this?”

“Of course.”

“Don’t tell her I’m coming. Not till I say.” She folded it carefully along its creases. “But maybe we can visit.”

“Whenever you’re ready.”

She put her arms round his waist. The last light was on the sea. Their hackathon had produced no code, no project and no documentation.

“Next time we’re actually coding,” she said. “And no more expensive surprises. And you have to stop your cousin ringing me with instructions about you.”

“I’ll try.”

“Try?”

“He likes you.”

“That’s not an excuse.”

“No,” he agreed, and kissed her, and rested his forehead on hers. “I’m glad you came.”

She looked at the letter in her hand, and then at him. “Me too.” For once she didn’t add anything to make it smaller.

chapters.title: The Fence
chapters.desc: Evangeline disappears from the flower market and comes back changed, and Eliana, who can find anyone, couldn’t find her in time. Afterwards she builds something to watch for the Lin name, and won’t tell even Yu Chen what it’s for.
chapters.epigraph: “I was three days too slow. It won’t happen again. That’s all I can tell you.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Eliana noticed was that Evangeline hadn’t answered.

It was the second Tuesday in October, and Evangeline went to the flower market under the old viaduct every Tuesday and Saturday at six, because the orchid sellers put their white trays out then and she liked to see them before anyone else had touched them. She always sent something afterwards. A photograph of a tray. A complaint about a supplier. A single line telling Eliana to stop worrying about whatever she was worrying about.

At seven there was nothing. At eight the man who walked three steps behind Evangeline rang the house from the market, and Eliana heard Baba’s voice go somewhere she’d never heard it go. By the afternoon she had rung her sister’s phone eleven times, and it rang out every time, and then it stopped ringing at all.

“Where did she go in?” Raiden was standing in the middle of the sitting room in his black windbreaker. He hadn’t sat down since he’d arrived.

“The east steps, under the arches. Her man says she went ahead to the orchids. He looked away for a minute. When he looked back she wasn’t there.”

“Who was she meeting?”

“Nobody. She never meets anybody.”

Raiden’s jaw went tight. “I know that isn’t helpful.”

“No,” said Eliana. “It isn’t.”

He didn’t argue. That frightened her more than anything else.

By midnight she’d stopped leaving her room. Curtains shut, three phones in a row on the desk, cold tea by the keyboard. A list of everywhere Evangeline might have gone: the market, the café on the corner, the pharmacy, the river road. Every line ended in something ordinary. A stallholder who remembered a woman in a coat like hers. A driver who thought he might have seen her. A camera pointed at the wrong bit of pavement.

She was good at finding things. She could dig a name out from under layers of false records and follow a person through the careless edges they left behind until a pattern stopped being a pattern and became somebody. But Evangeline had gone missing between one ordinary minute and the next, and Eliana couldn’t find her.

After one, Yu Chen knocked once and came in with a bowl. Congee, the plain kind he made when he knew she’d refuse anything that needed chewing. He put it by the keyboard, far enough away not to get in the way.

“I’ll eat later.”

“You said that three hours ago.”

“Then I’ll eat in four.”

He didn’t ask what she’d found. He never asked what she found. He put his hand on her shoulder instead, and she leaned into it before she could stop herself, and he bent and kissed the top of her head.

“I’m here.”

She nodded once and went back to the screen. He stayed.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday morning Raiden came with a sheet of paper. He looked as though he hadn’t slept, and he held the paper between two fingers as if it might break.

It was the flower market. All of it, from memory, in his hand: the arches of the viaduct, every row of stalls, the orchid sellers at the east end, the stairs and ramps and the service gate behind the fish lorries, and every camera he’d ever noticed on every pillar, with a little line drawn out from each to show which way it faced.

“So you can search,” he said. “You’ve got the footage. I’ve got where it’s pointing.”

She stared at it. The camera on the third pillar faced the ramp. Nothing covered the service gate.

“I tried to draw her,” he said. “Three times. I can’t do faces. I never could.”

Her throat closed. “This is better.”

“I know.” He looked past her at the monitors. “Anything?”

“No.”

“Right.” At the door he turned. “Don’t stop eating.”

“Yu Chen sent you?”

“I’m capable of an original thought.”

“That’s debatable.”

It was the first time either of them had smiled since Tuesday. It didn’t last.

The second night was worse. She’d started to recognise the exact moment a search turned into something else. First there was urgency, then concentration, then the hours stacked up and the possibilities got narrower and the empty spaces started to feel personal. By two she wasn’t looking for a person any more. She was looking for the moment she’d failed to notice. The call she hadn’t answered. The thing she’d missed.

She opened the last photo Evangeline had sent her, the Saturday before. A jar of pale flowers on a wooden counter.

Evangeline: these reminded me of you

Eliana had sent back a picture of a hideous porcelain rabbit.

Evangeline: you have terrible taste

Eliana: and yet you keep talking to me

She hadn’t known it would be the last thing.

“Eat,” he said behind her, and put down a plate: fruit, a small sandwich, a glass of water. He took the blanket off the back of her chair and put it round her shoulders, and pulled a chair up beside hers, and held her hand when he found it was cold.

“You’ve got your own things to do. You should go.”

“Do you want me to?”

She didn’t answer. He kissed her knuckles. “Then I’ll stay.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday she stopped answering anybody. Not on purpose. She just didn’t have the attention to spare. Messages piled up. Raiden. Elowen. Zhao, once. Yu Chen, from the next room.

At midnight a man who wouldn’t give his name telephoned the house and said, “Harbourside. The emergency doors. Before three,” and rang off.

Raiden rang every hospital in the district. Eliana was already in her shoes. Yu Chen had the car at the mouth of the lane before she’d reached the bottom of the stairs, and drove the river road with one hand on the wheel and the other on her knee, and said nothing at all, and she loved him for it more than she knew how to say.

Elowen’s car pulled in under the canopy at the same moment, and Elowen got out in a long dark coat over her nightdress with her hair down. Eliana went in behind her. Yu Chen stayed with the car. He wasn’t family, not out loud, and they both knew what a waiting room full of Lins would make of him.

Harbourside General was too bright for three in the morning. Raiden was already there with his hair wet and his glasses fogged. And in a plastic chair by the nurses’ station, in a black jacket three sizes too big that was buttoned to her chin, there was Evangeline.

Alive. Sitting up. Dirt on her face and her hair tangled and raw red marks on both wrists, and a graze at her temple, and her eyes as still as they’d always been.

Elowen went to her knees in front of the chair. Eliana stopped with both hands over her mouth. Then Evangeline looked at her, and Eliana burst into tears and put her arms round her sister carefully, as if she might break.

“I’m here,” Evangeline said into her hair.

“Three days.” Eliana couldn’t stop. “Three days.”

Zhao came last, in a beige suit at four in the morning with his collar open, Bao behind him as still as furniture. He didn’t go to the chair. He went to Raiden, and then he turned to Bao and said pleasantly that he wanted every van that had gone in or out of the West Basin since Tuesday morning, and the van from the flower market, and the men in it, and he didn’t care how far it went. His voice was so pleasant that Eliana stopped crying.

Baba came. A detective came, young and still as a post in a black coat with rain on the shoulders, and introduced himself to Baba and to Zhao, and pulled a plastic chair round so he could sit lower than Evangeline. It was Wei Long. He looked at Eliana once, over Evangeline’s shoulder, and then back at his notebook.

Evangeline told him in a voice so low they all leaned in. The market, a little after six. Two men. A van. A cloth. A box in the dark. A man who’d opened it. She didn’t know his name.

“What did he look like?”

“Tall.”

Wei Long wrote one word and asked nothing else about it.

Eliana sat in the chair by the window afterwards while the doctor checked her sister over and said dehydrated, exhausted, bruised, nothing that wouldn’t mend. She heard all of it and understood all of it, and part of her was still standing in front of the monitors looking at an empty search.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six Yu Chen drove her home. By the afternoon it had been decided that Evangeline would go up the hill to Elowen and Zhao, behind the gates and the dogs, a long way from the house that had known which Tuesday she’d walk ahead to the orchids.

That night Eliana stood beside his car in the lane and looked up at the tall house. Her window was dark. Then a light came on, on the landing below it. Baba was standing at the rail with one hand on it, looking up. Not at the front door. At her room. He stood there without moving. Then he turned and went back inside.

“Has he done that before?”

Yu Chen was slow to answer. “I’ve seen him there. More than once.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I didn’t know what it meant.”

She’d spent three days looking for someone who’d disappeared, and now there was a man in her own house standing under her room in the dark looking up at a light. She couldn’t decide which frightened her more.

She didn’t sleep. After one he found her at her desk with the blanket round her shoulders and her hair scraped back, and a new project open on the screen. She hadn’t opened a single file from the search. This was something else. A new directory, pages of notes, a long list of conditions. It had a plain name.

LIN WATCH.

“What are you building?”

“A fence.”

“For what?”

“For our name. Anything with it in. Anywhere it shouldn’t be.”

“Why?”

She kept typing. “I was three days too slow. It won’t happen again. That’s all I can tell you.”

He didn’t push. He looked at her face, pale, eyes red, not crying any more, set into something much harder. Then he looked at the empty cup by her keyboard and reached to move it back from the edge of the desk.

“DON’T.”

The word cracked across the room. He stopped instantly.

Her hands were frozen over the keys and her shoulders were rigid. “Don’t,” she said again, quieter.

He took his hand away. The cup had never been in any danger of falling. She knew that. He knew it too. But the thought of anyone moving anything on this desk, anything she’d set where she’d set it, had become unbearable.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“I didn’t mean to snap.”

“You don’t have to apologise.”

She reached for his hand after a while, and he let her take it. “I need this to be mine. All of it. Don’t touch it. Don’t ask what’s in it.”

“I won’t.”

He’d remembered her rules. He always did. But she could see the questions he wasn’t asking. What was she expecting to find? Who was she protecting? And why did one family’s name need its own alarm?

“Do you want me to stay?”

She nodded. He pulled his chair closer and kept his hands in his lap.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Saturday the fence had a shape. Not a search engine, not a list of people: a boundary that watched, and woke her with two short buzzes whenever the Lin name turned up where it shouldn’t. She hadn’t decided yet what she would do with what it saw. She only knew she wanted to see it first.

He brought breakfast. She ate it without being told. He noticed and didn’t say so.

Raiden rang at ten from the hill. “She’s sleeping. Did she tell you about the man?”

“Tall.”

“I keep trying to remember if I’ve seen anyone like that.”

“Have you?”

“No.”

“Then don’t invent a face,” she said, more gently. “You told me you can’t do them anyway.”

He was quiet. “She’s back,” Eliana said.

“I know.” He didn’t sound as if he’d believed it yet.

At noon Yu Chen brought her a fresh cup of tea and set it down well clear of the old one. “I didn’t move the other cup.”

Her face softened. “Thank you.”

They worked in silence for a while, her on the fence, him on a chapter of pathology. Then she said, without looking away from the screen, “Your cousin’s opened a file. It’s got a name on the front. Not mine. The one you heard him say at the sea.”

His hand stopped on the page. “How do you know?”

“I know.” She turned. “That was him at the hospital, taking her statement. He looked at me.”

“Does anyone else know you know?”

“Not from me.”

“Why are you telling me?”

“Because I don’t want you to hear it from somebody else.” She looked back at the screen. “I’m not asking you to stop him. I’m not asking you to do anything. I just want you to know that I know.”

“All right.”

“You’re not going to ask what I know?”

“You haven’t told me what the fence is for, either.”

A small tired smile. “You noticed.”

“I notice most things about you.”

“That sounds exhausting.”

“It can be.” He turned his hand over on the desk and she put her fingers in it. “He’s persistent. If he thinks someone’s dangerous, he won’t stop.”

Her smile went. “Neither will I.”

He knew that tone. It was the one she used when she’d already made a decision and didn’t intend to explain it. He kissed her knuckles. “Then be careful.”

“I am.”

He didn’t tell her he didn’t believe her.

That night she stood at her bedroom window. The landing below was empty and the house was dark. Behind her the fence was running, and it would watch, and wait, and notice. She’d built it because she couldn’t find her sister in time. Because somebody had taken Evangeline out of an ordinary morning and hidden her where Eliana couldn’t reach. Because a tall stranger had opened a box and given her back, and nobody knew who he was. Because her father stood under her window at night looking up. And because somewhere across the city, the cousin of the boy next door had a file with a name on the front.

On her desk the old cup was exactly where she’d left it. She touched the rim with one finger and checked the fence again.

It was quiet. For now.

chapters.title: The Detective Already Knows
chapters.desc: Wei Long has worked out that the person the Syndicate calls “the Eraser” is the girl next door, the one the boy he raised is seeing. He comes to the garden wall off the record, to decide what to do about her, and to ask Yu Chen about a lie.
chapters.epigraph: “I asked you to your face. You looked at me and you lied. I raised you better than that. Or exactly that well.”
chapters.content:
Song Wei Long had never liked surprises. He liked evidence. He liked things that could be checked and put in order: who came into a room, who left it, and why somebody had got interested out of nowhere in a person they’d ignored for years. Most of all he disliked being lied to.

Which was why he’d spent the better part of two months confirming something he’d already suspected.

The Syndicate’s Eraser, the man nobody had ever seen, the contractor with a drawer of false names three layers down, was Eliana Lin. The girl next door. The girl who used to sit on the front wall with scraped knees and a book she never finished, who’d once fallen asleep in his grandfather’s kitchen with a red-bean bun in her hand. The girl the boy he’d raised had followed up a hill, and apparently never once left alone.

He’d known her all her life. He’d known Yu Chen nearly as long. And it irritated him more than he liked to admit that he hadn’t seen how those two facts joined up sooner.

He could have called Yu Chen in. He could have rung and demanded an explanation and got the same calm answers he’d been getting since the autumn. Instead, on a Saturday in the middle of July, he went to the garden wall. Off the record. Without telling anyone at the station. Before he decided what to do about her, he wanted to know exactly how far his cousin had gone to protect her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late afternoon, the heat just starting to give. The jasmine on the back wall had gone wild over the summer and the persimmon threw half the garden into shade. Yu Chen was sitting on the wall with a book open on his knee and a glass of water beside him. He looked up at the gate.

“Ge.”

“You’re free?”

“For now.”

Wei Long looked at the tall house. “Is she home?”

“Yes.”

“Does she know I’m here?”

“No.”

“Good.” He sat on the other end of the wall. They’d shared enough silences over the years that Yu Chen knew when he was arranging his thoughts, and let him. “I know,” Wei Long said eventually.

“Know what?”

“Don’t insult me. I know who they call the Eraser. I know it’s Eliana.”

No raised voice. No accusation. Just the fact, put down between them. Yu Chen looked at his hands, and then nodded once.

“All right.”

“All right? I asked you to your face. You looked at me and you lied. I raised you better than that. Or exactly that well.”

“I told you I had nothing I could confirm.”

Wei Long gave a short disbelieving laugh. “You knew. You let me ask you about her. You let me warn you about the Syndicate. You sat across from me at New Year and listened to me explain why that person was dangerous.”

“I listened.”

“Do you know how that sounds?”

“I know why you’re angry.”

“I’m not asking about my feelings. Answer me.”

Yu Chen looked across at the tall house. The upstairs curtains were open and he could see the corner of her desk. “She didn’t ask me to lie.”

“I didn’t ask what she asked.”

“You were asking questions that would have made her life harder. I wasn’t going to give you something that wasn’t mine to give.”

“She’s not a file, Yu Chen. She’s not a piece of information you get to hide because you’ve decided the world doesn’t deserve to see it. Stop talking as if you’re the only one allowed to decide what happens to her.”

For the first time something in Yu Chen’s face went tight. “I haven’t decided anything for her. I’ve kept things from you. That’s about me, not her. You asked if I’d tell you who the Eraser was if I knew. I wouldn’t. If you asked again I’d give you the same answer.”

“You’d lie to me again.”

“Yes.”

The garden went still. Wei Long looked at him: the child who used to wait for him on the front step when he came home from school, the teenager who’d once refused to speak for an entire afternoon because Wei Long had told him he was too young to decide things for himself. The same stubborn composure, grown up.

“And if keeping her out of it means keeping her from help?”

“Then she can decide whether she wants help. She has the right to.”

Wei Long looked away. He’d expected defensiveness. Anger, even. He hadn’t expected his cousin to be so certain.

“You’ve built quite a life round her,” he said. “I’ve looked. Your records, your money, where you go. All clean.”

“It’s supposed to be.”

“Too clean. You’ve been keeping your name away from anything that could lead back to her. Careful about who you see and what you leave behind. You’ve been scrubbing every corner of your own life so nobody thinks to look at hers.”

Yu Chen didn’t deny it. “I don’t want her work to become mine,” he said at last. “She has enough people deciding what she is. I don’t need to be another one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana found them twenty minutes later.

He’d left his phone on her bed. She’d sent him three messages, the last a photo of two cups with if you don’t come back soon i’m drinking yours too, and when he didn’t answer she came out through the side door with both cups and saw who was sitting on the wall.

She stopped. “Hello.”

“Eliana.”

She looked at Yu Chen. There was something in his face she knew too well. Not guilt. A held stillness. She gave one cup to him and, after a moment, held the second out to his cousin.

Wei Long looked surprised, and took it. “Thank you.”

“What happened?”

“I told him I know who the Eraser is,” said Wei Long.

Her fingers tightened on the empty saucer. She looked at Yu Chen, and he met her eyes and didn’t look away. Then she pulled the old garden chair across and sat down.

“Oh.”

“That’s all?”

“What would you like me to say?”

He nearly smiled. “Your—“ He stopped. He’d been about to say neighbour. “He said much the same thing.”

“He’s my boyfriend. He’s allowed to be difficult.”

Yu Chen’s head turned. A faint smile came and went at the corner of his mouth. Wei Long saw it. He also saw that she’d said it without hesitating, and without any of the careful qualifications she’d once hidden behind, and that it was the first time anyone had heard her say it out loud.

“Do you know why I’m here?”

“To decide what to do about me.”

“Partly. I’m not going to ask you what you know. Not here. I know your name. I know the one they use. I know they’re the same.” He turned the cup in his hands. “And I know about the cameras. In March, when Zhao went missing. You went through every camera round the harbour, the service roads, the fuel station, the north quay. You found the one on the north access road that worked. And you sent it to Chen Si, not to us.”

The garden seemed to lose some of its warmth. She looked down. “I didn’t know who was watching.”

“That was sensible. You should still have told someone you trusted.”

“I did.”

She glanced at Yu Chen. Wei Long followed the look and sighed. “Of course you did.”

“You’re not going to ask for the files?”

“Not today.”

“Good.”

“You don’t make this easy.”

“I don’t think that’s my job.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.”

He stayed another half hour. He asked about her course, whether she’d eaten, whether Yu Chen was still keeping her up too late. She answered with varying degrees of politeness. When he asked if she’d been to see Nainai yet she went pink.

“She asks about you every time I ring.”

“You told her I was thinking about it,” Eliana said to Yu Chen.

“A while ago.”

Wei Long smiled into his tea. Then he took a small white card from his jacket and put it on the wall beside her. A name, a number. His own.

“I’ve got your number.”

“This one reaches me directly. Day or night. I want you to have a way out.” He held up a hand before she could speak. “Not out of everything. I can’t make what you’ve done disappear because you decide you’re tired. But if you ever want to step away from them, or something’s coming at you that you can’t handle on your own, ring me. Before you decide you’ve got no other choice.”

“Conditions?”

“One. No more lies. If you ring, tell me the truth. I won’t promise to agree with you or to keep you from every consequence. I’ll listen. And I won’t ask for your files.”

Yu Chen looked at him. “Don’t look so surprised,” said Wei Long. “I know when to leave something alone.”

She turned the card over. Nothing on the back. She put it in her pocket. “Thank you.”

He left as the sun went down. When the gate shut she turned to Yu Chen.

“Did he shout at you?”

“No.”

“Did you lie?”

He paused. “I told him I’d lie again.”

She let her breath out. “Of course you did. You shouldn’t have to. You shouldn’t have to keep your whole life clean so nobody looks at mine.”

“I don’t do it because I have to. I want my life to be mine. And yours to stay yours.”

She stepped in, caught the front of his shirt and kissed him hard. Not the careful kiss she gave him when they were alone. This one was sudden and full of everything she hadn’t said while his cousin sat there. He caught her waist and kissed her back, and then slowed it, his hand moving to her cheek, his thumb under her eye.

“You’re upset.”

“Not with you. I hate you lying to people because of me.”

“I’m not doing it because of you. I’m doing it because I choose to. And if I ever choose not to, I’ll tell you.”

She looked at his mouth. “I’m still trying to kiss you.”

“Then ask properly.”

“Can I?”

“Always.”

This time he let her set the pace. And when she’d kissed him long enough that her knees had stopped working, she took his hand and pulled him off the wall and across his own garden and in through his kitchen door.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t let him turn the lamp on. She found his room in the dark the way she’d found it a hundred times, and pushed the door shut with her back, and pulled him to her. The window was open. The last blue was going out of the sky over the Walled City, and the room was full of the smell of jasmine and warm stone.

“Eliana—“

“No lamp.”

He understood. Tonight she didn’t want to be looked at. She wanted to be touched.

She pulled his shirt over his head and pressed her mouth to his chest, his collarbone, the hollow of his throat where his pulse was going hard. His hands found the hem of her dress and drew it up and off, and he made a sound low in his chest when he found she had nothing on under it but her underwear, and she laughed into his shoulder, breathless. They got to the bed by feel. She pushed him down and he pulled her with him, and for a while it was all hands and mouths in the dark, his palms moving over her back, her waist, the curve of her hip, as if he were learning her again with his eyes shut.

“You’re shaking,” he said.

“So are you.”

He kissed down her body slowly, unhurried, her stomach, her hipbone, the inside of her thigh, until she had both hands knotted in his hair and was pressing the back of her wrist to her mouth to keep quiet, because the window was open and the whole lane could hear. He held her hips still and didn’t stop until she broke, arching off the bed, her whole body tightening and then coming loose all at once.

She dragged him back up by the shoulders and kissed him, tasting herself on his mouth. He reached across her for the drawer. She heard the small tear of the packet in the dark. Then he was above her, his forehead against hers, his breath unsteady.

“Look at me,” he said.

“I can’t see you.”

“Then feel it.”

He pushed into her slowly, and she wrapped her legs round him and held on. They didn’t hurry. There was nothing in it of the clumsy laughing first night, or the beach. This was slower, and darker, and she held his face in both hands and felt every movement of it, his mouth on her neck, the weight of him, the low helpless sounds he made against her skin. When she was close she said his name, and he said hers back, rough, and moved deeper, and she came again with her nails in his shoulders and her face turned into his neck. He followed her with a shudder that went right through him, holding her as if he could keep her there by holding on.

Afterwards they lay tangled in the dark with the sheet kicked off and the jasmine coming in through the window. She had her ear on his chest and could hear his heart slowing.

“He knows,” she said.

“Yes.”

“And he still gave me his number.”

“Yes.”

She lay and thought about that until she fell asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning he made eggs while she sat at the kitchen table in his shirt with the white card in front of her. She checked the number against everything she already had. It was real. It was his. No second contact, no hidden condition. She saved it, looked at the screen, and changed the name to NO FILES.

Eliana: if you ever ask me for files, i hang up. if you try to get them another way, i’ll know

Wei Long: Understood. No files.

Eliana: and don’t send anyone to ask me questions

Wei Long: I won’t.

She hesitated. and tell nainai i’ll come when i can

The reply took longer. She’ll cry. Don’t tell her I said so.

Yu Chen put a plate in front of her. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re smiling.”

She tried to stop. It didn’t work. He reached across and brushed his thumb over her knuckles. “I’m glad you’ve got his number.”

“Would you be angry if I rang it? If I wanted out?”

“No.”

“Would you try to stop me?”

“No.”

“Would you come with me?”

“If you wanted me to.”

There was something in that which made her chest ache. Not that he’d promised to follow her. That he’d left the choice with her.

In the afternoon she found him back on the wall where Wei Long had sat the day before. She stepped between his knees and he put his hands on her waist.

“I don’t want to leave,” she said. “Not because of him or the Syndicate or anything. I don’t want to leave this. Us.”

“You don’t have to.”

She leaned down and kissed him. “Don’t tell him I said that. And don’t tell Nainai I’m coming next week. Or next month. Or that I might bring her flowers.”

“I won’t.”

She put her arms round his neck. The light was going gold over the garden and the jasmine moved in the breeze along the wall. His cousin had come to decide what to do about the Eraser. He’d left her a number instead, and a choice, and a promise not to ask for what she wasn’t ready to give.

“Can we go inside?”

“Why?”

She smiled. “Because I want you to kiss me somewhere the neighbours can’t see.”

He laughed and stood up with his hand still at her waist. “Come on, sweetheart.”

She followed him in through the door and didn’t look back.

chapters.title: He Held the Ladder
chapters.desc: For Elowen’s flower-shop wedding, Eliana strings a sky of lights and won’t say why. The night before, a lanky boy holds her ladder for hours and slips out before anyone finds her asleep. At the wedding Raiden says “my wife” out loud, and nobody introduces the boy next door to anyone.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll hold it. You do the stars. Don’t look down — you never look down.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past seven on Friday evening, Eliana Lin was standing at the top of a stepladder in the middle of her sister’s flower shop, losing an argument with a string of lights.

“They’re tangled,” Yu Chen said.

“They’re complicated.”

“They’re tangled, and you’re leaning.”

“I’m reaching.” She had one end of the wire in her left hand and was picking at a knot with her teeth. Her claw clip had slipped to one side and her glasses were pushed up into her hair, where they did no good at all. “If you move the ladder I’ll have to start the whole beam again.”

“I wasn’t going to move it.”

“You were thinking about it.”

He had been, so he didn’t answer. He stood at the bottom with both hands on the rails and his sleeves rolled to the elbow, looking up at her as if nothing in the shop were worth watching except a girl on a ladder biting a wire.

Aurelia had run the shop for three days with two phones and a notebook, and had gone home at six promising to feed anyone who touched the guest list to the dogs. Tomorrow, three and a half years after a registry office on a Tuesday morning, Elowen was going to have the wedding she’d never had, here, among the buckets and the cooler and the long wooden counter where she’d made other people’s bouquets since she was twenty. Elowen had been allowed to choose the flowers. Eliana had been allowed to do the lights.

She had been planning them for weeks. Warm bulbs along every beam. Strips hidden under the shelves. Threads of tiny lights wound through the greenery so the leaves would seem to glow from inside. Nobody knew why the pattern had to be exactly this pattern, and she hadn’t told anyone, including the person holding the ladder.

“Pass me the coil behind you,” she said.

He reached for it.

“Your other behind.”

He gave her a look and passed up the right one. She hooked the wire over the beam, leaned out to pull it taut, and felt the ladder steady under her before it could even think about tipping.

“Don’t lean so far.”

“Then I’d need you to let go.”

“I’ll hold it. You do the stars. Don’t look down — you never look down.”

“I know,” she said, and went on working.

At eight Elowen came out from the back with a box of ribbons and stopped in the doorway. Eliana was sitting on the third step with a knot in her lap. Yu Chen was still holding the rails.

“How long have you been doing that?”

“Not long,” said Eliana.

“Almost two hours,” said Yu Chen.

Eliana looked down at him. “Traitor.”

“Have you eaten?” Elowen asked her.

“I had a biscuit.”

“At five,” said Yu Chen.

“It was a large biscuit.”

Elowen went into the kitchen and came back with two sandwiches on a plate. She gave them to her sister, looked at the boy at the foot of the ladder with an expression Eliana couldn’t read, and went home to sleep.

Eliana ate half a sandwich standing on the floor. Yu Chen looked at the other half.

“After this beam,” she said.

He waited.

She ate it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By ten the ceiling had begun to look like something. The long arcs crossed from beam to beam and dipped in soft loops over the middle of the room, and where they gathered most thickly, above the space by the counter where Elowen would stand, there was a cluster she had measured twice and rehung three times. By half past ten there was dust in Yu Chen’s hair and he was shifting his weight every few minutes without a word about his back, and every time she glanced down he was already looking up.

“Your arm’s shaking,” she said.

“It’s fine.”

“Swap hands.”

“I’m all right.”

“Swap.”

He swapped. She watched him do it, and then she said “Thank you” so low that he had to tilt his head to hear it.

“For what?”

She looked at the beams instead of at him. “Everything.”

At twenty to midnight she came down the last time, one hand on the rail, and he caught her elbow on the bottom step and didn’t let go of it. She went to the switch by the cooler door and turned the strings on, just for a second, to check them.

The shop went gold. Every beam at once, every shelf, every thread in the leaves. The white roses in the buckets along the wall caught it and seemed to float. She turned it off again before anyone in the street could see.

“Is that what you wanted?” he asked.

“Exactly that.”

He was looking at the switch, not the ceiling. She’d put a strip of masking tape over it that afternoon so no one would touch it, and on the tape in her own handwriting it said 9:41.

“Why nine forty-one?”

She hadn’t expected him to notice. She should have.

“On the seventeenth of March, three years ago,” she said, “Elowen and Zhao went to the registry on a Tuesday morning and signed at nine forty-one. Chen Si watched. Then they went home. Nobody took a photograph and nobody remembers the time except the man who wrote it down, and me.” She pushed her glasses back up her nose. “So tomorrow night, at nine forty-one, the lights come on.”

He didn’t say it was sweet. He reached up and put her claw clip back properly.

“You remembered,” he said.

“I always remember.”

“I know.”

They were meant to leave at midnight. At a quarter past she was sitting on the floor behind the counter with her back against the cabinet, looking up at the dark beams and telling him about the cluster over the counter, and at half past she’d stopped telling him. At twenty to one her head tipped sideways against the wood.

He crouched in front of her. “Sweetheart.”

“Finished?” she said, without opening her eyes.

“Yes.”

“Good.” And she was asleep again.

He could have woken her and walked her home. He looked at the claw clip already coming loose again, at her glasses on top of her head, and fetched the folded blanket from the back room instead, and eased it under her, and laid his leather jacket over her. She caught the sleeve in her fist without waking.

“I’m here,” he said.

Her fingers loosened. He filled his steel flask with milk tea from the urn in the kitchen, set it by her hand, and stood for a minute under the dark strings of lights. Then he bent and kissed her forehead and let himself out through the back, leaving the work lights on so she wouldn’t wake up in the dark. Nobody saw him go.

At half past one Elowen came back for her phone. Eliana didn’t know that until much later.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke at six to the sound of a lorry in the lane and the smell of leather. For a second she didn’t know where she was. Then she saw the blanket, and the jacket, and the flask, and knew exactly where she was and who had put every one of them there. The work lights were off. Somebody had turned them off.

Yu Chen: Morning.

Eliana: where are you

Yu Chen: Home. You looked comfortable.

Eliana: you left your jacket

Yu Chen: I noticed.

Eliana: come back

Yu Chen: Already outside.

He was, in a clean shirt with his hair still damp, holding a paper bag of egg tarts from the bakery that opened at half past five. She took the bag from him and put her arms round his waist and her face against his shirt.

“You should have stayed,” she said into it.

“You needed to sleep.”

“I sleep better when you’re there.”

“I know.” He rested his chin on her head. “Next time I’ll stay.”

She kissed him once, and then again because the first had been too short, and he smiled against her mouth and said, “Breakfast first,” and she called him unromantic, and he said he was responsible, and she said that was worse. Then he went home before Aurelia arrived at eight, because nobody had asked him to the wedding and he didn’t expect anyone to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The guests came at four, out of a grey afternoon that couldn’t decide whether to rain.

Granny Yip from the market had the second row and a packet of tissues. Xiao Pan wore a tie for the first time in his life and kept touching it. Chen Si came in a dark suit and stood beside Zhao, and the two of them talked in low voices by the cooler as if they were discussing a shipment. Song Wei Long arrived with a small box, stiffened when Elowen hugged him, and spent most of the evening at the window, looking up at the roof across the street, where there was nothing but a water tank.

Evangeline had come in the morning with Mama’s orchid in a pot, the one everyone had thought was dead, and set it on the counter. In the afternoon she stood by the door in a plain dress with her hands folded and watched the street.

Raiden arrived last, with a young woman Eliana had seen twice in her life and never been introduced to. The woman was carrying a steel box with handles, and inside the steel box, held level for half an hour on the back of a motorbike, was the bottom tier of Elara’s cake. At the door she set it down, took a ring out of her pocket and put it on. Raiden reached into his collar, broke the string he’d worn round his neck for as long as Eliana could remember, and put his on too.

Then he walked in with his hand on the small of her back.

“This is Jinx,” he said to the room. “My wife. She built Xiao Pan’s bike. Don’t touch her tools.”

Eliana, at the foot of her own ladder with a roll of tape in her hand, heard herself say, “Since when?”

Before Raiden could answer, Zhao looked up from the cooler and straightened his cuff. “Since her jacket on the chair,” he said to Raiden. “It was your marriage.”

Baba put his teacup down and went outside.

Eliana thought he’d gone. She went to the window to see which way the car would turn, and saw him on the pavement instead, with Jinx, who had followed him out. He was talking. Jinx was listening with her arms folded. Eliana couldn’t hear a word. She saw her father say something and hold one hand flat at the height of a workbench, and saw Jinx answer, one word, and saw her father nod as if a thing he’d been wondering for years had been settled. When they came back in, Jinx went to stand by the door beside Evangeline, and the two of them watched the street together without speaking. Baba sat down and picked up his tea.

At six a tall man in gold-rimmed glasses and a black turtleneck came in alone and went and stood beside the cake. Nobody introduced him either. He stood there all evening as if someone had asked him to guard it, and every time Elara walked past him with a tray he looked at her and she didn’t look back.

Eliana knew why. She’d known for six weeks, since a registry entry on a Friday in the middle of August had crossed her screen with two names on it. She had closed it and told no one. It wasn’t hers to tell.

Elara had a thin gold chain round her neck. Something on it had worked its way out from under her collar.

“Oh,” said Aurelia, at Elowen’s elbow. “Oh, indeed.”

“He’s a colleague,” said Elara, passing with the plates.

Across the room the man by the cake caught Eliana watching him. His eyes narrowed behind the gold rims, a warning as plain as a sign on a door. She smiled at him. He looked away, and she smiled more, and then she went to check the switch for the eleventh time.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain started at seven and stopped at half past nine. By then the shop was full of the last grey light and the smell of wet roses, and the strings overhead were still dark.

Baba stood up. Elowen had gone into the back to change her shoes, and he went and waited at the door of the back room, and when she came out he offered her his arm. Eliana hadn’t known he was going to. From where she stood by the switch she saw his face. It was composed, the way it always was. His eyes were wet.

He said something to Elowen, low. Eliana heard the end of it. “Her mother would have liked that.”

Then he walked her the length of the shop, between the buckets and the chairs, and put her hand into Zhao’s, and went and sat down in the front row next to Evangeline and took her hand instead. There was no celebrant. Elowen had said no. There was nothing to sign; they’d signed it three years ago. Chen Si stood beside Zhao. Aurelia stood beside Elowen. Granny Yip was crying and telling the woman next to her that it was the pollen.

Eliana watched her father’s hand around Evangeline’s. She had never once been the person he was tender with, and she’d stopped expecting to years ago, and it still went through her like cold water. She looked down at her watch so that nobody would see her face.

Nine forty. The second hand going round.

At exactly nine forty-one she turned on the lights.

The whole shop went gold at once. Every beam and every shelf and every thread of green, and above the counter, over the place where her sister stood, the cluster she had rehung three times shone brightest of all. Elowen looked up. Then she looked across the room at Eliana by the switch, and Eliana saw her understand, all at once, what her sister had been doing for weeks without saying. Elowen’s hand went to her mouth.

Zhao looked at the lights, and then at his wife, and took her face in both hands and kissed her under them, in front of everyone, long and slow. Granny Yip clapped. Chen Si cheered like a schoolboy. Aurelia wept openly into a handkerchief. Baba looked down at his hands and smiled.

The cake was lemon, four tiers, with sugar camellias so fine the light came through the petals. Raiden danced with Jinx between the buckets. Evangeline climbed onto the kitchen step stool to put a plate of cake up on the top shelf, out of everyone’s way, as if she were saving it for somebody who wasn’t there, and Raiden said “Evangeline, get down” from the middle of the floor without letting go of his wife, and Evangeline didn’t.

Eliana slipped out through the back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lane was wet, and the gold from the windows lay across the stones in long squares. He was leaning on the wall opposite the back door with his hands in his pockets, in the shirt from that morning, without his jacket, because she had it.

“I saw,” he said. “Through the window. When they came on.”

“You weren’t supposed to be here.”

“I know.” He looked up at the back window, where the light was coming through the leaves. “I wanted to see what nine forty-one looked like.”

She crossed the lane to him. Behind her the music was muffled by the door. Somewhere along the street a gutter was still dripping.

“You held the ladder for three hours,” she said.

“Three hours and twenty minutes.”

“You counted.”

“I was standing there.” He took one hand out of his pocket and touched her cheek, as if checking that she was warm enough. “One day I’ll put lights like that up for us.”

He didn’t say it like a promise she had to sign. He said it the way he’d say it was going to rain again. She looked up at the window, at the glow coming through it, and then at him.

“One day,” she said.

His hand slid from her cheek to her jaw. His fingers settled beneath her ear, and he tipped her face up and kissed her, and her back met the cool wet brick of the wall. It was slow. He held her as if he had all night, and she rose onto her toes and took a fistful of his shirt, and when he lifted his head to breathe she pulled him straight back down. His thumb moved along her jaw. Her heart was going so hard she was sure he could feel it through his shirt.

“Again,” she said, when he let her breathe.

He kissed her again.

Ten minutes later she went back inside wearing his leather jacket, which came halfway down her thighs and smelled of him and of the lane. She didn’t explain it. Elowen, by the cake, looked at the jacket and then at her sister’s mouth and said nothing at all.

Later still, when the music was slower and Elowen and Zhao had disappeared into the cooler and Aurelia was counting loudly to a hundred outside its steel door, Baba stood by the cake and looked at the man in the gold-rimmed glasses. The man looked across the room at Elara with a stack of plates in her hands, and back at Baba.

“Wang Xing Yue,” he said. “Her husband.”

Eliana, in a jacket two sizes too big, put her face in her collar so that nobody would see her laughing, and looked up at the lights.

chapters.title: The Photograph
chapters.desc: At nineteen minutes past three in the morning, the fence catches the one thing it was built to catch. By ten she’s home and hollowed out, and the boy next door is on the kerb with his bicycle, because he always is.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to be scared on your own. That part’s mine. You can give me that part.”
chapters.content:
At nineteen minutes past three on a Tuesday morning in October, the fence found what it had been built to find.

Eliana was awake.
