She’d been awake most of the night with one knee drawn up under her chin and a cup of tea going cold by the keyboard, reading code that didn’t need reading, because some nights the house was too quiet to sleep in. Baba’s light had gone out at midnight. A car went by in the wet street and its headlights slid across her curtains and were gone.

The alert was small. One match. One image. One name.

She opened it, and for a second she didn’t understand what she was looking at, and then she did.

Evangeline, on the floor of a bare room, one shoulder against a wall. Her hair loose and tangled. Her face turned a little away from the camera, not far enough. It had been taken with a flash, close, inside the place where she’d been kept for three days a year ago, and underneath it, in a private listing that was never meant to be found, someone was discussing a price.

Eliana’s chair went back so hard it hit the bed.

She had built the fence for exactly this. A year ago she’d been three days too slow, and she’d sat up for a week afterwards making something that would watch the family’s name in every place it shouldn’t be. It had watched for a year. It had found leaked addresses and a doctored photo of Raiden and a man in the north trying to sell a story about Baba to a magazine. It had never found this. Evangeline had been home for twelve months. She’d sat at their table and laughed at Raiden and stood under the lights at Elowen’s wedding three weeks ago, and all that time someone had been keeping this as a thing to sell.

She picked up her phone.

Eliana: i found something

Eliana: it’s ev

He rang before she could put the phone down.

“Don’t come over,” she said.

“What did you find?”

“Someone’s selling a photograph of her. From when she was held.”

The softness went out of his voice. “Are you on your own?”

“Yes.”

“Is your door locked?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“I need to take it down. All of it. Every copy.” She was already typing. “Don’t ask me to stop.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

She hated that he could hear the difference between her angry and her frightened. She hated that it helped.

“Yu Chen.”

“I’m here. You don’t have to be scared on your own. That part’s mine. You can give me that part.”

He didn’t tell her it would be all right. He stayed on the line while she began, and didn’t speak again unless she did.

By two minutes past four she had the first copy. By twenty-five to five she had the second. By eleven minutes past five she was inside a private exchange that had already been closed, where the image still sat in the history like something left in a drawer. There weren’t dozens. There were enough. She didn’t read what the men had said about it. She didn’t let herself think about who had wanted to buy it. She kept what she needed to prove where it had gone, and then she took it out of every place she could reach, one by one, until the listing was gone and the exchange went dark and the accounts that had passed it round couldn’t open it any more. Then she searched for it again. Then again.

At twenty-four minutes past six she sat back. The window had gone grey. She hadn’t seen the sun come up.

“It’s gone,” she said.

“All of it?”

“Everything I found.” She pressed her fingers into her eyes. “I should have found it a year ago.”

“You found it.”

“After someone had already sold it.”

“You found it,” he said again, and the repetition didn’t make it less ugly, but it gave her something to hold. “Eat something.”

“Don’t.”

“All right.”

She ended the call herself, a long time later.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten she came downstairs with her face washed and her hair up, looking exactly like herself, which seemed wrong. Ah Sim was at the stove. Ah Sim looked at her once and didn’t ask why she looked like someone who’d been a long way away all night. She put a bowl of plain congee on the table and stood over it until three spoonfuls had gone, and then took the bowl away and said “Good,” and that was all.

The boy next door was sitting on the kerb outside the gate with his bicycle on its side next to him.

“You should be at the hospital,” she said. It was Tuesday. Third years had wards on Tuesdays.

“I rang in sick.”

“You’re not sick.”

“No.” He stood up. “I wasn’t going to be much use today.”

“Yu Chen.”

“Can I come closer?”

It was such a small question. It nearly undid her. She nodded, and he came slowly, his eyes moving over her face without making her feel looked at.

“I’m going to Ev’s,” she said.

“I know.”

“I want to go alone.”

“Do you want me nearby?”

She hadn’t expected that. She looked down so that she wouldn’t have to answer with her face, and saw that his left shoelace was undone and trailing in the gutter. She crouched without thinking and tied it, a double knot, pulled tight.

“Now you won’t trip.”

He looked down at the top of her head. “Thank you.”

She stood up and took his hand, and they stood there in the late-morning sun at the edge of the pavement while a delivery van tried to reverse down the lane and failed twice.

“Yes,” she said. “Nearby.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Evangeline had moved in August to the sixth floor of an old textile building by the river, which nobody had explained to Baba. Elowen opened the door. Yu Chen sat downstairs on the low wall by the loading bay with his hands between his knees.

Ev was on the sofa with her feet tucked under her and a mug held in both hands. She looked up and said “Hi,” and then saw Eliana’s face and put the mug down.

Eliana sat beside her and took her hand. She’d planned what to say. None of it came. Elowen sat on Ev’s other side and said, “Take your time.”

“I found a photograph last night,” Eliana said. “From when you were held. Someone was selling it.”

Ev went still in the way some animals go still. Elowen’s hand found her shoulder.

“Did you see it?” Ev asked.

“Yes.”

“Was it me?”

“Yes.”

Ev looked at the window for a while. Then she nodded. “Okay.”

“I took it down. Every copy I could find. I kept the records, nothing else.” Eliana’s throat closed. “I should have found it sooner.”

“No,” said Elowen.

“If the fence had been—“

“No, Eliana.” Elowen took her other hand, so that she was holding both sisters at once. “You found it. You stopped it. Don’t turn that into one more thing to punish yourself with.”

Ev leaned her shoulder into Eliana’s. “You didn’t take it,” she said. “So don’t say sorry for it.”

At four the door opened without a knock.

He came in as if he lived there. That was the first thing Eliana noticed. The second was that Ev looked up at him before anyone else had moved, and that something in her face settled. He was a little older than Eliana, dark-haired, with a stillness about him that had nothing to do with calm. He looked at Ev first.

“All right?”

“Fine.”

He didn’t argue with it. He only looked at her a moment longer, as if reading something only he could read, and then he turned to Eliana.

“Jun Hyuk,” said Elowen.

“Eliana,” he said. Not a question. “Elowen said you found something.”

She didn’t take out her phone. She wasn’t going to put that image back into the room.

“A listing. A photograph taken while she was held. It was circulating privately. I’ve taken it down.” She hesitated, then gave it to him, because she could see in his face that he’d find it anyway. “There was a name on the original exchange. Hwang. The account was being run from a mahjong club over a car wash on Kiln Street.”

Jun Hyuk didn’t move at all.

“Hwang,” he said.

“That’s all I have. It could be an alias.”

“It isn’t.” He said it the way someone else might say the time. Then he looked at Ev, and his voice changed. “It doesn’t mean anyone knows where you are. It doesn’t mean anyone’s coming.”

Eliana watched him separate what they knew from what they feared, and do it for Ev’s sake and not his own. She noticed his hands, which were still. She noticed that he’d stopped asking questions, which meant he didn’t need answers. She noticed the thin silver band on Ev’s finger, and the black thread round his, and the two cups by the sink that had been washed and set upside down together.

She didn’t ask. There were enough questions in the room already.

“I’m not asking you to do anything,” she said.

“I know.” He looked at her properly then. “Thank you for telling me first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen took her home in a taxi at nine. She didn’t speak. He didn’t ask her to. At the gate he walked her to the front door and waited until she was inside and he’d heard the lock.

At two in the morning she was sitting on the front step in a cardigan too thin for October, with her knees pulled up and her forehead on them.

The street was asleep. A train went by somewhere beyond the rooftops. She could see the photograph every time she closed her eyes, and she’d stopped trying not to close them. She heard the side gate between the two gardens creak, and footsteps on the path, and someone sat down next to her and put a blanket round her shoulders.

“Your window was open,” he said.

“You can’t keep using that.”

“I’ve got others.”

She pulled the blanket closer. He sat with his shoulder against hers and looked at the empty street with her.

“I keep thinking about it,” she said.

“I know.”

“I thought I’d be angry. I am. But mostly I’m…” She couldn’t find the word, and he didn’t hand her one. “Tired.”

“You’ve been up all night.”

“That isn’t what I mean.”

“I know.”

She leaned her head against his shoulder. “I hate that she was still being hurt after she came home. All year. While we were having dinner.”

His jaw tightened. She felt it against her hair.

“Do you remember the ladder?” she said.

“Three hours and twenty minutes.”

She laughed, a small breath of a laugh. “You said one day you’d put lights up for us.”

“I meant it.” He turned his hand over under hers. “Not tomorrow. Not because you have to answer. One day.”

She looked at him. The streetlamp caught one side of his face and left the other in shadow. He looked exhausted. He’d rung in sick and sat on a kerb and then on a wall by a loading bay for five hours, and he hadn’t once asked her to make the day easier for him.

“I’ve got something to say,” she said.

“All right.”

She opened her mouth and nothing happened. She closed it.

“You don’t have to,” he said.

“I want to.” She looked at their hands, and then made herself look at his face. “I love you.”

It came out so low it barely crossed the gap between them. He heard it. She watched him hear it, and go still. He’d known. He’d known in a hundred ways, in the way she looked for him in rooms and kept his jackets and reached for his hand when she was frightened and pretended she hadn’t. She had never once said it. In two years of saying everything else, she had never been the one to say this first.

“Don’t look at me like that,” she said, going hot.

“Like what?”

“Like you heard me.”

“I did.” He lifted his hand to her cheek. “Sweetheart. I’ve got you.”

She turned her face up, and he kissed her. There was nothing hurried in it, nothing that tried to take the words and keep them. He kissed her as if he knew exactly what they’d cost, and her fingers curled into his jumper and held on.

“I love you too,” he said against her mouth.

“I know.”

“Of course you do.”

She laughed, and kissed him again.

At some point after that the front door opened behind them. Ah Sim stood in the doorway in her dressing gown and looked at the blanket, and the boy, and Eliana’s head on the boy’s shoulder. Then she went back inside. A few minutes later the door opened again, and Ah Sim came out with a plate of buttered toast and her own grey cardigan, and set the plate on the step beside them and put the cardigan over Eliana’s knees.

“It’s cold,” she said. And to Yu Chen, who had sat up straight: “Eat.”

She went in and shut the door. She didn’t ask anything. She didn’t say anything about how close they were sitting or what time it was or where the blanket had come from.

“She brought you toast,” Eliana said.

“She brought you toast.”

“She brought you a plate.”

He held a triangle up to her mouth, and she bit it, and they ate the whole plate under the porch light with Ah Sim’s cardigan over both their knees.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen rang at nine the next morning. Eliana was at the kitchen table with Yu Chen’s jacket round her shoulders and Yu Chen across from her, drinking Ah Sim’s tea as if he’d been doing it all his life.

“Have you eaten?” said Elowen.

“Yes.”

“Ah Sim says the ladder boy was on our step at two in the morning.”

Eliana shut her eyes. “Ah Sim tells you everything.”

“Is he still there?”

Eliana looked across the table. Yu Chen was looking with great concentration at his cup.

“Put me on speaker,” said Elowen.

She did. “Good morning, Elowen,” said Yu Chen.

“Good morning.” A pause, in which Eliana could hear her sister deciding something. “Is the ladder boy good to her?”

“Elowen.”

Yu Chen put his cup down. He thought about it, the way he thought about everything, as if the question deserved a real answer.

“I try to be,” he said. “I want her to be happy. Even when it’s got nothing to do with me.”

The line was quiet. Eliana looked down at her hands.

“Good,” said Elowen at last. “Because she’s good at pretending she doesn’t need anybody, and she’ll carry everything on her own if you let her, and she won’t tell you when it hurts.”

“I know,” he said.

Eliana put her face in the jacket. “Can you both stop.”

“Thank you, Yu Chen,” said Elowen, and rang off.

Eliana lifted her head. He was smiling into his tea.

“Ladder boy,” she said.

“Apparently.”

“You’re never getting rid of it.”

“I don’t want to.”

He had a ward round at eleven and two messages from Xing Yue asking whether he still intended to be a medical student. She walked him to the gate. He set his bicycle upright and told her to rest and to eat lunch, a real lunch, and she told him Ah Sim’s toast was a real lunch, and he tucked a piece of hair behind her ear and swung his leg over the bike.

She caught his sleeve.

“I love you,” she said, in daylight, at the gate, looking straight at him.

Something helpless came into his face. He leaned down and kissed her forehead. “I love you too.”

She let go. He rode to the end of the lane and looked back once before he turned the corner, and she stood at the gate until he’d gone.

chapters.title: The Night He Lost One
chapters.desc: On a Friday night in the emergency department, Yu Chen does chest compressions on a nineteen-year-old delivery rider, and nothing works. At two in the morning Eliana finds him on the east stairwell, and she stays until the sun comes up.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to say the right thing. You just don’t leave. I learned that from you.”
chapters.content:
At fourteen minutes to midnight on the last Friday in February, Wang Yu Chen was counting.

One, two, three, four. Elbows locked, shoulders over his hands, the heel of his right palm on the lower half of a stranger’s breastbone. The resuscitation bay at Harbourside was bright and crowded and loud in the particular way rooms got loud when everybody in them was trying not to hurry. A nurse was drawing something up. Someone called a time. The registrar stood at the head of the trolley with his eyes on the monitor and his voice as level as a ruler.

The boy on the trolley was nineteen. His name was Fung Ka-lok. His delivery jacket had been cut open down the front and his helmet was under a chair where a paramedic had dropped it. A van had turned across him at a junction three streets from the hospital, and the paramedics had been working on him since the kerb.

“Keep going,” said the registrar.

Yu Chen kept going. His shoulders burned. Sweat ran down under his cap. He had done this forty times on a plastic torso in a teaching room with a metronome, and the torso had never had a scrape on its thumb.

“Change.”

Another pair of hands took over. He stepped back, breathing hard, and stood at the foot of the trolley with his own hands hanging at his sides, and watched.

There was no single moment when he understood they were losing. There were only small things. A pause, a check, another round, the registrar’s voice not changing. A nurse looking at the clock and away again. He looked at the boy’s face. There was a faint crease between his eyebrows, as if he’d been puzzled by something. Yu Chen wondered whether he’d been frightened. He wondered whether anyone had a plate of food waiting for him somewhere, going cold.

“Time of death, twenty-three fifty-eight.”

The room went quiet in a way that felt wrong for a room so full of people. Someone drew up the sheet. The nurse began writing. Yu Chen looked at the boy’s right hand, which had fallen off the edge of the trolley, at the grime under one nail, at the scrape by the thumb. He’d been working. He’d probably had his phone in that hand when the van turned.

“Wang.”

He looked up.

“You all right?”

“Yes,” he said. It came out by itself.

The registrar looked at him a second longer. “Go and wash. Take ten minutes.”

He didn’t remember the corridor. At half past twelve he washed his hands. At twenty to one he answered a nurse’s question about a drug chart, correctly. At one he stood outside the staff room with a paper cup of water he didn’t drink. That was almost the worst of it, that everything still worked: his voice, his hands, his memory for doses. Somewhere under all of it was a boy who’d been alive at half past eleven and wasn’t now, and nobody needed Yu Chen to do anything about that, so there was nowhere to put it.

At eighteen minutes past one he looked at his phone.

Eliana: are you still at the hospital

Eliana: your rota says you finished at midnight

He stared at that. He’d never given her his rota. He opened his calendar and found his shifts in it, every one until June, in a shade of green he’d never have chosen, with a small lock symbol beside them that meant they were being fed in from somewhere else. He thought about being angry. He was too tired to find where he’d left it. He put the phone back in his pocket without answering and walked away from the staff room towards the east stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found him at six minutes past two.

She’d rung twice. He hadn’t picked up. She’d taken a taxi in her house shoes and an old jumper with the sleeves over her hands, and asked at the front desk, and been told nothing, and walked the long way round past radiology to the east stairwell, because he’d told her once that it was the only place in the building where nobody wanted anything from him.

The fire door wasn’t quite shut. She pushed it open.

He was on the landing between the third and fourth floors, sitting with his back to the wall and his elbows on his knees and his hands clasped between them. His hair was tidy. His scrubs were tidy. His face had the composed, closed look it got when he was keeping something behind it. His hands were shaking.

She let the door close. He looked up.

“Eliana?”

“Hi.”

“It’s two in the morning.”

“I can tell.”

“You shouldn’t be here.”

She came down the stairs and sat on the step beside him, close but not touching, and put the bag she’d brought down at her feet. She didn’t ask what had happened. She didn’t ask why he hadn’t answered.

“You don’t have to talk,” she said. “I’ll just sit here.”

He bent his head. She sat. The ventilation hummed in the walls. Somewhere above them a door opened and shut, and footsteps went away along a corridor, and it was quiet again.

At twenty-four minutes past two he said, “He was nineteen.”

She didn’t ask who.

“Fung Ka-lok. Delivery rider. A van at the junction by the market.” He looked at his hands, and flexed them once, as if checking they were still his. “I did compressions. I did what they told me. I kept the rhythm. I changed when they said change. I watched the monitor and waited for the next thing.” His voice went lower. “Nothing worked.”

She moved her hand onto the step between them, near his, not touching. Just there, in case.

“Someone asked if I was all right,” he said. “I said yes. I don’t know why I said yes.”

“Because they asked.”

“I keep thinking about whoever was waiting for him. Whether he’d told someone he’d be home after the shift. Whether they know yet.” He stopped. “He was just trying to get home.”

She took his hand. This time he let her. His fingers were cold right through.

His face changed slowly. His mouth went first, pressed tight. He tried to breathe through it and the breath caught halfway, and he turned his face to the wall so she wouldn’t see. She didn’t ask him to look at her. She didn’t tell him not to. She held his hand and waited, and his shoulders began to shake, and he put his free hand over his eyes as if he could hold it all in by covering it, and couldn’t.

She put her arm round him. He leaned into her, and then he broke. Not loudly. Like someone who’d been holding himself upright for hours because there had been work to do and questions to answer and no room anywhere for this. He cried into her shoulder with his whole body, and she took his weight and moved one hand slowly over his back and kept the other wrapped round his fingers.

“I’m here,” she said. “I’m here.”

At ten to three he lifted his head. His eyes were red. He looked away from her, embarrassed.

“Don’t,” she said.

“Don’t what?”

“Look like that.” She brushed a tear off his cheekbone with her thumb. “You don’t owe me sorry.”

“I wasn’t going to say it.”

“Good.”

She opened the bag. A bottle of water. A flask of rice porridge Ah Sim had made at nine for no reason she’d explained. A packet of tissues. He looked at it as if she’d brought him something from another planet.

“You brought food.”

“You haven’t eaten.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“I’m not asking you to finish it.”

He took the spoon. She watched him eat one mouthful, and then another, and she didn’t count them out loud or tell him how many more. When he stopped she screwed the lid back on.

Then she picked up his right hand and turned it over. The knuckles were pink. There were faint marks on his wrists from the gloves. She bent and kissed his knuckles, once and then again, and the back of his hand, and each of his fingers.

“Eliana.”

She looked up at him and kissed his cheek. His eyes closed. She kissed the other cheek, and his forehead, and the corner of his mouth, and felt his breath shake out of him.

He put his hands on her waist and drew her across into his lap. She went. He held her with one arm round her back and his face in her neck, and she wrapped her arms round his shoulders and held on.

“I couldn’t save him,” he said into her skin.

“I know.”

“I know the algorithm. I know what the team did. I know nobody in that room could have changed it.” His fingers tightened on her back. “I still couldn’t.”

“You were there,” she said. “You didn’t leave him on his own in a room full of strangers. You had your hands on him the whole time. That’s what you could give him.”

He didn’t answer. She felt his breathing slow against her throat.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-three minutes to four he stood up, one hand on the wall, and put his face back on. She watched him do it in the corridor. A nurse said goodnight and he said goodnight. A junior doctor asked if he was finally going home and he said yes, finally. It wasn’t that he’d forgotten. The building still needed him to be all right, so he was all right until the doors.

At the exit he stopped. “You came on your own?”

“Yes.”

“At two in the morning.”

She fixed his coat collar, which didn’t need fixing. “You were on your own.”

In the taxi he leaned his head against the window. At a red light she found his hand on the seat between them, and rubbed her thumb over his knuckles, and he turned his palm up and held hers properly.

His house was dark. She took him into the kitchen and heated the rest of the porridge and made him sit, and he sat, and ate four spoonfuls. Then she took him upstairs. His room looked the way it always did: textbooks squared on the desk, half a page of notes in his illegible hand, the bed made with hospital corners. She hung his coat on the chair, sat him on the edge of the bed, and knelt to undo his shoes.

“I can do that.”

“I know.”

She undid them anyway. She pulled back the covers and he lay down on his back and looked at the ceiling, and she climbed in beside him in her jumper and turned towards him.

“Can I hold you?”

“Yes.”

She put her arm across his waist and her head on his chest. His heart was steady under her ear. His hand came up and settled on her back.

“I don’t know if I’m going to be any good at this,” he said after a long while.

She lifted her head.

“When I’m studying I know what I’m doing. I know the answers. I know what to look for.” He was looking at the ceiling. “I don’t know how you go into the next cubicle and say good evening as if nothing happened.”

“Maybe you’re not supposed to act like nothing happened.”

“You still have to see the next one.”

“Yes. But you don’t have to pretend the last one didn’t count.” She touched his face. “You can remember his name. You can be sad. You can come home.”

He turned his head on the pillow and looked at her. “I didn’t know what to say to you. On the stairs. I didn’t know what you’d want me to say.”

“You don’t have to say the right thing,” she said. “You just don’t leave. I learned that from you.”

He knew what she meant. She saw it in his face: a June night nearly three years ago, two sets of front steps with a knee-high wall between them, a girl in rabbit slippers waiting for a well done nobody had said, and a boy who’d sat down on his side of the wall and stayed until she could go back inside.

She kissed his cheek. “You don’t have to be a doctor in here.”

“What am I in here?”

“Yu Chen.”

“Just Yu Chen?”

“My Yu Chen.” Heat climbed her neck the second she’d said it. “Don’t make me say it twice.”

“I won’t,” he said, and pulled her closer, and she tucked herself back against his side.

✦ ✦ ✦

The window began to lighten at sixteen minutes past five. Eliana hadn’t slept. He’d drifted in and out, and every time he surfaced she was still there. Once he reached for her without opening his eyes and she gave him her hand. Once he said something she couldn’t make out, and she kissed his shoulder until he was quiet.

When the curtains had gone grey he opened his eyes properly.

“You stayed,” he said.

“I said I would.”

“You’ve got a lecture.”

“Not today.”

“It’s Saturday,” he said, working it out.

“It’s been Saturday for five hours.”

He almost smiled. Then he looked at her for a while, and she let him.

“You put my rota in my phone,” he said.

“Both our phones.”

“I didn’t give it to you.”

“No,” she agreed.

“That’s a violation of about four hospital policies.”

“Six.” She didn’t look away. “You can take it off. It’s two taps. I’ll show you.”

He didn’t take it off. He brushed her hair back from her face instead.

“Stay a bit longer,” he said.

“I’m not going anywhere.”

He pulled her into his arms and she lay with her hand over his heart while the house next door woke up and the shutters went up at the bakery on the corner and somewhere across the city a family who’d been waiting for a boy to come home from his shift were being told he wouldn’t.

Yu Chen would remember his name. Fung Ka-lok, nineteen. He would remember there’d been a person under the cut jacket, a person who’d been working and trying to get home. For now he closed his eyes, and she held him until the sun was all the way up.

chapters.title: The Criminal Mind
chapters.desc: Eliana goes to a seminar to understand the men she hunts at night, and comes out with friends: a psychology student who never stops talking, her two sisters, and a cold profiler who looks at her half a second too long. Outside, Yu Chen breaks one of her rules.
chapters.epigraph: “I went to learn about monsters. I came home with a group chat.”
chapters.content:
Eliana had expected the seminar to be three hours of slides and men in good suits talking about criminal behaviour as if it were weather. She had not expected to be adopted before lunch.

It was in the new law building, all glass walls and polished floors, with a foyer big enough to make every conversation sound important. The programme said THE CRIMINAL MIND: PATTERNS, MOTIVES AND THE MOMENT BEFORE THE ACT, and under it, Arthur Cheung. She’d read his papers the night before, and an interview in which he said the most dangerous mistake investigators made was assuming that a predatory man’s next move would be logical. That was why she’d come. She didn’t want to know what men said they’d do, or what they believed they were doing. She wanted to know what they did next, when they thought nobody was looking.

She’d come alone. That had been the plan.

“Is this seat taken?”

A girl stood in the aisle with a notebook, three pens and a coffee, wearing the expression of someone who had already decided they were going to be friends.

“No,” said Eliana.

“Wonderful.” The girl sat. “I’m Si-Jie. Psychology, final year. Are you psychology?”

“No.”

“Criminology? Law?” Si-Jie leaned in. “Secret detective?”

“Computer science.”

“That’s exactly what a secret detective would say.”

Two more girls came down the row behind her, and Eliana looked from one face to the next and back and gave up trying to tell them apart. One carried a notebook with a business school crest on it and the look of someone who’d been got out of bed against her will. The other wore sunglasses indoors and a cap pulled low.

“You stole my seat,” said the one with the crest.

“Your bag isn’t a person,” said Si-Jie. “These are my sisters. Si-Wei does business, and she’s going to run the world and be rude to it. Si-Yuan’s an actress. She’s playing a detective next year and wants to know how to look clever.”

“I’m here to look at how he stands,” said Si-Yuan from under the cap, pointing at the empty lectern.

Si-Wei looked at Eliana over her coffee. “Don’t let Si-Jie talk you into anything. She’ll have you at lunch by twelve.”

Eliana, who did not smile at strangers, found she was smiling. Si-Jie saw it and looked as pleased as if she’d won something.

Arthur Cheung began at ten, without notes. He wasn’t tall. He wore a dark suit and a plain watch and the expression of a man who had removed from his face everything he didn’t need.

“People ask me what makes an offender dangerous,” he said. “They expect intelligence, or violence, or a bad childhood. Those matter. The more useful question is what he believes he’s allowed to do.”

Eliana stopped writing.

He talked about permission. About men who began with small violations and watched the response. About the ones who collected things, photographs and objects and private details, because having them was the point, because possession was a kind of control. Eliana wrote possession as control in her notebook, and under it, he doesn’t want her, he wants proof he can reach her, and underlined it twice.

She didn’t notice that Arthur Cheung, mid-sentence, had glanced down at her page.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie took possession of her at the break. There was no other word for it. By half past twelve Eliana was at a corner table in the canteen with three sisters and a plate she hadn’t chosen, listening to Si-Jie tell a story about a lecturer who’d failed to recognise her for two years, and that was when she noticed the man by the window.

Forties. A pressed shirt and an expensive watch and a face that would slide out of your memory as soon as you looked away. He wasn’t eating. He was looking at his phone, and the screen was turned just far enough that from where she sat Eliana could see it change. A woman in a bedroom, photographed through a gap in a curtain. He swiped. Another woman. Another.

Her face didn’t move. She looked away, ate a mouthful of rice, looked back. He’d put the phone to his ear and was talking low, and the thread on his screen was a list, with a price beside each name. At the top of the thread, a contact name she knew, because it was in a file Qian had sent her in the summer.

“You’re not listening,” said Si-Jie.

“Sorry. I need to make a call.”

She went out to the stairwell and sent four lines to Qian and two photographs of nothing in particular, a window and a coat rack, which happened to have the man and his table in the corner of them. She didn’t go near him. She didn’t touch his phone. She gave Qian enough to find the rest and let it go, and when she came back Si-Jie had put a slice of cake in front of her chair.

“You looked like you needed cake.”

“That’s not a diagnosis.”

“It’s a psychological one.” Si-Jie beamed. “I’ve been waiting all day to say that.”

In the afternoon Arthur divided them into groups with invented case files. Eliana spoke rarely, and when she did, she talked about behaviour: what a man repeated, what he hid, what he did when the first approach failed. When Arthur stopped beside her table she disagreed with the case file’s conclusion before she could stop herself.

“It says he wanted money,” she said. “The money’s convenient. Everything else he does says access. He wanted to know he could get something private and keep it.”

Arthur looked at her for half a second longer than he needed to. “You’re not in psychology.”

“Computer science.”

“An odd reason to come.”

“People leave traces,” she said.

“They do,” said Arthur Cheung, and moved on, and Si-Jie kicked her under the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five Si-Jie made her swap numbers, and Si-Wei added her to a group chat called YEN GIRLS AND ONE HOSTAGE, and Si-Yuan sent a photograph of Si-Jie looking outraged into it within the minute. They were standing in the foyer laughing about it when Dominic Ip came across the polished floor towards them.

She knew him from second year. They’d been on the same systems project for a term, him and his three friends and her, and she’d done most of the work and he’d done most of the talking at the presentation. He was well dressed and sure of himself and had always looked as though he enjoyed being heard.

“Lin Eliana,” he said. “I thought it was you.”

“Hello, Dominic.”

He smiled round at the sisters. Then, in a voice a good deal louder than the distance needed, he said, “Would you like to go out with me? Dinner. I’ve wanted to ask since second year.”

Heads turned. Somebody by the doors stopped talking. Eliana felt the foyer get bigger and brighter and louder all at once, and every face in it was waiting, and her mouth opened and nothing came out of it. She knew the word. It was two letters long. She couldn’t find it.

“It’s all right,” said Dominic, still smiling. “You can say yes.”

A hand closed round hers.

She knew it before she looked. Warm, steady, long fingers, a callus on the side of the middle one from his pen. Yu Chen had come through the glass doors without a sound, and he was standing at her shoulder, and he didn’t look at her. He looked at Dominic.

“She’s with me,” he said.

That was all. He didn’t raise his voice. He just looked, and kept looking, and after a few seconds Dominic’s smile went somewhere else. He glanced at their hands. “Oh. Sorry. I didn’t know.” He nodded at nobody in particular. “Have a good evening.”

Yu Chen watched him all the way to the doors.

Then he turned, and his face changed completely. “Sweetheart?”

“Hi,” said Eliana.

Si-Jie looked at Yu Chen. Then at their hands. Then at Eliana, with dawning joy. “Who is this?”

“Yu Chen,” said Eliana, going red.

“Your Yu Chen? The one who—“

“Please don’t.”

“Wang Yu Chen,” he said, and shook Si-Jie’s hand with his free one, and didn’t let go of Eliana’s with the other.

“You’re calm,” said Si-Wei, studying him.

“Not really,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d come on his bicycle. He wheeled it with one hand and held hers with the other, along the path under the camphor trees towards the north gate, and for the first few minutes he didn’t say anything. She knew that stillness. It made all his movements slow and exact.

“You froze,” he said at last.

“Everyone was looking.”

“I know.”

“I’m not interested in him.”

“I know that too.”

“Then why are you angry?”

He stopped walking. “Because he stood there and made you feel you owed him an answer in front of a room. And he was smiling while you couldn’t speak.” His hand tightened on hers. “I wanted to put him through the glass.”

“You can’t.”

“I know.”

“You’d have to explain it to the dean.”

“I know.”

“And pay for the glass.”

The stillness cracked. He laughed once, against his will. Then his face went serious again. “I was jealous,” he said plainly, as if reading out a result. “Not because I thought you’d say yes. Because he asked as if he could have you. And because I wanted to be the one holding your hand in that room before anybody else got near.”

She looked at their fingers.

“You broke a rule,” she said. “Rule one. Nobody knows. You said it in the middle of the law building.”

“I know.”

“And you answered for me.”

“I know that too.” He didn’t argue. “I should have asked if you wanted me to step in.”

“Yes.”

“I’m sorry.”

She thought about it, honestly. “I liked that you were there. Both things are true.”

“Both things are true,” he agreed, and kissed her knuckles, and they walked on.

“What was it like?” he asked at the gate. “The seminar.”

“I went to learn about monsters,” she said. “I came home with a group chat.”

Her phone buzzed in her pocket, as if to prove it. Then again. Then four times in a row.

✦ ✦ ✦

His house was dark and smelled of the jasmine coming in at the kitchen window. She stood by the counter while he filled a glass of water and gave it to her, and she drank half of it and put it down, and he was still looking at her.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing.”

“You’ve been looking at me like that since the foyer.”

“Am I not allowed?”

“Depends what you’re planning.”

His eyes dropped to her mouth. Hers went to his waist, and she hooked two fingers through his belt loops and pulled. He came. She rose onto her toes and kissed him against the edge of the sink, and the first kiss was quick and the second wasn’t. He put the glass down somewhere without looking. His hand found her waist and the other the back of her head, and he kissed her with everything he’d been holding behind his face since five o’clock.

“Trouble,” he said into her mouth.

“You like trouble.”

“I love trouble.”

His room was half dark, the streetlight coming in pale through the blind. He shut the door with his heel and stood in front of her and asked, as he always asked, “All right?”

“Yes.”

“Sure?”

She took his hand and laid it against her cheek. “I’m here.”

He kissed her forehead, and her cheek, and the corner of her mouth, slow, and then not slow. There was something in him tonight that hadn’t been there before, a pressure under the gentleness. She felt it in his hands on her back, the way they tightened when she moved and loosened the instant she came back. He pulled her jumper over her head and dropped it. She worked the buttons of his shirt open one at a time while he waited, breathing hard, letting her, and when she pushed it off his shoulders he caught her wrists and kissed the inside of each one where her pulse was racing.

He laid her down on the bed and undressed her as if he were memorising the order of it, and she lay in the blue half-light and watched his face, and saw the jealousy in it, and the want, and how hard he was holding both.

“Yu Chen. You don’t have to be angry any more.”

“I’m not angry with you.”

“I know.”

He lowered himself over her, skin to skin, his weight on his forearms. “I hated watching you freeze,” he said against her throat, and then he kissed her there, and lower, his mouth moving down over her collarbone and her breast until she arched under him and forgot the foyer and the glass and every face in it. When he slid into her she gasped and held his shoulders, and he went still, deep, and looked down at her.

“Mine,” he said.

It hung in the air. She saw him hear himself, saw the flicker in his face as he waited to find out if she’d pull away.

She didn’t. She slid her hands down his back and held him where he was. “Yours,” she whispered. “But not because you said so.”

He understood. She watched it reach him.

“Because I choose you,” she said.

He made a sound she’d never heard from him and began to move, and she moved with him, and it wasn’t gentle the way it usually was, and she didn’t want it to be. He held her hips and drove into her until the headboard knocked the wall and she had to put her hand over her own mouth, and he pulled it away and kissed her instead, and said her name, and the other name, Yu-er, the one only he used. Her release took her before she was ready for it, sharp and shuddering, her heels in the backs of his thighs, and he followed a few strokes later with his face in her hair and her name in his mouth, and held her so tight afterwards that she could feel his heart against her ribs as if it were her own.

They lay tangled in the sheet. She traced the bones of his wrist.

“Were you really that jealous?”

“Yes.”

“How jealous?”

He considered it with his usual care. “Enough that I had to remind myself I’m not allowed to put people through windows.”

She laughed against his chest. “How mature.”

“I’m proud of myself.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later he was at the bathroom sink washing his hands, and she leaned in the doorway in his shirt and watched him in the mirror.

“What?” he said.

“Nothing.”

He dried his hands and turned round. “You’re looking at me.”

“Am I not allowed?”

“Depends what you’re planning.”

She crossed the tiles and put her arms round his waist and looked up at him. “Next time,” she said, “hold my hand longer.”

His face went soft. “In the foyer?”

“Anywhere. Not only when somebody makes me uncomfortable. Just hold it. And don’t let go the second people look.”

“Even if Si-Jie starts asking questions?”

“Especially then.”

He laughed and kissed her forehead. She’d gone to a seminar to understand men who thought other people’s boundaries were negotiable, and she’d come home to one who sometimes wanted to step over a line for her and stopped when she asked. That mattered. So did the hand he’d held outside the glass doors.

She slid her fingers between his.

“Longer,” she reminded him.

He closed his hand round hers and didn’t let go.

chapters.title: The Boy Next Door, He Always Waits
chapters.desc: A bank wants Eliana quiet, so her family sends Serafina’s fiancé to drive her to her own talk. Nobody tells Yu Chen anything. He’s on the kerb by half past five anyway, and at two in the morning he stops pretending there’s no name for what they are.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody. The boy next door. He always waits.”
chapters.content:
At twenty-five to eight on a Monday morning in March, somebody rang the bell of the tall house, and Eliana opened the front door in an enormous grey university hoodie, black trousers and one sock. The other sock was in her hand. Her claw clip was holding up most of her hair and her glasses were on top of her head.

A man she’d never seen before stood on the step. Behind him, leaning on the gatepost, was Serafina Song.

“Where’s Zhendong’s replacement?” said Eliana.

“I’m taking you,” said the man.

She looked him up and down. Dark jacket, plain trousers, clean shoes that had been resoled. No earpiece, no badge, no card on a lanyard.

“Name?”

“Qin Haozhen.”

“Occupation?”

“Today? This.”

“That’s not an occupation. Identification?”

“I haven’t got any,” he said. “At the moment, officially, I’ve never existed. There’s a letter.”

Elowen had rung her at eleven the night before. Zhao was stuck in Rotterdam, his flight cancelled, and wouldn’t be back till Monday evening, and Zhao didn’t like her going anywhere this week without someone, because for a fortnight people had been ringing her department to ask which room she’d be speaking in. Elowen had found someone. Elowen hadn’t said he didn’t exist.

“Come in,” said Eliana. “I need to check you’re not terrible.”

“Good luck,” said Serafina.

“You’re the one with the car.”

“I’m the one with several cars.”

Eliana held out her hand to him, palm up. “Phone.”

He gave it to her, which told her more than his face had. She took it to the kitchen table and plugged it into her laptop and typed while he stood by the fridge and watched her hands, and told him to stop watching her hands, and he watched her screen instead. It took three minutes and fifty seconds. He timed her. She unplugged it and held it out.

“Done.”

He touched the screen. In place of his lock screen there was a matte black car with a white seven, coming over the last crest of the mountain road at Baizhang with two wheels nearly off the ground. When he touched it again to see the time, the phone made the sound of an engine on the limiter.

“What have you done?”

“Improved it. You had three things telling the world where you were. You’ve got a security update you’ve been ignoring for a year. And you’ve got a new group.” She’d called it PEOPLE WHO WILL ACTUALLY ANSWER. Serafina was at the top.

“She isn’t my emergency contact.”

“Your phone says she is now.”

“Three minutes fifty,” he said. “That was impressive.”

“Don’t patronise me.”

“It’s the only voice I’ve got,” said Qin Haozhen, and Serafina, at the kitchen door, laughed so hard she had to hold the frame.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lecture was at ten in the old physics theatre, which held two hundred and was half full by ten to. She went down to the front with her laptop bag. Haozhen sat at the back by the door, where he could see both exits and nobody would look at him twice.

“You’re not going to stand by the lectern?”

“No.”

“Good. I don’t want people thinking I’m important.”

“You are important.”

He said it as if it were the time of day. She didn’t know what to do with it, so she said “Don’t make it weird” and went down the steps.

Her talk was called Open Doors. Since the autumn she’d been following the money behind the man in the canteen and his list of women, and it had led her into a bank: not into its vault, which was locked well, but round the side, to a door nobody had shut. She showed the room how the bank’s systems had been built to keep strangers out and never designed to stop people already inside. How permissions had been handed down from one job to the next for nine years without anyone taking them back. How a contractor’s access token from 2016 had never been switched off. She used the bank’s own published documents, and records passed to her by someone inside who’d asked not to be named, and a demonstration on a dummy network she’d built herself. She didn’t touch anything real. Her point was simple. A locked front door means nothing if you’ve left the staff entrance open.

At the questions a man in the third row stood up. “You’re saying the bank’s negligent?”

“I’m saying its controls are inadequate.”

“Can you prove it?”

“To the regulator. On Thursday.”

He sat down. She took six more questions, and enjoyed every one of them, and didn’t notice the man in the grey coat by the side door, who’d come in twenty minutes late and hadn’t looked once at the slides. Haozhen noticed him.

He was waiting at the side entrance when they came out, a man in his forties with a phone held low by his hip, lens outward.

“Miss Lin,” he said. “I think we should have a word. Privately.”

“No,” said Haozhen, and stepped half a pace forward.

“I’m not talking to you.”

“I know.”

“You’ve made some allegations,” the man told Eliana. “People are worried about where they lead. You’re young. You don’t understand how these things are done.”

Her chin came up. “I understand enough.”

The man took a step towards her, and Haozhen moved once. He wasn’t fast about it. He just changed where he was standing, so that the man couldn’t reach her without going through him, and held out his hand.

“Phone.”

“What?”

“You’ve been recording her for six minutes. Give me the phone.”

The man laughed. Haozhen didn’t. He kept his hand out and kept looking, and after four seconds the man stopped laughing and gave it to him. Haozhen didn’t watch the video. He opened the call log and read out, pleasantly, the last number the man had rung at ten past nine that morning: a switchboard at the bank, a department, a first name.

“That’s who sent you,” he said. “I’ll ring him this afternoon and tell him he employs a man who stands outside lecture theatres filming girls of twenty-two on a phone registered in his own name. Then I’ll ring the regulator Miss Lin is seeing on Thursday and tell them the same.” He deleted the video, and the copy in the cloud, and held the phone out. “Or you can walk away and he’ll never know you were careless.”

Two campus security officers in yellow jackets came round the corner of the building. The man took his phone and went.

“You didn’t touch him,” said Eliana.

“No.”

“You didn’t even raise your voice.”

“No.”

“That was the most frightening thing I’ve ever seen.” She looked at him properly for the first time. “I think I see why Elowen rang you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They had coffee in the café by the north gate. She turned her laptop round on the table to show him a live map with a small blue dot going round an oval: the circuit in the north, where Serafina had gone straight from the Lin house, and the dot was Serafina, read from the phone in her race suit pocket every two seconds.

“She asked for location sharing for the team,” said Eliana. “In case anyone broke down on the motorway. I made it more useful. That’s lap nine. She’s a tenth up on lap eight.”

“Did she agree to that?”

“She agreed to location sharing.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“I know,” said Eliana serenely.

His phone went off on the table with the sound of an engine at full revs, and half the café turned round. It was Serafina, from the pit lane, asking why his phone sounded like that and telling him to bring egg sandwiches. He said “Love you” before he rang off, and found Eliana looking at him over her glasses with enormous satisfaction.

In the taxi home her own phone lit up on her knee.

Yu Chen: On your kerb.

“Who’s that?” said Haozhen, because she’d smiled.

She turned the screen face down. “Nobody. The boy next door. He always waits.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty past five a young man in a black leather jacket was standing on the kerb outside the tall house with two paper cups of coffee, looking at his watch. His hospital lanyard was still round his neck. He’d left the ward at half past three, which he wasn’t supposed to do in his final year, and hadn’t told her.

“You’re late,” he said.

“I was giving a lecture.”

“You said four.”

“It finished at four.”

“It’s twenty past five.”

“Then you’ve been waiting an hour and twenty minutes,” said Eliana. “Good arithmetic.”

He looked past her at the man getting out of the taxi. “Who’s he?”

“My bodyguard.”

“I’m not her bodyguard,” said Haozhen.

“Same thing.”

Yu Chen looked at him a moment longer. Whatever passed between the two of them, Eliana wasn’t part of it. “Thanks for bringing her back.”

“Look after her.”

“I can hear you both.” She took one of the coffees out of Yu Chen’s hand. “Go home, Qin Haozhen. Zhendong lands at seven.”

“Ring if anything happens.”

She waited until he’d turned. “Your wallpaper. Don’t change it.”

“I wasn’t going to,” he said, and got back in the taxi.

Inside the front door Yu Chen put her bag down and turned round and looked at her, at her face, her hands, all of her, the way he looked at a patient.

“Did anyone touch you?”

“No.”

“Did anyone get close?”

“One man. Haozhen stood in the way.” She put her coffee on the hall table. “I’m fine.”

“I know.”

“You don’t look like you know.”

“I left the ward at half past three,” he said, “and sat on your kerb for two hours because I wanted to see you come home.”

It was so simple that she didn’t know where to put it either. She took the front of his jacket in both hands and pulled, and he came down to her, and she kissed him. The first one was gentle. The second wasn’t, and he walked her back until the inside of the front door was against her shoulder blades, and kissed her slowly with his hand flat on the wood beside her head, until she forgot what day it was.

“All right?” he said against her forehead.

“Yes.”

“Really?”

“Really.”

She took him upstairs. In her room she opened a folder on her laptop she’d never shown anyone, and sat him at her desk, and stood behind his chair.

“Since January,” she said, “someone’s been sending me photographs.”

He went still.

“Anonymous. Some to my university email. Some left for me to find.” She reached past him and clicked. “Of the gate. The street. The flower shop. A café I’ve been to once. The bus stop by my faculty.”

He went through them slowly. She watched his face. When he reached the last one he stopped.

It was the front steps of the tall house, taken at night from across the lane. The three stone steps under the little tiled roof. The crack in the third one. The knee-high wall between her steps and his. The place where he’d brought her a blanket in October and she’d told him she loved him.

“When?”

“February.”

“Were you on the step?”

“No. I was inside.”

He studied the angle. “They’ve been watching your house since January,” he said. “And you didn’t tell me.”

“I didn’t want you involved.”

“I’m already involved.” He turned in the chair and took her hand. “Sweetheart. You can handle a great deal. That doesn’t mean you have to handle all of it alone. Does Qian know?”

“Yes.”

“Do you think it was the man today?”

“I think it’s the same people.”

“Then we’ll be careful.”

“We?”

“Yes,” he said, and she didn’t correct him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to two in the morning she was on the front step with the door open behind her, letting a strip of warm light out across the stones. He came round from his side with two cups of tea and stepped over the little wall and sat down beside her.

They watched the lane. A cat went along the top of the opposite wall and dropped out of sight.

“Haozhen asked who you were,” she said into her cup. “In the taxi.”

“What did you tell him?”

She didn’t look up. “I said you were nobody. The boy next door.”

He didn’t answer. A car went by at the end of the lane, and its lights went over them and away.

“I didn’t know what else to say,” she said. “I wasn’t ashamed. I didn’t know how to explain something that hasn’t got a name.”

“Do you think it hasn’t?”

“I don’t know.”

He put his cup down on the step. “Eliana.”

She looked up.

“I’ve waited a long time,” he said. He wasn’t angry, and that made it harder. “I waited when you didn’t know what you wanted. I waited when you couldn’t say it. I waited when you needed rules and no name and nobody knowing. I don’t regret a day of it.” His hand found hers. “But I don’t want to be nobody.”

Her eyes began to sting.

“I want to marry you,” he said.

She stopped breathing.

“I want to marry you,” he said again, lower. “Not because of the photographs, or because somebody’s watching your house, or because I want to keep you somewhere safe. Because I want a life with you. An ordinary one. I want to argue with you about breakfast. I want to know where you’ve left the keys. I want to be the one you ring when something goes wrong, and the one you tell when something goes right.” He held her hand tighter. “You don’t have to answer tonight. Or tomorrow. I’m not asking you to decide anything because I’m sitting here. I just don’t want you to think there’s no name for what we are.”

She stood up.

The tea went over on the step. He looked up at her.

“Eliana?”

“I can’t.”

He stood too. “Sweetheart—“

“I can’t.”

She went inside and shut the door. He heard the bolt go across.

He didn’t knock. He didn’t say her name again. He knew the sound of that bolt, and what it meant when she needed the other side of a door, and he’d spent years learning when to wait. He sat back down on the step in the spilled tea and looked at the strip of light under the door.

On the other side of it Eliana stood with her back against the wood and her hands over her face. She could imagine it. That was the terrible part. His shoes next to hers in a hall. His books on a table. His voice from another room. His name beside hers on a piece of paper. She could imagine every bit of it, and then she imagined it gone, the way her mother was gone, the way her father had been gone for twenty-two years while living in the same house, and she couldn’t make herself believe that something that permanent could belong to her and stay.

Her phone lit up in her pocket.

Yu Chen: I’m outside. I won’t come in.

Yu Chen: You don’t have to answer tonight.

She typed something, and deleted it. Typed, deleted. She went upstairs and sat on the edge of her bed and put the phone face down on the blanket.

Below her window the boy next door sat on her step, where he’d sat at two in the morning for four years, and didn’t go home.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.desc: She doesn’t answer him. She doesn’t leave, either. For nine days they live on either side of a garden wall and say nothing that matters, until she knocks on his door at two in the morning.
chapters.epigraph: “Teach me forever”
chapters.content:
She didn’t open the front door on Tuesday. Not when the tea came, or when he knocked once at half past seven, or when he sent a message at noon asking whether she’d eaten. She saw all three. She answered none of them.

The tea was on the little table by the door when she finally opened it, still warm, with a paper bag under the cup and a sesame bun inside from the bakery on the corner. There was no note. She ate the bun. She washed the cup and put it back on the table. At five she left by the back gate into the alley, in the gap between the man opposite watering his pots and Ah Sim going out to the market, and didn’t look at the garden wall, or the kerb, or the house next door.

When he found the empty cup at seven he looked at the ring of tea in the bottom and smiled a little, because she’d drunk it. He washed it again and put it back.

On Wednesday there was sliced pear beside the cup, and a folded note under the container. You don’t have to talk. She read it twice and put it in the drawer of her bedside table. At lunch Si-Wei caught her looking at her phone without turning it on and pushed a bowl of noodles across the table at her without asking any questions at all, which was somehow worse. That evening there was a second note. I made too much tea. He had never once in his life made too much tea. She kept that one too.

On Thursday she went to the regulator in her one good jacket and talked for two hours about open doors, and came home and slept for three, and at sixteen minutes past one in the morning Qian rang.

“An old man,” Qian said. “Retired. His wife’s ill. Someone’s been taking his savings for months with promises about returns. He thinks the first payment comes next week.”

“Send it.”

“You sound tired.”

“I didn’t ask how I sounded.”

It was ugly the way these always were. A man who’d spent a year being patient with lonely people, learning what frightened them about their savings and their bodies, making himself the one they rang. He’d told the old man’s wife the money would pay for her care. Eliana read it all twice and got quieter as she went. By dawn there was no operation left. She’d put the evidence where the right people would find it, warned the families she could reach, and made sure his next promised payment would arrive nowhere. She didn’t feel anything like satisfied.

Qian: He’s been told. His daughter is with him.

She read it until the words stopped meaning anything. Then her phone lit again.

Yu Chen: Tea’s outside.

He’d sent it at twelve minutes to six. She hadn’t heard him. There was a small jar of honey by the cup and a note. You don’t have to explain anything to me. She stood in the doorway holding it for long enough that the tea went lukewarm.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Friday he’d stopped knocking. He still left the tea. He still sent one message a day. He still waited, but he’d stopped standing at her door, and she noticed, and hated that she noticed. She hated that she could tell his footsteps from everyone else’s in the lane. She hated that she knew he’d come home by the tick of his bicycle chain.

On Saturday Ah Sim came into the kitchen with a basket of laundry and found her eating cold watermelon in front of the open fridge at four in the afternoon.

“You haven’t slept.”

“I have.”

“Not enough.” Ah Sim began to fold. “Your father rang. He wants you home on Friday. He’s arranged for you to meet Chen Si about work.”

Eliana lowered the watermelon. “What work?”

“He didn’t say. He said it was arranged and you should be grateful.” Ah Sim folded a shirt into a perfect square. “He also said the boy next door is to stop waiting on the kerb outside this house. He said the lane isn’t a place for him to stand about. People will talk.”

The kitchen went still.

“He said that to you?”

“To me.”

“And?”

“I told him I’d pass it on.” Ah Sim put the shirt on the pile. “I haven’t.”

In twenty-two years her father had never once asked whether she’d got home safely. He’d never asked who walked her back from the bus or sat with her on the step at two in the morning when she couldn’t sleep. But he cared where Yu Chen stood. He cared what the lane would say.

She went upstairs and opened his messages and typed my father says you’re not allowed to wait outside any more. She looked at it until the screen dimmed, and deleted it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday the tea wasn’t on the table. She looked for it and felt her stomach drop, and then she saw that the loose brick in the garden wall, the one by the old fig, had been pulled out and put back slightly crooked.

There had been a jar behind that brick since they were nine and ten. Nainai’s plum-jam jar, washed and dried, sent down from the north with a parcel of jam one winter and kept by a boy who’d decided it was exactly the right size for notes. She’d left him drawings in it. He’d left her sweets and, once, a dead beetle he’d thought was beautiful. Neither of them had opened it for years.

She pulled the brick out. The jar was there, with the cup beside it, and a folded paper inside the jar.

In his hand, in capitals, as if for someone who might need to find it years later:

I’M NOT GOING ANYWHERE

She laughed, a small helpless sound in the empty garden, and sat down on the cold path with her back to the wall and the jar in her lap, and drank the tea.

On Monday she worked. Qian sent another job and she took it, and when it was done she asked for another, and he sent it without comment. A man who rang widows pretending to be a grandson in trouble. A woman had sold her wedding ring for him. Another hadn’t told her children because she was ashamed. Eliana connected his seven names and his four bank accounts and the one phone he’d used for all of them, and gave Qian enough to warn every family on the list, and closed the laptop at twenty past four in the morning, and sat in the dark with the jar on her desk.

The other notes were in the drawer. You don’t have to talk. I made too much tea. You don’t have to explain anything to me. She touched their edges. She was eighteen again on the front step at two in the morning, waiting for a well done nobody had said, and a boy came out on his side of the little wall and sat down and stayed. He had never once asked her to be easier to love.

She put the heel of her hand over her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday afternoon, the eighth day, she was waiting outside the psychology building for Si-Jie when Si-Wei came and leaned on the wall beside her with a coffee.

“Can I ask you something?”

“No.”

“I’m going to anyway.” Si-Wei looked across the courtyard instead of at her. “Are you afraid he’ll leave?”

Eliana didn’t answer. That was its own answer, and they both knew it.

“You plan for everything,” said Si-Wei. “I’ve watched you. You keep the exits open. You always know what you’ll do when someone lets you down. But you can’t plan for somebody staying. If they stay, you have to believe they’ll still be there tomorrow, and then the day after, and there’s no end to it, and that’s the part you can’t stand.” She drank some coffee. “You’re treating losing him as if it’s safer than keeping him.”

“That isn’t fair.”

“Maybe not. But being terrified of losing someone isn’t proof you should run.” Si-Wei pushed herself off the wall. “It’s proof you’ve got something you don’t want to lose.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday the ninth day the cup was on top of the wall, on the flat brick by the fig, and the note under it said I’ll be home tonight.

She heard his bicycle at six. She watched from her window as he wheeled it up his path with his bag over one shoulder, looking more tired than she’d ever seen him, and went in and shut the door.

At eighteen minutes past ten she typed are you awake and didn’t send it.

At three minutes past two she knocked on his door.

She’d climbed the wall in her socks and cardigan and nightshirt, because the front way meant the lane and the lane meant her father’s rule, and the stones of his path were cold through the wool. He opened the door before she’d knocked a second time. He’d been awake. There was a book in his hand with his thumb still in it.

He looked at her feet. “It’s cold.”

“I know.”

“Come in.”

She didn’t. She held the cuffs of her cardigan in her fists and made herself look at his face.

“Teach me forever,” she said.

He went completely still.

“I don’t know how to do it. I don’t know how to promise something that long. I don’t know how to wake up and not wait for the terrible thing.” Her voice shook and she let it. “But I want to. I want to learn. I can’t promise I won’t panic again. I can’t promise I’ll know what to say. I might need time. But I don’t want to call you nobody any more. I don’t want to call you the boy next door when you’re the person I want next to me.”

He reached for her hand. She let him take it.

“Then what are you asking?” he said.

“Tomorrow. Can we start with tomorrow?”

He didn’t answer straight away. Then something gave in his face. “Tomorrow.”

“And the day after?”

“Tomorrow first,” he said, and she laughed, and it came out broken.

She stood on her toes and kissed him, and he didn’t stop this time. His hand went to the back of her head and his other arm came round her waist and he pulled her over the threshold into the doorway and kissed her again, and again, and when she held his face between her hands she found it wet. She’d seen him cry once, on a hospital stair. Never like this.

“I thought you weren’t coming back,” he said.

“I was always coming back.”

“You bolted the door.”

“I know. I wanted you to wait. I didn’t know how to ask you to.” She was crying too. “I’m sorry. I’m sorry.”

“Don’t make me guess for nine days again.”

“I’ll try.”

“That’s enough,” he said, and closed the door behind her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs he gave her a pair of thick socks, and hung her cardigan over the chair, and put a glass of water by the bed and drew the curtains, the same small things he’d been doing for years whether she was there or not, and the sight of them made her chest ache. When he turned round she held out her hand. He came and stood between her knees and she put her arms round his waist and her cheek against his stomach, and his hand settled on her hair.

“Are you angry?”

He thought about it, because he always did. “I’m hurt.”

“I hurt you.”

“Yes.” He tipped her chin up. “And you came back. If you need space, tell me. If you can’t talk, send me one word.”

“What word?”

“Anything.”

“Tomorrow,” she said, and he smiled, and she pulled him down by the front of his T-shirt.

He let her set the pace. She took his T-shirt off over his head and put her mouth on his collarbone, on the place where his heart was, and felt it going under her lips as fast as hers. She lifted her arms and he drew her nightshirt off and stood looking at her in the lamplight as if he’d been afraid he’d never be allowed to again, and then he knelt on the floor in front of her and kissed the inside of her knee, and her thigh, slow, until she was holding the edge of the mattress with both hands. When he finally put his mouth between her legs she said his name out loud into the quiet house and didn’t care who heard. He didn’t hurry. Nine days had gone into it. He held her open with his hands on her thighs and took her apart slowly, so slowly, and when she came she curled forward over his shoulders, shaking, her fingers in his hair.

He climbed up beside her and she pulled him over her and reached down between them and guided him in herself, and they both stopped breathing. For a long moment neither of them moved. She could feel all of him, his weight, his heat, the tremor in his arms. She looked up at him in the lamplight.

“I’m not afraid of you,” she said.

“I know.”

“I’m afraid of losing you.”

He pressed his forehead to hers. “I’m afraid of losing you too.”

“You never say that.”

“I didn’t want you to feel you had to carry it.”

She kissed him, and began to move under him, and he moved with her. It was slow and deep and they bumped noses once and laughed into each other’s mouths, and then they stopped laughing. He laced his fingers through hers on the pillow above her head. She wrapped her legs round him and held on, and when it built in her again it went through her more gently than the first time, a long rolling wave, and she felt him break a moment after with his face in her neck and her name and Yu-er in a whisper against her skin.

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest and her hand over his heart. His fingers moved through her hair.

“Can I stay tomorrow?” she said.

“Whenever you want.”

“Don’t say whenever. I might.”

“Then I’ll make breakfast.”

“What if I want to sleep?”

“Then I’ll let you sleep.”

“What if I want you to stay in bed?”

“Then I’ll stay.”

She seemed satisfied. She was quiet for a while. Then she said, into his chest, “I want to marry you too.”

His hand stopped. She felt his breath catch under her ear. She didn’t look up.

“Not because I know how to do forever,” she said. “Because I want to learn it with you.”

He bent and kissed the top of her head. “All right.”

“That’s all?”

He smiled into her hair. “For tonight.”

“Tomorrow?”

“Tomorrow.”

She fell asleep with one hand curled in the sheet over his heart. At twelve minutes to six he woke and read a message from the ward and answered it and put the phone face down, and she opened her eyes a little.

“Where are you going?”

“Nowhere,” he said.

chapters.title: In Front of Everyone
chapters.desc: After nine days and a knock at two in the morning, Eliana does the bravest thing she can think of. She holds his hand on the hill, in daylight, where the whole university can see. It takes her the entire walk to the gates.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m only brave for six hundred metres.”
chapters.content:
On the ninth of April, at the long table in the tall house, Ah Sim had brought out two cakes, the way she had every year since the spring of 2023: one with Raiden’s name piped on it and one with Evangeline’s, side by side on the same tray, so that nobody had to share. Eliana had filmed the candles. It was a crooked fifty seconds. Raiden complained that the wax was dripping on the icing. Evangeline put one hand flat on her brother’s forehead to stop him leaning in too soon, and said “Wait. Make a wish,” and he said he already had, and she said that didn’t count, and he looked at her and smiled and shut his eyes.

Afterwards, with the video still on her screen, Eliana had sat on the stairs and thought about who to send it to. Her family was in the next room. She sent it to Yu Chen first.

She had never once sent him anything first. She’d sent him things last, or late, or after everyone else had seen them, so that he’d never be the person she’d chosen. That night she didn’t think about it. She just wanted the first person to see something she’d thought was worth keeping to be him.

Yu Chen: They’re happy.

Eliana: obviously. there’s cake

Yu Chen: You filmed them for nearly a minute.

Eliana: the candles were important

Seventeen days later, on the last Saturday in April, she was standing in front of her mirror at half past ten in the morning having changed her jumper three times to go to a university where she had no classes, which she considered deeply unfair.

Yu Chen: Are you coming in today?

Eliana: maybe

Yu Chen: I’ll be by the lower gate.

Eliana: you always are

Yu Chen: You noticed.

At the front door Ah Sim was doing the flowers. Eliana stopped with her hand on the latch.

“Do I look strange?”

Ah Sim looked at her over a spray of white lilies. “You look like yourself.”

Eliana thought about that all the way to the bus.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at the lower entrance with his bicycle, a paper bag hanging off the handlebars, his sleeves pushed up to the elbow and the blue-and-copper wire bracelet she’d made him at Christmas on his left wrist. He was reading something on his phone with his head bent, and she saw him before he saw her, and slowed down.

She knew how he stood when he was waiting. She’d seen him in hospital corridors and on roofs and on the step outside her house at two in the morning, and on a kerb for an hour and twenty minutes with two coffees going cold. She’d seen him cry and seen him sleep. She’d spent nine days trying not to see him at all.

He looked up. His whole face changed.

“You came,” he said.

“I said maybe.”

He held out his hand.

He’d held her hand a thousand times. In his room and in hers, under blankets and tables, in his coat pocket in the cold, behind doors. Never here, in the open, at the bottom of the hill with students going past them in the sun. He didn’t move it closer. He didn’t say anything. He just held it out and let it be there.

She put her fingers in his. His hand closed round hers.

“Don’t look so pleased,” she said.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I’ve held your hand for years.”

“Not here.”

He looked at her then. “No,” he said. “Not here.”

The path from the lower gate to the main gates at the top of the hill was six hundred metres. She knew because she’d measured it once on the campus map in a bad lecture, and got six hundred and twelve or five hundred and ninety-eight depending on which way you went round the library. Today it felt like six kilometres. A girl carrying a coffee looked at their hands and then at their faces. A bicycle bell rang behind them. Somebody laughed at something that had nothing to do with them, and Eliana’s fingers tightened anyway.

“Do you want to let go?” he said.

“No.”

“All right.”

At the first bend two girls from her year said “Lin!” and their eyes went down to the hands and up again, and one of them said “Morning, Wang,” with an enormous grin. At the second bend somebody from his year shouted his name from the library steps and lifted both eyebrows nearly into his hair. Yu Chen raised his free hand and kept walking. His thumb moved over her knuckles.

“You’re enjoying this,” she said.

He considered it honestly. “A little.”

At the third bend Professor Szeto was coming down the hill with a folder under her arm and the expression of a woman who’d read three disappointing reports before breakfast. She ran Eliana’s department and had once returned a project of hers with a single word in red at the top, Show-off, and a mark of ninety-four. Eliana felt her own fingers begin to loosen. Yu Chen didn’t tighten his. He didn’t pull her on. He just kept walking at the same pace, and let her decide.

She didn’t let go.

“Lin,” said Professor Szeto. “Wang.”

“Good morning, Professor.”

The professor’s eyes went to their hands and stayed there for exactly one second.

“I see,” she said. “Saturday’s an odd day to be on campus.”

“I’ve got some work,” said Eliana, going red to the collar.

“Of course you have.” Professor Szeto looked at Yu Chen. “And you?”

“Meeting someone.”

“Apparently,” said the professor, with the corner of her mouth, and went on down the hill.

“That went well,” said Yu Chen.

“She knows.”

“Knows what?”

She looked at him, and his smile deepened, and she didn’t hit him only because both her hands were busy, one with his and one with her bag strap.

By the top she’d stopped counting who had noticed. Something strange had happened to her somewhere round the library. She felt light. As if she’d been carrying something heavy so long she’d forgotten it had a weight, and had put it down by accident halfway up a hill.

✦ ✦ ✦

The triplets were on the steps by the upper courtyard. Si-Jie saw them first and stopped in the middle of a sentence with her mouth open.

“Don’t,” said Eliana.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re about to.”

“I am about to.” Si-Jie put a hand over her heart. “Are you two finally—“

“Yes,” said Yu Chen.

Eliana turned and stared at him.

“You were taking too long,” he said.

Si-Jie made a noise like a kettle. Si-Yuan took off her sunglasses to see better. Si-Wei looked at Eliana over her coffee with the face of someone who had predicted this on a whiteboard, and said only, “So that’s why you smile at your phone.”

“I don’t smile at my phone.”

“You absolutely do,” said all three of them.

Si-Jie, who couldn’t help it, said she needed to know what she was allowed to tell people. Eliana opened her mouth to say nothing, the way she’d said nothing for four years. Yu Chen was looking at her. He didn’t say anything. He was waiting to see what she’d choose.

“You can tell people we’re together,” she said.

Si-Jie stepped forward and hugged her. Eliana went stiff for half a second, and then hugged her back, and over Si-Jie’s shoulder she saw Yu Chen watching her with a look she’d never seen on him in public. Proud. Not because she’d held his hand. Because she’d stayed.

Dominic Ip was by the main gate, talking to a boy from the business school. He saw them. His eyes went to their hands and his face rearranged itself.

“Lin,” he said.

“Dominic.”

He glanced at Yu Chen. “Morning.”

“Morning,” said Yu Chen.

It was perfectly polite. It was delivered in a tone so cold that Dominic seemed to forget what he’d been going to say next, and his mouth opened and closed again, and by then they were past.

“Was that necessary?” said Eliana.

“I said good morning.”

“You said it as if you were reading out a death certificate.”

“That’s unkind,” he said, and she laughed out loud in the middle of the courtyard.

✦ ✦ ✦

His bicycle was chained just inside the gates. She stopped beside it and looked back at the campus: the hill, the steps, the students taking photographs under the university sign. She’d made rules. She’d hidden kisses behind stairwells and held his hand under tables and left his room before dawn and told people he was nobody. Now she was standing at the top of the hill in daylight with her hand in his, and it seemed the whole university knew that the boy next door wasn’t just the boy next door.

“Sweetheart?”

“It’s strange,” she said.

“Does it feel wrong?”

“No.”

“Then we can keep going.” He lifted their hands and kissed the back of hers. “You don’t have to be brave every second.”

“I’m only brave for six hundred metres.”

“That’s a long way.”

“It’s exhausting.”

He’d been unlocking the bicycle with one hand. He stopped. He seemed to decide something, and he let go of the handlebars, and the bicycle tipped over against the railing with a crash that made two girls by the noticeboard jump. He didn’t look at it. He took her face in both hands and kissed her, right there under the university gates, in front of the noticeboard and the two girls and a boy with a skateboard who stopped dead.

Her hands found his shirt and held on. He kissed her as if there were nobody else on the hill. When he lifted his head his forehead stayed against hers.

“Hello, girlfriend,” he said.

“Hello, boyfriend.”

He smiled at her then the way he didn’t smile in front of people, open and boyish, all the way up. Then he turned to pick up the bicycle, which was lying on its side with the front wheel still spinning.
