“Your bicycle,” she said.

“Worth it,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Study room 4B was on the third floor of the medical library, and on Saturdays nobody booked it. It had been theirs every Friday since the March of his first year. He sat at the table with his notes for the cardiology block laid out in order and his tea at his elbow, and she sat across from him for twenty minutes with her laptop open, pretending to work.

“Are you busy?” she said.

“A little.”

She stood up and walked round the table. He watched her come. She put her hands flat on either side of his notes and looked at him, and then she climbed onto the table and sat down on the notes.

He looked at the pages under her. Then up at her.

“Sweetheart. That’s the heart.”

“I know.”

“You’re sitting on the whole conduction system.”

“I know.” She leaned down. “It’s intentional.”

He put his pen down. He looked at her mouth. “Should I ask what you want?”

“You can guess.”

He put his hands on her waist and she bent and kissed him. She was smiling too much for it to be graceful, and he pulled back and asked what was funny, and she said “Nothing,” and he said “You’re smiling,” and she said “So are you,” and then he drew her down off the table and into his lap in one movement, notes and all, and she made a small surprised sound against his mouth.

“I’m supposed to be distracting you,” she said.

“You are.”

The cardiology notes slid off the table one page at a time. Neither of them picked any of them up. He kissed her slowly with one hand at the back of her neck and the other spread across her ribs, and she sat sideways in his lap with her arms round his neck and forgot that the door had a window in it until somebody’s footsteps went past in the corridor and didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five she was lying on his bed with her phone held up over her face while he showered.

She’d taken photographs all day without meaning to. The gates. The hill. Si-Jie’s face at the moment she understood. His bicycle on its side, which she deleted, because he’d looked too pleased with himself standing next to it. Then she found the one she’d taken halfway up the hill without thinking about it, looking down. It wasn’t good. The focus was soft and the sun had bleached half the path and the frame was crooked. But their hands were clear in the middle of it: his fingers round hers, her thumb against the side of his hand, the wire bracelet on his wrist, and behind them, out of focus, the hill going up towards the gates.

The bathroom door opened. He came out rubbing his hair with a towel.

“What are you looking at?”

“Nothing. It’s private.”

“From me?”

“Especially from you.”

He sat down beside her and she turned the screen. He looked at it for a while without saying anything.

“The light’s bad,” she said. “And it’s crooked.”

“I like it.”

She opened her settings. She cropped it until their hands sat in the middle and saved it, and locked the phone, and woke it again, and there they were on the lock screen. The hill. The gates. Their hands.

“How many times do you think you’ve held my hand?” she said.

“I stopped counting at a thousand.”

“That’s a lie. You’ve never stopped counting anything.”

“Nine hundred and forty,” he admitted, and lay down beside her, and she laughed into his shoulder. “Today was the first time everyone saw,” he said.

“Does it feel different?”

He thought about it the way he thought about everything. “Like I don’t have to let go when someone walks past.”

She took his hand and kissed his knuckles. “You don’t.”

Her phone lit up on the bedside table with a message from Si-Jie that was mostly exclamation marks, and the lock screen came on under it. Their hands, together, on the hill.

“Are you happy?” he asked her.

She looked at the boy who’d followed her to university on purpose and waited nine days without asking her to be less frightened.

“Yes,” she said, and didn’t lower her voice.

chapters.title: Two Gowns
chapters.desc: On the same afternoon, in the same hall, Eliana gets a degree in computer science and Yu Chen gets one in medicine, which was the point of four years of “coincidence”. On the steps afterwards she kisses him in front of both families.
chapters.epigraph: “You can stop now. Elara. You can stop.”
chapters.content:
At nine minutes past two on the second Thursday in June, the camera in the corner of Jinx’s workshop went white.

Eliana was awake, because she usually was. She’d put that camera in herself in March, over Jinx’s objections, pointed at the charging bench where the batteries for the electric conversions sat in a row overnight, and she’d told Jinx then that one day she’d be glad of it. Jinx had said that one day Eliana could say I told you so and until then she could get out of her workshop. Now the little square on Eliana’s second monitor had gone from grey to white to orange, and the orange was moving.

She rang Raiden. It rang out. She rang the fire service with her other hand, gave them the street in Tai Hing and the name of the garage and the words lithium, upstairs flat, two people, and was in a taxi by seventeen minutes past with her shoes in her hand.

By the time she got there the street was full of blue light. Smoke was coming out of the top of the roller shutter in a thick black sheet and folding back down over itself, and a fire crew had a hose through the side door. Evangeline was across the road in a coat over her nightclothes with both hands over her mouth. Jun Hyuk was beside her, motionless, looking at the roof.

“Where are they?”

“Out,” said Evangeline. “They’re out. They’ve gone to Harbourside.”

Eliana’s knees went. She sat down on the kerb without deciding to.

It came to her in pieces over the next hour, from Ev and a fireman and finally from a message Raiden dictated to a nurse. A battery had gone up on the bench. Jinx had smelt it first and gone down the back stair, the narrow iron one from 1974 that nobody else ever used, to get the extinguisher from the yard. Raiden had woken to an empty bed and smoke under the door and gone down the front way, and found the shutter locked from inside, and pulled on it to get to her. It had been hot. He’d pulled anyway. She’d been in the yard the whole time.

At a quarter past three Elara, three months back on the surgical floors at Harbourside, came through the curtain of the end bay in her scrubs and found her brother on one trolley with both palms in dressings like white boxing gloves and his wife on the next with oxygen under her nose and soot in the lines round her eyes, and said “Again?” so loudly that a porter turned round. Raiden had grinned at her. Eliana heard that part from Jinx later, in a voice like gravel.

Yu Chen found her on the kerb at four. He’d come straight from a night shift, in the clothes he’d left home in at seven the evening before, and he crouched in front of her and looked at her face before he said anything.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Did you go in?”

“No.” Her hands were shaking. She pushed them into her pockets. “They’re at Harbourside. Raiden’s hands. Jinx breathed smoke. Elara’s with them.”

He took her hands out of her pockets and held them.

“Breathe,” he said.

She breathed. He waited, and she did it again, and his thumbs moved over her knuckles.

“It’s all gone,” she said. “The benches. Her lathe. The bike she was building for Xiao Pan’s cousin. Everything.”

He didn’t tell her it would be fine. He didn’t tell her it could be replaced. He pulled her forward into his arms on the kerb, with the hose still running behind them, and held her while she shook.

“I’m going to rebuild it,” she said into his shirt.

He didn’t ask if she’d thought about it. He knew she’d begun.

“Then we’ll make sure you eat while you do,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop was closed for six weeks. The fire had taken the front benches and the stock and the lathe and most of the wiring, and the water had taken a good deal of what the fire hadn’t. There were inspectors and loss adjusters and estimates and delays. Raiden, with his hands bandaged, wanted to do everything himself and couldn’t hold a spoon. Jinx told him to sit down. He didn’t.

On the first Saturday Eliana arrived with her laptop and her tool roll and a box of cable and a licensed electrician, a patient man called Mr. Ching who’d done the wiring on her father’s warehouses for twenty years. She rewired the whole back wall herself with Mr. Ching checking every joint behind her. She rebuilt the alarm and the cameras and the inventory system from what had survived on Jinx’s cloud account. She refused to be paid. At the end of the day, sitting on an upturned crate with soot on her face, she looked at Jinx and said, “I’ve been waiting three months to say this.”

“Don’t,” said Jinx.

“I told you so. About the camera.”

Jinx looked at the new camera in the corner, pointing at the new bench, and then at her sister-in-law, and the corner of her mouth went up. Nearly.

On the Monday, Elara stood on the tall ladder holding the new shelf brackets against the wall while Jinx drilled, and her hands didn’t move a millimetre. When the last one was up Jinx looked at it with her spirit level and said “That’s level. Nobody does them level. Eliana’s are all a degree off and she says it’s the wall.”

“It is the wall,” said Eliana from under the bench.

On the second Saturday Baba came. Eliana hadn’t known he was going to. He got out of the silver car with Uncle Mok and stood looking at the burnt shutter, and then Jinx’s father arrived from the flyover in a van with a rod and a bucket, and the two of them went round the back without a word to anybody and spent four hours in the yard clearing the drain that the firemen’s water had silted up. Neither of them said anything to the other that Eliana could hear. When they came out they were both filthy to the elbows, and Baba washed his hands at the yard tap and got back in the car and went home.

She worked on the shop by day and on her final project by night. Professor Szeto had given her a week’s extension on account of the fire, which she’d asked for in a two-line email she’d rewritten nine times. Yu Chen brought food. Sometimes he sat on the floor of the shop with a textbook while she ran cable. Sometimes he sat on the floor of her room while she wrote code, and fell asleep against the bed with the book open on his chest, and she put a blanket over him without stopping typing.

“You’re staring,” she said one night without turning round.

“I’m reading.”

“Your book’s upside down.”

He looked. It was. He turned it the right way up with great dignity.

She submitted the project at four minutes to midnight on the extended deadline, checked the confirmation, checked it again, took a screenshot of it and shut the laptop, and put her head down on the desk.

“Finished?” he said from the floor.

“I hate university.”

He laughed. She held out her hand behind her without lifting her head, and he took it, and stayed like that until she fell asleep.

The marks came out on the second of July. First class. She read the email four times in the queue at the bakery and then rang him on the ward and said “first” and hung up before he could say anything, because she was in a bakery and her face was doing something she couldn’t control.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth of July they graduated on the same afternoon, in the Great Hall, in two different gowns.

She stood in the queue backstage with the computer scientists, adjusting a tassel she’d already adjusted four times, holding a card that said LIN ELIANA, BACHELOR OF COMPUTER SCIENCE, FIRST CLASS HONOURS. Four years of deadlines and presentations and pretending she wasn’t frightened. Four years of a boy who’d turned out, by coincidence, to be at the same university, on the same hill, in the same library room every Friday. Across the corridor the medical graduates were gathering. She found him at once. His cap was straight. He was listening to somebody from his year and nodding. Then he looked up, straight at her, as if he’d known exactly where she’d be standing, and mouthed something.

She narrowed her eyes. He mouthed it again.

Beautiful.

She looked away and went red to the roots of her hair.

The families were in. She’d seen them from the wings: Elowen and Zhao, Evangeline and Jun Hyuk, Raiden with his hands in light dressings now and Jinx beside him with her arm through his. Near the front, Xing Yue in a dark grey suit with his back straight, and Elara next to him. He’d been Yu Chen’s mentor for four years and had been asked to come. Wei Long sat at the end of a row with something in the inside pocket of his jacket that he kept touching.

At the end of the Lin row sat Baba.

When they called her name she walked out into the lights, and the hall went quiet in her ears, and her shoes were too loud on the boards. She could see the vice-chancellor and the scroll and the rows of faces beyond. Then she saw her father.

He was looking at her. Not at the stage or the scroll or the programme on his knee. At her. His eyes followed her the whole way across.

She’d spent most of her life trying to make him do that. She’d tried being quiet and being useful and being excellent. She’d tried being invisible. She’d tried needing nothing at all. And now, at twenty-two, in a borrowed gown, he was looking at her as she crossed a stage, and she almost forgot to put her hand out for the scroll.

She shook the vice-chancellor’s hand. She turned to the hall. Baba was still watching. She smiled at him, small and uncertain, and went down the steps.

When the medical graduates went up, Xing Yue clapped for his cousin exactly as hard as everybody else did, and Eliana, watching from the side, saw Elara look at her husband sideways and say something, and saw his jaw go tight, and understood that the man was nearly in tears and would rather have died than show it.

Yu Chen crossed the stage the way he did everything, unhurried, his gown sitting neatly on his shoulders, as if it were any afternoon. She knew better. She knew what this had cost him. The nights on the wards. A boy called Fung Ka-lok. The mornings he’d come home grey and still sat beside her while she worked. He took his scroll and turned and found her across the hall in one look, and she clapped until her palms stung.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards there were the steps.

The Great Hall had thirty of them, wide and shallow and full of gowns and families and flowers and phones. He came down towards her with his scroll in one hand and his hood slipping off one shoulder.

“Congratulations, Doctor,” she said.

“Not quite.”

“Medical graduate.”

“Better.”

“Four years,” she said.

“Four years.”

“You really followed me.”

“I applied to a university.”

“You applied to my university.”

“Coincidence,” he said, as he had said for four years.

She reached up and took hold of the edge of his hood and pulled him down and kissed him.

Not quickly. Not behind a door or under a table or with one eye on a corridor. On the steps of the Great Hall, at three in the afternoon, with both their scrolls crushed between them and both their families close enough to see. His hand came to her waist. He kissed her back as if nobody else were there.

Somebody whistled. Raiden. Somebody else laughed. Then Elara burst into tears and came down three steps at once and hugged her little sister so hard that Eliana’s cap fell off and rolled down two steps, and Eliana stood with her arms out stiff at her sides and said, “You can stop now. Elara. You can stop.”

Elara didn’t stop. Yu Chen, with his ears red, went past them both to his cousin, and Xing Yue shook his hand.

“Emergency,” said Xing Yue. “You’ll be good at it. You don’t panic and you don’t like being thanked.”

Yu Chen looked at him as if he’d been handed something heavy and didn’t know where to put it down. “Thank you.”

Eliana, still being hugged, looked over her sister’s shoulder for her father.

He’d been at the top of the steps. He’d seen. She could tell from the way he stood, as if a door had shut inside him. He looked at his youngest daughter in a young man’s arms, and something closed in his face, and he turned and walked away along the colonnade towards the gate where Uncle Mok had the car, and didn’t look back.

She watched him go. Then Elara let go of her, and Evangeline picked up her cap, and she put it back on crooked, and didn’t let herself think about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long found them under the camphor trees at the edge of the lawn, away from the crowd.

“Nainai asked me to bring this,” he said, and took out a letter. The paper was soft from being carried. “She said to read it to you out loud, exactly as she wrote it, because I’d try to improve it.”

He unfolded it and cleared his throat.

“My dear Eliana. We have not met yet, which is my grandson’s fault, because he is a careful boy who believes that waiting is a reasonable way to spend his life. I have known your name since the summer of 2021. He writes to me every month. I know that you forget to eat when you are working, that you draw in the margins of other people’s books, and that you once fixed his phone so that it would not let him stay up past two. I know you are clever. I hope you know that you do not have to be clever to be loved. You do not have to be useful. You do not have to earn a place at our table. I will tell you what I have told him: you are family now. Come north when you can. I will make you something warm, and I will not make you finish it. With my love, Nainai.”

He folded it up again and held it out to her.

She didn’t take it at once. She stood under the camphor trees in her gown, holding her scroll, and her mouth wasn’t doing what she told it to.

“I haven’t even been to see her,” she said.

“She knows.”

“I should have.”

“She didn’t write it to make you feel guilty.” Wei Long put the letter in her hand and closed her fingers over it. “Keep it.”

She held it against her chest with the scroll. Wei Long looked at his cousin, who was looking at Eliana.

“You’ve done well,” he said to Yu Chen.

“I had a good reason.”

“Don’t get unbearable about it,” said Song Wei Long, and went to find his car.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening Yu Chen put both scrolls side by side on the desk in his room and stood back to look at them. Eliana came and straightened his, because it was a degree off.

“Yours on the left,” he said.

“Why?”

“You always sleep on the left.”

“That has nothing to do with anything.”

“It seemed relevant.”

She leaned back against him and he put his arms round her waist. Computer science and medicine, side by side under the lamp. Four years of coincidence.

“We graduated,” she said. “Both of us. Same hall. Same afternoon.”

“Same afternoon.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“A little,” he said, and kissed the top of her head. “And now?”

She thought about her father’s back going away along the colonnade. About Nainai’s letter in her bag. About a burnt shutter in Tai Hing and a new one going up on the twenty-sixth, and Jinx’s face when she saw the camera.

“Tomorrow first,” she said.

“Tomorrow first,” he agreed.

chapters.title: The Neighbour and the Cold Gaze
chapters.desc: At the first Sunday lunch after graduation, Lin Jian tells the table, and not his daughter, that she won’t be wasting a Lin future on a policeman’s nephew. Yu Chen, who has never raised his voice in that house, stands up.
chapters.epigraph: “Wanting your father to love you isn’t a weakness.”
chapters.content:
Elowen asked Yu Chen to Sunday lunch on a Thursday, over the phone, while Eliana sat on his kitchen counter eating cherries out of a paper bag and pretending not to listen.

“Sunday,” Elowen said. “One o’clock. Baba’s table.”

There was a pause on Yu Chen’s side of the kitchen. Eliana stopped chewing.

“I’d be glad to come,” he said.

“Good. Ah Sim will cook for twenty and Raiden will complain about it. Jinx and Ev are coming, and Jun Hyuk. Zhao.” Another pause. “Don’t bring anything, Yu Chen. You’re not a guest I’m trying to impress. I want everybody at one table, and I want my father to have to look across it.”

When he’d rung off she put another cherry in her mouth. He came and stood between her knees.

“You were listening.”

“I was eating.”

“Attentively.” He wiped a trace of cherry juice off the corner of her mouth with his thumb. “Are you all right with Sunday?”

“Are you?”

“I’ll be fine.”

“That wasn’t the question.”

“I know,” he said.

She held a cherry out to him and he took it from her fingers with his mouth.

“Don’t let him ruin your Sunday,” she said.

“I won’t let him ruin yours.”

“That’s an ambitious promise.”

“I’ve had practice,” he said, and kissed her forehead.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday was clear and hot. They came in through the red door in the alley wall, because everyone did on Sundays: Raiden and Jinx with a bag of lychees nobody had asked for, Evangeline and Jun Hyuk, Elowen and Zhao, and last of all Eliana in a pale blue dress with Yu Chen beside her carrying nothing, as instructed. Ah Sim met them in the courtyard with her sleeves rolled up. She looked at Yu Chen, and at his empty hands, and nodded once as if he’d passed something.

“You came,” said Elowen, kissing her sister’s cheek and then, after the smallest hesitation, touching his arm.

“I said I would.”

“Stop looking polite. It makes me feel old.”

“You are older,” said Yu Chen, and Elowen stared at him and then laughed, and Eliana felt something in her chest unclench a notch.

Zhao appeared in the kitchen doorway with a tea towel over his shoulder. “Wang Yu Chen. Come and help me get Raiden away from the duck.”

“I heard that,” said Raiden, from inside, with his mouth full.

“Good,” said Zhao.

Evangeline came and stood beside Eliana in the courtyard. “He’s nervous.”

“He isn’t.”

“Then why are you doing that with your hands?”

Eliana looked down. Her fingers were knotted together. She untied them.

“It’s hot,” she said.

“Of course,” said Ev.

Baba came down at ten to one. He nodded to Elowen and Zhao. He nodded to Raiden, and to Jinx, a little longer. He nodded to Ev and Jun Hyuk. Then his eyes came to Yu Chen and stopped.

“Mr. Wang.”

“Mr. Lin.”

That was all. Baba went to the head of the table and sat down in the carved chair.

“Baba,” said Eliana.

He looked at her. “Your hair’s untidy.”

She put her hand up to it before she could stop herself. Yu Chen didn’t move, and didn’t speak, and waited until she came and stood beside him. His hand brushed hers. She took it for a second and let it go. She wasn’t afraid. She wanted to walk into her father’s dining room on her own feet.

✦ ✦ ✦

For a while it was a family lunch. Ah Sim’s steamed fish, the duck, the soup that had taken her two days. Elowen asked Yu Chen what he’d do now he’d graduated, and he told her about the foundation year at Harbourside starting in August, carefully, without making it sound like anything. Raiden complained there was too much food. Jinx told him he could stop eating. Ev asked whether the new lights at the shop were finished.

“The last fitting’s on Saturday,” said Eliana.

“She labelled every box,” said Raiden. “Every single one.”

“Because you put the wrong stock on the wrong shelf.”

“Once.”

“Seventeen times.”

“Seventeen is still one category,” said Raiden, and Jun Hyuk laughed into his tea.

Yu Chen sat beside her with his knee against hers under the table. Twice he moved a dish nearer to her when she hadn’t reached for it. She ate the fish. He noticed her eating it, and she noticed him noticing, and neither of them said anything, and for half an hour it was almost ordinary.

Then Baba put his chopsticks down.

“I hear the ceremony went well,” he said to the table.

“It did,” said Elowen.

“Both of them graduated.” He didn’t look at either of them. “Medicine is a hard field. And there’s a great deal one can do with computer science.” He picked up his tea. “A Lin education should lead somewhere. There’s no reason for her to waste the future this family has built for her on a policeman’s grandson.”

The table went still.

Raiden’s face changed first. Jinx put down her bowl. Ev looked at Eliana. Elowen’s mouth went thin. Zhao set his cup down without a sound.

Eliana looked at her father. He wasn’t looking at her. He was looking at Yu Chen, as if Yu Chen were a delivery left at the wrong door, something that would go away if he spoke firmly enough.

She’d heard him say crueller things. She’d never heard him say a thing like that in front of everyone, about the man sitting next to her, as if she weren’t in the chair.

Yu Chen put his chopsticks down. He didn’t push his chair back hard. He didn’t raise his voice. He stood up, and the room turned to him because he had never once stood up in this house.

“You talk about her as if she isn’t here,” he said.

Baba looked at him.

“She’s sitting at this table,” said Yu Chen. “You can speak to her.”

“This is a family matter.”

“Then speak to your daughter.”

“You’re in no position to tell me how to speak in my own house.”

“No,” said Yu Chen. “I’m not. But she isn’t someone you can discuss as if she has no say in her own life.”

Baba pushed his chair back. “Do you imagine one degree from the same university makes you suitable for her?”

“No.”

It came so fast that Baba blinked.

“I don’t think a degree makes me suitable,” Yu Chen said. “Or my family, or my grandfather’s photograph by the front door. I don’t think anything I say at this table will make you approve of me. But she isn’t yours to approve or refuse on her behalf.”

Baba stood. The carved chair scraped on the tiles.

“Young man—“

“Baba.”

Eliana’s voice was low. Everyone turned. She was still sitting, with her hands in her lap.

“I’m here,” she said. “I’m sitting right here.”

He looked at her as if he’d only just seen where she was. Then his eyes went back to Yu Chen, and he came round the end of the table, and Yu Chen stepped between them.

He didn’t touch her father. He didn’t threaten him. He simply stood where he was, between the head of the Lin family and the youngest Lin daughter, with his hands at his sides.

“Move,” said Baba.

“Please sit down, Mr. Lin.”

“Move.”

“I won’t.”

Eliana stood up. She put her hand on Yu Chen’s arm. She could feel how hard he was holding himself still under her fingers. He turned his head, and she shook hers a fraction, and he understood that she wasn’t asking him to go. She was asking him to let her speak. He stepped back half a pace and she came and stood beside him.

“You don’t have to like him,” she said to her father. Her voice shook. She didn’t stop. “But you don’t get to decide I leave him. You’ve spent my whole life talking about me to other people. To Elowen. To Ah Sim. To the table. You talk about my future as if it’s a room you’ve already furnished and all I have to do is walk in. I’ve got a degree. I’ve got work. I’ve got my own life.” She took Yu Chen’s hand, in front of all of them. “And I’ve got him. I chose him.”

Baba’s eyes went down to their hands.

Something changed in his face then that she’d never seen in it. Not anger. Something less sure of itself. For a second, so fast she might have imagined it, she saw fear: as if he were looking at someone he could no longer reach just by saying her name. Someone who might go. Someone who’d learned how.

“Your mother—“ he said, and stopped.

The room held its breath.

“Don’t,” said Eliana. It came out small. “Don’t use her to tell me what to do.”

His face closed like a shutter coming down. He picked up his jacket from the back of the carved chair and walked out of the dining room, and they heard his study door shut overhead.

Nobody moved for a long moment. The clock in the passage ticked.

“I’m going to—“ said Raiden, getting up, and Jinx put two fingers on his wrist and he sat down again.

Elowen came round the table and put her arms round her sister. Eliana let her. She didn’t cry. Yu Chen stood beside them with one hand not quite touching her back, and waited until she looked up and found it, and took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ah Sim packed the fish into boxes for everybody without a word. At the front of the house, on the three stone steps under the little tiled roof, Eliana stopped.

These were the steps where she’d sat at eighteen waiting for a well done. The crack in the third. The knee-high wall between her steps and his. Above them, behind a closed window, her father’s study.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“What for?”

“For making you sit through that.”

He took her face between his hands. “You didn’t make me do anything.”

“He shouldn’t have spoken to you like that.”

“No.”

“Or about me.”

“No.”

“You stood up,” she said. “You never stand up in that house.”

“I know.”

“Were you angry?”

“Yes. But it was worse watching you sit there while he talked as if you weren’t allowed to answer.”

“I could have answered.”

“I know you could.”

“So why did you get between us?”

He thought about it, as he did everything. “Because he came towards you,” he said, “and I didn’t want you standing there on your own.”

Her mouth trembled. She took the front of his shirt in her fist and pulled him down and kissed him.

On her father’s front steps, in the middle of a Sunday afternoon, under his study window. On purpose. His hands found her waist and he kissed her back slowly, and then not slowly, with everything he’d held still through two hours at that table.

“I’m not hiding you,” she said against his mouth. “Not from him. Not any more.”

“I know, sweetheart.”

She stepped over the little wall onto his side, still holding his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

His room was full of afternoon. The curtains were open and a long bar of sun lay across the floor and up over the edge of the bed. He put his keys on the desk and took off his watch, the way he did, and when he turned round she was standing in the light in the pale blue dress looking at him as if she were trying to memorise something.

“Come here,” he said.

She came. He held her without saying anything, her cheek on his chest and his hand moving slowly up and down her back.

“I hated how he looked at me,” she said. “As if I’d done something wrong.”

“You haven’t.”

“I thought it’d be different after I graduated. I thought if I had the degree and work and my own money, he’d finally—“ She stopped.

“Finally what?”

She shook her head against him. “I don’t know how to stop wanting him to want me.”

“You don’t have to stop.” He kissed her hair. “Wanting your father to love you isn’t a weakness.”

She lifted her face. “Do you still want to marry me? After today?”

“More than I did yesterday.”

“Why?”

“Because I want you to have one place where you never wonder whether you’re welcome.” He touched her cheek. “But I don’t want you to marry me to get away from him.”

“I’m not,” she said. “I want to marry you too. Not today. Not because of him. Because I want you.”

He closed his eyes for a second. Then he kissed her, and she reached behind herself for the zip of her dress.

He took over. He drew it down slowly, the whole length of her spine, and the dress slid off her shoulders and pooled at her feet in the sun. He undressed her the rest of the way the same way, as if there were all the time in the world, as if nobody in the house next door had ever said a word about her. She pulled his shirt over his head and pressed her mouth to his chest and felt his heart going hard, and he lifted her and laid her down across the bar of sunlight on his bed.

Everything was bright. She could see all of him and he could see all of her. She’d always wanted the dark before, the lamp off and the blind down, and today she didn’t. He kissed her throat and her collarbones and the soft inside of her arm, and down over her breasts and her stomach, slow, unhurried, until she was arching off the sheet and saying his name. When he came back up over her she pulled his weight down onto her and wrapped her legs round his hips and took him inside her with a long, shaking breath.

He held still. He looked down at her in all that light.

“I’m here,” he said.

She began to cry.

She didn’t make a sound. The tears simply ran out of the corners of her eyes into her hair, the way she’d learned to cry as a child in a quiet house, where even grief had to be quiet. He saw them. He didn’t stop and he didn’t ask her to. He kissed them off her temples one side and then the other, and moved in her slowly, deep, steady, his forehead against hers, until the crying and the wanting were the same thing and she was holding on to him with her whole body. It built in her like heat. When it broke she turned her face into his shoulder and shook, and he followed her with his breath ragged in her ear, and held her afterwards as if she were something he’d carried a long way.

They lay in the sun with the sheet half off. Her cheek was on his chest. He stroked her hair.

“He should have been proud of you today,” he said.

She didn’t answer. She didn’t need to.

Later she fell asleep there, and he stayed awake and watched the bar of light climb the wall and go gold, and thought about a girl on the step in rabbit slippers, and a roof, and a typed list of rules, and nine days, and a knock at two in the morning, and a hill. He would never make her prove she belonged. Not to him, not to anybody. She already did.

When she woke the light had gone soft.

“Were you watching me?”

“Yes.”

“Creepy.”

“You were dribbling.”

“I was not.”

“A little,” he said, and she pushed his chest, and he caught her hand and kissed the palm.

“Can we stay here a bit longer?” she said.

“As long as you want.”

Nobody in that room asked her to be useful, or impressive, or to earn anything at all. She put her head back on his chest and stayed.

chapters.title: A Job Offer and a Night Shift
chapters.desc: Her father summons her to the fishing-net building, where the Syndicate offers her the Syndicate’s top security post, full time, for life. The same night Yu Chen works his first night as a real doctor, and she takes dinner up to the top of the car park.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t take a thing just because somebody’s finally decided you’re worth keeping.”
chapters.content:
The fishing-net building hadn’t changed. The paint was still coming off the stairwell in long grey curls, the lift still made its small sick noise between the third and fourth floors, and someone had left a bag of oranges on the security desk as if the building were a shrine. Eliana had always thought it looked like a place the city had forgotten. That was presumably the point.

She came at a quarter past eleven on the first Thursday in August, in black trousers and a white blouse and the small silver earrings Yu Chen had given her on graduation night. The man on the desk knew her.

“Miss Lin. Qian’s upstairs.”

“Is my father here?”

He hesitated a fraction too long. “Yes.”

“Of course he is,” said Eliana, and took the stairs.

On the fourth floor the long room was open. Qian sat at the table with a folder in front of him and the face he always had, as if somebody had once told him expressions were expensive. Uncle Mok stood by the window with a paper cup of tea. At the far end, with his back to the light, sat Baba.

They hadn’t spoken since Sunday lunch three weeks before. Not a word. They’d passed on the stairs at home twice.

“Sit,” he said.

She sat opposite him. The folder was thick, much thicker than anything Qian had ever sent her.

“What’s this?”

“An offer,” said Baba.

Qian slid it across the table. She didn’t open it.

“You’ve graduated,” her father said. “First class. Your work for the Syndicate has been consistent. Chen Si says so. Qian says so.” He folded his hands. “The Syndicate needs someone to run its security. All of it. Systems, people, the weak places outsiders look for. It should be someone who already knows where they are.”

She almost looked over her shoulder to see who he meant. In twenty-two years he’d never said a sentence about her work to her face.

“Head of security,” said Qian.

“Full time?”

“Yes.”

“Permanent?”

“For life,” said her father.

The room was quiet except for the fan.

She opened the folder. A formal letter of appointment. A salary she didn’t need to read twice. A team of eight, hers to choose. Offices on the ninth floor of a building on Harbour Road with a car to take her there and bring her back. Authority over every system the Syndicate touched, answerable to nobody but Chen Si and her father. She turned the pages. She understood the shape of it long before she reached the end. Permanent meant always available. The work would stop being something she could take and finish and put down. It would be where she lived. Her movements would be known, because that was what security meant. Her time would belong to it.

“You’d have everything you need,” Baba said.

“Everything?”

“Your own people. Your own office. No more waiting for Qian to send you jobs at one in the morning.” He paused, and then said it, as if it were the kindest thing in the folder. “You’d never need to go anywhere.”

Her fingers stopped on the paper.

There it was. He said it the way someone else might offer a coat. A house you couldn’t leave. A room with no door in it. A life in which she would never again have to wonder where she belonged, because she would never be allowed to need anywhere else.

The salary was real. The title was real. The resources were real. And underneath all of it, between the clauses, she could see the bars.

She closed the folder.

“I’ll let you know,” she said.

His face changed. “You need time?”

“Yes.”

“What is there to think about?”

“Whether I want it.”

“You’re qualified for it.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

Uncle Mok lowered his tea. Qian’s eyes moved to her father and back.

Baba looked at her for a long moment, as if she were a line in a ledger that wouldn’t balance. Then he turned to Qian. “Give her whatever time she needs.”

“Thank you for the offer,” said Eliana, and stood, and left the folder on the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

Qian followed her into the corridor and shut the door.

“You should read the whole thing.”

“I did.”

“You read the first half.”

“I understood the second half.”

He nearly smiled. “Did you know it was coming?” she said.

“I knew they were discussing it.”

“And you didn’t stop them.”

“It’s a good position, Eliana.”

“I know. That’s the problem. A bad one would be easy to say no to.” She leaned on the peeling wall. “He wants me where he can see me.”

Qian didn’t answer. He went back into the room and came out with the folder, and put it on the little table by the lift, and laid his hand flat on top of it for a second. Then he took his hand away and said nothing at all, and went downstairs.

Uncle Mok was waiting at the turn of the stair with his tea.

“Finished?”

“For now.”

He looked at the folder under her arm. “He’s been planning that since before your exams.”

“I gathered.”

Uncle Mok drank some tea. Then he said, looking down the stairwell rather than at her, “Your mother used to make him wait too.”

She went still.

“When they were young,” he said, “he’d decide something and expect her to agree. She’d let him explain the whole thing. She’d listen with great care. Then she’d go and do what she liked.” The corner of his mouth went up. “She made him stand outside shops for an hour at a time. He’d stand there pretending he wasn’t waiting. I sat in the car and watched him do it for twelve years.”

Eliana had never heard this. Not from Baba. Not even from Elowen. In their house her mother was a photograph on the stair, a date in February that was also her birthday, a name that made rooms go quiet. She’d never been a young woman who kept a man waiting outside a shop.

“Was he angry?” she said.

“Often.”

“Did she mind?”

“Not in the slightest.” He laughed under his breath. “He loved her for it. He was never any good at saying what he wanted. She was never any good at pretending she didn’t know.” He looked at her then. “You’ve got her face when you’re deciding something.”

“People keep telling me that.”

“Maybe they keep being right.” He patted her shoulder once, a big dry hand. “Don’t take a thing just because somebody’s finally decided you’re worth keeping. Go home, girl.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to seven Yu Chen sent her a message.

Yu Chen: First night.

Eliana: i know

Yu Chen: Are you going to wish me luck?

Eliana: no. you’re a doctor. you’re meant to be confident

Yu Chen: Confidence and luck are different things.

Eliana: good luck sweetheart

Yu Chen: Better. Have you eaten?

She looked at the folder open on her desk. For life.

Eliana: yes

Yu Chen: What?

Eliana: food

Yu Chen: Convincing.

His shift started at eight. He’d walked those corridors for four years as a student, following registrars and trying to remember everything, but tonight his own name was on the rota and his own card was clipped to his coat. Dr. Chan, the registrar on nights, gave him five minutes before the department filled up.

“Don’t try to be impressive,” she said. “Be thorough. If something doesn’t feel right, say so. If you don’t know, ask. And eat before midnight.”

“I will.”

“That’s what they all say.”

The first hours were a blur of small decisions. A toddler with a temperature. An old man who’d fallen in his bathroom. A woman with stomach pain who was frightened mostly because she lived on her own. He listened and examined and wrote things down and called for help when he needed it. He was slower than he wanted to be. He checked everything twice.

At twenty to eleven a man of fifty-eight came in with his wife, annoyed to be there.

“Indigestion,” he said. “Something I ate.”

“He’s been sweating for an hour,” said his wife.

“It’s hot.”

“He said his chest hurt.”

“I said it was uncomfortable.”

Yu Chen looked at him. Grey under the tan. A line of sweat along his hairline in an air-conditioned room. “Can you show me where?”

The man pressed his palm flat to the middle of his chest. “Pressure. Comes and goes.”

“Does it go anywhere?”

A pause. “My left arm feels odd.”

Yu Chen asked for observations and an ECG straight away. The man complained that this was a great deal of fuss for a bad dinner. Yu Chen didn’t argue with him. He stood beside the trolley until the tracing came off the machine, and looked at it, and looked again, and felt his stomach drop.

“Dr. Chan?”

She looked at it for two seconds. “Resus. Now.”

It went fast after that, and it wasn’t his to run, and he didn’t try to. He gave the history in four sentences and fetched what he was asked to fetch, and when the curtain closed he went out to the wife, who was standing in the corridor with her handbag held against her chest.

“Is it a heart attack?”

He didn’t soften it into something untrue. “We think it may be. The team is treating it as urgent.”

“Will he be all right?”

“They’re doing everything they can,” he said, and stayed with her until a nurse came.

When the man had gone up for treatment Dr. Chan passed him at the sink.

“Good catch,” she said. “You didn’t take indigestion for an answer. Don’t get ahead of yourself.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten to midnight Eliana was at the side entrance with a paper bag.

Eliana: outside

Yu Chen: Where?

Eliana: your hospital. i brought food. find me

He found her in four minutes. His coat was creased and his hair had given up, and there was a tiredness round his eyes she’d learned to read years ago, and when he saw her his face changed.

“You came.”

“You said it was your first night.”

“You haven’t eaten either.”

“Hello to you too,” said Eliana.

He had twenty minutes. He didn’t take her to the staff room. He took her up in the lift to the top deck of the multi-storey car park, where the air was warm and the wind came through the concrete and the whole city lay beyond the barriers in lit windows, and his old grey car sat on its own at the far end under a lamp. They sat on the bonnet with the bag between them. Rice and chicken and greens, in two of Ah Sim’s tins.

“You made this?”

“I supervised.”

“From the kitchen?”

“From a chair.”

He laughed and ate, properly, and she watched him eat, and felt something warm and fierce settle under her ribs.

“How was it?” she said.

“A man came in with chest pain. He thought it was indigestion.” He told her. The ECG, Dr. Chan, the curtain, the wife with her handbag. “I don’t know yet if he’ll be all right.”

“You noticed.”

“It’s my job.”

“It’s your first night.”

“It’s still my job.” He looked at her sideways in the lamplight. “Are you proud of me?”

He said it half as a joke. She heard what was under it. She put her hand on his face.

“Yes,” she said, and kissed him.

He kissed her back, and then again, longer, his hand on her waist, and she slid closer along the warm metal until she had her fingers in the front of his white coat and he had her back against the windscreen.

“Are you allowed to do this on shift?”

“I’m on a break.”

“Is kissing your girlfriend part of a break?”

“It’s the best part,” he said, and kissed her until his phone went in his pocket and they both groaned. He kissed her once more, hard, and slid off the bonnet. “Don’t wait up.”

“I’m going to wait up.”

“I know,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t sleep. At seventeen minutes past two he sent Still awake? and she sent unfortunately and he asked if she wanted to talk about the offer, and she said not yet, and he said I’m here when you are.

At three she gave up and went next door with a toothbrush in her cardigan pocket. Auntie Tsoi opened the door in her dressing gown and looked at her and said “Ah,” the way she’d said it since Eliana was nine, and stood aside.

“He’s not home.”

“I know.”

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

Auntie Tsoi narrowed her eyes.

“No,” said Eliana.

She got a bowl of soup at the kitchen table and instructions. Don’t ask him too many questions. Make him wash his hands. Make him drink water. “Yes, Auntie,” said Eliana, and went up to his room to wait.

He came in at seventeen minutes to six. She heard the front door, and his keys go down on the hall table, and his feet on the stairs, slower than usual. He stopped in the doorway and looked at her sitting on his bed in his old university sweatshirt.

“Sweetheart.”

“Hello, Doctor. Hands.”

He blinked. “Auntie Tsoi?”

“Obviously.”

He washed his hands. When he came back he took off his watch and then the coat, and she folded it over the chair, and he reached for her and put his head down on her shoulder and stayed there.

“The man?” she said into his hair.

“Transferred. Stable when I left.” He breathed out. “I kept thinking how quickly it could have gone the other way.”

“But it didn’t. You noticed. You did your job.” She kissed his forehead. “And you came home.”

“I came home,” he agreed.

She’d already turned the bed down. He changed into a clean T-shirt and lay down and she climbed in beside him and fitted herself against his side, and he kissed her forehead, and her cheek, and she turned her face up and he kissed her mouth. It was slow and sleepy and tasted of hospital toothpaste. There was no hurry in it. He kissed her as if he’d finally got somewhere safe.

“You should sleep,” he said.

“So should you.”

“I’m trying.”

“You’re not trying hard,” she said, and slid her hand under his T-shirt and across his stomach, and felt it jump under her palm.

“Eliana.”

“I’ve been awake for hours. I’m sure.”

The curtains were open a hand’s width and the first grey of morning was coming in. She drew the sweatshirt over her head and dropped it off the side of the bed, and he looked at her in the half-light as if he’d forgotten how tired he was. They undressed each other clumsily, laughing under their breath when his elbow caught the lamp, when he forgot halfway through what he’d been saying and she finished the sentence for him. He was careful with her. She was patient with him. She pushed him onto his back and climbed over him and took him inside her slowly, so slowly, and watched his eyes close and his mouth open on her name. She moved on him in the grey light with her hands flat on his chest, unhurried, the way you’d rock something to sleep. His hands came up to her hips and held on. When it built it built gently, a long warm swell rather than a wave, and she felt it take her and let it, and leaned down so that her forehead was on his when he followed her, with a sound like a man setting down something heavy.

“I’m proud of you,” she whispered.

He didn’t open his eyes. He pulled her down onto his chest and held her there.

He was asleep in two minutes. She lay with her cheek over his heart and his arm round her waist. His watch was on the desk. His card lay beside it, his photograph unsmiling over WANG YU CHEN, and she reached across carefully and picked it up and looked at it and put it back.

Her phone lit on the bedside table.

Qian: Have you looked at it again?

She looked at the door, and at the boy asleep under her cheek with one hand still holding the hem of her shirt.

Eliana: not yet

She didn’t know what she’d choose. But she knew she wouldn’t take a lifetime just because someone had made it hard to leave. She put the phone face down and closed her eyes.

chapters.title: The Breach
chapters.desc: For the first time in her life, someone gets through Eliana’s walls — a crew called Magpie, let in by an old key she handed out herself in second year. It isn’t just data. It’s the family’s safe-house addresses, and a clock starts.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re not on your own in this room”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past four on a Friday morning in September, her phone rang on Yu Chen’s bedside table, and Eliana was awake before the second buzz.

Qian. He never rang. He sent short messages at one in the morning and expected her to work out the rest.

“What’s happened?”

“Your fence has gone quiet.”

She sat up. “What?”

“Eleven minutes ago it stopped reporting. The second line too.”

“The outside copy?”

“Gone.”

She already had her laptop open on her knees. “Don’t touch anything. Don’t let anyone touch anything.”

“I haven’t.”

She hung up on him.

Beside her Yu Chen breathed slow and even, one arm flung across the place where she’d been. The bedroom was dark except for her screen. She opened the fence and it was there, all its lights green, its last report ordinary. Too ordinary. She went past it to the logs she kept somewhere else, and past those to the ones behind them, and found the place where the reporting simply stopped, clean, at four minutes past four. It hadn’t broken. Somebody had taught it to believe there was nothing to see.

Her stomach turned over. She opened the vault where she kept the family’s safe-house register.

It was empty.

She looked again. The names were gone. The addresses were gone. The notes were gone: which flat had a back stair, which had a doctor two doors down, which old lady in which harbour town would open her door to anyone who said a particular word. She searched the second copy. Empty. Her hand went cold on the trackpad.

It had never been a simple list. It was the places people in her family went when a home stopped being safe. Where a sister could disappear for a week. Where a man could be moved at night without anyone in the rest of the family knowing which night. Some of the addresses were twenty years old. Some had never been written down anywhere else. She’d built six walls round it because she knew exactly what it meant in the wrong hands.

Her phone rang again.

“It’s gone,” she said. “Qian, the whole register.”

“I know. I’ve started calling people.”

“How long have they had it?”

“We don’t know yet.”

“Who?”

A pause. “A crew who call themselves Magpie. They buy access and information through other people. They’ve been quiet since spring.”

“Someone let them in,” she said.

“Yes. Call you back,” said Qian, and went.

She didn’t realise she was shaking until the mattress moved behind her.

“Sweetheart?”

His voice was rough with sleep. He looked at her laptop and then her face, and he was awake.

“Someone got in,” she said. “They took the safe-house list.”

He didn’t ask what was on it. He didn’t ask how. He understood enough of what she did to understand that. “Is anyone in danger?”

“I don’t know.”

“Does Qian know?”

“He’s ringing them.”

He nodded. Then he got out of bed and put on a T-shirt, and when he came back from the kitchen ten minutes later he had a bowl in his hands. She didn’t look round.

“Have you eaten?” he said.

“Someone has the addresses,” she said, “and you’re asking me about food.”

“Yes.” He put the bowl down beside the laptop and his hand on her shoulder. “Let me look after the part you’re not going to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At two minutes past five a name came up on her screen.

Not in the fence: in an old exchange Qian had dug out of the wreckage and sent across: a credential, the one Magpie had used to walk in through the staff entrance. She knew the format. She’d made it.

DOMINIC IP. Second year. The systems project.

She sat back so hard the chair hit the wardrobe.

She remembered it. A study room in the engineering library on a Tuesday afternoon, three years ago. Dominic across the table asking for access to a shared environment so his half of the team could review their code before the presentation. She’d checked the request. She’d made the key. She’d told him it was temporary. She’d been late for 4B and in a hurry. And she had never once gone back to take it away.

She’d handed it to him. Nobody had stolen it or guessed it. She’d given it to him with her own hands, and it had sat in a dead project for three years like a key under a mat.

“It’s the same credential,” said Qian on speaker.

“I closed that project.”

“You closed the project. You didn’t close the key.”

She went to the window. Outside, the lane was still dark. She thought of Dominic in the foyer of the law building, loud, smiling, saying you can say yes. She thought of Yu Chen’s hand closing round hers. She’s with me. She’d thought Dominic was only a man who’d mistaken politeness for interest. She’d been wrong about something.

“Did he sell it?” she said.

“We don’t know yet whether he passed it on himself or whether someone took it from him.”

“But the key came from me.”

“Yes.”

“I trusted him.”

“You were in second year,” Qian said. “You made a decision with what you had.”

“I should have revoked it.”

“Yes,” said Qian.

He didn’t tell her it wasn’t her fault. He didn’t pretend it hadn’t happened. It was the reason she trusted him.

“I’m coming in,” she said.

“No. You’re no use to me half awake and deciding things out of guilt. Stay where you are.”

At a quarter past six she found the second thread. A payment. Not large enough to stand out, not odd enough to catch anybody’s eye. But the source was clear when she followed it far enough.

CALDER RISK PARTNERS.

She knew that name. She’d seen it in the bank’s letters in the spring: the firm the bank had hired after her lecture, to manage the risk of her. The firm whose man had stood outside the physics theatre filming her for six minutes. They’d wanted her quiet. Now they’d paid a crew of thieves to take the addresses of the places her family ran to.

“It’s Calder,” she told Qian.

“We have the same record. We’re treating it as true.”

“They don’t need the list. They’re consultants.”

“Apparently they think they do,” said Qian. “Stay somewhere secure. Not alone. Don’t go near the building. Don’t go near Dominic. Don’t go near Calder. And don’t try to get it back by yourself. Say it.”

“I understand.”

He rang off. She closed the laptop and sat with both hands flat on it.

She needed to ring her father.

The thought was there before she could stop it. Baba had people. Resources. The Syndicate’s own men could move faster than anything she could put together, could empty the safe houses and fill new ones by tonight. All he’d have to do was ask her to take the job. The folder was in her desk drawer next door. She could hear his voice. You’d never need to go anywhere.

She found his number. Her thumb stayed over it.

She put the phone down.

She needed help. She also knew precisely what that help would cost. Protection would become a debt. The debt would become the job. The job would become her life. She’d spent too many years learning that every kindness in that house came with a condition, and she wasn’t going to sign a lifetime because somebody had found the one thing that could frighten her into it.

But the people on that list were real. They weren’t an argument. They weren’t leverage.

“I don’t know what to do,” she said to nobody.

Yu Chen came back with the bowl, which he’d taken away and warmed again. Congee. He pulled the other chair beside hers and put the spoon in her hand.

“Three spoonfuls,” he said.

“I’m not five.”

“Five-year-olds argue less.”

She almost smiled. She took one mouthful, and he waited, and she took another, and a third, and put the spoon down.

“Someone used a key I gave them,” she said.

“Dominic?”

She looked at him. He’d already understood.

“I gave it to him in second year. It was meant to be temporary.”

“Did you know it was still live?”

“No.”

“Then you didn’t knowingly give him this.”

“I should have checked.”

“Yes,” he said. She flinched. He didn’t take it back. “But that isn’t the same as meaning it. People may be in danger because somebody chose to use something you trusted them with. You can learn from it without turning yourself into the person who deserves the punishment.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eight he rang the hospital. She heard only his side, in the corridor.

“I’m not safe to come in today. A family emergency. Yes. I’ll follow the procedure. Thank you.”

“You’ve got patients,” she said when he came back.

“They’ve got a team. I’ve told the department and my list is covered.” He picked up the empty bowl. “I’m staying. You can be angry with me after you’ve eaten something else.”

By ten he’d made her drink two glasses of water and sit away from the screen for twenty minutes. He’d also checked the front door twice. The first time she didn’t notice. The second time she did.

“It’s locked.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you checking?”

“Because I want to.”

“You’re guarding the door.”

“Yes.”

“You can’t guard every door,” she said. “Or every person. Or fix this.”

“I know.” He took her hand. “I’m staying with you while you fix the parts you can. And making sure you eat.”

She laughed, a small broken sound, and put her forehead against his chest.

At noon Qian rang again, on speaker this time, with Yu Chen at the other end of the table. The families on the list were being reached. Some had moved. No one had been approached that they knew of. Calder’s payment chain was being followed. Dominic Ip wasn’t answering his phone.

“Don’t go looking for him,” said Qian. “I’m not asking you to forgive him. I’m asking you not to become the next problem. And Eliana. Your father knows.”

Her fingers froze on the table. “You told him?”

“Not me. Someone did. He hasn’t rung.”

When the call ended Yu Chen said, “Are you going to ring him?”

“No.”

He didn’t argue.

“Even though he could help,” she said.

“All right.”

“Even though people could get hurt while I don’t.”

“All right.” He turned her hand over in his. “I think you should decide whether you want that job on a day when you’re not being frightened into it. You don’t owe anybody your whole life because they could get you through one bad day.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven minutes past four in the afternoon a message came from a number she didn’t know.

You should have kept your old friends.

Then a second.

Magpie remembers who opened the door.

She didn’t answer. She took a screenshot and sent it to Qian and closed the window, and found that her hands had gone completely still in a way that was worse than shaking.

Yu Chen read it over her shoulder and his face went still.

“Come away from the screen.”

“I’ve got work.”

“One minute.”

He held out his hand. She took it. He walked her into the bedroom and sat her on the edge of the bed and crouched in front of her and looked up into her face.

“Are you frightened?”

She tried to say no. Nothing came.

“Yes,” she said.

“That’s all right.”

“I hate that they know where to find me. I hate that they know I gave him the key.”

“You’re not on your own in this room,” he said.

“You don’t have to keep saying that.”

“I’ll keep saying it till you believe it.”

She leaned forward and he caught her, and she put her arms round his neck and held on.

“I want to forget all of it,” she said into his shoulder. “For one minute.”

“Then come here,” he said, and she climbed into his lap.

It was an old habit. It had survived the secret years and the rules and the nine days. She settled sideways against him with her arms round his neck and her forehead against his, and his hands held her waist, and for one minute there was no Magpie and no Calder and no list and no key and no father waiting to turn an emergency into a debt. There was only Yu Chen, and the slow thud of his heart under her arm.

“You’re shaking,” he said.

“I’m tired.”

She kissed him. He kissed her back, gentle, and she took his face in both hands and kissed him again, harder, and felt him smile against her mouth.

“Sweetheart,” he said. “You’ve got work.”

“Don’t ruin it.”

He kissed her once more, slowly, with his hand at the back of her neck. Then he drew back and touched his forehead to hers.

“Go,” he said.

“You’re telling me to get off your lap?”

“I’m telling you to finish what you started. Come back when you need me.”

She looked at him. Then she kissed the corner of his mouth and slid off his knees, and at the doorway she turned round.

“Don’t go anywhere.”

“I won’t,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-six minutes past seven the front door was still locked and the curtains were drawn. The fruit plate was empty. The water glass had been filled twice. He was in the kitchen doing something with soup.

Qian: Families are being moved. No confirmed approach. Stay where you are.

She read it twice and closed the laptop, and for the first time all day she didn’t open it again straight away.

He’d made soup and rice. He put a bowl in front of her and sat down across the table.

“You took the whole day off,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You could have been doing something important.”

“I am,” he said, and picked up his spoon. “Eat.”

Somewhere in the city a crew called Magpie had a list they should never have touched. Somewhere a firm of consultants was waiting to see what it had bought. Somewhere her father knew she had a reason to ring him, and was waiting for the phone.

She reached across the table. He took her hand. He was watching her, not the door, not her phone. Her.

The clock had started. She could hear it. For tonight, she wouldn’t let it decide who her life belonged to.

chapters.title: Thirty-Six Hours
chapters.desc: She doesn’t sleep for a day and a half, hunting the crew that holds her family’s addresses. Yu Chen doesn’t leave. When she finds them, the choice is hers: give it to her father, who would make them vanish, or hand it to the law.
chapters.epigraph: “You didn’t give me a file, or ask me to make anything disappear. You asked me to help you bring it into the light.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past nine on Friday night she rang her sister.

“Where are you?”

“At home,” said Elowen. “Why?”

“Is Zhao there?”

“In the kitchen.”

“Put me on speaker.”

The rustle, and then Zhao’s voice, level. “Here.”

Eliana looked at the dark window of Yu Chen’s study and the two screens in front of her. “Don’t open the shop tomorrow. Don’t go to the market. Don’t go to Jinx’s. If you need anything, Zhao goes.”

“What’s happened?”

“Nothing yet.”

“That isn’t an answer, Eliana.”

“It’s the one I’ve got.” She shut her eyes. “Someone’s got hold of the family’s safe-house addresses.”

The silence on the line was immediate.

“Which addresses?”

“I’m not reading them to you on a phone.”

“Are we in danger?”

“I don’t know yet. Stay in. Don’t talk about it to anyone outside the family.”

“Have you told Baba?”

“No.”

“You can’t do all of it on your own,” said Elowen.

“I know.”

She didn’t know how to say the rest. That she’d been doing it on her own for years. That this time the hole in the wall was hers. That she was afraid of what their father would ask in return if she told him.

“We’ll stay here,” said Zhao. “Nobody goes out.”

She rang Fig Tree Lane next. Jun Hyuk answered on the first ring, which meant he’d been holding the phone.

“Keep Ev at home,” she said. “All weekend.”

“She isn’t going anywhere,” said Jun Hyuk, and that was all he said, and she believed him completely.

When she put the phone down Yu Chen was in the doorway in a dark T-shirt with his hair on end. He’d been trying to sleep.

“You told them?”

“What they need.”

“Good.” He put a glass of water by her elbow. She hadn’t seen him fetch it. “It doesn’t have to solve everything tonight. It has to keep them home tonight.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By midnight his study had turned into something she hadn’t meant to build. Her laptop, his old monitor dragged in from the bedroom, a notebook, a pen she’d chewed flat, and a printout of the safe-house register that she’d kept in a sealed envelope behind the bookcase in her room, because she’d never trusted any single copy of anything to survive. It was three years out of date. It was enough to tell her what had been taken.

He sat on the sofa behind her with a blanket and a textbook and read the same page for twenty minutes. She knew because she looked over her shoulder at it.

“You can sleep,” she said.

“I can.”

“Then do it.”

“I will,” he said, and turned the page he hadn’t read.

At twenty-five to one Qian rang. No confirmed approach on any of the addresses. Nobody had knocked on any door that they knew of.

“No confirmed approach isn’t the same as none,” she said.

“I know. Don’t chase them.”

“I’m not chasing them. I’m tracing them.”

“Eliana.”

“I heard you,” she said, and hung up.

Yu Chen closed his book. “Come and lie down.”

“No.”

“You’ve been at it for nineteen hours.”

“People’s addresses are in somebody’s hands.”

“I know.” He came round the desk and put his hand on the back of her chair. “I’m not asking you to stop. I’m asking you to let your body catch up before it makes a decision your head wouldn’t.”

“Five minutes.”

“Ten.”

“Seven.”

“Eight,” he said, and she almost laughed, and let him take her hand and walk her to the bed.

She lay on top of the covers in her clothes and stared at the ceiling. He sat beside her.

“Do you think they know where everyone is?” she said.

“I don’t know.”

“What if they do?”

“Then we deal with what we know. Not everything we can imagine.”

“That’s easy for you.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t. I’ve stood with families outside a resus bay at four in the morning waiting for somebody to tell them whether someone they love is coming out. I’ve been the one who has to go and tell them. I don’t like waiting any more than you do.” He touched her cheek. “Shut your eyes for eight minutes.”

She didn’t sleep. But for eight minutes she stopped looking at a screen, and he held her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes past three she found the first address.

Not one of theirs. A small commercial lease in the old electronics district, registered to a company with no visible connection to anyone. The lease was old. The money paying it was new. She followed the money through two intermediaries and a third, and the third was a name she’d seen once that afternoon, in the exchange Qian had sent her.

“Yu Chen.”

He was awake at once. He came and stood beside her and didn’t lean over her shoulder or touch the keyboard. He read what she’d put on the screen for him.

“Is that them?”

“A flat above a phone shop. I think it’s where they meet.”

“Tell Qian.”

Qian said wait. He said they’d confirm it themselves. He said, in more words than she’d ever heard him use at once, that a woman who’d been awake for twenty-one hours turning up at a phone shop at four in the morning would make nobody on that list any safer.

“You’re not going on your own,” said Yu Chen when she’d put the phone down.

“I’m not going at all.”

“Good.”

She didn’t go. She did something else. The crew had kept the stolen register on a rented server two countries away, and they’d been careless about the door in the way people often are when they’ve just walked through somebody else’s. At ten to six, while the grey came up behind the curtains, she went in and took it back. Every copy she could find on that machine, and the two it had synced to, folded up and locked and carried home to her own wall, and in their place she left nothing at all. They would know someone had been. They wouldn’t know what else she’d seen.

She didn’t feel triumphant. She sat back and found that her tea had gone cold hours ago and that her hands were shaking again.

“Legal?” said Yu Chen from the doorway.

“Mostly,” said Eliana.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came in without her noticing. She ate half a piece of toast because he stood beside the desk until she did.

At twenty to nine Qian confirmed the phone shop. Nobody there at the moment. A second location somewhere. And something else.

“The list wasn’t all they wanted,” he said. “They’ve been collecting the people round it. Names. Who’s married to who. Who drives which car. Whatever they could get.”

“Calder?”

“We’re still finding out how far.”

At twenty-six minutes past eleven she found how far. The flat above the phone shop had a tenant whose name meant nothing, paying rent from an account that also paid one of Calder Risk Partners’ suppliers. Same chain. Magpie hadn’t just found an old key and helped themselves. Somebody had commissioned them. Somebody had wanted to know where the family went when it needed to disappear.

“That’s enough to escalate,” said Qian.

“To who?”

“People who’ll do it properly.”

“Properly,” she said. “Meaning slowly.”

“Meaning legally.”

She hung up and looked at the drawer she’d brought the folder over in.

She knew exactly what her father would do. He wouldn’t wait for warrants. He wouldn’t wait for interviews or a court. He’d make one call. Magpie would stop existing by Monday, and perhaps Calder too, and the addresses would be safe, and there’d be a desk on the ninth floor of a building on Harbour Road with her name on the door for the rest of her life.

At five past one she stood in his kitchen while he cut vegetables, and said it out loud.

“If I ring my father, he makes it go away.”

He put the knife down. “Probably.”

“He’s got people. He could find Magpie. He could find Calder.”

“What would he want?”

“The job.”

He nodded and leaned on the counter. “Then that’s one door. Your father’s. It’s fast and it’s certain and it’s safe, and you know what it costs.” He paused. “The other door’s the law. Slow. Maybe not certain. People might get hurt while it works.”

“So which?”

“I won’t choose for you.”

“Why not?”

“Because you’ll have to live in whichever life it opens on, after today. I can tell you what each one costs. I can help you think. I’ll stand next to you whichever you pick.” He took her hand. “But I won’t tell you which life to have.”

“What if I pick wrong?”

“Then we’ll deal with what comes.”

“That isn’t reassuring.”

“It’s honest,” he said, and pulled her in against his chest, and she stood there with her eyes stinging. “You don’t have to make the choice that looks strongest. Or the one that makes your father proud. Or the one that proves you aren’t frightened. It belongs to you. That’s all.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to four she didn’t ring her father, and she didn’t ring Qian. She scrolled to a number she’d saved two summers ago under a name she’d chosen herself.

NO FILES.

It rang twice.

“Eliana?”

She heard the surprise in it, small and quickly put away.

“You’re using your own phone,” said Wei Long.

“Yes.”

“Are you safe?”

“I’m with Yu Chen.” She looked across the room at him. He didn’t come closer. He stood by the window and waited. She took a breath. “My name is Eliana Lin. I’m the Eraser.”

The silence went on long enough that she heard his breathing change.

“I know,” he said carefully.

“I need to give you something. A crew called Magpie. And a firm called Calder Risk Partners.”

“Tell me.”

She told him. Not every door she’d walked through, but enough: the key and the breach and the register, Dominic’s name, the payment, the flat over the phone shop, the people Magpie had been collecting round the list. She told him where the evidence was and how it could be checked by someone with the right to check it. He didn’t interrupt once.

“Have you told your father?” he said at the end.

“No.”

“Would he help?”

“Yes.”

“Would he ask you to take the position?”

“Yes.”

“I see.” A breath. “Then you don’t have to give it to him.”

“I want the families safe. I want Magpie found. I want Calder looked at by someone who can’t be bought.” She swallowed. “Can you do it legally?”

“Yes.”

“Even if it’s slow?”

“Yes.”

“Even if my father doesn’t like it?”

“Especially then,” said Song Wei Long. “I won’t promise you an outcome I can’t guarantee. I can put this in front of people who’ll act lawfully and keep the evidence clean and look after the people on that list.” He was quiet for a second. “You gave me your name. You didn’t give me a file, or ask me to make anything disappear. You asked me to help you bring it into the light.”

“Yes,” she said, and her eyes went.

“I’m glad you rang,” he said.

He didn’t ask her to go into the flat. He didn’t ask her to confront Dominic. He asked her to keep everything she had exactly as it was and write down how she’d come by it, and let the investigators do the rest. For once in her life she did as she was told and didn’t try to outrun the process.

At eighteen minutes past seven he rang back. The team had what they needed to begin.

“Tonight?”

“They’re working through the steps.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No. It’s the honest one. Go and rest. You’re not required to stay awake until somebody knocks on a door.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At six minutes past nine she sat down on the camp bed.

He’d brought it into the study at teatime because she wouldn’t leave the desk, and made it up properly: sheet, pillow, folded blanket, a bottle of water on the floor beside it. She sat on the edge. He crouched to straighten the blanket.

“There’s a bed next door,” he said.

“I want to be here when he rings.”

He didn’t argue. He sat down next to her. After a while she turned and said “Come here,” and climbed into his lap with her knees either side of his hips, and he caught her without thinking.

“You’ve been here thirty-six hours,” she whispered.

“Not quite.”

“Don’t correct me.”

He smiled. “All right.”

“You didn’t go to work. You fed me. You checked the door. You made me drink water.”

“Somebody has to.”

“I don’t know how to thank you.”

“Then stay here,” he said.

She kissed him. It was a tired kiss, a little clumsy. Her lips were dry and her eyes were heavy and her fingers got tangled in his hair. But she kissed him as if she’d found the one place in the city where she didn’t have to keep watch, and he held her closer and kissed her back, forehead and cheek and mouth again.

“Sweetheart,” he murmured. “You’re exhausted. Lie down.”

“Will you stay?”

“I’m not going anywhere.”

She slid off his knees onto the camp bed, and he sat on the floor beside it with his hand over hers, and her eyes closed.

At fourteen minutes past one on Sunday morning her phone went and she was awake before it finished the first ring.

“We’re moving,” said Wei Long. “The phone shop. The team has the authority.”

“And Calder?”

“Separate team. Separate warrant.”

The news came in pieces after that. At twenty-seven minutes past three: arrests at the phone shop. At ten past four: Magpie’s records and devices secured and sealed. At twenty-four minutes to six: Calder’s offices searched under warrant, several people taken in to be questioned. It wasn’t over. There’d be interviews and lawyers and months of it. But the people who’d held those addresses weren’t free to do what they liked with them any more.

“Are you all right?” said Wei Long.

She looked at Yu Chen, sitting on the floor beside the camp bed with his hand round hers.

“I think so.”

“You called me by my name tonight. And you gave me yours.” He was quiet. “You can ring again.”

When it ended the room was silent. She put the phone on the floor.

“It’s done,” she said.

“Not all of it.”

“No.”

She looked at him, and her face crumpled. Not dramatically. Just a small collapse of everything she’d been holding up for two days. He opened his arms and she went into them.

“I rang him,” she said into his neck. “I gave him my name. I didn’t ring my father.”

“I know.”

“I thought I’d have to.”

“You didn’t.”

“I was so frightened.”

“I know, sweetheart.”

He helped her up. She was unsteady on her feet, and he put his arm round her waist and walked her to the bedroom, and she changed into one of his shirts while he pulled the covers back, and when she climbed in she reached for him straight away and tucked herself against his chest.

“Do you think my mother would have rung him?” she said after a while. “Uncle Mok says she made Baba wait. She didn’t just agree because he wanted something.”

“I don’t know.”

“Maybe he loved her because she didn’t.”

He kissed her forehead. “You don’t have to be like her to deserve what she had.”

“What did she have?”

“Someone who waited,” he said.

She kissed him once and said “Good night, Doctor,” and he said “Good night, sweetheart,” and at eight minutes to nine on Sunday morning she woke up in sunlight.

Elowen: Everyone’s home. Zhao made breakfast. Nobody’s gone anywhere. Thank you for telling us.

Elowen: Are you safe?

Eliana: yes. it’s being dealt with. i’ll ring later

She put the phone down and turned over. He was awake, watching her.

“I didn’t take the job,” she said.

“You haven’t.”

“You’re not going to ask if I’m going to?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because you haven’t decided,” he said.

She smiled. “I’m starting to like that answer.”

Outside, Sunday went on. Somewhere people in rooms with strip lights were sorting through hard drives and sealing them in bags. A crew had been found. A firm had been opened up. And a woman who’d spent years building walls round everyone she loved had let somebody stand next to her while she opened a door herself.

This time, she slept.

chapters.title: Someone Else’s Blood
chapters.desc: The breach turns physical. A man is sent to frighten Eliana at the dawn flower market, the crowd breaks, and a stallholder is crushed under a van. Yu Chen is there, off duty, and Eliana sees for the first time exactly what he chose to do with his life, and what else his hands can do.
chapters.epigraph: “Same job. Two sides of a wall.”
chapters.content:
The flower market was awake before the sun. At thirteen minutes to five on the last Tuesday in September the narrow streets were already full of handcarts and buckets and men unloading chrysanthemums under yellow shop lights, and the air smelled of wet leaves and cardboard and, somewhere further in, lilies.

Eliana walked beside Elowen with two paper cups of hot soy milk. Yu Chen came half a step behind them with his hands in his jacket pockets. He’d finished a late shift at ten the night before and slept five hours. She’d slept seven, which she counted as a victory.

“You’re walking too slowly,” said Elowen.

“I’m carrying something.”

“It’s soy milk.”

“It’s hot.”

“You’re holding it by the sleeve.”

Eliana looked down, and held it more carefully, and behind her Yu Chen smiled.

“Don’t encourage her,” Elowen told him.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

“His face is perfectly normal,” said Eliana.

“Thank you,” said Yu Chen.

“Don’t look pleased.”

Elowen laughed and pulled her sister away by the arm towards a stall where a man was cutting the strings off bundles of seasonal stems. It had been a week since Wei Long’s teams went into the phone shop. Magpie’s men were in custody. Calder’s partners had lawyers.
