Elowen had decided, on Sunday, that she was not going to stop going to her own market on her own Tuesday because of people who were in custody and people who had lawyers, and Eliana had decided she was going with her.

Yu Chen watched them go. There was a version of Eliana that only came out round Elowen. Less guarded. More childish. She complained and sulked and stole food out of her sister’s hand. He’d known that version since she was nine. He wanted her to have more mornings like this, ordinary ones, mornings that didn’t need anyone to disappear.

✦ ✦ ✦

The man in the grey jacket was standing by a delivery van, and Eliana noticed him because he wasn’t looking at the flowers.

He was looking at Elowen. Not openly. Not all the time. Just often enough.

She slowed. Yu Chen saw her slow and followed her eyes. The man looked away. Forties. Clean-shaven. Grey jacket zipped to the throat, a paper cup in one hand, the other hand in his pocket. He looked like someone waiting for a delivery, except that he’d been waiting too long.

“Jie,” said Eliana. “Go into the warehouse.”

Elowen looked round. “Why?”

“Please.”

Whatever Elowen saw in her face made her stop asking. She went the long way round between two stalls. The man in grey watched her go. Then he came over.

“Lin Eliana?”

She didn’t answer.

“Your sister has a lovely routine,” he said, pleasantly. “Every Tuesday. Same supplier. Same time. Same little walk through the market.” He looked at the warehouse door. “People get comfortable.”

Yu Chen stepped forward. “Who are you?”

“I’m not here for you.”

Eliana looked at the man’s jacket, and his shoes, and the cup, and then at his face.

“Did Calder send you?”

The smile went. Only for a second. She saw it go.

“Never heard of them.”

“That’s a pity,” she said, “because I know you.” She took one step closer. Her voice didn’t rise. “Your name’s Luk Ming-kit. You rent a flat on the twelfth floor of a block in the north estates. Your daughter’s in Primary Three at the school by your mother’s building, and you pick her up on Thursdays because your ex-wife works late on Thursdays.”

The cup trembled in his hand. Yu Chen’s eyes went to her and stayed there.

“You should be careful,” Eliana said, “about bringing your own family into other people’s business.”

“Are you threatening me?”

“No. I’m telling you I know you’ve got a daughter. And asking you to remember that before you frighten anybody else’s family.”

He leaned in. “You think you know everything?”

“I know enough.”

He looked past her at Yu Chen. “You should keep your girlfriend under control.”

Something went out of Yu Chen’s face. Not much. The warmth. “Don’t talk about her,” he said.

Eliana touched his wrist. A small warning. Not yet.

“Your father,” said Luk Ming-kit, “used to be a lot more careful who he let near his family.”

“Then you should ask him what happened to that,” said Eliana, and turned her back on him.

It should have ended there.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first shout came from the far end of the lane. Then another. A loaded trolley went over with a crash. Luk had stepped back into a stack of empty crates, and they came down round him, and a van driver behind them, startled by the noise and the sudden rush of people, leaned on his horn. The van jerked forward. Someone screamed. And the market broke.

People went every way at once. A woman dropped a bucket and chrysanthemums went across the wet stones. Elowen came out of the warehouse door just as a knot of people surged towards it.

“Jie!”

Yu Chen moved first. He got Elowen by the arm and pulled her out of the crush and shoved her back towards the doorway, where two stallholders were dragging people inside.

Eliana turned and saw the van. It was going too fast for the lane. A stallholder in a blue apron was trying to pull a cart of potted orchids out of its way.

“Mrs. Siu!” somebody shouted.

The van hit the cart. Metal screamed on concrete. The woman went down. The van stopped only when its front wheel climbed the kerb of her stall.

For one terrible second the whole market was silent. Then the screaming started, and Eliana ran.

Yu Chen got there first. Mrs. Siu was conscious, grey with pain, her left leg trapped under the cart and the corner of the van’s bumper.

“Don’t move,” said Yu Chen.

His voice was different. Not louder. Clear. He dropped to his knees on the wet stones beside her.

“Mrs. Siu, can you hear me?”

She nodded, gasping. “My leg.”

“I know. Don’t try to move it. I’m going to stay with you.”

“I’m calling an ambulance,” said Eliana.

“Do it.”

Her fingers shook once on the screen and then went steady. She gave the dispatcher the street and the stall, a vehicle against a pedestrian, one woman with a serious lower-leg injury, conscious and breathing. Yu Chen looked up without stopping what he was doing.

“First-aid kit. Somebody’s got one.”

“First-aid kit!” Eliana shouted down the lane, and a man ran.

Yu Chen checked her breathing, her colour, where the blood was coming from. He didn’t try to pull her free. He didn’t try to straighten anything. When the kit came he tore open a dressing and took Eliana’s hand and put it flat on the wound and pressed down.

“There. Hard. Don’t lift it to look. Just keep pressing.”

She pressed. The blood came up warm round her fingers. Her knees were soaked. Her hands were shaking. His weren’t.

“Look at me, Mrs. Siu,” he said. “The ambulance is coming. I’m right here.”

“My flowers,” said the woman. “They’re ruined.”

He glanced at the orchids broken all over the stones. “Then we’ll get you new ones.”

She made a sound that might have been a laugh.

Elowen came out of the warehouse with another dressing and knelt in the wet on the other side. “Tell me where.”

“Here. Help her keep pressure.” He moved Elowen’s hands for her. For a few minutes the three of them knelt round a stranger in a blue apron, Eliana’s hands and Elowen’s together on the dressing, Yu Chen talking the whole time, small questions, her name, what her daughter was called, keeping her looking at him. The sirens took six minutes. It felt like an hour.

When the paramedics knelt down he gave them a handover in under a minute: what had hit her, how she’d been when he reached her, what they’d done, what had changed since. One of them nodded. “We’ve got her.”

He stood up and stepped back. Only then did Eliana see his hands. The blood was up to his wrists. It was on his cuff. He looked down at it once and then at Mrs. Siu being lifted, and at her daughter, who’d come running up the lane in her nightclothes and was asking if she could go in the ambulance.

The doors closed. The ambulance pulled away.

“Your hands,” said Eliana.

“It isn’t mine.”

“I know.” She took his wrist. Now that it was over there was a faint tremor in his fingers. “You were so calm.”

“Somebody had to be.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Look what you did.”

Luk Ming-kit was standing by the fallen crates. His grey jacket was filthy and his face was wild.

“You brought this here,” he said to Eliana. “You threatened me. You started it.”

“I didn’t touch you.”

“You think you’re clever?” He looked at Yu Chen. “And you think you’re a hero because you can play doctor?”

Yu Chen said nothing. He moved so that he was a little in front of her.

“Tell your father Calder isn’t finished,” said Luk.

“Calder’s under investigation,” said Eliana.

“Investigations end.”

“So do prison sentences. Eventually.”

He laughed. And then he shoved her.

It wasn’t a hard push. But the stones were wet, and she was tired and off balance and kneeling a minute ago in a puddle of someone else’s blood, and her heel went. Yu Chen caught her before she fell.

And then something changed.

He moved so fast that she didn’t see it happen. One moment Luk was standing in front of them. The next he was turned away from her, bent forward over a crate, with his right arm locked up behind his back and Yu Chen’s weight on it, and he was crying out.

“Let go!”

“Don’t touch her,” said Yu Chen, low and cold, close to his ear.

The arm was at an angle that made Eliana’s stomach lurch. Luk tried to twist. Yu Chen’s grip shifted, one exact degree, and the man made a high, frightened sound.

“Yu Chen.”

He didn’t look at her.

“Let him go.”

“He pushed you.”

“I know.”

“He could have hurt you.”

“He didn’t.”

Luk tried to wrench free again. She saw Yu Chen’s jaw set. She saw it then, under the calm: not the boy who brought her tea, or the man who remembered which side of the bed she slept on, or the doctor who’d knelt on the stones talking to a frightened woman with his hands full of her blood. Something else. An anger that was frighteningly precise. His hands knew exactly how much force they were using, and exactly how much more there was.

“Yu Chen. Please.”

His eyes came to hers. For one second he didn’t move.

Then he let go and stepped back. Luk stumbled away clutching his shoulder.

“Stay there,” said Yu Chen.

“You’re insane,” said Luk.

Yu Chen didn’t answer. He didn’t go near him again. He stood between him and her and watched him until two market security men came, and then the police. Luk tried to tell them she’d provoked him. Eliana gave them his words about Calder, word for word. Yu Chen stood next to her while she did it, with his hands still red.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove home. He wouldn’t let her, because her hands were still shaking. At a red light he looked across at her.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Your wrist?”

“It’s fine.”

“Let me look when we’re home.”

The light changed.

“You nearly broke his arm,” she said after a while.

His hands tightened on the wheel. “I know.”

“Did you mean to?”

“I meant to stop him.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

He didn’t answer straight away. “I was angry. I didn’t like seeing him put his hands on you.” He breathed out. “I don’t know if I’d have stopped quickly enough if you hadn’t said my name.”

There was no pride in his face. No satisfaction. Only a quiet recognition of something in himself he hadn’t liked.

She reached over the gearstick and touched his fingers. “You stopped.”

“Because you asked.”

“That matters.”

He turned his hand over and held hers. “Yes.”

“I saw you today,” she said, looking out of the window. “With Mrs. Siu. You knew what to do. You didn’t panic. You didn’t make it about you. You just kept talking to her.” She looked at their hands. “I think I understood for the first time. That you chose this. You chose to spend your life putting your hands between people and the worst thing that can happen to them.”

“Not every time,” he said.

“No. But you try.” She swallowed. “And then I saw what the same hands can do to someone who hurts me.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be sorry you stopped him. Be sorry you nearly went too far.”

“I am.”

“I’m not pretending I wasn’t frightened,” she said. “But I’m not afraid of you.”

He looked at her a second longer than he should have, and then back at the road.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home he washed his hands twice. The first time to get the blood off. The second because he couldn’t quite convince himself it was gone. She stood in the bathroom doorway and watched the pink go down the drain.

“Come here,” she said.

He turned the tap off. She held out a towel and he dried his hands. Then she stepped past him and turned on the shower.

“What are you doing?”

She stepped under it in her clothes. The water darkened her shirt and flattened her hair. She held out her hand.

“Eliana.”

“Come here.”

He looked at her for another second. Then he stepped in after her, fully dressed, and the water ran down over both of them.

She reached for his face. He caught her wrists, gently. “You’ll catch a cold.”

“Probably.”

She kissed him. He went still, and then his hands came down to her waist. Nothing about it was playful: the kind of kiss that asks someone to come back from wherever you watched them go. He kissed her carefully, his hand at the back of her wet head.

“I saw your hands,” she said against his mouth. “I saw you hold Mrs. Siu’s. And I saw you hold his arm.”

“I’m sorry you had to see that.”

“I didn’t want to look away.” She touched his cheek. “I know you’re gentle. I know you can hurt someone too. I don’t want you to become someone who thinks that’s the only way to look after me.”

“I don’t want that either,” he said.

She undid his shirt under the water, button by button, and peeled it off his shoulders, and it fell with a wet slap on the tiles. He pulled hers over her head. They got the rest off between them, clumsy, laughing once when her jeans wouldn’t come down over her wet hips, and then not laughing. He turned the water warmer. She put her palms flat on his chest and felt his heart and stood there.

“Can you hold me?” she said.

He held her under the water, skin to skin, his chin on her hair, until her shoulders stopped shaking. Then he turned the water off and wrapped her in a towel and carried her to bed with her wet hair soaking the pillow.

There was no hurry in it. He didn’t try to make her forget the morning. He touched her as if he understood that some things can’t be kissed away, only carried more gently. When she trembled he drew her closer. When she kissed him he answered. He moved down her body slowly, kissing the bruise coming up on her wrist, the inside of her elbow, her ribs, her hip, and she pulled him back up and over her and guided him in and wrapped herself round him. He moved in her slow and deep and careful, his forehead against hers, his eyes open, and she held his face and watched him the whole time. When it came for her she said his name and he said hers, and afterwards he stayed inside her a long time, not moving, just holding her.

“Today I understood something,” she said into his neck. “We do the same job.”

“Do we?”

“You stand between people and the things that hurt them.” She touched his chest. “I stand on the other side of a wall and try to stop those things before they get there. Same job. Two sides of a wall.”

“Maybe,” he said. He brushed her wet hair off her face. “I think you spend too much time thinking you’re on the other side. You’re one of the people I’m trying to protect too. You don’t have to be useful to deserve that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past six she woke. He was beside her, reading on his phone, and put it down the second she moved.

Elowen: Mrs. Siu’s daughter says she’s stable. They’re working on the leg. Thank you for staying with her.

She showed him. He read it and nodded.

“Your hands are clean,” she said.

He looked at them. “Yes.”

She took one and turned it over and kissed the palm. Then the other.

The market would open again in the morning. Mrs. Siu’s stall wouldn’t. A man in a grey jacket would be answering questions about who’d sent him. And Eliana would remember Yu Chen’s voice telling a frightened woman not to move, and his hands full of a stranger’s blood, and the way he’d let go the moment she said his name.

“Yu Chen,” she said. “Next time, don’t let go of my hand.”

His fingers closed round hers. “I won’t.”

chapters.title: The First Child to Say No to His Face
chapters.desc: At the Mid-Autumn table, with the whole family watching, Lin Jian announces the job as a thing already decided. Eliana turns it down, and him, out loud and to his face. Nobody in the house has ever done that before.
chapters.epigraph: “But not wanting something is enough not to give my life to it.”
chapters.content:
At thirteen minutes past eight on the morning of Mid-Autumn, Wei Long sent one word.

Wei Long: Done.

Then, a minute later:

Wei Long: Charged this morning, all of them. Magpie and Calder both. The evidence is sealed and the case goes on properly. The addresses are protected. You can breathe.

She was sitting on Yu Chen’s kitchen counter in his shirt with a cup of tea gone cold in her hands. He was at the stove. She turned the phone so he could read it.

“It’s over?” he said.

“The charging is. The rest will take a year.”

“That’s good.”

“Yes.”

It wasn’t a clean ending. There’d be a court and lawyers and months of it, and outcomes neither she nor her father could decide. But it was an ending she hadn’t had to pay for with her life. She sat looking at the screen until he put a plate of eggs beside her on the counter.

“I’m not hungry.”

“That’s a pity. I made two.” He kissed her temple on his way past. “Happy Mid-Autumn.”

“It’s tonight.”

“I’m early. I’m a doctor. I’m allowed exceptions.”

At twenty to twelve someone knocked. A young woman in a cardigan stood on his front step holding a bunch of yellow chrysanthemums wrapped in brown paper.

“Is Eliana here? I’m Siu Wing-yan. Mrs. Siu’s daughter. From the market.”

Eliana came down the hall so fast she nearly slid. “How is she?”

“Better. Much better.” The young woman held out the flowers. “My mother wanted you to have these. They kept her leg.”

Eliana took the paper in both hands. “They kept it?”

“She’ll need months of physio and she won’t be standing at a stall all day for a long while. But the surgeons are happy.” Wing-yan smiled. “She tells everyone on her ward about the young doctor who wouldn’t let her move, and the two sisters who knelt in the wet with her.”

“She was brave,” said Yu Chen, behind Eliana.

“She says you promised her new orchids.”

He blinked. Then he smiled. “I did.”

“She intends to collect. She also says you were handsome.” Wing-yan considered him. “And frightening, when you were shouting at people not to touch her.”

“That’s more accurate,” said Eliana, and Wing-yan laughed and went.

Eliana stood in the doorway holding the chrysanthemums. He came and put his arms round her from behind.

“She kept her leg,” she said.

“Yes.”

She turned and put her face in his shirt and stayed there without explaining. He didn’t ask her to.

“I want to buy her orchids,” she said eventually.

“Then we’ll buy her orchids.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The tall house smelled of pomelo and roast duck and incense. By six the courtyard was hung with lanterns, red and gold under the eaves, and out in the lane the neighbours’ children were running up and down with paper rabbits on sticks, their ears bobbing. A big plate of mooncakes sat in the middle of the long table. It was the same evening Eliana had sat through every year of her life, and she’d never once felt it belonged to her.

Elowen and Zhao had come in through the red door with her. Raiden and Jinx were at the end of the table already arguing. Evangeline was stealing pomelo off Raiden’s plate. Elara and Xing Yue sat across from Wei Long. Ah Sim was everywhere at once.

Baba sat in the carved chair at the head. He looked up when she came in. His eyes went over her face once, and then back to his tea.

Yu Chen came last, because Elowen had asked him and because Auntie Tsoi had sent him with a box of her lotus pastries and instructions not to come back with it. He put the box down beside the mooncakes and took the empty chair next to Eliana. Under the table his knee found hers and stayed.

For a while it was warm. Raiden complained about the traffic and Jinx told him he was the traffic. Xing Yue said something dry about the number of lanterns that made Elara laugh into her napkin. Ev asked Elowen when the shop would take seasonal orders again. Eliana ate duck and felt Yu Chen’s knee against hers and let herself believe, for twenty minutes, that it was an ordinary dinner.

Then Baba put his chopsticks down.

“I have something to say.” The table quieted. “The position we discussed in August has been arranged. The Syndicate has made its preparations. Qian has been told. Her office will be ready on Monday.” He picked up his cup. “She starts then.”

Nobody moved.

He went on as if he were talking about the gutters. “The first month she reviews the existing structure. After that she takes it over.”

Eliana put her tea down. “I’m not starting on Monday.”

He didn’t look at her. “The arrangements have been made.”

“I know.”

“Then there’s nothing to discuss.”

“There’s something to discuss.”

“Not at this table.”

“Then look at me,” she said.

It wasn’t loud. It stopped him. He raised his eyes.

She stood up. Her chair went back on the tiles. She could feel the whole table: Elowen’s hand tight on her napkin, Ev gone completely still, Yu Chen beside her not reaching for her and not interrupting.

“I’m not taking the position,” she said.

“Eliana.”

“No.”

It was a small word. It was the first time she’d ever said it to him like that. Not through Elowen. Not in a message. Not behind her bedroom door. To his face, at his table, in front of everyone.

“I won’t work for the Syndicate full time. I won’t be its head of security. I won’t sign a contract that ties me to this house for the rest of my life.”

“You’ve been offered something most people would spend their whole lives trying to get.”

“I know.”

“Then why refuse it?”

“Because I don’t want it.”

“Wanting isn’t enough to build a life on.”

“No,” she said. “But not wanting something is enough not to give my life to it.”

He looked at her as if she were a problem he hadn’t planned for. “You’re being childish.”

Her throat closed. She almost looked down. Then she thought of the flat over the phone shop and the blood to Yu Chen’s wrists and the night she’d had her thumb over his number and hadn’t pressed it. She’d done the hard thing once. She’d asked for help without handing herself over. She could do this.

“I’m twenty-two,” she said. “I’ve got a degree. I’ve got work I chose myself. I’m not a child waiting for you to decide where to put me.”

“You’re a Lin.”

“I know my name.”

“Then behave like one.”

“What does that mean?” He didn’t answer. She heard herself laugh, a small hard sound. “You say I’m a Lin when you want me to do as I’m told. When have you ever wanted to know who I am?”

His face went still.

“Eliana,” whispered Elowen.

But she’d started. “You made arrangements for me without asking. You told this whole table I’d take it. You decided where I’d work and what I’d do and how long I’d stay, and you never once asked me.”

“Someone has to think about your future.”

“You don’t know anything about my future.”

His eyes went past her. “Does he?”

Yu Chen didn’t move.

“Don’t bring him into this,” she said.

“He has no idea what this family carries.”

“Then you should have taught me.” She took a breath that hurt. “I grew up in this house watching everyone else know where they belonged. Elowen had you. You walked her down the aisle and cried. You knew how to be proud of her. You knew how to worry about her. You knew how to look at her when she talked.” Elowen looked down at her plate. “With me you always had something else to do.”

“You don’t understand.”

“Then explain it.”

He said nothing.

The words came out before she could soften them.

“I know what I am to you. I’m the day she died.”

The table went completely silent. Out in the lane a child laughed, and a paper lantern caught a gust and rattled.

“The day your wife died having me,” she said. “That’s what I’ve been in this house. Not your daughter. Not somebody you wanted to know. The day she died.”

Something changed in his face. Not anger. Something much older, and much worse.

“Don’t speak about things you don’t understand.”

“I don’t understand because you never told me.”

He stood up. The carved chair scraped back and she flinched before she could stop herself, and under the table Yu Chen’s hand found hers and held on. He didn’t stand. He didn’t speak.

Baba looked at their hands, and then at him. “You have no place in this.”

“I haven’t said a word, Mr. Lin.”

“Then don’t.”

“Stop it,” said Eliana. “Don’t talk to him like that because you can’t answer me. I’m not taking the job. I’m not staying because you want me where you can see me. And I’m not spending the rest of my life trying to make you look at me.”

For a second she thought he’d say something about her mother. He didn’t. He looked down at the table, at the mooncakes and the chrysanthemums and the faces gone quiet all round it.

“Sit down,” he said. “Dinner isn’t finished.”

“I am,” said Eliana, and picked up her bag, and walked out through the courtyard with Yu Chen behind her.

✦ ✦ ✦

On her front step, against the knee-high wall, sat a rabbit lantern.

White paper, pink ears, a round tail, and a little light glowing inside it. She stopped.

“Yours?” she said.

“I bought it last night. I wasn’t sure if it was too childish.”

“So you brought it anyway.”

“I thought it deserved to be seen,” he said.

She sat down on the step. He sat beside her with the lantern between them.

“Did you hear all of it?”

“Yes.”

“I said it in front of everyone. To him.” Her voice went small. “I’ve never done that.”

“I know.”

“Was I cruel?”

He thought about it, because he always did. “No.”

“I said I was the day she died.”

“You said that’s what you’ve been to him. You told him what it was like to grow up in a house without being seen.” He brushed his thumb under her eye. “You were allowed to say it.”

“I don’t know if he understood.”

“Maybe he didn’t.”

“That’s not comforting.”

“I don’t want to lie to you,” he said.

She looked at him in the warm paper light, an ordinary young man in a dark shirt with his sleeves rolled up, and found she could breathe because he was there. She leaned across the lantern and kissed him. He caught her by the waist. The rabbit’s light fell over their hands. She kissed him once, and then again, with the lane full of other people’s children shrieking over their paper animals.

“Happy Mid-Autumn, sweetheart,” he said against her forehead.

“Happy Mid-Autumn,” she said, “my Yu Chen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen found her an hour later sitting on the floor of her bedroom in pyjamas with the lantern on the windowsill.

“I stole a mooncake,” said Elowen, and sat down beside her.

“From the table?”

“Obviously.”

“Baba’ll notice.”

“Let him.”

Elowen broke it in half and gave her the bigger piece. Lotus paste and a salted yolk. They ate in the light of the paper rabbit.

“I never thought you were the day she died,” said Elowen. “I was seven. I don’t remember much about Mama. I remember you. You were so small. I used to think if I stayed close enough you wouldn’t feel alone.”

“You did.”

“Not enough.”

“You were my sister,” said Eliana.

“I still am.” Elowen put an arm round her. “Nobody’s ever said no to him like that. Not once. You were terrifying.”

“I was shaking.”

“I know,” said Elowen, and kissed the top of her head. “That’s what made it brave.”

It was nearly midnight when she went. Eliana walked her down and came back up and put the rest of the mooncake in a tin and washed her hands and sat on the edge of the bed.

A shadow came under her door.

She knew the shape of the shoes. The stillness. The way he never knocked unless he’d already decided he could bear the answer.

She didn’t move. The shadow stayed. She heard a small shift of weight on the boards. For years she’d wished he would come in. Not to talk about her work or what she’d done wrong or her mother. Just to sit down on the end of the bed and ask if she’d eaten. If she was happy. If she wanted anything at all.

The shadow stayed another minute. Then the footsteps went away along the passage.

She didn’t cry. She turned off the big light and left the rabbit glowing.

Across the courtyard Lin Jian stood under the eaves looking up at the curtain with the little light behind it. I’m the day she died. He remembered a different woman in a flower shop years ago, refusing to let him choose. He remembered standing outside on the pavement while she took far too long to decide, and her laughing at him through the glass. He remembered the corridor. He’d spent twenty-two years refusing to look at the resemblance too closely. Tonight his daughter had stood up at his table and made him look.

He stood there until the lantern went out.

Yu Chen: Home?

Eliana: home

Yu Chen: Lantern safe?

Eliana: yes

She typed something and deleted it, and typed it again.

Eliana: i said no

Yu Chen: I heard you.

Eliana: i think i’m proud of myself

Yu Chen: You should be.

Outside her door the passage was quiet. For the first time in her life she didn’t lie awake listening for whether he’d come back. She shut her eyes under the glow of the paper rabbit and let herself be proud.

chapters.title: The Eldest Sister Takes Her Side
chapters.desc: The eldest sister comes to the tall house and says to their father the thing the family has let him avoid for twenty-two years. It doesn’t mend him. But it makes him stop, and that evening, on the roof next door, Eliana says she’s leaving.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re not leaving your family. And you’re not losing your home. You’re choosing another one.”
chapters.content:
For six days after Mid-Autumn, Baba didn’t leave his study.

He ate when Ah Sim carried a tray up. He slept, though nobody knew how much. He took the calls that mattered and let the others ring out. The house learned to move round the shut door the way water moves round a stone. Nobody mentioned the dinner. Nobody mentioned the job. Nobody said out loud the sentence his youngest daughter had left on the table.

On the first day Elowen waited. On the second she asked Ah Sim whether he was eating. On the third she went upstairs and stood outside his door. On the fourth she knocked, and he didn’t answer. On the fifth she went home to Zhao. On the sixth, a Sunday, she came back at seventeen minutes past ten in the morning and went into her father’s study without knocking.

He was at his desk with papers in front of him and his reading glasses pushed up on his forehead and a cup of tea gone cold at his elbow.

“You should knock,” he said.

“I did. On Thursday.”

“You didn’t wait.”

“I’ve waited six days.” She shut the door behind her. “I need to talk to you about Eliana.”

His pen stopped. Then it went on. “She’s made her decision.”

“I know.”

“Then there’s nothing to talk about.”

“That’s what you always do,” said Elowen. “You decide a thing is finished because you don’t want to talk about it.”

He looked up. “Elowen.”

“No. You’re going to listen.”

She had hardly ever spoken to him like that. Even after her own wedding, even with a life of her own on the hill with Zhao, she’d kept a careful distance round him. She’d learned to disagree without making him angry. She’d learned to steer a conversation away before it turned. She’d learned to protect her little sister without ever quite standing in front of him. She’d spent thirty years being the eldest, and she’d mistaken that, for most of them, for being in charge of keeping the peace. She was only just beginning to understand that the peace had usually meant Eliana being quiet.

“Do you think she doesn’t know why you treat her the way you do?” she said.

He put the pen down. “She doesn’t understand the circumstances.”

“She understands them better than you think.”

“She was a child.”

“She was a child when you stopped looking at her. She’s twenty-two now. She remembers every time you looked straight through her.” Elowen’s hands were trembling. She held them together. “I remember Mama too. I remember the house before. I remember her laughing. I remember her making you wait outside shops because she couldn’t decide. I remember you happy.”

“That’s enough.”

“It isn’t. You loved her. I know you did. But Eliana didn’t take her away from you.”

“I never said she did.”

“You didn’t have to say it.” The words sat between them on the desk. “You never said it. You just made her live with it. Every birthday. Every dinner. Every time she tried to show you something and you turned your head.”

He looked down at his hands.

“She was always reminded of that day,” he said.

Elowen frowned. “Who was?”

He didn’t answer, and she understood: he hadn’t meant Eliana. He’d meant himself.

“Then you should have told somebody,” she said, more gently, not retreating an inch. “You should have gone away for a while. You should have let us help. You should have found a way to grieve that didn’t make your daughter carry it.”

“You don’t know what it was like.”

“No. I didn’t lose my wife. I was seven.” She paused. “But I lost my mother too. And Eliana lost hers before she ever had the chance to know her. We both did. But you made sure Eliana lost something else as well.”

“What?”

“Her father.”

He looked away to the window.

“You walked me down the aisle,” said Elowen. “You cried at my wedding. You came to the hill the week Zhao and I moved and stood in the garden telling him where the drains should go. You ask whether Ev’s eating. You know Raiden’s work schedule. You know which Saturday Jinx’s father comes for fish.” Her voice cracked. “You know how to love people, Baba. You just never let yourself love her.”

His face changed then. Elowen had seen him angry and cold, and frightened, though he’d have denied it. She’d never seen him look so completely tired.

“Every time I look at her,” he said at last, “I’m in that corridor.”

She went still.

“The hospital. The doctor coming out. The way they all looked at me.” His fingers curled against the desk. “I remember being told she was alive.”

“And your first thought?”

He didn’t answer.

“Baba.”

“I couldn’t understand why,” he said, so low she barely heard it. “Why she was alive and your mother wasn’t.”

The room was silent. A car went by at the mouth of the alley.

“Every time I looked at her I saw the doors. I heard them telling me there was nothing more they could do. I thought if I looked at her long enough I’d see her mother in her. Some part of her that would explain where she’d gone.” His voice went rough. “When I didn’t, I couldn’t bear it.”

“So you made her bear it instead,” said Elowen. There were tears on her face now. “She was a day old. She needed you to pick her up. To tell her she was wanted. To say happy birthday. To ask if she’d eaten. To be proud of her when she graduated. You could have loved both of them.”

His eyes dropped.

“I know,” he said.

Two words. She’d never heard him say them in her life. Not I understand. Not you don’t know. Just I know.

“I can’t forgive you on her behalf,” she said. “And I won’t ask her to. But I’m not going to let you go on pretending she was the problem.” At the door she turned round. “She doesn’t need you to turn into a different man overnight. She doesn’t even need you to explain it all today. She just needs you to stop making her feel she should apologise for being alive.”

She went out and shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-four minutes to one Eliana’s phone lit up on Yu Chen’s dining table.

Elowen: are you at his house

Eliana: yes

Elowen: can I come round? don’t cook. I’m bringing lunch

“Your sister’s coming,” said Yu Chen, from behind a journal.

“How do you know?”

“You smiled at your phone.”

“I smile at my phone all the time.”

“Not like that,” he said, and turned a page.

Elowen arrived with two bags of shopping and a box of pastries she claimed had been on offer. They ate at his table. She talked about the shop and an order of four hundred white roses for a funeral and Zhao’s attempt to mend a cupboard door that had been fine until he touched it. Eliana laughed. Yu Chen put in a sentence now and then. It was easy, and ordinary, until Elowen put down her chopsticks.

“I spoke to Baba this morning.”

Eliana’s smile went. “Oh.”

“I went into his study. I didn’t knock.” Elowen folded her hands. “He told me something. He said every time he looks at you he’s back in the hospital corridor. He said when they told him you’d lived, he couldn’t understand why you were alive and Mama wasn’t.”

Eliana looked at the table.

“I thought so,” she said at last.

“You knew?”

“Not exactly. I knew he couldn’t look at me without remembering. I didn’t know if he remembered the day, or if he thought I was the reason.” She gave a faint smile. “Did he say I wasn’t?”

“No,” said Elowen. “But he knows. I told him he’d made you carry something that was never yours.”

“To his face?”

“To his face.”

Eliana let out a breath that was almost a laugh. “Jie. You’re terrifying.”

“I’m your eldest sister,” said Elowen, and Eliana leaned across the table and hugged her, and Elowen held on hard.

“I should have said it years ago,” Elowen said into her hair.

“You were always there.”

“Not enough.”

“You were there,” said Eliana, and Yu Chen got up without a word and went to make tea.

When he came back with the pot, Elowen was wiping her face with a napkin and looking at him with an expression he couldn’t read.

“I’ve known about you since my wedding,” she said. “In case you two were wondering.”

Eliana sat bolt upright. “What?”

“I came back for my phone at half past one on the Friday night. You were asleep behind the counter on a folded blanket with your claw clip falling out and your glasses on your head.” Elowen looked at Yu Chen over the napkin. “There was a man’s leather jacket over you, far too big. And a steel flask of milk tea by your hand. I knew whose jacket it was. I’d seen it on the boy next door leaning on our garden wall every winter since he was fourteen.”

Yu Chen looked at the teapot.

“So you knew,” said Eliana.

“I put the flask closer to your hand,” said Elowen, “and turned off the work lights, and went home. And the next night you came in from the back lane wearing it.”

“You turned the lights off,” said Eliana slowly. “I woke up and they were off. I thought—“

“You thought he’d done it.”

“I left them on,” said Yu Chen, “so you wouldn’t wake up in the dark.”

Elowen smiled at him then, properly, for the first time Eliana could remember. “I know. That’s when I decided you were all right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty past four Ah Sim came across from the tall house with a paper bag.

“Your father asked me to bring these,” she said, and put it in Eliana’s hands.

Persimmons. Six of them, bright orange and firm, with their little green caps still on. From the branch of the old tree in the Song garden that had hung over the Lin side of the wall for thirty years, the one Yu Chen had climbed onto his roof by since he was ten.

“He said they were ripe,” said Ah Sim. “He said—“ She stopped, and looked at Yu Chen, standing by the window. “He said to tell you to take some to the boy.”

Nobody spoke. Elowen looked down at her hands.

Eliana held the bag. She remembered, from somewhere she couldn’t place, that her mother had liked persimmons. That she’d said the ones from that branch were sweeter if you left them a few days.

“Did he say anything else?”

“Only that,” said Ah Sim.

She didn’t know what it meant. A peace offering. An apology. A reminder of someone they’d both lost. Or six ripe persimmons that her father had finally remembered she might like. She decided not to make it bigger than it was. But she didn’t put them away. She set them on his kitchen counter, where she’d see them.

“That’s something,” said Elowen.

“It’s a quiet yes,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she went next door to the tall house for some books. She stood in the doorway of her own room with a bag on her arm and looked at it. The same desk. The same window. The same curtains. The corner where she’d once hidden a drawing of the two of them under a chemistry textbook. She’d spent years making this room into a place she could disappear into. She didn’t know any more whether she wanted to go on living in it.

She went back across the garden, climbed the old persimmon onto his flat roof, and found him sitting by the low parapet with two cups of tea.

“You brought a bag,” he said.

“I did.”

“Are you moving out?”

“Maybe.”

She sat down next to him. The evening was cool. Lanterns left over from Mid-Autumn still glowed in the windows round the Walled City, and down in the lane a child was practising with one, swinging it too hard.

“Yu Chen,” she said. “I think I want to move in.”

He turned his head.

“Properly. Not staying over. My clothes, my books, my computer. I want to have breakfast with you without pretending I’ve got to go home after. I want my own key. I want to leave my things in your bathroom without you putting them back in my bag. I want to complain that you take up too much of the bed.”

“I don’t take up too much of the bed.”

“You do.”

“You steal the blanket.”

“Because you take up too much bed.” She looked at him. “So?”

“Not because of your father?”

“Partly,” she said honestly. “Mostly because I want to live with you.”

He looked at her a long moment.

“Yes,” he said.

“Yes?”

“Yes, sweetheart.”

She leaned in and he caught her face and kissed her, and she laughed against his mouth, and he kissed her again. Then he stood up and pulled her up with him, put both arms round her waist and lifted her clean off the roof.

“Yu Chen!”

He spun her once. She shrieked and grabbed his shoulders. He spun her again, laughing now, really laughing, and set her down just long enough to kiss her properly. She was out of breath when he let her go.

“You’re ridiculous,” she said.

“You’re moving in.”

He was smiling in a way she almost never saw on him. Not the small held-back one he used for teasing. Open, all the way up, like a boy.

“You’re happy,” she said.

“Yes.”

“How happy?”

“More than I can say,” he said, and for once she let him off.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty minutes later she was standing in front of his wardrobe. She opened the left door, and the right. Half of it was empty. A lot of it.

“You cleared this.”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“A while ago.”

“How long is a while?”

He considered. “Several months.”

She opened the bottom drawer. Folded blankets, a spare pillowcase, and a small box of hair ties. At the top, the pale blue one she’d lost in his bathroom in the spring.

“Why are there hair ties?”

“You leave them everywhere. I collected them.”

She started laughing. Then she stopped, because she’d turned round and seen the chair.

It stood by his window. Simple, warm wood, a curved back, a pale cushion. It was almost exactly the chair in her bedroom, the one she’d drawn in and read in since she was fifteen.

“Why do you have my chair?”

“So you could sit here.”

“When did you buy it?”

“Four months ago.”

“How did you get it the right height?”

He looked, for the first time in her memory, mildly embarrassed. “I measured yours.”

“When?”

“One afternoon.”

“When I was asleep?”

He didn’t answer.

“You measured my chair while I was asleep in it?”

“I didn’t want to wake you. You were comfortable.”

She stared at him, and then she burst out laughing so hard she had to sit down, and she sat down in the chair, and her feet reached the floor exactly the way they did at home.

“You got it right,” she said.

“I know.”

“You’re strange.”

“I know.”

“So strange,” she said, and pulled him down by his shirt and kissed him.

Later they sat by the window with the persimmons, washed and sliced on a plate.

“They’re sweet,” she said.

“Ripe.”

“My father used to bring them in for my mother. I don’t remember him ever bringing them for me.” She turned a slice over. “Do you think it means yes? To me moving?”

“I think it’s a quiet one,” he said.

At eighteen minutes past eleven she went back across to the tall house for the rest of her books. He went with her, because she said she could carry books and he said he knew she could, and she said then why was he coming, and he said because he liked helping her, and she let him carry the books.

At the front door of the tall house she stopped and looked up the dark stairs.

“I’m really leaving,” she said.

She didn’t mean books. He knew. She was leaving the house where she’d spent twenty-two years trying to become somebody her father could look at without remembering the worst day of his life. The room where she’d learned to be quiet. The step where she’d waited for a happy birthday.

“You’re not leaving your family,” he said. “And you’re not losing your home. You’re choosing another one.”

She looked at their joined hands, and smiled, and pulled the door shut behind her, and walked next door with him.

chapters.title: Two Boxes and a Monitor
chapters.desc: Eliana moves out of the tall house where she’s lived at the top of the stairs in the dark. It takes two boxes, a suitcase of hard drives and one monitor. He carries the monitor. She doesn’t go far, only next door, which was always where she was going.
chapters.epigraph: “Now you can just turn over.”
chapters.content:
Her whole life, it turned out, fitted into two cardboard boxes, one suitcase of hard drives, and a monitor that Yu Chen wouldn’t let her carry.

“This is ridiculous,” she said.

He was standing in the doorway of her bedroom in the tall house on the second Saturday in November, holding the monitor against his chest with both arms.

“Which part?”

“You’re carrying it as if it’s a sleeping kitten.”

“It’s expensive.”

“So am I.”

He looked at her over the top of it. She smiled.

“I’m joking.”

“I know,” he said, and edged it sideways round the doorframe without touching the wood.

She looked round the room. The desk was nearly bare. The books she wanted were in the boxes. Most of her clothes had already wandered next door over the past month and the rest were folded in the suitcase on top of the drives. Chargers, headphones, notebooks, and the small collection of things she insisted weren’t sentimental and would never throw away. At the back of the desk drawer she found a drawing on squared paper, two houses side by side joined by a crooked line, and folded it small and put it in the front pocket of her bag.

“Anything else?” he said.

“No.”

The room looked bigger with nothing in it. The shelves bare. The chair gone from the window. For years this was where she’d gone when the house was too quiet or too cold. She’d lain here at night listening to footsteps in the passage, waiting for a door that never opened. She’d thought leaving would feel like something. It felt like forgetting her keys.

“Come on, sweetheart,” he said.

She picked up both boxes at once.

“I can take those.”

“They’re light.”

“Give me one.”

“No.”

“Eliana.”

“Yu Chen.”

He sighed. “Then I’ll carry the monitor and the suitcase.”

“Good compromise.”

“It’s not a compromise. It’s me giving up,” he said, and she laughed and went past him down the stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ah Sim was waiting in the hall with her hands folded.

“Miss.”

“Ah Sim.”

“Today?”

“Today.”

Ah Sim looked at the two boxes. “That’s all?”

“Most of it’s already next door.”

“Still. Two boxes.” She looked past Eliana at Yu Chen coming down with the monitor held level like a tray of soup. “Doctor Wang. Don’t let her carry everything herself.”

“I won’t.”

“I can hear you,” said Eliana.

“Good,” said Ah Sim, and took one of the boxes from her. At the shoe cabinet Eliana stopped and took out the slippers she’d worn all through university. Ah Sim watched her.

“You’ll come back for breakfast,” she said. It wasn’t a question. “Every day. If you don’t, I’ll send someone to fetch you.”

“I’m moving next door, not to the other side of the sea.”

“Exactly,” said Ah Sim. “So there’s no excuse.”

“That’s fair,” said Yu Chen, and Eliana told him not to take sides, and he said he wasn’t, and Ah Sim looked deeply satisfied.

Baba was in the front hall.

She hadn’t heard him come down. He was standing by the door to the study in his house clothes, as if he’d been on his way somewhere and stopped. They hadn’t spoken properly since Mid-Autumn. Five weeks. The persimmons. Breakfast at the same table, twice, in silence.

He looked at the monitor in Yu Chen’s arms, and then he stepped aside.

“Careful with the corner,” he said.

“Thank you,” said Yu Chen, and carried it through.

Baba’s eyes went to the boxes. “What’s in those?”

“Books. Clothes. Some things.”

“Your computer?”

“In the suitcase.”

He nodded. Then: “That monitor. Is it connected to the cameras?”

“No. The cameras run on their own.”

“Then make sure none of the old equipment’s still wired in here. Nothing left listening in the walls.”

“I checked on Thursday.”

He nodded again. It was an ordinary question. A practical one. He’d asked it, all the same. He looked at the open front door, and stepped forward, and held it wider.

“Go,” he said.

She didn’t know what to do with it. She walked past him with her box.

“Thank you, Baba.”

He didn’t answer. But he held the door until the second box was through.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took less than a minute to walk next door. He’d left his front door open. The house smelled of coffee and clean washing. The monitor was already on the long desk in his study, the suitcase by the wardrobe, the boxes on the floor. In his bedroom her chair stood by the window, the one he’d bought four months ago and measured against hers while she slept.

“You really got everything ready,” she said.

“I wanted you to have somewhere to put your things.”

“You could have given me a drawer.”

“I did. And a wardrobe. You needed the space.”

She walked round the room touching small things as if to make sure they were real. The second lamp. The little dish for earrings. A second toothbrush in the bathroom. Her clothes hung on the left of the wardrobe and his on the right, and hers had more room.

“You left me more space.”

“You have more clothes.”

“I do not.”

He looked at the wardrobe. He looked at her.

“Don’t,” she said, and put her arms round his waist.

He rested his chin on her head. “Welcome home.”

She shut her eyes and couldn’t answer.

“I’m home,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night was the first night in her life she didn’t have to leave.

It began with her complaining that his bedside lamp was too bright, and him tilting it. Then that the duvet was too warm, and him folding it back. Then that he was laughing at her. He said he wasn’t. She said his face was. He laughed properly, and she kissed him to make him stop, and it was meant to be quick.

It wasn’t. He drew her in and she put her arms round his neck and they kissed slowly, with the ease of people who knew each other too well to hurry. He stopped once to look at her.

“Comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“Happy?”

“Yes,” she said, and pulled his T-shirt over his head.

There was nowhere she had to be by morning. Nobody to creep past. No gate to climb back over before Ah Sim was up. He undressed her as if he had a whole lifetime to do it in, which, she thought, with her heart going, perhaps he did. He kissed her shoulder and the inside of her wrist and the soft skin under her breast, and she lay back on sheets that smelled of both of them and watched him in the lamplight. When he came into her she said his name out loud, at an ordinary volume, in an ordinary voice, for the first time in four years, because nobody would be climbing a wall at dawn and the only other person in the house was Auntie Tsoi, who slept like a stone downstairs and had known about them since before Eliana did. He went still and looked down at her as if she’d given him something.

They didn’t rush any of it. He moved in her slowly and she moved with him, and when it built too fast she put her hand flat on his chest and he slowed, and they lay joined and kissing until it came back gently on its own. She came the first time with her face in his neck. He held her through it and didn’t stop, and the second time it took them both, deep and long, and he said Yu-er into her hair over and over like a word he’d just learned.

Afterwards they lay in the dark talking about nothing: the tap in the bathroom that dripped, whether her monitor would fit on the left of the desk, what Ah Sim would make for breakfast. Somewhere after three they reached for each other again without either of them deciding to.

At eighteen minutes past four she lifted her head from his chest because he was awake beside her, and looking at something.

“Why are you awake?”

“Nothing.”

She followed his eyes. Across the narrow gap between the houses, there was a light on in the tall house. In her old bedroom. The curtains were open.

Baba was sitting on the edge of her empty bed.

She went still. She could see the bare desk, the empty shelves, the open wardrobe, the place by the window where her chair had been. Her father sat in the middle of it with his hands on his knees. He wasn’t looking at anything. He was simply there.

Yu Chen didn’t speak.

After a while Baba got up and went to the window. For a second his face turned towards the house next door. Towards them. Then he turned away and sat down again.

“Do you think he misses me?” she whispered.

Yu Chen thought about it. “I think he’s noticed you’ve gone.”

“That’s not the same.”

“No.”

The light stayed on. At twelve minutes past five the first grey came over the roofs. At twenty-one minutes to six her father stood up and turned off the lamp, and the room disappeared.

She put her head back on Yu Chen’s chest.

“I’m not going back,” she said.

“I know.”

“I’m not leaving him because I hate him. I just can’t keep living there.”

“You don’t have to,” he said, and kissed her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week was a strange adjustment. She found out he folded towels in thirds. He found out she owned eleven chargers. She found out he checked the front door was locked twice every night. He found out she left her glasses in places that made no sense, on top of the fridge, in the bread bin, once in his shoe. She learned he liked coffee before breakfast and not after. He learned she couldn’t be trusted to know where her phone was if she was thinking about anything else.

They’d shared beds and meals and blankets and secrets for years. Living together was different. There was nothing to announce. No reason to be leaving. No pretending she’d go home after breakfast. She was home already. So was he.

At twenty-four minutes to eight every morning Ah Sim rang.

“Miss. Breakfast.”

“It’s early.”

“Your father has eaten. Congee.”

Sometimes she went alone. Sometimes he came, because, he said, he liked breakfast, and she said he liked Ah Sim’s congee, and he said that was also true. Sometimes Elowen was there, or Ev called in on her way past, or Zhao turned up to collect something he’d left. Sometimes Baba was already at the table. He didn’t say much. Neither did she. But he’d stopped pretending not to see her come in. One morning he asked if she wanted more tea. Another, he asked whether the equipment next door was set up properly. She answered. He nodded. Nothing was mended. Nothing was forgiven. But there was a small movement where there had been none, and she learned not to demand it be more than it was.

On the Thursday he passed her the vinegar before she’d reached for it. She sat looking at the little dish in her hand after he’d gone back behind his newspaper. She didn’t tell anyone. It didn’t need to be a story. But she ate every grain of the congee, and when Ah Sim took the bowl away she said “Good,” as if Eliana had done something difficult, and perhaps she had.

On the second Sunday she woke at thirteen minutes past two because the bed shifted. He was sitting up.

“Yu Chen?”

“Sorry. Go back to sleep.”

He was looking at the window. Across the gap, her old room was dark.

“Are you checking my window?”

He rubbed his face. “I wake up sometimes.”

“At two?”

“Usually.”

“Why?”

“Habit.” He breathed out. “I used to check whether your light was on. If it was dark, you were probably asleep. If it was lit, you were awake.”

“Even when we were together?”

“Yes.”

“Even when I was asleep here?”

He looked at her. “Sometimes.”

“How often?”

“Most nights. For years.”

“Yu Chen.” She sat up. “That isn’t the same as knowing I’m all right.”

“No,” he said. “But it was the only thing I could do.”

Her chest tightened. She took his face in her hands.

“You don’t have to check any more. I’m here. Look at me.”

He did.

“I’m not going anywhere tonight,” she said, and lay down and pulled his arm over her waist, and he followed her down. “And you can wake me. If you need to.”

“I don’t want to disturb you.”

“You’re allowed to disturb me.”

“That’s generous.”

“I’m a generous woman,” she said, and when he woke again later he didn’t sit up. He turned towards her and listened to her breathing instead.

The next night she found his glasses on the bedside table. He was sitting on the edge of the bed reading a message from the ward.

“Put them on.”

“Why?”

“Because I said so. No. Let me.”

She put them on his face herself and stood back and looked at him through them.

“What?”

“I like your face.”

“That’s fortunate,” he said, and she pushed him over backwards onto the bed and climbed on top of him and pinned both his wrists above his head.

He didn’t look alarmed. He looked delighted. “Are you arresting me?”

“Maybe.”

“What for?”

“Checking my window at two in the morning.”

“That’s a serious charge. What’s the sentence?”

She leaned down and kissed him. He smiled against her mouth. She kissed him again, slower, and his hands stayed exactly where she’d put them until she let go, and then they came to her waist.

“Do you know what I think?” she said. “You spent years watching my window. Now you can just turn over.”

He took her hand off his chest and kissed the palm.

“I’m right here,” she said.

“I know,” said Yu Chen, and took his glasses off with great care and put them on the table, and turned out the lamp.

chapters.title: The Red Egg
chapters.desc: The first February she wakes up next door, there’s still a red egg on the step, and this time she catches who leaves it. At the grave at dawn her father turns to her and says the words. That night she writes one word on a sticky note and puts it in Yu Chen’s textbook.
chapters.epigraph: “It was always me.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Eliana saw when she opened Yu Chen’s front door on the morning of her twenty-third birthday was a red egg.

It sat in a small white bowl on the top step, its shell dyed a deep uneven red, with a folded square of tissue under the bowl so it wouldn’t scratch the stone. She stood in the doorway in his sweatshirt with her hand on the latch, and didn’t move.

There had been a red egg every birthday she could remember. Some years it was on the step of the tall house before dawn. Some years Ah Sim brought it up with breakfast and said someone had left it outside. Nobody had ever said who. She’d decided long ago that it was Ah Sim, and loved her for pretending it wasn’t.

Down by the knee-high wall, someone was walking away.

Her father. In the dark coat he wore to the cemetery, hands in his pockets, shoulders a little bent against the cold. He hadn’t seen her.

She picked up the bowl and stepped out onto the stone in her bare feet.

“Baba?”

He stopped. He turned. Neither of them said anything. His eyes went to the bowl in her hands.

“You’re awake,” he said.

“It’s my birthday.”

“I know,” he said, and seemed to hear himself say it.

“Did you leave this?”

He looked at the egg, and then at her. “Yes.”

“Every year?”

He didn’t answer straight away. Then: “It was always me.”

All those years. The eggs on the step, the ones she’d eaten alone in her room, sometimes with a little soy sauce, sometimes still warm. The ones she’d thanked Ah Sim for in her head. It had been him. He’d boiled an egg and dyed it red on the eighteenth of February for twenty-three years, and carried it to her step before she was up, and never once let her see.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I didn’t know what to say,” said Lin Jian.

She looked down at it.

“It’s getting cold,” he said.

She nearly laughed. “It’s an egg.”

“I know.”

“You could leave it warm next time.”

He nodded once, as if she’d given him an instruction, and turned to go.

“Baba.”

He stopped.

She held up the bowl. “Thank you.”

Something went across his face. Then he nodded. “Happy birthday,” he said, awkwardly, to the wall rather than to her. But he said it.

She stood on the step long after he’d gone in through his own front door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen came out ten minutes later doing up his watch, his hair still damp. He looked at the bowl in her hands, and at her face.

“You found it,” he said.

She stared at him. “You knew.”

He paused a fraction too long.

“Yu Chen.”

“Good morning.”

“Don’t good morning me. You knew my father left red eggs on my step every birthday?”

“I knew he boiled them,” he admitted.

“Since when?”

“Since I was eleven. I came home early from school one February and he was standing outside your gate with a bowl. He saw me.” Yu Chen considered. “He didn’t exactly ask me not to tell. He just looked at me.”

“You could have told me when you were twelve.”

“I suppose I could.”

“Or thirteen. Fourteen. Fifteen—“

He caught her hand. “I didn’t think it was mine to tell.”

She looked at the egg a while longer, and then put her forehead against his chest.

“Happy birthday, Yu-er,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were at the cemetery before the sun. The path up the hill was slick with the night’s rain and the air smelled of wet grass and other people’s incense. She carried the flowers. He carried the egg.

“Why are you carrying it?”

“Because you asked me to.”

“I didn’t.”

“You looked at it.”

“That isn’t asking.”

She let him keep it.

Her mother’s grave was near the old stone wall at the top. Elowen and Zhao were already there, and Ev with Raiden, holding a small bunch of white freesias. Jinx had come with him. Ah Sim stood a little way back talking to one of the groundsmen. Baba stood in front of the stone. He turned when they came up, and looked at the flowers in her hands and the egg in Yu Chen’s.

“Put it there,” he said, and Yu Chen set the bowl down beside the stone.

Eliana knelt and arranged the stems. Pale pink and white, because those were the colours Elowen remembered their mother liking.

“Morning, Mama,” she said.

She’d never known her. She had photographs, and stories, and the odd sentence that seemed to belong to somebody else’s life. That her mother laughed loudly. That she liked flowers and persimmons. That she made Baba wait outside shops. That she’d loved Elowen. That she’d died on the day Eliana was born, of Eliana being born. For years Eliana had wondered whether her mother would have liked her. Whether she’d have held her. Whether she’d have told her she was wanted. She’d imagined the answers so often they’d begun to feel like memories.

Her father stood beside her. She didn’t look at him.

Then the first sun came over the wall onto the stone, and he said:

“Happy birthday, Yu-er.”

She went completely still.

Nobody had ever called her that but Yu Chen. In her father’s voice it sounded strange, not because she’d never heard it but because she’d never heard it from him, about her. She turned her head slowly. He was looking at her. Not past her, or at the grave. At her.

“Happy birthday,” he said again. Then: “I’m sorry.”

She didn’t move.

His hands were clasped in front of him. He seemed to be searching for words and finding none that were big enough.

“I couldn’t look at you without remembering that day,” he said. “I thought if I stayed away from you I could keep it somewhere I could bear it. But I made you carry it.” His voice went rough. “You were a day old. You were my daughter. You deserved a father.”

The tears came before she could stop them.

He didn’t reach for her. Perhaps he didn’t know whether he was allowed. Perhaps he was afraid she’d step away.

“I wanted you to say happy birthday,” she said. “I waited. Every year.”

“I know.”

“I didn’t need anything else.”

“I know,” said Lin Jian. There was no excuse in it. No explanation he was asking her to accept. Just the thing itself, admitted.

“I don’t know what to say.”

“You don’t have to say anything.” He looked at the stone. “Your mother would have liked you. She’d have liked you so much.”

Eliana couldn’t speak.

“I wish I’d met her,” she said at last.

“So do I,” said her father.

They stood together in front of the grave. Nothing was mended and they had not become close all at once, but they were standing on the same side of it, looking at the same person, and for the first time she didn’t feel she was standing there alone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards they went for breakfast at the old dim sum place by the harbour, the one with the cracked green tiles that Baba had been going to since before any of them were born. She sat between Yu Chen and Elowen. Baba sat opposite and ordered for the table, and when the congee came he told the waiter hers was to have less ginger, which she’d never once told him.

It was ordinary. Almost unbearably ordinary. She kept looking at him, not because she expected anything else, but because she wasn’t used to being able to look at her father without feeling she’d done something wrong.

Halfway through he put his chopsticks down and looked across the table.

“Doctor Wang.”

Yu Chen sat up. “Yes?”

“Are you working on Sunday?”

“I have the morning off.”

“Come for lunch.” A pause. “Next New Year as well. Dinner. If your family can spare you.” Another pause, longer. “Will you?”

Not an order, and not a decision made on Yu Chen’s behalf: a question, and her father was waiting for the answer to it.

Yu Chen held his eyes. “Yes. I’d like to.”

Baba nodded once and picked up his tea.

Eliana looked down into her bowl. Her mouth was trembling. Under the table Yu Chen’s knee found hers, and she turned her hand over on her lap, and he slid his fingers into it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seventeen minutes past three her phone buzzed on the sofa.

Elara — voice message, 6:04

She stared at it.

They’d spent the day before at Fig Tree Lane, all of them, because Elara couldn’t face the red door yet and Baba had said that if she couldn’t come to the table, the table would go to her. Red lanterns in the fig tree. Ah Sim in Ev’s kitchen criticising the stove. Elara had sat by the window most of the afternoon with her right hand in her lap in its soft grey sleeve, and said Happy New Year, Baba to their father at the door, and little to anyone else. She hadn’t said anything to Eliana since November that wasn’t pass the rice.

November. The last Sunday of it, after lunch, in the alley outside the red door. A man in a seaman’s jacket with a knife, coming for their father, and Elara getting in the way. Eliana had been in a hoodie at the gate next door and had seen it, and run, and cleared the alley of the neighbours coming out of their doors while Yu Chen knelt on the stones in his grey jumper and held Elara’s forearm up exactly where Xing Yue told him to. She still saw the stones sometimes when she shut her eyes. Afterwards Elara had stopped talking to anyone. In January she’d gone to stay with Ev at Fig Tree Lane for five weeks, and Xing Yue had sat on the porch step outside every night of it. They’d only gone home together the week before New Year.

Eliana pressed play.

“Happy birthday, Eliana.”

Elara’s voice was softer than she remembered.

“I know I hardly spoke to you yesterday. I’m sorry. I didn’t know if I could do this. Xing Yue says you’ve moved next door at last, and that Yu Chen’s been clearing space for you for months. I told him that sounded exactly like Yu Chen.” A small breath. “I hope the house is warm. I hope you can sleep without listening for things outside the window.”

A pause.

“I haven’t been good at talking to anyone. I read the messages and think I’ll answer later, and later turns into another week. You sent me a photograph of the cats on the step of the red door, in December, and I looked at it every night and never said thank you. So. Thank you.” A wavering laugh. “I’m going out more. Not far. Down to the bottom of the road. Xing Yue says that’s progress and I’ve told him not to sound so pleased with himself.”

Eliana sat down.

“I heard about Baba this morning. Ev told me. I’m not going to tell you to forgive him. I don’t think anyone gets to tell you how fast that should happen. But I’m glad he said it. I’m glad you got to hear it.”

A long silence on the recording.

“Happy birthday, Yu-er. I hope you get loved loudly and gently and in all the ordinary ways. Breakfast with your sisters, and arguments about blankets, and somebody who always knows where you’ve left your glasses.” A breath. “And I hope I can see you soon. Properly. I don’t know when. But I want to.”

The message ended. Eliana listened to it again.

Yu Chen found her on the sofa with the phone in both hands.

“That’s not your nothing face,” he said.

“It’s Elara. Six minutes.”

He sat down beside her and she played it to him, and he listened without a word, and kissed her temple when it ended.

“Tell her she doesn’t have to hurry,” he said. “And tell her you’re glad she sent it.”

Eliana: i listened twice. i miss you. you don’t have to hurry but i’ll be so happy when i see you. and i want to hear more about xing yue being pleased with himself

She stopped, and then added:

Eliana: i love you. take your time

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he was at the desk with a textbook open for his membership exam, highlighted in three colours, and she was on the bed in pyjamas and her glasses with a pad of yellow sticky notes.

“What are you doing?” he said, without looking round.

“Nothing.”

“Should I be worried?”

“No.”

She wrote one word. Crossed it out because the letters were too big. Wrote it again. Signed it. Then she got up and went to the desk and leaned over his shoulder.

“Don’t look,” she said, and slid the note between the pages of his cardiology chapter, and went back to the bed and picked up her phone and became absorbed in it.

He looked at the yellow corner sticking out of the book. He opened it.

Official.

— Yu-er

He went still. He read it once, and again. Then he looked at the bed, where she was not looking at him at all.

“Sweetheart.”

“Hmm?”

“What’s this?”

“Your textbook.”

He stood up. She looked up just in time to see him coming, with the note held between two fingers.

“Official?” he said.

“Official.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes,” she said, and smiled.

He leaned down and, with great deliberation, stuck the yellow note to the middle of her forehead.

“What are you doing?”

“Making it official.”

She laughed and reached up for it, and he caught her wrists. He looked at the note on her forehead and kissed it, right in the centre. Then her forehead underneath it, and her nose, and finally her mouth, slow and warm, until she’d stopped laughing and had her hands round his neck.

“Do you like it?” she said against his lips.

“I’ve been waiting years for that word.”

“You’ve had it for years.”

“I know. But you wrote it down.”

He took the note gently off her forehead and pressed it to the inside cover of his textbook, flattening the corners with his thumb.

“You’re keeping it?”

“Of course.”

“It’s a sticky note.”

“It’s important,” said Yu Chen.

Later, with the lights off, she lay with her head on his chest and thought about the day. The egg on the step. Her father’s voice at the grave. Will you? at breakfast. Elara’s six minutes. One word on yellow paper.

“Do you think next year will be different?” she said.

“Different how?”

“Maybe Baba will say happy birthday without looking at the ground. Maybe Elara will come to dinner. Maybe Ah Sim will stop ringing every morning.”

“That one seems unlikely.”

“Maybe you’ll stop looking at my old window.”

He kissed her forehead. “I’m trying.”

Downstairs on the kitchen counter, a small white bowl sat washed and empty. For once nobody had to wonder who’d left it.

chapters.title: Legal, Mostly
chapters.desc: Eliana opens her own security firm in two rooms above a dumpling shop, with a sticky note for a sign. Si-Wei writes the business plan. Yu Chen bought the building a week ago and mentions it on opening night, which goes about as well as he expected.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s what Baba does.”
chapters.content:
The sign was a sticky note.

Yellow, slightly crooked, held to the glass of the door with two strips of clear tape. In black marker, in capitals, it said FENCE, and underneath, smaller:

Security, risk, and the things people should have thought about earlier.

Eliana stood on the landing on the first Monday in March with a paper cup of coffee and looked at it. Then at the two rooms behind it. Then back at the sign.

“It’s crooked,” she said.

Si-Wei was sitting cross-legged on the floor inside with her laptop on her knees. She didn’t look up. “It has character.”

“It looks like a ransom note.”

“It looks like a start-up.”

“It looks like we can’t afford a printer.”

“We can’t afford a printer.”

“Si-Wei. We are a security company.”

“Exactly. Security companies should understand the value of not spending money on things they don’t need.”

The front room was half painted. One wall was a soft grey and the next was a slightly different soft grey, because Eliana had chosen it under the strip lights in the paint shop and been wrong. There was a second-hand desk against the wall and two chairs and a filing cabinet with one drawer that stuck. The back room held a server cabinet, two workstations, a whiteboard, and a kettle borrowed from Si-Wei’s flat and never returned. The whole thing sat over a dumpling shop on a street of old shophouses near the ferry pier, and every morning the smell of steamed dough and ginger came up the stairs, and the owner, Auntie Au, had already decided that anyone working upstairs was too thin.

It wasn’t glamorous. Nobody would photograph it for a magazine. But it had a door with her company’s name on it, even if the name was on a sticky note, and she had the key.

“Do we have a business plan?” said Eliana.

Si-Wei looked up at last. “Of course.”

“Can I see it?”

“No. You’ll edit it.”

“I might have suggestions.”

“You have a compulsion. You corrected the menu at the noodle place.”

“They’d spelled coriander wrong.”

“It was in Chinese.”

“Exactly,” said Eliana.

Si-Wei turned the laptop round. “Come here. I need you to sign something.”

It was a business plan, properly formatted: a summary, the market, the costs, what they’d sell. Security assessments, incident support, risk reviews for small firms that couldn’t afford the big ones. Conservative numbers for the first year. No vague promises. No claims they couldn’t back. Eliana scrolled down in silence until she reached the page about who owned what.

Yen Si-Wei — 15%

“What’s this?”

“Equity.”

“I can read.”

“Then we’re making progress.”

“You gave yourself fifteen percent.”

“You asked me to write the plan, set up the structure, negotiate the lease and get the company registered. I did all of it, in four weeks, while finishing my dissertation.” Si-Wei shrugged. “I’m not taking it for nothing. I’m taking it because I intend to work here.”

“You’re doing a business degree.”

“And this is a business. One of us should know how to run it.” She smiled sweetly. “You know how to break into it.”

Eliana opened her mouth and shut it again.

“Fifteen is a lot,” she said.

“It’s less than I wanted.”

“How much did you want?”

“Twenty.”

“Si-Wei.”

“Seventeen. Sixteen. Fifteen and a half.”

“Stop negotiating with yourself.”

Si-Wei laughed. “Fifteen. Final.”

Eliana looked at the page again. There was something unexpectedly steadying about seeing someone else’s name beside hers. She’d started this because she wanted work that belonged to her, work she could do without being folded back into her father’s world, without a desk on Harbour Road and a contract that ran for life. She hadn’t expected not to do it alone.

“Fifteen,” she said. “With a proper agreement.”

“Already drafted.”

“Of course it is. And you stop calling me your assistant.”

“What should I call you?”

“Co-founder,” said Si-Wei, and held out her hand, and Eliana shook it. “Now fix the sign.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first customer was Auntie Au, who came up the stairs at eleven with a bamboo steamer.

“Eat.”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Don’t thank me. You’re too thin. Both of you.” She put the steamer on the desk and looked round the half-painted room. “What do you do up here?”

“Security.”

“For people?”

“Mostly for companies.”

“Do you stop thieves?”

“Sometimes.”

“Good. Then stop my nephew taking money out of the till.”

Si-Wei choked on a dumpling. Eliana said, carefully, that that was probably a family matter, and Auntie Au said it was a security matter if he was stealing, and Si-Wei said “I like her” with her mouth full, and Auntie Au pointed at her and told her to eat more, and went back down the stairs.

“That’s our first client,” said Eliana.

“She’s not paying.”

“She paid in dumplings.”

“It’s a good model,” said Si-Wei.

By three they had an internet connection, a printer borrowed from the stationer two doors down, and a sign that was still a sticky note. Eliana was reading the registration documents for the fourth time when her phone went.

“Have you eaten?” said Yu Chen.

“Dumplings.”

“How many?”

“Enough.”

“That’s not a number.”

“I’m working.”

She heard a door close at his end. “I’ll come over after my shift.”

“Why?”

“I miss you.”

She glanced at Si-Wei, who was now looking at her own screen with tremendous concentration.

“It’s been five hours,” Eliana said, lowering her voice.

“It’s been a long five hours,” he said. “See you tonight, sweetheart.”

“Five hours?” said Si-Wei, without looking round.

“Don’t.”

“I’m thinking about our revenue.”

“Think quieter,” said Eliana.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at eighteen minutes to eight, still in the clothes he’d worn under his coat on the ward, with a paper bag of dinner in one hand and a small bunch of white flowers in the other.

“What’s that?”

“It’s your first day.”

She took them. White, tied with plain ribbon. She stood up and kissed his cheek. Si-Wei had gone down to talk to Auntie Au about the nephew.

“It’s nice,” he said, looking round.

“It’s small.”

“It’s yours.”

He put the bag on the desk, and she saw what was under it. A document. A thick one, in a blue folder.

“What’s that?”

He looked down. “Oh.”

Her smile went. “Yu Chen. What is that?”

He took off his coat. “Something I wanted to show you.” He opened the folder on the desk. “It’s the building.”

“What about it?”

“I bought it.”

Silence.

“I’m sorry?”

“The owner was thinking of selling. I spoke to him last week. There were other people interested.”

“The whole building?”

“Yes.”

“The dumpling shop?”

“Yes.”

“This office?”

He nodded.

She laughed once, and not because anything was funny. “You bought the building.”

“I thought it would make things easier. You wouldn’t have to worry about the rent going up, or the landlord changing his mind, or selling to someone who’d want you out. You could stay as long as you liked.”

“I found this place,” she said. “I negotiated the rent. I signed the lease. And you bought the whole building behind my back.”

“Sweetheart, I wasn’t trying to—“

“Don’t.”

She stepped back. He stopped where he was. She looked down at the papers. The price. The date. His name as the registered owner. All of it done before she’d put the sticky note on the door.

“You decided,” she said. “You decided what was best for me.”

“I thought it would give you stability.”

“That’s what Baba does.”

He went completely still.

“He decides what I need,” she said. Her voice was shaking. “He puts it in front of me and tells me it’s for my own good. He makes it impossible to say no without looking ungrateful. You know what I left that house to get away from. You know. And you did the same thing.”

He didn’t answer. For the first time since he’d walked in, he seemed to understand that this wasn’t something he could fix by explaining what he’d meant.

She grabbed her jacket and went out to the fire escape.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was narrow, iron, with a rail and a view of the alley behind the shop. Below her, Auntie Au was stacking stools. The smell of sesame oil came up through the cold.

He came out after a minute and stopped two steps away.

“Can I come closer?”

“It’s a fire escape. Stand where you like.”

He stayed where he was. “I’m sorry.”

She looked round. He wasn’t defending himself. That made it worse.

“You can’t buy things for me without asking.”

“I know.”

“You can’t decide that because you love me you get to make my decisions.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you?”

He looked down at the iron grating. “Because I was frightened. Of you losing this. There was another buyer. I thought if I had it, nobody could interfere with your work.”
