“You could have told me. You could have asked me. You could have let me decide whether I wanted to take the risk.”

“Yes,” he said. “Yes. Yes.”

“So why didn’t you?”

He was quiet a long time. “When you were little, I used to watch your light go off at night and wonder if you were warm. If you’d eaten. If your father had come home. For years I thought if I could only give you somewhere safe, it would make up for all the nights I couldn’t do anything.” He looked at her. “I know now that isn’t the same as asking you what you want.”

The rail was cold under her fingers.

“I don’t want to be managed,” she said. “I don’t want somebody to build a cage round me and call it looking after me. I’m not yours to arrange. I’m your partner. You’re supposed to stand next to me. Not in front of me.”

“I know,” he said. “I understand.”

She looked at him a moment longer. Then she reached out, took the front of his shirt in her fist and yanked him towards her and kissed him.

There was nothing gentle in it: furious, frustrated, full of everything she hadn’t managed to say properly. He kissed her back for a second and then drew away just far enough to look at her.

“Are you still angry?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” he said. “You should be.”

She kissed him again, slower, still holding his collar.

“You’re going to sign something,” she said.

“What?”

“A lease. FENCE rents its rooms from you. FENCE is a separate company. It pays rent. You don’t get to own my business because you own the walls. No changing the rent. No coming into the office without asking. No access to the systems. No special treatment.”

He considered. “Can I still bring you dinner?”

“That’s not a property matter.”

“Then I’d like to apply for permission.”

She tried not to smile. “Granted.”

“What’s the rent?”

“Dumplings,” said Eliana. “Depends on the month.”

He laughed, and she held his collar tighter. “I’m serious.”

“I know,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lease was signed the next morning with Si-Wei as witness and Auntie Au as catering. Eliana read every clause. Yu Chen read every clause. Si-Wei read every clause and asked if she could add one requiring the landlord to provide food during working hours.

“No.”

“Staff welfare.”

“You’re a shareholder.”

“Exactly. I deserve welfare.”

The rent was a modest commercial rate with a review in two years and no hidden conditions. The building belonged to Yu Chen. The rooms belonged to FENCE. The paper made sure it stayed that way. Eliana put it in the drawer of the filing cabinet that stuck, and kicked the drawer shut, and kissed him, and Si-Wei said “Please remember we’re at work,” and Eliana said it was lunch, and Si-Wei said it was ten in the morning.

That evening the front room was still half painted. She’d insisted on doing the last stretch of wall herself and he’d insisted on holding the ladder and they’d argued about the ladder for twenty minutes and the grey for another twenty, and then she climbed down and announced the wall could stay as it was until Monday.

“Are you sure? It isn’t even.”

“I know.”

“Would you like me to—“

“No.”

He smiled. She put the brush down on the lid of the tin and took his hand. The dust sheet was still spread over the floor. The desk lamp threw warm light across the unfinished wall.

“Do you know what I like about this place?” she said. “I chose it. The rooms. The name. The work.” She touched his face. “And I chose you. Don’t forget that.”

“I won’t.”

She kissed him. He drew her in, and paused when she leaned back.

“Still angry?”

“A little.”

“Do you want me to stop?”

“No,” she said. “I want you.”

The shop downstairs had closed. The street had gone quiet. She pulled him down onto the dust sheet, and they undressed each other on the floor of her company with paint on her fingers and the lamp making long shadows up the uneven wall. She was still angry and she let it be part of it: she pushed him onto his back and pinned his wrists and kissed him hard, and he let her, and when she let go he rolled her under him and kissed his way down her throat to her breasts, slow, until the anger turned into something else and she was arching up into his mouth. She guided him inside her herself. They moved together on the rough cotton, her heels pressed into the backs of his legs, the cold floor under the sheet and his heat over her, and she held his face and watched him in the lamplight and said mine before he could, and he laughed, breathless, and said yours into her mouth. When she came it was sharp and sudden and she bit his shoulder to keep quiet in an empty building, and he followed a moment after with his face buried in her neck.

Afterwards she lay with her head on his shoulder on the dust sheet. There was grey paint on his sleeve where it had been thrown over the tin.

“Your shirt,” she said.

“I’ll survive.”

She kissed the small smear of paint on his wrist. “Sorry.”

“Worth it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At thirteen minutes past eight the next morning the first email arrived.

Subject: Security consultation — customer data exposure

A woman called Michelle ran a small online stationery business from her flat. Someone had got into her customer list. She’d told her web host, and they’d told her not to worry, and she was worrying anyway, and she wanted somebody independent to tell her the truth. It was short and careful and a little frightened. Eliana read it twice.

“We’ve got a client,” she said.

Si-Wei spun her chair round. “A real one?”

“A real one.”

At the bottom of the email there was one more line.

I found your website through a friend. I don’t know why, but I think you’ll understand. I love you already.

Si-Wei burst out laughing. “Oh, she’s ours.”

“She’s a client, not a pet.”

“She’s a client who loves us.”

Eliana looked at the line again and felt something warm settle under her ribs. Not the thrill of finding something hidden. Something quieter. Somebody had found the two rooms over the dumpling shop with a sticky note on the door and decided to trust them.

Hi Michelle,

Thank you for writing to FENCE. I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. Asking for an independent review was the right first step. We’ll find out what happened, tell you plainly what we find, and help you with what comes next. You don’t have to work it out on your own.

Eliana Lin

She sent it.

“Your dumplings are getting cold!” shouted Auntie Au up the stairs.

Eliana looked at the clock, and the email, and the sticky note on the door. Then she switched off the lamp and went down to lunch.

chapters.title: The First Client Is Very Loud
chapters.desc: FENCE’s first real client is Ren Hao, who hires Eliana at top volume, hugs everyone in the building and says “I love you” to the dumpling woman. Two weeks later, at Serafina’s wedding, Eliana leaves early with cake, because Yu Chen is on nights.
chapters.epigraph: “Ren Hao can say it to the whole building. I put it in your textbook.”
chapters.content:
The first time Ren Hao came to FENCE, he announced himself to the entire building.

“HELLO! IS THIS THE SECURITY COMPANY?”

Eliana looked up from her laptop. Si-Wei shut her eyes. Downstairs, Auntie Au dropped something metal.

A man filled the top of the stairs: a beautiful suit, a leather briefcase, and the smile of somebody who had never once wondered whether a room was ready for him before he walked into it. Behind him a younger man was trying to carry three archive boxes up a staircase built for one.

“Ren Hao,” he said. “I have an appointment. I think. Someone downstairs said come up. Is this the right place?”

“Mr. Ren,” said Eliana. “Your appointment’s at ten.”

He looked at his watch. It was two minutes to. “Excellent. I’m early.”

“You’re two minutes early.”

“That’s what I said.” He stepped inside and looked round: the two rooms, the second-hand desks, the wall that had finally been painted the same grey all over in April and still somehow looked two different colours in the afternoon. The sticky note on the glass. He read it aloud. “FENCE. Good name. Short. Memorable. Slightly threatening.”

“That’s what we were going for,” said Si-Wei.

He laughed loudly and shook Eliana’s hand hard enough to slop her coffee. “I’ve heard about you. You’re the one who found the hole in the Calder business.”

“I did part of the assessment,” said Eliana, more carefully.

“And now you’ve got your own firm. Wonderful. I love independent businesses. I love women who know what they’re doing. I love a good dumpling.” He went to the top of the stairs. “WHO MAKES THE DUMPLINGS?”

“ME,” shouted Auntie Au.

“I LOVE YOU!”

A pause downstairs. “THEN BUY SOME!”

“I WILL!” He came back in, glowing. “I like this building.”

“I think we’ve found our target market,” murmured Si-Wei.

He sat down for four seconds and stood up again. His firm advised private clients on risk. It had a good reputation, an expensive office, and an IT department that told him everything was fine, which was exactly why he didn’t believe it.

“Test us,” he said. “Everything you’re legally allowed to test. The systems, the procedures, the people, the habits. I want to know where we’re soft before someone else tells me. No courtesy reports. No pretending something’s fine because someone senior might be offended. If there’s a hole, tell me. If someone’s incompetent, tell me. If I’m incompetent, tell me that too.”

“It won’t be comfortable,” said Eliana.

“Wonderful.”

“It’ll disrupt your operations. We’ll need a written scope, signed authorisation and named contacts. We won’t go anywhere outside what we agree. We don’t promise to find everything. And we don’t claim anything we can’t back up.”

“Good. Good. How much?”

She told him. He listened.

“Triple it,” he said.

“That’s not how we price.”

“Then price properly. You’re taking responsibility for my company for six weeks. I want you to have the time to do it right. I’m not paying for a cheap report that tells me what I want to hear.” He beamed. “Besides, I like your face.”

“That’s not a pricing metric,” said Si-Wei.

“It should be.” He stood, shook both their hands, picked up his briefcase, and turned at the door. “Thank you. I love you already.”

He said it with such uncomplicated sincerity that Eliana didn’t know whether to laugh. He was halfway down the stairs before he came back up.

“Where are the dumplings?”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time he left he’d bought four boxes, hugged Auntie Au, promised to bring his whole office for lunch, and called Si-Wei the brains of the operation. He’d also signed the proposal before he reached his car.

“Triple,” said Eliana, looking at it.

“Triple,” said Si-Wei.

“He didn’t even negotiate.”

“Some people have a different relationship with money.”

They looked at each other. “First real client,” said Si-Wei.

From the street, Ren Hao’s voice rose again. “KEEP THE RECEIPT, AUNTIE. I’M CLAIMING THESE.”

“I’m going to regret this,” said Eliana.

His firm took up three floors of a tower in the business district, with a client services floor, a research team, and a risk department of two: one excellent, Ren Hao said, and one excellent at explaining why the first one was wrong. He turned up to meetings unannounced. He brought food every time. Pineapple buns on Tuesday. Coffee for an entire floor on Thursday. A bag of oranges on Friday, and a question about whether anyone had had lunch. Si-Wei started a table on the whiteboard headed REN HAO, UNPLANNED VISITS, with a column at the end for Likelihood of food (%) that she filled in, every day, with 100.

He was loud. He wasn’t careless. He signed every approval, found them every person they asked for, and when somebody tried to steer a meeting towards something flattering he said “Let her finish,” and they let her finish.

In the second week she found the pattern. Not a break-in. Not a stranger. Client files opened at two in the morning by an account that had no reason to be awake. Copies made on the nights before three accounts moved to a rival firm. Records that showed information leaving by a door marked staff only. She checked it twice and then a third time and called Si-Wei over to her screen.

“That’s not a mistake,” said Si-Wei after a long minute.

“No.”

“Someone’s taking files.”

“Someone with senior access.”

“Ren’s going to hate this.”

“He asked us to tell him,” said Eliana. “He paid us triple to tell him.”

He didn’t shout when they presented it. That was how she knew it was serious. He sat at the head of his own conference table with his hands folded and listened to the whole report without interrupting once. The account belonged to one of his oldest partners. The report didn’t accuse him of anything the records didn’t show. It set out what had been accessed and when, what could be proved and what couldn’t, and recommended that everything be preserved and the rest left to lawyers.

“You’re sure?” Ren Hao said at the end.

“I’m sure the access broke your own policies. I’m sure files were copied and taken out by a route nobody approved. I can’t tell you everything that was taken. That’s for an investigation.”

He looked at the table for a while. “His name’s on the wall downstairs. He was here when we had six people.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be sorry for finding it.” He stood up. “Send me the final report. Nobody goes near him until the lawyers have it.” He looked at her then, and smiled, worn out but genuine. “You know what? I really do love you.”

Si-Wei looked at the ceiling. Eliana pressed her lips together. “Thank you, Ren.”

“Triple was worth it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen heard about Ren Hao over dinner, which she hadn’t meant him to. She’d simply been talking while he chopped vegetables, and the name had come up often enough that he asked.

“Is he the one who brings food?”

“Yes.”

“The loud one?”

“Yes.”

“The one who says he loves everyone?”

She smiled. “Yes.”

He went on chopping. “How many times has he said it?”

“Today? Twice.”

“Yesterday?”

“Three, I think.” She watched him. “Are you counting?”

“No.”

“You’re counting.”

He put the knife down. “Does he mean it?”

“In the moment. I think he just says it.”

“That’s convenient,” said Yu Chen, picking the knife up again. “Being able to tell people you love them without having to think about it first.”

She understood. She came up behind him and put her arms round his waist.

“Are you jealous?”

“No.”

“Then why are you cutting that carrot like it owes you money?”

He stopped. She laughed into his back. He turned round.

“I don’t enjoy hearing another man tell you he loves you.”

“He tells the printer he loves it.”

“I’m not jealous of the printer.”

“Good.” She put her hands flat on his chest. “He says it because he’s happy and he likes people and he fills rooms. You don’t say it like that. You say it like you’ve checked it first.”

“Do you want me to say it more?”

“Only if you mean it.”

“Do you?”

She reached up and touched his cheek. “I love you. When you’re quiet.” She kissed the corner of his mouth. “When you’re jealous.” Another kiss. “When you cook. When you don’t.”

“Don’t encourage me,” he said, and kissed her.

“Ren Hao can say it to the whole building,” she said against his mouth. “I put it in your textbook.”

“I’ve still got it,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The invitation came on a Wednesday: cream envelope, Serafina’s handwriting, a pressed flower under the ribbon. Ren Hao was at FENCE when Eliana opened it, eating a dumpling on the edge of Si-Wei’s desk.

“A wedding!” he said. “Whose? Yours? When’s yours?”

“It’s not mine.”

“When is it, though? Yours.”

“Ren,” said Eliana, and he put both hands up and grinned.

No ballroom, Serafina had written on the card. No stage. The people we want, nine dishes, and our garage.

Yu Chen was on nights that week. He’d have to leave the house at half past seven on the Saturday.

“Go,” he said. “Stay as long as you like. Take photographs.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The registry was at ten past nine on the last Saturday in April. Eliana wasn’t inside for it; there were only two witnesses, Aurelia and Chen Si, and Aurelia came out with a handkerchief already wet. But Elowen had brought her to the steps, and when the doors opened she saw Haozhen come out with Serafina’s hand in his and his face doing something she’d never seen it do.

Zhao had brought an armful of white peonies he said weren’t from him. Raiden and Jinx were there, and Ev in silver. Eliana went straight up to the new husband.

“Can I see it?”

He gave her the certificate. She studied it with great seriousness, both names, the date, the stamp, the registrar’s signature.

“So you’re married now,” she said.

“Don’t make him cry,” said Aurelia. “He’ll ruin my photographs.”

By eleven the garage under the railway bridge had stopped being a garage. Warm bulbs ran along every girder. There were trestle tables in long rows under white cloths and two hundred borrowed chairs and flowers in old glass bottles, and over the shutter on a sheet in painted capitals: QIN & SONG. Trains went over every eleven minutes and the bulbs swung a little each time. Two hundred people. Racing teams old and new, a crew who’d flown in from abroad, a tiny old woman in the middle of the first table called Granny Shum who seemed to be in charge of everyone. The cook, Mr. Kwok, had insisted on nine dishes, and there were nine: a whole steamed grouper with ginger on the top table, roast duck, prawns in their shells, braised mushrooms, chicken in a clay pot, greens with garlic, a soup he’d stood over since dawn, and two more that appeared after everybody had said they couldn’t possibly.

Baba had come, in his dark suit, with Ah Sim and a gift bag, and sat at the Lin table looking faintly uncomfortable under the bulbs. Halfway through the meal, while he was talking to Zhao, he moved the plate of prawns across the cloth until it was in front of her. He didn’t look round.

“Thank you,” she said.

“Eat them before they go cold.”

“Yes, Baba,” she said, and ate them.

When Granny Shum stood up, the whole garage went quiet for her. “To the girl who always wanted to go faster,” she said, “and the man who learned he didn’t have to chase her. Now he can sit in the passenger seat.”

Haozhen found Eliana afterwards by the old service carriage at the back, holding two glasses of sparkling water.

“Where’s Yu Chen?”

“Nights.”

“Terrible excuse.”

“A convincing one.” She took the glass. “Congratulations.”

He looked at her the way he’d looked at her on her own doorstep thirteen months ago. “Can you do something to my phone?”

“That’s what people say right before they ask for something illegal.”

“I’m asking you. Explicitly. You told me not to change the wallpaper. So I haven’t. Now I’d like you to.” He glanced across the garage at his wife, who had kicked off her shoes and was arguing with somebody about a gearbox. “Something funny.”

She held out her hand. “Phone.”

Two minutes later she gave it back. The Baizhang crest was gone. In its place was a photograph she’d taken on the registry steps that morning: Serafina in her wedding dress, one hand on her hip, looking straight into the lens as if daring it. Across the top in big white letters it said SHE DRIVES. Underneath, smaller: I am merely the passenger.

Haozhen looked at it. His face went perfectly blank. Then he laughed so hard that Serafina turned round across two hundred people.

“What?”

“Nothing!”

She came over. “What’s she done to you?”

He held the phone out. Serafina read it. There was a long silence. Then she looked at Eliana.

“Keep it,” she said, and patted her husband’s cheek. “You look better in the passenger seat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When the bride and groom went out to the car at five the rice started with a handful from Eliana and turned into a cupful from someone at the back, and Serafina shrieked and Haozhen put his arm over her head, laughing with rice in his collar. A silver-grey car was waiting outside, polished till it shone. They drove off towards somewhere with an airstrip and a sunset, and Eliana stood in the road with rice on her shoes and a slice of white cake with cream between the tiers, wrapped in a napkin in a borrowed box, because Yu Chen liked the cream.

“Leaving?” said Elowen.

“He starts at eight. He’ll forget to eat.”

Baba looked at the box in her hands. “Taking food?”

“For Yu Chen.”

He nodded. “Tell him Sunday lunch is still Sunday lunch.”

She was at the top deck of the hospital car park at twenty past seven. His old grey car was in its usual corner under the lamp, and he was leaning on the bonnet in his scrubs with his coat over his arm, because she’d sent him one line from the taxi and he’d come down before handover.

“How was it?” he said.

“Beautiful. Nine dishes. A grandmother who made the best toast I have ever heard. Baba gave me his prawns.” She held out the box. “Wedding cake.”

“For me?”

“Unless you want to share it with the car.”

They sat on the bonnet. He ate it with a plastic fork while she told him about the registry and the certificate and the rice and the wallpaper, and at the wallpaper he stopped chewing.

“You changed his wallpaper. At his wedding.”

“He asked.”

“To what?”

“She drives.”

He looked at her and then started laughing. She took a smear of cream off the edge of the box with her fingertip, meaning to eat it herself, and he caught her wrist.

“You missed some.”

“Where?”

“There,” he said, and drew her finger into his mouth and licked the cream off it, slowly, watching her face.

She didn’t move. “That’s an inefficient way to clean it.”

“I disagree,” he said, and did it again with the next finger, and then leaned across the box and kissed her with sugar on his mouth, his hand at the back of her neck, the city lit up beyond the barrier and the lamp humming over them, until his pager went and he swore against her lips.

“I missed you,” she said.

“I missed you all day.” He kissed her forehead and slid off the bonnet with the empty box. “Go home. Sleep. Don’t wait up.”

“I’m going to wait up.”

“I know,” said Yu Chen, and went back in to work.

chapters.title: He Matches to Emergency Medicine
chapters.desc: Yu Chen is offered emergency medicine training at City Hospital, the first thing in years he has chosen entirely for himself. He doesn’t know how to say it out loud. Eliana throws him the loudest party a quiet person can stand.
chapters.epigraph: “Making your life smaller before I’ve even asked you to.”
chapters.content:
The email came at eighteen minutes to seven on a Friday morning in May, while Yu Chen was standing in the kitchen in a clean T-shirt with his hair still wet from the shower, waiting for the kettle after a night shift.

City Hospital — Emergency Medicine Training Programme

He didn’t open it straight away. The kettle clicked off. He poured the water and watched the tea bag colour it, and then he picked up the phone and read the message once, and again. A place on the next intake. Emergency medicine. City Hospital, starting in August, subject to the usual paperwork.

He’d expected to feel something enormous. Relief. Triumph. Instead he felt still, as if the house had gone quiet round him to see what he’d do.

He put the phone face down. The tea was too hot to drink.

“You’re home.” Eliana stood in the doorway in his university sweatshirt with the sleeves over her hands, half asleep. “Why are you standing like that?”

“Like what?”

“Like someone’s told you the kitchen’s closing down.”

“Good morning,” he said.

She came and kissed his cheek and looked at the phone. “Work?”

“Something like that.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

“I haven’t lied.”

“You’re doing the thing. The thing where you say nothing and your eyebrows have a private meeting.” She smiled. “Tell me.”

He could have handed her the phone. “I’ve had an offer,” he said. “Training. Emergency medicine. At City.”

For a second she didn’t move. Then her whole face lit up.

“You got it.”

“They’ve offered me a place.”

“You got it.” She threw both arms round his neck and squeezed hard enough to make him laugh. “Emergency medicine! City!”

“Yes, sweetheart.”

She pulled back with her hands on his shoulders. “Why are you so calm? Aren’t you happy?”

“Yes.”

“Really?”

“Really.”

She kissed his cheek and his mouth and then took his face between her hands and kissed his forehead. “I’m so proud of you.”

Something in him loosened. He shut his eyes. “Thank you.”

“Have you accepted?”

“Not yet.”

“Why not?”

He hesitated. “It’s a hard programme. The hours. Nights, weekends, rotations that change. I won’t always know my rota far ahead. I don’t know how much time I’ll—“

“Yu Chen.”

He stopped.

“Are you making this about me?”

“No.”

“Because it sounds a little as if you’re asking whether you should choose something because it might be inconvenient for me.” She looked at him. “I need you to be careful with that habit.”

“What habit?”

“Making your life smaller before I’ve even asked you to.” She touched his cheek. “Do you want it?”

He nodded.

“Then that’s your answer. I want you to have things that make you happy even when they’ve got nothing to do with me. Especially those.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t accept that day. Not because he was unsure about the work. He’d wanted emergency medicine since a Friday night in February two years ago, and before that, if he was honest. He liked the speed of it and the breadth, the need to decide with half the information while staying aware of everything he didn’t know. He liked that no two nights were the same. He liked the people.

But the offer made the choice real. For the first time in years he was being asked what he wanted with nothing else attached. No coincidence. No family expectation. No quiet pull of a life that had arranged itself round a girl next door. He’d followed her to university. He’d built his timetable round hers. He’d stayed in the house beside hers when he could have lived anywhere. None of it was false. He’d never regretted a day of it. But when he looked at the offer he realised he’d never once asked himself what he’d choose if nobody else were part of the question.

And he wanted this. He just didn’t know how to say so without it sounding like stepping away from her.

That afternoon he met Xing Yue for coffee near the hospital, to look over a document for a clinic project. They finished it in twenty minutes. Then Xing Yue saw the envelope on the table.

“Your offer?”

“Yes.”

Xing Yue read the heading and something close to a smile crossed his face. “Congratulations. And you haven’t accepted.”

“No.”

“Why?”

Yu Chen looked out of the window. “I don’t know how to tell Eliana.”

Xing Yue stared at him. “Tell her what?”

“That I want it.”

“Does she not want you to take it?”

“She does.”

“Then you’re making it more complicated than it is.” Xing Yue tapped the envelope. “Tell Eliana first. Then accept. Not because she gets to decide for you. Because she’s your partner and you want her to know what matters to you before you take the next step.” He paused. “You’re treating your own future like something you need to apologise for. You don’t need permission to want something.”

“I know.”

“Then act like it.” Xing Yue picked up his coffee. “And if you turn it down because you’re afraid she’ll be lonely, she’ll find out, and she’ll be furious, and I won’t help you.”

Yu Chen laughed, and for the first time that day the decision felt simple.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found her at FENCE at seven, sitting cross-legged in her chair with a client report. Si-Wei had gone home and left half a cup of tea on her keyboard and a note saying DO NOT FORGET THE FOLLOW-UP.

“Did you eat?”

“Properly,” he said, and kissed the top of her head, and put the envelope on her desk.

She read the first page and looked up.

“I want to accept,” he said. “I want emergency medicine. I want to train at City. And I know the hours will be hard. Nights, weekends, rotas that change—“

“You don’t have to sell me the disadvantages. I’ve known what being with a doctor means for years.”

“I wanted to tell you first.” He looked down at her hand in his. “And I wanted you to know this is something I want for myself. It’s the first thing I’ve chosen in years that isn’t about you.”

She didn’t move.

“I don’t regret anything,” he said carefully. “I’d choose you again. The university again. This house again. But this is different. I think I needed to say it.”

“I think you did,” she said. “Then become one.”

He leaned down to kiss her forehead and she caught the front of his shirt. “Wait.”

She stood up on her chair, which made her taller than him for once, took hold of both his ears, and pulled him up to her.

“Accept it,” she said, and kissed him.

Nothing small about it: it was delighted and wholehearted and almost laughing, and he caught her round the waist to stop her falling off the chair, and she didn’t stop.

“That’s my answer,” she said against his mouth.

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me for letting you have your own life.”

“I’m not,” he said. “I’m thanking you for being happy with me.”

He accepted the next morning on the sofa with her beside him, one leg tucked under her and a mug in both hands. She watched him read the terms and click the box. Your acceptance has been received.

“Doctor Wang,” she said, and shook his hand with great formality. “Welcome to the next bit.”

“I love you.”

“I know. And I’m throwing you a party.”

“How many people?”

“Not many.”

“Eliana.”

“Quiet people,” she said, “are allowed loud parties.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She did one other thing that week that she didn’t tell him about until he found it.

On the Tuesday he went down to the bike shed at the back of the house before an early shift and found a small black camera, no bigger than a matchbox, clipped neatly under his handlebar, and a second one facing backwards under the saddle. When he opened his calendar at the first red light, his new rota was in it, every shift from August to February, in the same shade of green as the old one, with the little lock beside it.

He rang her from the hospital gate.

“There’s a camera on my bicycle.”

“Two.”

“And my rota’s in my phone. The new one. That I haven’t been sent yet.”

“The department sent it to the new starters’ portal last night. The portal’s terrible.” A pause. “Are you angry?”

He thought about it, standing at the gate with his bike. “Why the cameras?”

Her voice went quieter. “Fung Ka-lok was on a bike. A van turned across him three streets from Harbourside. You’ll be riding to City at six in the morning and home at nine at night, through the market junction, for four years.” She breathed out. “I’m not losing you to a junction because I didn’t do the one thing I know how to do.”

He stood there a while with the bicycle against his hip and the traffic going past.

“You can take them off,” she said. “Two screws each. I’ll show you.”

“No,” said Yu Chen. “Leave them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The guest list became a problem by Monday. She’d meant to keep it small. Then she remembered Xing Yue and Elara, who’d been there through all his training. Elowen and Zhao had to come. Raiden and Jinx would be offended if they didn’t. Ev was in town. The triplets went everywhere together. Auntie Au from under FENCE announced she was doing the food whether anyone asked her or not. And somehow Ren Hao found out.

“ELIANA! I HEARD! YU CHEN IS GOING TO EMERGENCY MEDICINE!”

She held the phone away from her ear. “How?”

“I’M COMING. I’LL BRING FOOD.”

“What food?”

“Everything.”

“That’s not a quantity.”

“It’s a promise,” said Ren Hao, and hung up.

The party was on Saturday the thirtieth of May in the garden behind the house. She strung warm bulbs through the persimmon and along the back wall, and propped small cards on the table that said CONGRATULATIONS, DR. WANG. Auntie Au brought dumplings and buns and enough dishes for the whole Walled City. Elowen brought a cake. Ev brought flowers. Raiden and Jinx brought a coffee machine that was much too expensive and Jinx had obviously chosen. Si-Jie brought wine, Si-Yuan brought pastries, and Si-Wei brought a printed timetable.

18:00 Arrival. 18:30 Food. 19:00 Toast. 19:15 Unstructured celebration. 20:00 Cake.

At the bottom: No speeches longer than three minutes.

“Who’s that for?” said Eliana.

“Ren Hao.”

“Fair.”

Then Xing Yue came through the side gate with Elara.

Eliana hadn’t seen her sister properly since February. They’d sent messages. She knew Elara was going out more, teaching first-years in the anatomy rooms two mornings a week, working her hand on Jinx’s steel rig at the back of the garage before dawn. Still, seeing her step into the garden in a pale dress with her right wrist in its soft sleeve made something rise hot in Eliana’s chest. She went to meet her.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

They hugged. It was awkward for a second and then it wasn’t, and Eliana held on longer than she meant to.

“You did all this?” said Elara, looking at the bulbs.

“It’s a bit much.”

“That’s what a celebration is supposed to be,” said her sister.

Xing Yue shook Yu Chen’s hand. “You earned it.”

Ren Hao arrived last, not because he was late but because he’d stopped downstairs at FENCE to buy more dumplings on the way, and came through the gate with three bags. “WHERE IS THE DOCTOR?” He hugged Yu Chen hard enough to lift him off his heels. “EMERGENCY MEDICINE! YOU’LL SAVE LIVES!”

“That’s the plan,” said Yu Chen, winded.

Ren Hao turned on Eliana. “YOU DID THIS? YOU’RE A WONDERFUL WOMAN.” He hugged her too. Over his shoulder her eyes found Yu Chen’s, and she smiled at him, and Yu Chen smiled back, and didn’t look at all like a man cutting a carrot.

It was louder than he’d have chosen and it wasn’t unpleasant. He moved between people. Raiden explained that emergency medicine was the only job where you could be exhausted and starving and still expected to know everything, and Jinx told him not to listen to Raiden. Elara asked if he was excited. He was. More than he’d expected. There was something good in being surrounded by people who were glad for him without asking what it meant for anybody else. Across the garden Eliana was laughing at something Si-Wei had said, her hair tied back and a cardigan over her dress and a small plate in one hand. She looked happy. She turned and found him looking, and smiled. It was enough.

At seven Si-Wei tapped a glass.

“Toast.”

She held out a microphone. Eliana stared at it.

“You said no speeches.”

“Three minutes.”

She took it. There were too many faces. He was standing by the table with his hands in his pockets, looking at her.

“Yu Chen has spent a long time looking after other people,” she said. “Sometimes he forgets he’s allowed to want things for himself. I’m proud that he’s chosen something he loves. I hope he gets everything he’s worked for, and that he always remembers there are people waiting for him at home.”

Four sentences. Exactly four. The garden was quiet for a beat, and then Ren Hao clapped like a firework and everyone followed.

Yu Chen didn’t move. He was looking at her. Then he walked over and took the microphone out of her hand and put it down on the table, and in front of everybody, without a word, he went down on one knee on the grass.

The garden went completely silent.

“Yu Chen?” she whispered.

He took her hand and kissed the back of it. A sound went through the guests. He kissed it again.

“Get up,” she said, going scarlet. “Everyone’s watching.”

“I know,” he said, and stood, and kept her hand. “Thank you.”

Then he kissed her. Not a peck and not a show. A real kiss, slow and long, his hand at her waist and her fingers knotted in his, in front of her sisters and his cousin and three triplets and a loud man from Vancouver, who made a noise that was probably heard at the ferry pier.

“THAT’S LOVE!”

She buried her face in Yu Chen’s chest. He laughed into her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when the cake had been cut and the party had broken into smaller knots of people, she slipped up the persimmon onto his roof. He found her there on the low parapet looking down at the bulbs in the garden, and put his jacket round her shoulders, and sat beside her.

“Happy?” she said.

“Yes.” He looked out over the roofs. “I meant what I said. Before. About wanting to marry you. I still want it. Not because I want you to look after me, or so I can arrange your life. Because I want to come home to you. Even when I’m tired. Even when we’ve got nothing interesting to say. I want the ordinary days too.”

She took his hand.

“Keep wanting it,” she said.

He blinked. “That’s your answer?”

“For now.”

“I’m allowed to keep wanting it?”

“As much as you like.” She looked at their hands. “I want you to keep becoming who you want to be. And I want to be there when you come home.”

“That’s enough,” he said.

“It’s more than enough.”

Below them Ren Hao was probably telling someone he loved them, and Auntie Au was certainly telling someone to eat. Someone shouted his name up the stairs. He began to get up, and she caught his hand.

“Wait,” she said. “One more minute.”

He sat back down and gave her every minute she asked for.

chapters.title: Three Flats and a Porch
chapters.desc: They look at three new flats with harbour views and buy none of them. Instead they rebuild the old Song house as theirs, keep the porch, and take down the little wall between the two porches, which needs her father’s permission and costs him more than he lets show.
chapters.epigraph: “Old because we chose to keep them.”
chapters.content:
The first flat had floor-to-ceiling windows. The second had a kitchen island large enough to land a small plane on. The third had a private lift, a view straight down the harbour, and a bathroom that Eliana described to the agent as unnecessarily romantic for a room where people brush their teeth.

Yu Chen liked the third one. He didn’t say so. He stood at the window while the agent listed the pool, the gym, the residents’ lounge and the concierge who could arrange almost anything, and looked out at the water.

“It’s beautiful,” said Eliana.

“One of the most sought-after units in the building,” said the agent.

The harbour was bright under the June sun. Boats went slowly across it, and the towers on the far shore looked painted onto the sky. She could imagine waking up here. She could imagine him coming home after a night and leaving his shoes by the door and finding her at the window with her laptop. A quiet life. A comfortable one.

“Is there anywhere outside?” she asked.

There was a balcony. She stepped out onto it. A small table would fit. Two chairs. A plant or two. She tried to imagine leaving the door open while she worked and hearing him call her from the steps, and couldn’t, because there weren’t any steps.

“Thank you,” she said, coming back in. “We’ll think about it.”

In the lift he said, “You didn’t like it.”

“I liked it.”

“But?”

“It isn’t ours.”

“It’s an empty flat.”

“Exactly,” said Eliana, and took his hand. “Let’s see the next one.”

They saw all three, and then they sat in a café with three glossy brochures on the table while she drew boxes on the back of the receipt.

“What are you doing?”

“Comparing.”

“You’ve compared them.”

“I’m comparing again.” She pushed the receipt across. Three rectangles with little windows. One with a balcony, one with an island, one with a bath. “Evidence,” she said, “that I don’t want any of them.”

He laughed.

“They’re lovely,” she said. “They’re new and safe and they’ve got everything. And I keep thinking about the steps. I want the steps. The crack in the third one. The rail that needs painting. The place where you used to sit and pretend you weren’t waiting for me.”

“I wasn’t pretending.”

“You read the same page for forty minutes.”

“Reading takes time,” said Yu Chen.

“I want the lane,” she said. “I want to hear Ah Sim shouting over the wall about breakfast. I want to know which neighbour’s arguing with the delivery man. I want to leave the door open when it’s cool. I want somewhere that already knows us.”

He reached across and took her hand. “Then we won’t buy a flat.”

“Just like that?”

“Just like that.”

“You liked the third.”

“I liked the bathroom.”

“You’re impossible.”

“We can build a bathroom,” he said, and watched her face change.

“Wait,” she said. “The Song house.”

He went still.

It had been his home since he was eight, but it had never been his. It was Old Song’s house, the policeman’s house, with the sergeant’s photograph inside the door, and Wei Long had raised him in it and then left it to him two years ago with a key and a shrug and a list of everything that needed doing. The roof had problems. The plumbing was older than Ah Sim. Half the windows didn’t close. The back room had been damp since a typhoon in 2018.

“We could rebuild it,” she said, leaning forward. “Make it ours. Keep the steps.”

He looked at her for a long moment.

“Yes,” he said.

“It’ll be a lot of work. And expensive. And I want a long room with both our desks in it.”

“I know.”

“How do you know?”

“You’ve mentioned the long room fourteen times.”

“Fourteen?”

“Approximately,” said Yu Chen, and she folded the receipt and put it in her pocket to remember the three flats they hadn’t bought.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden and Jinx came on the Saturday. Raiden had a folder and Jinx had a tape measure.

“Where’s the damage?” said Raiden at the door.

“Good morning to you too.”

“Good morning. Where’s the damage?”

“Ignore him,” said Jinx, stepping past. “He’s excited.”

“I’m a professional.”

“You once measured a wall from the wrong side.”

“That was a design decision,” said Raiden.

They walked the house for an hour. The floors creaked. The kitchen was too small. The bathroom was a crime. Raiden lay on his back in the damp room and looked at the ceiling with deep satisfaction. Eliana followed with a notebook.

“What do you want to keep?” said Raiden.

“The steps.”

“Obviously.”

“The front windows. The sergeant’s photograph. The old rail.”

Jinx put her hand on it. “It’s in a bad way.”

“Repair it. Don’t replace it.”

“Repair it,” Jinx agreed.

Yu Chen stood in the doorway between the front room and the hall. “I want the middle room open. Enough for both desks.”

“Facing?” said Eliana.

“Slightly angled.”

“Why angled?”

“So I can see you without having to look up every time.”

She stared at him. Raiden made a noise.

“That’s disgusting,” said Raiden.

“It’s a desk arrangement,” said Jinx.

“It’s a desk arrangement with emotional consequences,” said Raiden, and wrote it down: two desks, angled, emotional consequences included.

The drawings came a week later, three versions in Raiden’s clean draughtsman’s hand: no faces, he never drew faces, but every hinge. One kept the old layout. One opened the middle of the house into a long room with light at both ends. One was ambitious and would have cost as much as the third flat. She sat on the floor with all three spread round her and put her finger on the second.

“The kitchen’s close enough to the desks that I can make tea without crossing the house. The front room still opens onto the steps.”

“And the bathroom?”

“New.”

“Good. I’ve never trusted that shower.”

“It’s older than us.”

“Exactly,” said Yu Chen.

“I want it to feel old in the right places,” she said. “Not old because things are broken. Old because we chose to keep them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The steps were the first real argument, and it wasn’t between the two of them.

The knee-high wall ran between the Song steps and the Lin steps under the two little tiled roofs. It had been there as long as she could remember. She’d sat on one side of it at eighteen at two in the morning while he sat on the other. They’d passed things over it all their lives: books, sweets, notes, a broken hair clip, an orange she’d once handed across as a peace offering at seven for stealing his toy car. Low enough to talk over. High enough to make each porch its own.

She wanted it gone. Jinx could run a bench along the front where it had been, a long seat following the old rail, so the two sets of steps became one.

“There’s one problem,” said Jinx, looking at it.

“My father,” said Eliana. The wall was the boundary. The tall house side was his.

“He might say no,” she said to Yu Chen that night, on her stomach on the bed with the drawings.

“Then we keep it.”

“Just like that?”

“It’s his house too.”

“Sometimes I hate how reasonable you are.”

“You don’t.”

She shut his book. “Come with me. Now.”

Baba was in his study. She put the drawings on his desk and stood in front of it, and Yu Chen stood beside her.

“We’re rebuilding the Song house,” she said.

“I’d heard.”

“Raiden’s drawn it. Jinx is doing the steps. We want to take down the little wall between the two porches.”

His eyes came up. “The wall?”

“So it’s one porch.”

“It’s a boundary wall. You’d need the line surveyed. The footing checked.”

“Raiden’s arranging all of it. Nobody touches anything until it’s signed off.”

He looked at the drawing for a long while. Then he looked past her through the study window, which looked down on the two front steps and the wall between them and the rail.

“Your mother wanted that wall gone,” he said.

Eliana’s fingers tightened on the edge of the paper.

“She said it made the two porches look as if they were arguing. She complained every summer. She wanted it down and I said it was unnecessary work, and she said I always found a reason not to do things, and I said I’d look at it later.” He paused. “Later went on a long time.”

“Uncle Mok said she always got her way in the end.”

“Not with the wall.” His mouth moved, barely. “She’d have liked the bench.”

He looked at the drawing again.

“Keep the rail,” he said. “She liked the rail.”

“I’m keeping it.”

“Then take the wall down. I’ll sign whatever the surveyor needs.” At the door he said, “Yu-er.”

She turned.

“Don’t let them rush. It’s an old house.”

“I won’t.”

“Your mother would have liked what you’re doing with it,” said Lin Jian, and looked back down at his papers before she could answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The wall came down on a Saturday in late June. He didn’t come to watch. He said he had a meeting. She suspected he didn’t want to see it go.

She stood on the steps with Yu Chen while the men took it apart brick by brick. A little dust went up. Then the last of it came away, and there was no wall, only two sets of steps under two roofs that had become one porch, with the old rail running along the front of both.

“It’s strange,” she said. “I’ve looked at that wall my whole life.”

He took her hand. She turned and pulled his face down and kissed him on the place where it had been, in front of the lane: the neighbour watering his pots, two schoolboys, the man from the bakery on his bicycle, who rang his bell.

“I’m still here,” said Raiden from behind them.

“Congratulations,” said Eliana, without letting go.

“Your girlfriend has no respect for the design team.”

“She’s the client,” said Yu Chen.

“That’s worse,” said Raiden.

Jinx built the bench herself in Tai Hing out of an old ferry plank, with Raiden carrying the wood and complaining. It ran along the front of the porch under the rail, sanded smooth and oiled warm, long enough for two people or three who didn’t mind sitting close. Eliana sat on it the day it went in and stretched her legs out and said, “Sit,” and Yu Chen sat, and their shoulders touched.

“Better than the harbour,” she said.

He looked at the lane. “Much better.”

Baba came over one afternoon in July without ringing. She was working in the half-finished long room. He stood on the new porch and looked at the bench and ran his hand along it.

“Jinx made this?”

“Yes.”

“Good work.” He put his hand on the rail. “Your mother would have sat here and made everyone else sit down.”

“And complained about the cushion.”

“She’d have said it was too hard.” Something nearly like a smile. “She always did.” He looked at her. “Have you eaten?”

“Not yet.”

“Ah Sim made soup. Come home for dinner.”

“I am home,” she said.

He looked at the house behind her. Then he nodded.

“Come to my house for dinner,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang her on a Tuesday evening while she was in the new kitchen trying to decide whether a soup needed salt.

“I need to ask you something,” said Baba. “It’s about Elara. She and Xing Yue want a safe room at Banyan Terrace. Not because of anything now. Somewhere she can go if she has to.” He paused. “I thought you’d know how to do it.”

“Baba,” said Eliana, “that’s literally my job.”

“I know.” A longer pause. “I wouldn’t ask if I didn’t trust you.”

Not a grand thing, and not an apology. Something, all the same.

“I’ll ring her tomorrow,” she said.

“Thank you.” And then, before he rang off: “Yu-er. Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She put the phone down and looked at Yu Chen at the table.

“He said he trusts me.”

“I heard,” he said.

“I think he’s trying.”

“Yes.”

“I think I’m trying too,” she said, and sat down beside him and leaned on his shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of July the house was nearly done. The roof didn’t leak. The windows shut. The kitchen was new and the long room was exactly what she’d drawn on the back of a lecture handout in second year: two desks, one long run of light, her monitors on one side and his books on the other, angled so that he could look up and see her without making it obvious, and so could she, when she was pretending not to.

“Come here,” she said the afternoon the desks went in, and pulled him by both hands between her knees as she sat in her chair. “Look. This is ours. Not your house. Not my father’s.”

“Ours,” he said, and kissed her forehead.

“Now sit at your desk. I want to see what it looks like when you’re working.”

“I’m not a display.”

“You’re an expensive decorative feature,” she said, and he laughed and sat down and opened a book, and every few minutes one of them looked up.

The bathroom was finished on the last Friday in July. New tiles warm underfoot. Proper pressure in the shower. A bath deeper than she’d expected. She turned the taps on.

“You’ve already tested it,” he said from the doorway.

“Not enough.”

When it was half full she turned it off and came and took his hand and sat him on the edge.

“Do you remember the first flat? I couldn’t imagine living there.” She looked round. “I can imagine getting old here.”

“So can I,” he said.

“Then we should test the bath properly.”

“You’re thorough.”

“I’m a professional,” said Eliana, and pulled him down by the front of his shirt.

He caught himself on the wall. She undid his shirt and pushed it off his shoulders, and he pulled her T-shirt over her head, and they got the rest off between them, laughing, with the steam coming up off the water. She stepped in first and sank down and held out her hand. He climbed in behind her and the water rose to the rim and slopped over onto the new tiles, and neither of them cared. She leaned back against his chest between his knees. His hands came round and spread flat on her stomach under the water, and then moved, slow, up over her breasts, down over her hips, between her thighs, while she lay back against him with her head on his shoulder and her breath going shallow. He touched her until she was gripping his knees under the water and turning her face into his neck, and when she came she pressed her mouth to his throat to keep the sound in, and then remembered she didn’t have to keep it in any more, in this house, and let it go.

She turned round in the water and straddled him and sank down onto him with a long sigh, her wet hair falling round both their faces. The water moved with them. He held her hips and kissed her collarbone and her mouth, and she rode him slowly, unhurried, in the house they’d rebuilt, until he was saying her name like a man saying a word he loved, and she felt him shudder and hold her down hard against him, and she followed him a second time, smaller and sweeter, with her forehead against his.

“I trust the bath,” he said eventually.

“More than the shower?”

“Much more,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday the third of August he started his emergency training at City.

He woke before the alarm and lay still for a while looking at her asleep with one hand under her cheek. Then he got up carefully, showered, dressed, checked his bag twice. When he came into the kitchen she was already there, in his shirt and a pair of shorts, with two cups on the table.

“Sit,” she said.

“You made tea?”

“No, the neighbour did.”

He sat. It was exactly right: not too strong, the milk he liked, the heat he liked. She never made the tea. He looked at her over the cup.

“You got up early.”

“It’s your first day.” She came round the table. “You don’t have to be brilliant today. You just have to turn up, listen, and remember you’re allowed to ask.”

“That sounds familiar.”

“I’m wise,” said Eliana, and kissed him. “Go and be a doctor.”

“I’ll come home.”

“I’ll be here.”

At the door he turned round. She was standing in the kitchen holding her own cup.

“Have a good first day,” she said. “My Yu Chen.”

She listened to his feet cross the porch, over the place where the wall had been, and the gate click, and his bicycle go off down the lane with two small cameras on it. Then she carried her tea to the long room and sat down at her desk. Across from her, angled just so, his chair was empty.

She hoped he’d remember lunch.

chapters.title: Nainai
chapters.desc: Yu Chen takes Eliana north to meet the grandmother he has written to every month for years. Nainai has kept every letter, has known Eliana’s name since the summer of 2021, and before they leave she gives him his mother’s ring.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t mind that you loved me. I mind if you forget I’m allowed to go.”
chapters.content:
Forty-three minutes out of the city, on a Saturday in September, Eliana began to think seriously about getting off the train.

She liked trains. She didn’t like what was waiting at the end of this one: A grandmother who’d apparently known about her for five years. Who’d kept every letter. Who, according to her grandson, was nice, which was exactly what a person said when he was keeping something back.

There was a paper bag on her knee with tea and almond biscuits in it and an embroidered handkerchief she’d taken two evenings to choose. He was opposite her with one long leg stretched into the gap between the seats, reading something on his phone, completely at ease. Of course he was. Wang Yu Chen could have walked into a room of people who’d waited twenty years to judge him and asked if they’d had lunch.

He looked up. “What’s wrong?”

She lowered her voice. “What if she doesn’t like me?”

“She will.”

“You can’t know that.”

“She’s been waiting to meet you for five years.”

“That makes it worse. That’s an exam I didn’t revise for.”

He held out his hand across the little table, and she gave him hers.

“She’s going to ask why I didn’t bring you sooner,” he said. “That’s all.”

“That’s a question with a trapdoor under it.”

“Then I’ll answer it. I’ll say I wanted to bring you when you were ready.”

He said it plainly, and that was the worst part, because it was true. When she’d hesitated in the spring he’d said another time, and hadn’t asked again until she raised it herself.

She looked at the door at the end of the carriage.

“I could still get off.”

“Yes,” he said.

He didn’t even hesitate.

“We’d miss the connection.”

“There are other trains.”

“She’d be disappointed.”

“Probably. I’d ring her.” He turned her hand over. “It’s your choice.”

It was ridiculous how much she loved him for that. She’d spent years learning not to need anyone. He’d spent years learning how to stay. Sometimes the two things still met awkwardly in the middle.

“I’m not getting off,” she said.

“I know.”

“Don’t say you know.”

“All right, sweetheart.”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little,” said Yu Chen, and caught her hand before she could hit his knee with it, and kissed her knuckles, and the train carried them north.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house stood in the hills above a small grey town, behind a long whitewashed wall. It was old, built round a courtyard, with dark timber beams and stone steps worn smooth in the middle by a hundred years of feet, and a camphor tree in the yard older than any of them. There was a camera under the eaves, and a long drive curving away to another gate.

Eliana stopped dead in the gateway.

“That’s your grandmother’s house?”

“Yes.”

“She lives here? On her own?”

“With Auntie Mui. And two people in the day.”

“Your family’s rich,” said Eliana.

He paused. “Yes.”

“How rich?”

“It’s a relative term.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“I know,” he said, and took her hand. “Come on. She’ll be waiting.”

She was. She was standing on the top step in a dark cardigan with a polished stick in her right hand, a small woman with silver hair pinned back hard and a face like a walnut. She didn’t lean on the stick. The moment her grandson came through the gate she pointed it at him.

“Look at your face.”

“Hello, Nainai.”

“Don’t hello me. You’re thinner.” He went up the steps and bent and put his arms round her, careful and unhurried, and she held his face in both her hands and inspected it as if he’d come home from a war rather than a train. Then she let go of him and turned the stick on Eliana.

“This one?”

“Yes,” said Yu Chen.

Nainai looked at her for a long, unnerving moment. Down at the paper bag. At their hands, which had found each other again without either of them noticing. Her face changed.

“So,” she said. “Eliana.”

It wasn’t a question.

“Hello, Nainai,” said Eliana, whose mouth had gone dry, and the old woman took her free hand in both of hers.

“I’ve waited a long time,” she said.

“I’m sorry we didn’t come sooner.”

“Don’t be. He’s a difficult boy. He thinks he has to arrange everything perfectly before he’s allowed to do it.” She looked at her grandson. “Am I wrong?”

“No, Nainai.”

“Then don’t interrupt.” She saw Eliana trying not to smile, and her own mouth went up at one corner. “Good. You can laugh at him. Somebody has to.”

“I do,” Eliana admitted.

“Excellent,” said Nainai, and took her inside by the hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch was on the table in the long dining room: a steamed fish, braised tofu, greens, chicken in a clay pot. Nainai told Eliana he’d fed his vegetables to the dog at eight and the dog had been ill for two days. Across the table he separated the tender meat near the bone of the chicken from the rest, without thinking, and put it in Eliana’s bowl, because that was the part she liked. Nainai saw. She didn’t say anything. She looked down at her own bowl, and something in her face settled, as if she’d confirmed a thing she’d been told.

Afterwards Yu Chen was sent to help Auntie Mui clear. Eliana offered and was told to sit.

“You’re a guest. Sit with me. That’s helping.”

In the sitting room there were photographs on every shelf: Yu Chen at six asleep in a fruit crate, Yu Chen beside a tall serious boy in gold-rimmed glasses who could only be his cousin. And a young woman with dark hair and a wide smile, holding a child against her shoulder with one hand cupped round the back of his head.

“His mother,” said Nainai, behind her.

Eliana had seen photographs before, never one so clear. The same eyes. The same way of looking at the camera as if it might be about to say something worth hearing.

“She had a strong mind,” said Nainai. “Stronger than my son liked. Yu Chen has it from her.” She sat down and pointed at the sofa with the stick. “He writes to me every month. Since August 2021, he has written about you.”

The date went into her like a stone into water.

Nainai got up again, went to a cabinet, and came back with a long dark wooden box with a brass clasp. Inside, envelopes in rows by date, black ink and blue, a few with folded photographs under them, in the neat slanting hand she’d know anywhere.

“Some are short,” said Nainai. “Some are long. He writes more when he’s worried.” She took out the first and put on a pair of glasses from her cardigan pocket. “August 2021. Dear Nainai. The girl next door has started at the university. She says she doesn’t need help with her books, but she brought three textbooks and a laptop in one bag and nearly fell down the library stairs.” She looked over the glasses. “That was you?”

Eliana covered her face. “Unfortunately.”

Nainai laughed out loud and took another. “September. She doesn’t like being asked if she’s all right. She says something rude, even when she isn’t. I’ve learned not to ask more than once.”

Yu Chen had come to the doorway with a tray of tea, without a sound. He stood there with an expression Eliana couldn’t read.

“Nainai. You’re embarrassing her.”

“I’m reading your letters.”

“Exactly.”

“Then you should have written fewer,” said Nainai, unrepentant, and took out another. “February 2022. I saw her in the yellow jumper today. She was in a doorway arguing with someone on the phone, and she kept smiling, because the person on the other end couldn’t see her face. Her hair was tied up badly. She had a pencil behind her ear. I wanted to tell her she looked pretty. I didn’t, because she’d laugh at me. I think she knows anyway.”

There was a long silence. Yu Chen looked at the floor. His ears had gone red.

“You wrote that,” said Eliana. “To your grandmother. About my jumper.”

“Apparently,” he said.

She started to laugh, helplessly, bent over with her hands over her face, and Nainai looked delighted.

“He’s always been like this,” she said. “Quiet. But once he likes someone there’s no end to it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Then, somewhere in the second year of letters, Eliana stopped laughing.

It was the details. Where she’d been. When she came home. Whether she’d eaten. One letter said he’d waited outside the engineering library for an hour because she hadn’t answered a message. Another said he’d walked her home after a late lab and stood in his own garden until her bedroom light came on. Another said she’d been quiet for three days and he didn’t know whether to ask. Another, from the nine days, was only four lines long, and she couldn’t read it at all.

Nainai saw her face change, and put the letters down.

Eliana looked at Yu Chen. He’d gone still in the doorway.

“Did you write about all of it?”

He didn’t pretend not to understand. “Some of it.”

“How often you waited for me?”

“Yes.”

“How often you checked I was home?”

“Yes.”

“How often you watched my window?”

A pause. “Yes.”

Her eyes filled. She didn’t know she was going to cry until she was doing it. She wasn’t angry. That seemed to frighten him more than anger would have.

“Why?” she said.

He put the tray down and sat opposite her. “Because I was young,” he said, “and I didn’t know what to do with how much I wanted to be near you. I was afraid something would happen to you and I wouldn’t know. I was afraid you’d stop coming home one night and I wouldn’t notice soon enough.” He looked at her. “I know it wasn’t fair. I know wanting to keep you safe doesn’t give me the right to know where you are every minute. I don’t want to make your life smaller because it makes me less frightened.”

She wiped her face with Nainai’s embroidered handkerchief, which she hadn’t even given her yet.

A younger Eliana would have been angry, the one who treated every kind of love as a debt that would one day be collected. She knew he’d loved her before he understood what loving someone asked of you, and that he was still learning not to turn fear into something that closed round her.

She reached across and took his hand.

“I don’t mind that you loved me,” she said. “I mind if you forget I’m allowed to go.”

“I won’t.”

“If you’re worried, you tell me. You don’t decide things for me in secret.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise.”

“I promise.”

She squeezed his hand. “And I want to read the yellow jumper one myself.”

“Of course you do,” he said, and Nainai laughed so hard she had to reach for her tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

It came out by accident, while Nainai was asking about her family.

“Elowen’s married to Zhao,” said Eliana. “And Elara’s married to Xing Yue.”

Nainai’s cup stopped halfway to her mouth.

“Xing Yue,” she said. “My Xing Yue?”

“Your—“ Eliana looked at the photograph of the tall boy in gold-rimmed glasses, and at Yu Chen, and back. “He’s your grandson too.”

“His father is my elder son,” said Nainai. “Yu Chen’s father was my younger.” She put the cup down. “Xing Yue married a doctor called Elara three years ago and has refused every New Year since to bring her north. That Elara is your sister?”

“Yes.”

“And you,” said Nainai, pointing the stick, “are the girl next door.”

“Yes.”

“He never wrote your surname,” said Nainai to the room in general. “Two years of the girl next door and then Yu-er. Not once a Lin.” She sat back and looked at her younger grandson. “The world is smaller than I was told.”

“Fourteen,” said Nainai. “And a medical school. And a port. My husband built them. My elder son is chairman, and tiresome about it. And this one—“ the stick again “—has a share of his grandfather’s trust coming to him at twenty-five, next April, which he has spent the last year pretending isn’t going to happen.”

Eliana turned slowly to Yu Chen. “That’s how you bought FENCE’s building.”

“With my mother’s money. The trust is April.” For once he didn’t look unrepentant at all.

“I wanted you to know me before you knew what my family owned,” he said.

She looked at the hand he was still holding. “Well. I know you.”

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, while he was upstairs, Nainai took a small velvet box out of a drawer in the little sitting room and opened it on her knee. A ring. Warm old gold, thin, a small stone set in the middle. Not extravagant. The kind of ring somebody wears every day for years.

“His mother’s,” said Nainai, and closed the box. “I wanted you to see it first. It isn’t a promise he’s made on your behalf. I’ll give it to him, and I’ll tell him to wait. Not until he thinks enough time has passed. Not until he’s arranged it all. Until you ask.”

Eliana’s eyes stung.

“He’ll want to give you everything,” said Nainai. “He’ll want to decide what everything looks like. Don’t let him. He needs somebody who’ll tell him when he’s wrong, and who chooses him freely. Not because we have money. Not because he waited.”

“I don’t want him to wait forever,” said Eliana.

“Then don’t make him,” said Nainai.

When Yu Chen came down she called him over and put the box in his hand.

“Your mother’s ring,” she said. “Wait until Eliana asks. Don’t turn this into one more thing you’ve decided in advance. Don’t make her feel she owes you an answer because you’ve waited. Let her come to you.”

He looked at the box for a long moment, and closed it.

“All right.”

“And look after the life you’ve already got while you’re waiting,” said Nainai, and pulled his head down and kissed his forehead. “Good boy.”

His ears went pink. Eliana pretended not to notice.

At the door she gave them food for the train and a jar of salted plums. “Write when you get home,” she told her grandson. “A letter.” And to Eliana: “Come again.”

“I will,” said Eliana, and meant it, and turned at the bottom of the drive to wave, and the small figure on the worn top step lifted the stick.

✦ ✦ ✦

The night train south had compartments with two narrow bunks, a fold-down table, a window and almost no floor.

The train jolted as it pulled out, and she lost her balance and fell forward into him, and he caught her by the waist and her palms landed flat on his chest. For a second neither of them moved. Then he kissed her before she could say sorry.

It wasn’t careful. His hand tightened at her waist and her fingers curled into his shirt, and the train rocked under their feet, and she laughed into his mouth from surprise.

“Sorry,” he murmured, against her lips.

“You kissed me before I could apologise.”

“I’ll apologise properly.” He kissed the corner of her mouth. “Sorry.” Her cheek. “Sorry.”

“You’re getting worse,” she said, and pulled him closer.

The bottom bunk was not wide enough for two people. This became obvious about thirty seconds after he climbed onto it.

“Where would you like me to put my body?” said Yu Chen after the third elbow, and she laughed so hard the bunk shook.

They worked it out. She lay half on top of him with the blanket over them both and the reading lamp throwing a yellow circle on the ceiling. They kissed slowly, interrupted by her knee and his elbow and a bend in the line that slid them both towards the wall. She undid his shirt under the blanket. He pushed her sweatshirt up and kissed her stomach and her breasts in the cramped dark, and the rhythm of the wheels went on under everything. There was no room to do anything quickly. She sat up astride him with her head bent under the top bunk and took him inside her and they both went still, breathing, and then the train found the rhythm for them, a long steady rocking that she didn’t have to do anything but give in to. He held her hips and watched her face in the yellow light, and when it came for her she put her hand over her own mouth because the walls were thin, and he took her hand away and kissed her instead, and followed her a moment after, holding her down against him while the whole carriage swayed.

Afterwards she lay on his chest with the blanket over her shoulders.

“Does Nainai know about the first time you kissed me?” she said.

“I told her that month. That I’d wanted to for years and I was afraid I’d want to again.”

“What did she say?”

“She told me to stop being a coward,” said Yu Chen, and Eliana laughed until he had to hold her still so she wouldn’t fall off the bunk.

After midnight she woke. He was awake, with the velvet box in his bag on the floor.

“Will you wait?” she said.

“Sweetheart,” he said, “I’ve been waiting for you since before I knew what I was waiting for.”

“That’s unfair. It makes me want to kiss you,” she said, and did, and then tucked herself back against him in the narrow bunk, and the train carried them south, towards the house they’d made.

chapters.title: The Ring in the Jar
chapters.desc: After the hillclimb, and after a night in the emergency department when she nearly loses him, Eliana leaves a note in the jar in the wall: “Ask me again.” He does, at two in the morning, on the porch where it started, with his mother’s ring.
chapters.epigraph: “Ask me again.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Eliana heard was Raiden shouting. The second was Jinx telling him to shut up. The third was the man on the loudspeaker, crackling across the hillside, announcing the sidecar class: first place by one point four seconds.

She turned in time to see Jinx come off the last bend of the old pass road on the dark green machine with ARCHITECT on its brass plate, flat over the tank, and Raiden in the chair beside her hanging so far out over the tarmac that his helmet nearly brushed the bales. They crossed the line and Jinx sat up and Raiden threw both arms in the air and nearly fell out.

Raiden climbed out of the chair, tripped on a tyre barrier, was caught by the back of his leathers by his wife, and pulled her helmet off and kissed her at the finish, in front of the marshals, with her hair stuck to her forehead and the engine still ticking. Somebody cheered. It might have been Mrs. Tong, Jinx’s old landlady, who’d been brought up the mountain on the club coach in a hat and had cried on and off since the first practice run.

It was the first Sunday in October, and half the family had come up out of the city to the hill climb with folding chairs and food boxes and enough flasks to supply an army. Zhao watched the result go up on the board and said “Hm,” which from Zhao was a standing ovation. Elara was wrapped in a jacket, laughing at something Xing Yue said. Ren Hao, who’d invited himself, was explaining the rules to a stranger.

A little way back, on two folding stools at the start line, sat Baba and Jinx’s father, Cao Tiehan, from under the flyover. Neither of them had said much all morning. Between them, on the grass, was a single flask, and every so often one of them unscrewed it and poured into the lid and passed it across, and the other drank and passed it back.

“Is there enough for one more?” said Eliana, and Baba hesitated, and poured, and held out the lid.

“Thanks, Baba.”

His hand paused on the flask. “Mm.”

Nobody turned to look. Nobody announced anything. But when a message from Si-Wei took her attention and she stood there reading it, he moved his stool a foot to the left so that the sun stopped falling across her face, and didn’t mention it.

Yu Chen saw. He didn’t say anything either. He came up behind her and put his hand flat against the small of her back for a second as he passed.

“What’s that for?” she said.

“Nothing.”

“You’re touching me.”

“Because I can,” said Yu Chen, and kissed her temple, and went to throw the cups away.

Baba watched him go. “He’s attentive.”

“He’s also annoying.”

Something moved at the corner of her father’s mouth. “Good. Someone should be.”

At the end of the afternoon Raiden held the little silver cup over his head on the back of a flatbed lorry, and Jinx held it by the base so he wouldn’t drop it. Eliana photographed them, and Yu Chen rested his chin on her shoulder and said “Send me that one,” and when she asked why, since he wasn’t in it, he said “Because you took it.”

He kissed her cheek. A small, ordinary kiss. She’d remember it later.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nineteen days later, on a Friday, the emergency department at City smelled of antiseptic and coffee and the particular tiredness that settles into a hospital after midnight.

He’d been on since four. A fall, two chests, a feverish toddler, a man who’d waited three days before admitting his stomach hurt. Nurse Bernie, twenty-two years on that floor, had been beside him most of the evening telling him coffee wasn’t food.

At thirteen minutes to midnight the ambulance brought in a man in his thirties found wandering outside a block of flats, sweating, agitated, his words coming out in the wrong order. Something taken. Nobody knew what. For half an hour he seemed to settle in the monitored bay. Then he got frightened. He started pulling at the leads and shouting that someone had followed him in. Bernie went to him in the steady voice she used for frightened people.

“You’re in hospital. You’re safe. Nobody’s going to hurt you.”

“Don’t touch me.”

“I’m not touching you.”

He sat up. Someone reached for the call bell. Yu Chen was at the foot of the trolley when the man’s hand found the empty glass bottle the paramedics had bagged up with his things and left on the locker.

It happened too fast for thinking. The man swung it. Bernie turned to shield the student nurse beside her. Yu Chen stepped in between.

The bottle caught his forearm and then the side of his head above the eyebrow as he turned, and broke against the rail of the trolley. Someone shouted. He felt a hot line open over his eye, and a strange delayed warmth running down the side of his face. The man swung again with what was left of the bottle, and this time the registrar and two porters had him, and security came through the doors at a run.

Yu Chen put his hand to his head. It came away red.

“Dr. Wang. Sit down.”

“I’m fine.”

“You’re bleeding.”

“Yes,” he agreed, and looked across at Bernie, who’d gone white. “Are you hurt?”

“You’re asking me?”

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Good,” he said, and his knees went, and he sat down on the floor.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t dangerous. That was what they told him. It wasn’t nothing either: eleven stitches above the left eyebrow, cuts along the forearm, a CT that came back clean, and a night under observation in a side room because rules were rules. The consultant told him he wasn’t going back on the floor tonight, or next week. He didn’t argue.

His phone was in his locker. He’d decided to ring Eliana in the morning, when he could tell her he was fine with a voice that proved it, instead of now, at one in the morning, when she’d come straight across the city in the dark and sit in a plastic chair being frightened for hours for no reason.

He’d said so to his cousin when Xing Yue came down from nine in his scrubs to look at the stitches. “Don’t ring her. Not till morning.”

Xing Yue had looked at him for a long moment over the gold rims, and said nothing, and gone away.

At twenty past one the door opened and Xing Yue came back in.

“She’s in the car park,” he said.

Yu Chen shut his eyes. “I asked you—“

“You did.” Xing Yue sat down on the chair by the bed. “I rang her anyway. I’m her brother-in-law and your cousin, and you don’t get to decide that she finds out you’ve been hit with a bottle from somebody else at breakfast. I drove over and fetched her. She didn’t drive. She was with me.” He looked at the dressing. “Eleven?”

“Eleven.”

“You’re a doctor. You should know how to avoid a bottle.”

Yu Chen’s mouth twitched. “I’ll remember.”

Xing Yue stood. At the door he stopped.

“She’s been pacing for twenty minutes,” he said. “Don’t make it worse.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came in carrying a paper bag and stopped just inside the door.

He was sitting up in bed in a hospital gown, paler than she’d ever seen him under the strip light, with a dressing over his left eyebrow and the beginning of a bruise at his temple and a bandage down his forearm. He looked tired. He looked alive.

“Hi,” she said.

“Hi, sweetheart.”

She came to the side of the bed and stood there and went through it like a checklist. “Eleven stitches. Eyebrow. Arm. Did they scan your head? Did you lose consciousness? Are you staying in?”

“Yes. Yes. No. Yes.”

She nodded. Then she said, “Are you stupid?”

His mouth moved. “Possibly.”

“Possibly?”

“I haven’t ruled it out.”

Her chin went. She looked away. He reached for her hand and she let him take it.

“Bernie?” she said.

“Fine. The student too.”

“Did you get in front of her?”

He didn’t answer. That was the answer. She put her forehead down on the back of his hand on the blanket and stayed there breathing.

“I know you didn’t think,” she said into it.

“She was in front of him. I couldn’t—“

“I know.” Her voice broke on it. Then she sat up and wiped her face with her sleeve and became businesslike. “I brought noodles.” She opened the box. Ginger and sesame and spring onion. She picked up the chopsticks. “Open.”

“Eliana—“

“Open.”

He opened. She fed him a mouthful and watched him chew. “Too hot? Does it hurt? Dizzy? Headache?”

“A little.”

“How bad? On a scale of—“

“Did you eat?” he said.

She stared at him.

“Before you came. Did you have anything? Did you finish the noodles you made for yourself at—“

“You’ve got eleven stitches in your face,” said Eliana, “and you are lying in a hospital bed checking up on my noodles—“

He took hold of the front of her hoodie in his good hand and pulled her down and kissed her, right in the middle of the sentence.

She made a small startled sound against his mouth. Then her hand came up to his face, careful of the dressing, and she kissed him back, leaning over the rail of the trolley, the chopsticks still in her other hand. It wasn’t long. He was hurt and she was still shaking. It was enough to make her shut her eyes.

“Sorry,” he whispered, against her forehead.

“What for?”

“Scaring you. And asking Ge not to ring you.”

“Don’t do that again. Don’t make me find out from somebody else. Don’t decide I shouldn’t come.”

“I won’t.”

“I was coming anyway,” she said, and kissed the side of his forehead that wasn’t hurt, once and twice and three times. “Eleven stitches.”

“It’s not that many.”

“Don’t you dare,” said Eliana, and he stopped, and she picked up the chopsticks and they ate the noodles out of the same box.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xing Yue was by the corridor window when she came out to fill the water jug.

“Thank you,” she said. “For ringing.”

“He thinks if he keeps you away from the frightening parts, you won’t be frightened,” said Xing Yue. “Does it work?”

“No.”

“Then he should stop.” He put his phone away. “Don’t thank me for waiting. You’re family.”

She fell asleep in the plastic chair at about four with her hand on the edge of his mattress.
