He woke and saw her, her hoodie off one shoulder and her hair coming down, and reached for the blanket at the foot of the bed, and stopped, because he’d learned that even small decisions about her comfort were better made with her than for her.

She stirred. “Why are you awake?”

“Couldn’t sleep.”

“Headache?”

“A little.”

She stood up, put the blanket over his legs, sat down again, and took his hand. “Go to sleep. That’s an order.”

“Yes, sweetheart,” he said, and did.

✦ ✦ ✦

The jar was in the wall by the porch.

When Jinx rebuilt the porch she’d found Nainai’s plum-jam jar behind the loose brick by the old fig and moved it to a little niche beside the front steps with a small wooden door, which Eliana painted yellow. They’d started leaving notes in it without deciding to. Buy tea. Kiss me before you go. You looked handsome today, don’t let it go to your head. I know you’re tired. Come home.

On the evening after he came home from hospital, she stood in front of it with a folded piece of paper in her hand.

It had taken three days to write. Not because the words were hard. Because they weren’t. She’d written them and crossed them out and written them again and sat on the kitchen floor for twenty minutes wondering whether she was allowed to want something this much.

She opened the yellow door and put the note in with the others and shut it, and stood with her hand flat on the bricks.

The porch light came on. He was in the doorway, still moving carefully, with the dressing over his eye.

“You’re supposed to be sitting down,” she said.

“I was looking for you. What are you doing?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at the yellow door. She put her hand over it.

“Nothing,” she said again.

He looked at her face, and smiled, and didn’t ask. He kissed her forehead and took her in.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning on the seventh of November, a Saturday, he was awake.

The stitches had come out on the Thursday. Bernie had called him an idiot in front of the whole department and then brought him a bun. He’d been looking for the water bill reminder in the jar that evening and found a new piece of paper among the old ones, folded twice, with nothing written on the outside. He’d opened it.

Three words.

Ask me again.

He’d stood in the kitchen with it. Then he’d remembered Nainai at the cabinet. Wait until she asks. She hadn’t asked him to propose. She’d asked him to ask. There was a difference, and he understood it.

He went upstairs and touched her shoulder.

“Sweetheart.”

“Mm?”

“Come downstairs with me.”

She opened one eye. “Is the house on fire?”

“No.”

“Did you break something?”

“No.”

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

He held out his hand. She looked at it, and then at his face, and something began to dawn in hers.

“All right,” she said.

He found her slippers. She pulled a cardigan over her nightshirt. They went down through the dark kitchen and he opened the front door, and the cold came in, and they stepped out onto the porch under the light.

The lane was silent. The bench ran along under the old rail. He stopped on the place where the wall had stood.

He’d imagined this a hundred ways, and understood at last that there was no perfect moment, only the one she’d given him.

He took the velvet box out of his pocket.

“Yu Chen,” she said.

He opened it. His mother’s ring lay on the velvet, warm old gold under the porch light.

She put her hand over her mouth.

“I’ve wanted to ask you for years,” he said. “I know I’ve said it before. I asked before you were ready, and I made you feel I’d already decided what our future looked like. I don’t want to do that.” He took a breath. “I want to marry you. Not because we’ve been together for years, or because I waited, or because of the house or the ring. I want every ordinary day with you. I want to argue about how warm the bedroom should be. I want to take you to the doctor when you won’t admit you’re ill. I want to come home and find you at the table in a nest of cables and empty cups.”

She laughed through her tears. “I don’t leave cups everywhere.”

“You do. I want to grow old with you. I want to keep choosing you when we’re tired and difficult and nothing goes the way we planned.” He lowered the box a little. “And I only want you to have this if you want it. It was my mother’s. I’d be honoured if you wore it. You don’t owe me that.”

She was crying openly now.

“Eliana Lin,” he said. “Will you marry me?”

For one second she couldn’t speak. Then she nodded.

“Yes.”

His face changed.

“Yes, Yu Chen.”

“Yes?”

“Yes.”

His hands were shaking when he took the ring out of the box. He slid it onto her finger. It fitted.

She looked down at it, a thin circle of gold that had belonged to a woman she’d never met, and touched it with her other hand, and then took his face in both of hers.

“You’re going to be my husband,” she said.

“If you’ll have me.”

“Yu Chen. You’re going to be my husband.”

She pulled him down and kissed him. Once, twice, a third time, barely letting him breathe between them. “Yes,” she said against his mouth. “Yes. Yes.”

“I heard you.”

“Yes.”

“I know, sweetheart,” he said, and held her face, and kissed her until the yeses turned into laughing and the laughing turned into something quieter.

Behind them, on the other half of the porch, a light came on in the tall house.

She didn’t notice at first. She was looking at the ring. Then a second light. A window went up. A curtain moved. The landing light. The light in Elowen’s old room, where Elowen and Zhao were staying the weekend. The light in Baba’s.

She stared.

“Someone saw,” said Yu Chen.

“Everyone saw.”

A silhouette stood behind the upstairs curtain. She put her face in his chest and laughed until she couldn’t breathe.

“It’s two in the morning,” he said into her hair.

“That doesn’t make it better.”

“Do you want to go in?”

“No,” she said, and held her hand out between them so the ring caught the porch light.

“Mrs. Wang,” he said.

“Not yet.”

“Not yet,” he agreed, and smiled all the way up.

“Soon,” she said, and kissed him again, and across the joined porch every window in her father’s house was lit, and for the first time in her life she didn’t feel any need at all to hide from the people watching.

chapters.title: A Wedding Between Two Gardens
chapters.desc: They marry where they both lived for years, across both back gardens, under the persimmon tree, through a gate cut in the wall. She means to walk to him on her own. At the gate her father is waiting, and for the first time in her life he asks her something.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll come out. Every night.”
chapters.content:
The first string of lights was crooked.

Eliana stood in the middle of the two gardens holding one end of it while Yu Chen stood on the ladder at the other, trying to work out why the bulbs kept sagging towards the persimmon.

“You’re pulling,” he said.

“I’m holding.”

“You’re pulling.”

“I’m holding enthusiastically.”

The ladder creaked. “Don’t move.”

“I’m alive. Living things move.”

From the porch Jinx made a sound that was probably a laugh. Raiden, who was meant to be helping, sat on the bench eating a persimmon.

“I’m providing moral support,” he called, with his mouth full, and Eliana threw a fallen leaf at him, which missed.

The waist-high brick wall between the Song garden and the Lin garden had stood for sixty years. Three weeks ago, with her father’s signature on the surveyor’s form, Jinx had cut a gate into it: an opening framed in dark timber, with a stone path running through. The rest of the wall stayed. The old persimmon stood just to one side of the opening, its branches over both gardens as if it had been waiting for the two houses to stop pretending.

She’d wanted the wedding here from the start. Not a hotel ballroom. Not one of the Wangs’ hospitals’ function rooms, though Xing Yue’s father had offered three. Here, where she’d grown up looking over a wall and finding him on the other side.

The bulbs finally settled into a curve from the persimmon to the porch roof. He climbed down.

“Still crooked,” she said.

“It isn’t.”

“Third bulb.”

He looked. There was, in fact, a dip. He stared at it. She smiled.

“You’re pleased with yourself,” he said, and pulled her against him.

“You’re getting dust on my dress.”

“You’re not wearing your dress.”

“That isn’t the point.”

He kissed her forehead and looked at the gate. “This is where I learned how to love you,” he said. “And where you learned you could come home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The scale had been a negotiation. Between the Wangs and the Lins there were enough properties and connections and well-meaning relations to stage a wedding that would have needed a security plan and a seating chart like a battle map. She’d refused. She wanted the two gardens and the people who’d been part of their lives, food she liked, music she could dance to, and a ceremony short enough that she wouldn’t cry before the vows.

He’d agreed to everything, and then made sure the old people had proper chairs, the path was level for Nainai’s stick, and there was a canopy in case of rain. She’d found the weather plan and accused him of preparing for the end of the world.

Aurelia made the dress. That was the part Eliana had found hardest to give up. She’d wanted something she could move in, something that felt like her and not a costume. Aurelia had listened, and asked about necklines and sleeves and which details Eliana wanted hidden rather than shown, and made a dress of soft ivory silk with a fitted bodice and sheer sleeves embroidered with tiny flowers you couldn’t see until the light caught them. And thirty covered buttons down the back.

On the morning of the twenty-third of October the dress hung on the wardrobe in her old room in the tall house, where she’d once kept her textbooks. She stood looking at it.

Elowen came in first and put an arm round her. “You used to say you’d never get married.”

“I know.”

“You don’t have to be that girl any more. You get to have this. And you get to be happy about it.”

Evangeline came with a box of pins and an expression of deep concentration. Elara came with a little case of make-up, her right hand nearly as quick as it had ever been. Aurelia came last with a sewing kit, looking suspiciously calm.

“Sit,” said Aurelia.

Eliana sat. Elara did her face, lightly, so that she still looked like herself. Ev pinned her hair back soft, with a few strands loose. Elowen kept looking at the clock.

When they turned her to the mirror she looked like a bride. It came slowly and then all at once, and her eyes filled.

“No,” said Elowen. “Not yet.”

“They’re allowed.”

“Not yet.”

Aurelia stood behind her and looked at her in the glass. “I made it for you,” she said. “Not for anybody looking at you. So you’d be comfortable in it.”

“I am,” said Eliana, and hugged her carefully.

“Good. Don’t eat anything that stains.”

“That’s cruel.”

“That’s marriage,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

The guests came into both gardens from four. From the window Eliana watched them find their places among the chairs set out in a curve under the persimmon: Serafina and Haozhen, Serafina stopping dead when she saw the dress through the glass and putting her hand over her mouth, Haozhen bending to tell her she’d ruin her make-up. Chen Si beside Aurelia. Zhao looking more formal than she’d ever seen him, with his hand on the back of Elowen’s chair. He Si-Mei, who’d once fixed Eliana’s worst mistake and sent her a bill for it, with a small gift and a sealed envelope. The triplets in a row like three exclamation marks. Ren Hao, already talking. Ah Sim in the front row in her best grey.

And Nainai, who’d come south three days early with her stick and used it to rearrange the chairs, sitting front and centre in dark blue with a small bunch of white flowers in her lap. She looked up at the window. Eliana lifted her hand. The old woman lifted the stick.

Baba was at the gate.

Not at the front with the guests. Not by the celebrant. At the new gate in the old wall, in a dark suit with a persimmon leaf pinned to his lapel, one hand on the timber frame, looking at the house.

“He’s been there half an hour,” said Elowen beside her.

The ceremony was at half past five, to catch the last of the light. At half past five the guests were seated. At twenty-five to six Raiden was told to stop talking. At twenty to six Eliana was still upstairs, because she’d asked them to wait.

There was a knock. “Baba’s at the gate,” said Elowen. “Do you want me to walk you down?”

Eliana looked at her sister and smiled. “No.”

Elowen touched her cheek and stood aside.

She went down the stairs of the tall house alone, through the kitchen where she’d eaten twenty-two years of Ah Sim’s congee, out of the back door into the Lin garden. The first thing she saw was the gate. The second was her father.

He hadn’t moved. When he saw her his face changed. His shoulders came down a fraction. His mouth opened and shut, as if he’d forgotten what he’d come to say.

“Baba.”

“Yu-er.”

“I thought you’d be with the guests.”

“I wanted to wait here.” His hands were clasped in front of him. For the first time in her life he looked unsure whether he was allowed to ask for something. “Can I walk you?”

It was such a small question. She felt it somewhere under her ribs. He’d told her for years where to go, what to become, which future to take. He’d never once asked her anything that mattered and waited for the answer.

She looked at the grey in his hair. At the lines round his eyes. At the man who’d left a red egg on her step every February for twenty-three years and never said so, who’d sat alone in her empty room until dawn the night she left.

“Yes,” she said.

Something moved in his face. “Thank you.”

He offered his arm. It was stiff under her hand at first, and then, slowly, it wasn’t. They went through the gate together.

✦ ✦ ✦

The two gardens had become one under the persimmon. The chairs curved round the trunk. The unlit strings ran overhead from house to house, over the gate and on to the porch. The old rail along the front had ribbons on it. The persimmon was heavy with fruit.

Yu Chen was waiting under it in a dark suit with a white flower in his lapel. His hair was tidy; she knew he’d have his hand through it by eight. His face was calm, and his jaw was tight, and his hands were clasped hard in front of him. When he saw her the tightness went out of him, most of it. His eyes went over her face and the dress and her hand on her father’s arm, and he smiled.

At the front Baba stopped. He looked at Yu Chen, and the two men stood there a moment. Then he took her hand off his arm and put it into Yu Chen’s.

“Thank you,” said Yu Chen.

Baba looked at his daughter. “Be happy.”

“I will,” she said, and he stepped back and sat down beside Ah Sim.

She barely heard the celebrant’s first words. She was too aware of Yu Chen’s hand, the slight tremor in it, his thumb moving once over her knuckles. She squeezed his fingers. He looked at her. She smiled. His mouth softened.

He said his vows first, to her and not to anybody else.

“I used to think loving you meant making sure you never had to be afraid. I thought if I watched closely enough and stayed close enough, I could keep every hard thing away from you. I know now I can’t promise you a life without fear.” His voice was steady. “I can promise I’ll never make your choices for you. I’ll stand next to you, not in front of you. I’ll listen when you tell me I’m wrong. I’ll come home to you. I’ll tell you when I’m frightened. I’ll let you look after me, even when I think I don’t need it.” A soft laugh went through the chairs. “And when it’s a hard day, and the house is quiet and the lights are off, I’ll still come out. I’ll come out. Every night.”

Her tears went before she could stop them. She laughed through them.

“I used to think that if I loved someone enough, they’d leave,” she said. “I thought it was safer not to ask for too much. Safer to promise nothing. Safer to keep one foot outside the door. Then you kept turning up. When I was difficult. When I was frightened. When I couldn’t say what I needed. You never once made me feel I had to be easier to love.” Her fingers tightened round his. “You gave me a home without asking me to disappear into it. You let me go when I needed to, and you let me come back because I wanted to. I can’t promise I’ll never be afraid again. I can promise I won’t make you guess for nine days. I’ll tell you when I need you. I’ll let you see me when I’m not brave. I’ll keep choosing you. Not because you waited. Because you’re who I want beside me.” She smiled at him with her face wet. “Tomorrow. And the one after.”

His eyes were wet too.

“Do you, Lin Eliana,” said the celebrant, “take—“

“Yes,” said Eliana.

At the back of the garden, Raiden, who’d been put in charge of the switch and told clearly to wait for husband and wife, heard the yes and hit it.

Every bulb in both gardens came on at once. Through the branches of the persimmon, over the gate, along the porch, down the old rail. The whole place went gold, the way a flower shop had gone gold at nine forty-one four years before, and every head turned up.

“That’s early,” said Yu Chen.

“Do you mind?”

“No.”

“YOU’RE WELCOME,” shouted Raiden from the back, and Jinx pulled him down by his tie.

The rings came. He slid hers on beside his mother’s. She put his on with fingers that wouldn’t keep still. The celebrant cleared his throat.

“And so by the authority—“

Yu Chen leaned in.

“Wait—“ said Eliana, laughing.

He kissed her before the celebrant got to the end of the sentence.

The gardens erupted. Elowen cried openly. Nainai laughed and banged her stick on the grass. Ren Hao made a noise they probably heard at the ferry pier. Baba sat still with Ah Sim holding his arm. Yu Chen kissed her again, smiling against her mouth.

“I was going to say you may now kiss,” said the celebrant.

“Sorry,” said Yu Chen.

“He’s been waiting,” said Eliana.

✦ ✦ ✦

The reception was loud. She’d expected loud. She hadn’t expected Ren Hao to take the microphone and announce that Yu Chen was the luckiest man in the city, that Eliana was terrifying in the best way, and that he personally had no idea how anyone survived being in love for six years with a woman who could take apart a bank’s security and still lose her phone in her own kitchen. She threw a napkin at him. He caught it. “See? Terrifying.”

Yu Chen didn’t stop smiling all evening. Every time she turned round he was looking at her. Once, while she was talking to Serafina, he came up behind her and put his hand at her waist.

“You’re hovering,” she said.

“You’re my wife.”

She stared at him. He looked entirely serious. Then she laughed. “You’re enjoying that. Go and eat something, husband,” she said, straightening his tie, and he said “Yes, sweetheart,” and went.

Late, with the music slow, she found her father alone under the persimmon looking up at the lights.

“Baba.”

“Yu-er.” He nodded at the gate. “It looks better.”

“I think so.”

“Your mother liked this tree.” He reached into his jacket and took out a small cream envelope with her name on it in his careful hand. “For you. Open it later.”

She kissed his cheek. He went completely still, and then he patted her hand. “Go. Your husband’s looking for you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went through the gate after midnight with her shoes in her hand, across the porch, into their house.

“Say it again,” he said at the door.

“You’re greedy.”

“Yes,” he said, and she stood on her toes.

“My husband.”

The bedroom was quiet. She stood in front of the mirror still in the dress. He came up behind her and looked at her in the glass for a long moment, and then his eyes went to the back of the dress, to the thirty small covered buttons running from her nape to below her waist, and he breathed out.

“Thirty,” she said.

“Thirty,” he agreed, and began.

His fingers were careful. The buttons were tiny and the silk was fine and he took them one at a time, and she watched his face in the mirror, grave with concentration. After the fifth he stopped.

“All right?”

“Yes.”

“Tell me if you want me to stop.”

“You’re not performing surgery.”

“Surgery’s easier,” he said, and kissed the back of her shoulder where the silk had begun to fall open, and went on.

At the fifteenth she reached back and touched his cheek. “You’re my husband.”

His fingers paused. “Yes.”

“Just checking.”

He kissed the knob of her spine. “Wife.”

At the thirtieth the dress loosened all at once and slid forward off her shoulders. He caught it before it fell and laid it over the chair as carefully as if it were still her, and turned her round. She stood in front of him in nothing but her rings.

“Wife,” he said again, as if he were learning a word.

She pulled him down by his tie. He laughed against her mouth, and she undid the tie and his shirt, button by button, slower than he’d been, deliberately, watching his face, until he was the one breathing hard. He lifted her onto the bed. He kissed her everywhere he’d kissed her a thousand times, and it felt like the first time, because she was his wife and he was her husband and the words were new in both their mouths. When he went down between her thighs she put her hand in his hair and said his name and then husband, and felt him smile against her. She came with her back arched and the lights from the garden still glowing at the edge of the curtains.

When he moved over her and into her she wrapped her legs round him and held his face so that he had to look at her the whole time.

“Tomorrow,” she said.

“And the one after,” he said, and moved, slowly, deep, his ring cool against her cheek where his hand cupped it. They found each other’s rhythm the way they always had, and it built long and steady between them until she was saying yes again, the way she had on the porch, and he broke with his forehead pressed to hers and her name and wife in the same breath.

Much later she lay with her head on his chest and remembered the envelope.

Inside was a photograph. Her mother, young, laughing, under the persimmon tree, one arm up to a branch, about to pull down a fruit before the birds got to it. On the back, in her father’s careful hand: She would have wanted to see you happy.

Eliana looked at it a long time. Yu Chen didn’t speak. He held her.

“She’d have liked the lights,” she whispered.

“I think so.”

For once, thinking about the mother she’d lost, she didn’t feel she had to choose between missing her and being happy. She could have both.

“Sleep, wife,” he said.

“Goodnight, husband.”

Outside the last of the bulbs glowed over both gardens. The gate stood open.

chapters.title: 2 A.M., The Porch
chapters.desc: Epilogue. On the night she turns twenty-five, Eliana sits on the porch at two in the morning, not because the house is too quiet but because it’s exactly quiet enough. She has something to ask. The boy next door comes out and sits down beside her.
chapters.epigraph: “I just want to keep finding you.”
chapters.content:
At twenty-five, Eliana Lin had finally learned that a quiet house didn’t always mean something was missing. Sometimes it meant everything was where it belonged.

At two in the morning on the night of her birthday the refrigerator hummed downstairs and the curtains shifted in the air from the vent and somewhere out in the lane a scooter went by and was gone. Yu Chen was asleep beside her. His wedding ring was on the little wooden tray on his side of the bed next to his watch, because he’d taken it off to wash his hands after his shift and forgotten it. She’d remind him in the morning. He’d say he knew. She’d say knowing and doing were different things. He’d kiss her until she forgot what she’d been complaining about.

She smiled in the dark. Then she got up.

She wasn’t restless. She wasn’t afraid. She had something to ask him, and she wanted to ask it somewhere that belonged to the beginning.

She pulled on a cardigan and her slippers and went down through the kitchen and out of the front door. The porch light was on. It always was. The bench ran along under the old rail where the wall had been. Beyond the gate in the garden wall the tall house was dark except for a small light in the kitchen, where Ah Sim had left the lamp on for twenty-five years.

She sat down on the bench and tucked her feet under her and looked at the lane.

Two in the morning. Twenty-five. She thought about the girl who’d sat on these steps at eighteen in rabbit slippers, waiting for a well done. The girl who’d thought being loved meant being watched and corrected and kept close enough that leaving would feel like a crime. The girl who’d nearly got off a train because she was frightened of an old woman with a stick. The girl who’d bolted her door at two in the morning because somebody had said marry.

She wondered what that girl would think of her now. Perhaps she’d cry. Perhaps she wouldn’t believe it. Perhaps she’d ask whether the boy next door was still next door.

He was. He always had been.

✦ ✦ ✦

The day had begun at the cemetery.

Baba was there before anyone else, standing in front of the stone in his dark coat with a small bunch of white flowers and a cloth bag in his hand.

“Baba.”

“Yu-er.”

“Happy birthday to me,” she said.

He looked at her, and nodded. “Happy birthday.”

It came easily now. Not perfectly, not without the odd pause, but easily enough that she’d stopped holding her breath for it. He took a red egg out of the cloth bag and set it on the stone beside the flowers.

“Twenty-five,” he said.

“Yes.”

“You’re getting older.”

“That’s usually how it goes.”

“Still talking too much,” said Lin Jian, and she laughed.

She’d brought a photograph from the wedding and propped it beside the flowers: the two of them under the persimmon in October, both laughing at something Raiden had shouted. Her mother had never met her. Eliana didn’t feel any more that she had to guess what her mother would have thought of every choice. She could simply miss her, and carry on.

“You look happy,” said her father, looking at it.

“I was.”

“Was?”

“I still am.”

“Good.” He adjusted the flowers. “How’s FENCE?”

“Busy. Four staff. Two floors. A proper sign.”

“Two floors? Did you need two floors?”

“We needed more room.”

“Then you should have found more room.”

“Baba. That’s what we did.”

His mouth moved. “Good.” He looked at her sideways. “Does Si-Wei still say she does all the work?”

“Every day.”

“Does she?”

“Absolutely not.”

He nodded, as if that settled an important business matter. “Make sure she knows.”

He asked about her work often now. Not the way he used to, when every question had been a test she was failing. He asked because he wanted to know what she was doing. Sometimes he even listened all the way to the end without telling her what to do instead. It was progress. Small and ordinary.

There was a second egg in the bag.

“Two?” she said.

“One’s yours.” He hesitated. “The other’s for your husband.”

She looked at him, and a smile spread right across her face. “You brought Yu Chen a red egg?”

“He’s family,” said her father. “Take it home.”

The others came up the hill in ones and twos. Elowen and Zhao with a basket of fruit. Raiden and Jinx arguing about where they’d parked. Ev and Jun Hyuk with freesias. Elara with Xing Yue’s hand resting lightly at her back. Nobody made a speech. Elowen put her flowers beside Eliana’s. Jun Hyuk bowed to Lin Jian. Raiden said something to Jinx that made her elbow him.

Yu Chen came last, straight from a night shift, with a small paper bag.

“You’re late,” said Eliana.

He looked at his watch. “I’m on time.”

“You’re late in my heart.”

“Happy birthday, sweetheart,” he said, and kissed her knuckles, and took something out of the bag. “Your red egg.”

It was lopsided. Badly lopsided. The shell had a crack at one end and the dye had gone on in patches like a map of some unfortunate island.

“What happened to it?”

“Nothing. I boiled it. It was meant to be round.” He looked at it with dignity. “I made another one. It’s in the kitchen. It’s better.”

“Why didn’t you bring that one?”

“This one was yours,” he said.

Her laughter went soft. She took the cracked egg in both hands. “I love it.”

Baba cleared his throat. Yu Chen turned.

“Baba,” he said. He’d started calling him that at the wedding dinner, without asking, and her father had stopped, and looked at him, and gone on eating, and that had been permission.

Lin Jian held out the second egg. “For you.”

Yu Chen looked at it, and at Eliana, who was already smiling, and took it in both hands. “Thank you.”

Her father, and her husband. Two men who’d once stood on either side of a wall each certain he knew what was best for her. Now they were handing each other red eggs in front of her mother’s grave.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch was at the tall house, where Ah Sim had cooked for twice the number of people there were. Raiden ate as if he hadn’t seen food in a week. Yu Chen put the two red eggs in a small bowl beside his plate.

“You kept the ugly one,” she said.

“Especially the ugly one.”

Halfway through, her father asked about FENCE again. She told him about the second floor, the four staff, the bigger clients, the ones she still turned down.

“Do you still do the work yourself?”

“Some. Si-Wei runs most of the operations. The team does most of the assessments. I do the client meetings, the reviews, the hard conversations. And the technical work when it’s interesting.”

He nodded. He drank some tea.

“You built something,” he said.

He didn’t add anything. He didn’t need to.

“Yes,” she said.

“Your mother would have liked that,” said Lin Jian, and she reached across the table and took his hand, and he let her keep it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen drove them home. She sat in the passenger seat watching the afternoon light slide across the buildings.

“You’re quiet,” he said.

“I’m thinking.”

He waited. He’d learned not to fill every silence.

“FENCE has been asked to do a job abroad,” she said. “A regional group. An independent security review across five sites. It’s big. Too big to do from here. Three months, maybe more. Singapore first, and then two other places.”

“Three months.”

“I’d like you to come with me.” She turned in her seat. “I know your training’s complicated. I know you can’t just vanish from City. I’m not asking you to give anything up. I just wanted to ask.”

He kept his eyes on the road. “Do you want me there because you want me there, or because you don’t want to be away from home?”

“Both,” she said honestly.

He smiled. “I’d like to come.”

“You don’t have to say yes because it’s my birthday.”

“I’m not.”

She looked at him all the way back to the lane.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home he went up to change. She stayed in the kitchen putting Ah Sim’s leftovers in the fridge. His phone was on the counter. It lit up.

City Hospital — Leave request approved.

She didn’t open it. She didn’t need to. The preview was enough. Four weeks.

He came down with his sleeves pushed up and his hair damp, and saw her face, and saw the phone, and stopped on the bottom stair.

“Four weeks?” she said.

“Yes.”

“You booked leave. Before I asked you.”

He came closer. “I saw the proposal two weeks ago. You’d left it open on the long desk.”

“I was reviewing it.”

“I know. I read the page that was open.” He held up a hand before she could speak. “Only that page. I didn’t touch anything else. I saw the dates. I read the hospital’s leave policy and spoke to my supervisor. I didn’t ask for anything till I knew the dates might work.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I didn’t know if you’d want me there. I didn’t want you to think I’d already decided.” He looked at her. “Four weeks is all they’d give me. I thought it would let us work out whether I could join you again later, or whether you’d rather do the rest on your own.”

“How did you know when to ask?” she said. “You can’t have known it was real from one page.”

He looked almost embarrassed. “Your noodles.”

“My what?”

“You order the same noodles from the place by the pier whenever you’re working on something that matters to you. You ordered them three times in one week.” He paused. “And you asked whether the hotel by the client’s office had a proper kitchen. And you left the flight tabs open.”

She put her hands over her face. “You investigated my noodle habits.”

“I noticed.”

“That’s worse.”

He took her hand. “I haven’t booked anything else. No flights. Nowhere to stay. Only the leave. I wanted to ask you first.”

She looked at their hands. He hadn’t bought a building. He hadn’t decided for her. He hadn’t silently arranged her life round his idea of what she needed. He’d taken a possibility seriously and left the choice with her.

“Four weeks,” she said.

“Yes.”

“That’s romantic.”

“I thought so.”

“You’re ridiculous,” she said, and stepped into him, and kissed him. Not the quick kitchen kiss they gave each other going out of the door, or the one she used to stop him being serious. She kissed him slowly because she was happy and because she wanted to.

“Happy birthday?” he said, when she let him breathe.

“The best one,” she said, and meant it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning he came out onto the porch in a soft T-shirt with his hair on end.

“Sweetheart?”

“Hi.”

“Couldn’t sleep?”

“I could.” She patted the bench. “Come and sit.”

He sat. The bench creaked. The bulbs from the wedding were still strung through the persimmon over the gate, switched off, their outlines faint in the light from the lane. He put his arm along the back of the bench behind her.

“Do you remember the first time you sat with me out here?” she said.

“You were eighteen.”

“And you’d been in love with me for years.”

“Yes.”

“You’re not even going to deny it?”

“No,” said Yu Chen.

She leaned her head on his shoulder. “I’ve got something to ask you.”

“All right.”

“I want to take the job. I want to see what FENCE can do outside the city. I want to work with people I’ve never worked with. I want to find out if we can build something bigger.” She looked up. “And I want you there. Not for four weeks. For as much of the three months as we can make work. I’m not asking you to put your life on hold. I want us to work it out together.”

He thought about it. “What do you need from me?”

“Your company.”

“That’s all?”

“For now.”

“Then yes,” he said. “I’ll talk to my supervisor. If I can’t be there the whole time I’ll come when I can. And you don’t turn it down because of me.”

“I won’t.”

She put her hand flat on his chest.

“I used to think forever was a frightening word,” she said. “I thought it meant I’d never be allowed to leave. That if I promised, I’d lose the right to change my mind.” She looked out at the gate standing open in the old wall. “I don’t think that any more. I think it’s the freedom to keep choosing the same person. I don’t need to know what the next ten years look like, or where we’ll live, or how many times we’ll move. I just want to keep finding you.”

He didn’t say anything. He looked at her as if she’d given him something he’d waited for since he was ten.

She turned on the bench and took his face in her hands, and kissed him first, slowly, on the step where she’d sat at eighteen and he’d sat down on the other side of a wall and stayed.

“Forever,” she said against his mouth.

“Forever,” said Yu Chen.

They stayed out there until the sky began to thin over the roofs. When they went in he paused at the door and looked back at the garden, at the dark persimmon and the open gate.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing.” He looked at her. “Twenty-five.”

“Twenty-five.”

“Happy birthday, sweetheart.”

She stood on her toes and kissed him once more, and he held the door, and she went in, and the boy next door followed his wife home.

chapters.title: A History of Untangled Headphones
chapters.desc: Six years of Yu Chen untangling Eliana’s wired headphones, mending the ones she breaks, and buying the last forty pairs in the city when the make is stopped. He has never once complained. Then she finds the one pair she untangled for him.
chapters.epigraph: “A lifetime.”
chapters.content:
By the time she was twenty Eliana had broken six pairs of headphones, and Yu Chen had watched every death.

One crushed under a textbook. One caught in the hinge of her desk drawer. One whose left cup simply stopped, though she swore she’d done nothing to it. One she’d tried to mend with a paper clip, which he’d banned. One sent through the wash in a pocket. One that survived all of it and then died when she yanked the cable too hard trying to get a knot out.

He’d never once complained. Not when she dropped a snarl of wire in his lap in the middle of a lecture. Not when she knocked at his door at eleven at night holding a pair so knotted they looked like a small furious sea creature. He took them, and sat down, and untangled them. Sometimes while she complained about something else. Sometimes while he read. Once, in second year, he did an entire cable without looking up from his anatomy notes. She’d thought of it as a useful domestic skill. She hadn’t thought of it as anything else until she found the drawer.

It was a Sunday at the end of November, five weeks after the wedding. He was on a day shift at City. She was meant to be sorting the spare room, which had become the room where they put things they meant to sort later. She’d found three reams of printer paper, a box of old lecture notes, two chargers that belonged to neither of them and a mug she’d been looking for since September, and then she opened the bottom drawer of his old desk.

Cables, coiled. A box of adapters. And a pair of black headphones, the over-ear kind with the soft cups and the long cord, wound neatly round themselves and held with a strip of Velcro. There was a tiny scuff on the left cup. On the cable, near the jack, a little flag of yellow tape with a number on it in his handwriting.

7.

She sat back on her heels. She knew pair seven.

She’d broken it in the autumn of 2022, the evening the invoice came. He Si-Mei had found the flaw in a system Eliana had built, fixed it without being asked, and sent a bill with a covering note that called the flaw an avoidable oversight. Eliana had read it on the bus and come home so angry she’d ripped the headphones off her head in his doorway and a wire had come away inside the right cup. She’d thrown them on his table.

“Don’t,” she’d said.

“Don’t what?”

“Say anything. You’re thinking I’m careless.”

He’d turned them over in his hands. “I’m thinking the solder joint’s come loose,” he’d said, and fixed it that night with the little iron he kept for his bicycle lights. She’d worn them the next morning to the café where Qian had arranged for her to meet He Si-Mei in person, and argued for forty minutes, and walked out with the invoice halved and a grudging you’re better than your mistake, which she’d counted as winning. She’d kissed him in the kitchen afterwards holding the receipt up like a trophy. She’d forgotten the headphones.

Apparently he hadn’t.

There were more in the drawer. A pair still sealed in its box. Another. Another. All the same make, all the same model, black, the one she’d liked since a paper bag of ten had appeared on her desk in her first September. She took them out one at a time and stacked them on the floor round her until she was sitting in a small black fortress of boxes.

Forty. Under the last one was a folded receipt from three years before. Discontinued stock. Clearance. 40 units.

Eliana: why do you own forty pairs of my headphones

It took him six minutes.

Yu Chen: I wondered when you’d find those.

Eliana: that isn’t an answer

Yu Chen: I’m at work.

Eliana: you can answer at work

Yu Chen: They stopped making them. You hated the replacements.

She had. One had been too sharp. One tangled if you looked at it. One wouldn’t stay on her head. She’d complained about all three, and he’d listened, and apparently made a purchase.

Eliana: you bought the last forty

Yu Chen: The last forty I could find.

Eliana: you’re insane

Yu Chen: Probably.

Eliana: i married you

Yu Chen: Yes.

Eliana: i’ve made a terrible mistake

Yu Chen: I love you too. Don’t lose pair seven.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he came home at eight she was at the kitchen table with all forty arranged in front of her in rows.

He stopped in the doorway, looked at the headphones and then at his wife, washed his hands first, dried them, folded the towel, and sat down beside her with the composure of a man who’d bought forty pairs of discontinued headphones and saw no reason to treat it as an event.

“You could have bought ten,” she said.

“You’d have used them.”

“Twenty.”

“You’d have used them.”

“Thirty.”

He considered. “Possibly.”

“Forty?”

“The man had forty,” said Yu Chen.

She pressed her lips together. He’d known she liked something, learned it was going, and made sure she’d never have to go looking. It was absurd. It was entirely him.

“Do you know how many I’ve broken?” she said.

“Since first year? Twenty-three.”

“You counted?”

“No.” He turned one of the boxes over in his hands. “You break more when you’re having a bad month. Three in four months in second year. Two during the breach. One you kept pulling off your head while you worked, so you could hear the door.” He paused. “One last year. The spring you opened FENCE.”

She stopped smiling.

There it was again: the quiet, slightly unnerving way he had of reading her through the most ridiculous things. Which noodles she ordered. Whether she’d stopped wearing earrings because she was tired. How fast a pair of headphones died in a hard month. Sometimes it was a comfort. Sometimes she wanted to confiscate it.

“That’s a little creepy,” she said.

“I know.”

“You’re not supposed to agree.”

“Would you rather I hadn’t noticed?”

She looked at his hand round hers on the table. “No.”

“Then?”

“Then at least pretend to be normal.”

“I’ll try,” he said.

“You won’t.”

“No,” he agreed, and she leaned on his shoulder and laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the other pair three days later, and it wasn’t in the drawer.

It was in the shallow drawer of his bedside table, under an old watch strap and a packet of spare shirt buttons. His own headphones, the cheap grey ones with the silver rings round the earpieces that he wore on the bicycle under his helmet. The cord was wound round itself in a lumpy, uneven coil, with one loop twisted the wrong way and the end tucked through in a way that made them hard to undo.

She knew that coil. She’d made it.

It was the week after his stitches, a year ago. He’d been home on orders to rest and had sat at the long desk trying to read a journal with one eye, and his headphones had been lying on the desk in a knot. She’d picked them up.

“Those are mine,” he’d said.

“I know.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I’m aware.”

She’d made it worse. Then better. Then worse. It had taken her ten minutes and a good deal of language, and the result had been neither elegant nor, strictly, untangled. She’d held it up.

“Done.”

He’d looked at the lump of cord, and then at her, and said “Thank you,” gravely, and put them down with great care beside his journal. She’d forgotten all about it by dinner.

He came out of the bathroom and found her sitting on the bed holding them.

“You kept these,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I didn’t untangle them. I made them worse in a different direction.”

“You did it for me,” he said. He took them out of her hands and put them back into her palm. “That’s all.”

She looked down at the lumpy coil.

She’d handed him tangled things for six years without thinking. Cables and headphones and bad days and her father and a frightened girl in a doorway at two in the morning. He’d taken all of it without a word and sorted it out and learned the difference between a broken wire and a hard week. And he’d kept the one knot she’d ever tried to undo for him.

“Do you remember the breach?” she said.

“The register.”

“Do you remember what I did with the cable for the drive case?”

He thought. “You tied it to the handle. With Jinx’s knots.”

“A reef knot and a bowline. She taught me on the workshop floor the week before. Everyone said I was being ridiculous.”

“You were.”

“It worked.”

“It did,” he said. “It didn’t catch once all night. I watched you carry that case up and down the stairs nine times.”

He remembered that too. Of course he did.

“You’ve made a whole history out of my not being able to look after headphones,” she said.

“Not only that. I remember pair seven going into that café. I remember you on my floor in first year untangling the black ones and crying because you thought you’d ruined something important.”

“I hadn’t.”

“No.” He looked at her. “I remember you asking me to hold your hand while I did one. Second year. You were too tired to say why. I did the whole cable one-handed.”

She’d forgotten that one entirely. “That sounds inconvenient.”

“It was,” said Yu Chen. “I didn’t mind.”

She stood up on the bed so that she was taller than him, and looped the grey headphone cord round the back of his neck, and took one end in each hand.

“What are you doing?”

“Keeping you.”

“With headphones?”

“You bought forty pairs. You’re responsible for the investment.”

He laughed. She pulled gently on both ends until his face came up to hers, and kissed him, slow, with the cord loose round his neck and her hands flat on his chest. His arms came round her waist without tightening.

“Was that payment?” he said against her mouth. “For six years of untangling?”

“That was interest.”

“How much do I owe you?”

She kissed the corner of his mouth. “A lifetime.”

Something changed in his eyes. His hand moved from her waist to the small of her back.

“That’s a long time,” he said.

“You kept the broken ones. You kept the one I untangled.” She smiled. “I think you can afford it.”

He kissed her again, and the lumpy grey headphones went back in the shallow drawer under the watch strap and the spare buttons, exactly where he’d kept them for a year.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning he was at the kitchen table with pair seven in his hands, frowning at the jack.

“The joint’s going again.”

“Give it to me.”

He raised an eyebrow. “Do you know how?”

“No. Don’t interrupt the process.”

She sat beside him and began winding the cable round her fingers. In under a minute she’d produced a knot.

“Sweetheart. That’s the wrong end.”

“Do you want to do it?”

“No.”

“Then be quiet.”

He was quiet. A second knot appeared. He pressed his lips together.

“Don’t,” she said, pointing at him.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face is saying things.”

He looked away, smiling. After another minute she’d got the cord loose, with one kink near the jack and a twist that would never come out. She held it out.

“Fixed.”

He took it from her as if it were something precious. “Thank you.”

He put it down beside his cup and took her hand, and they sat in the quiet kitchen with their fingers laced between the teacups.

“Next time you buy forty of something,” she said, “tell me.”

“All right.”

“You’re only saying that.”

“Probably,” said Yu Chen, and she leaned over and kissed him, and then put pair seven carefully beside his phone.

“Don’t lose those,” she said. “I untangled them.”

“I know,” he said.

It had never really been about the headphones. It was all the things she’d handed him without thinking. All the knots and the messes and the ordinary, inconvenient pieces of her life. He’d never asked her to turn up with everything neatly put away. He’d made room beside him, taken whatever she held out, and stayed until it came undone.

chapters.title: The Library Booking System
chapters.desc: Study room 4B has been booked to “Wang Y.C.” every Friday since the March of his first year, and nobody has ever beaten him to it. The librarian who has watched it for four years has her suspicions. She never finds out how.
chapters.epigraph: “For the librarian who kept our mornings safe.”
chapters.content:
Mrs. Cai had worked on the front desk of the medical library for twenty-seven years. In that time she’d watched several generations of students fall in love, fall out of it, cry over results, cheat on results, and sleep so deeply in the reading room that the fire alarm hadn’t moved them. She considered herself hard to surprise.

Then there was Wang Yu Chen, and study room 4B.

The first time she noticed the booking was in March of his first year. Wang Y.C. — 4B — Friday 08:00–12:00. An ordinary booking. The following Friday it was there again. And the one after. By the end of the term she’d noticed that it was always 4B: not the big rooms on the second floor, not the ones with the good windows over the camphor trees, not the ones by the reference shelves. A small room on the third floor with a table, four chairs, a noticeboard and one window. By his second year it was most mornings, not only Fridays.

He was punctual and polite and had once carried a box of donated journals up two flights for her without being asked. There was only one odd thing.

The booking system opened at midnight, two weeks ahead, and there were three hundred medical students and twelve rooms. In four years, nobody beat him to 4B. Not once. Mrs. Cai had looked at the timestamps. Every booking had gone in at between four and nine seconds past midnight.

She’d also noticed he always booked it for one, and always put out two chairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

By his second year she had a theory, and it was not an unreasonable one.

The girl was called Lin Eliana. Computer science, not medicine, which made her use of a medical study room technically irregular, which Mrs. Cai chose not to see. Small, in enormous jumpers, with a claw clip and round glasses that were usually on top of her head, and a habit of carrying three books more than she could manage and losing her student card. She wasn’t especially quiet. Mrs. Cai had once heard her arguing with the printer by the stairs. The printer had won. Wang Yu Chen had fixed it.

And whenever she came up the stairs, his head turned towards the door of 4B before she’d reached it. A small movement. But Mrs. Cai had been watching people across a desk for twenty-seven years, and she knew what waiting looked like.

One morning the girl came in at seventeen minutes past eight with a laptop, a drink and three books, and pushed the door open with her shoulder.

“Sorry.”

“You’re late,” he said, without looking up.

“I know.”

“Did you eat?”

“Good morning to you too.”

He pushed a small paper bag across the table. She looked inside. Her whole face changed.

“You’re annoying,” she said.

“Eat.”

Mrs. Cai, who had been checking the room was occupied, withdrew from the doorway. She didn’t need to know anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first incident was in their third year. She remembered it because a law student complained to her about it at the desk.

He’d come up at five past eight and found the girl in the chair by the window of 4B and informed her the room was booked.

“Is it?” said Eliana, looking up from her laptop.

“I booked it.”

“Okay,” she said, as if she had no strong views.

“So you can move.”

Before she could, the door opened behind him. Wang Yu Chen came in with two drinks in one hand and four books in the other, and looked at the law student, and at Eliana, and at the chair.

“What’s happened?”

“I’ve booked this room. She’s in my seat.”

Yu Chen put the drinks down. He took his phone out and showed the law student the confirmation. “4B is booked to me. You’ve got 4D. Across the corridor.”

The boy looked at the slip on the door, and went red. “I thought—“

“She’s sitting where she belongs,” said Yu Chen.

He didn’t raise his voice. It wasn’t even unfriendly. But something in his face made the law student decide that arguing would be an unproductive use of his morning, and he went across the corridor and complained to Mrs. Cai instead.

She went up later with a returned book as an excuse. The door was ajar.

“She’s sitting where she belongs?” the girl was saying. “That’s possessive about a chair.”

“It’s your chair.”

“Since when?”

“Since you started sitting in it.”

“That isn’t how ownership works,” said Eliana.

“Drink,” said Yu Chen, and put the cup in her hand.

Mrs. Cai went back down to the desk and read the same paragraph of her newspaper four times.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were other things. Small ones.

The window chair was always left empty until the girl came in. He never put his bag on it. He put her water on the right side of her laptop, because she was left-handed and kept knocking it over when it was on the left. When she rubbed her eyes he’d take her glasses off her face without a word, clean them on a cloth from his pocket and put them back on her nose, and neither of them stopped working. Mrs. Cai had never seen a young man so entirely domesticated.

One afternoon she went up to fetch a book somebody had left in 4B, and the door was half open, and she stopped.

The girl was sitting in the window chair with her legs folded under her, reading. He was standing beside her. He said something. She shook her head. She looked up at him with an expression Mrs. Cai recognised as the beginning of an argument, and he reached down and took her glasses off.

“Hey.”

“Your eyes are tired.”

“I’m reading.”

“You’ve been reading for four hours.”

“That’s usually what happens in a library.”

He smiled. Then he bent down and kissed her. Not hurried and not accidental: a familiar kiss, given with the calm of someone who’d done it many times. The girl took hold of the front of his shirt when he began to straighten up, and kissed him back.

Mrs. Cai turned round in the corridor and walked straight back downstairs. She had seen nothing. Absolutely nothing. She was, after all, a professional.

The next morning there was a yellow sticky note on her desk under the stapler. A small drawing in pencil of a dark blue flask with a dent in its side, and under it, in a round untidy hand: sorry about the noise. — 4B.

She’d never mentioned noise. She put it in her drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

The nine days were different. She remembered them because the room stayed booked.

It was the spring of their last year, the March before his finals. Wang Y.C. — 4B — 08:00–12:00. Every morning. On the first day she assumed the girl was ill. On the second she wondered whether they’d argued. By the third she’d noticed that he was coming in earlier than usual, putting his books down and sitting in his chair, and that the window chair stayed empty. He didn’t use it for his bag. He didn’t move it. He didn’t look at it for long. But every time the door at the top of the stairs went, his eyes lifted.

On the fourth day she took him a cup of tea.

He looked up, startled. “Thank you, Mrs. Cai.”

She glanced at the empty chair. “Your friend’s not coming today?”

Something moved in his face. “No.”

“Is she unwell?”

A pause. “Not exactly.”

She didn’t ask any more.

On the seventh he didn’t come. On the eighth he was back at two minutes past eight, grey with tiredness, and sat beside the empty chair all morning.

On the ninth he came in carrying two drinks. Tea, and the sweet iced coffee the girl always got. He put the coffee on the table by the window chair and sat down.

Mrs. Cai looked away. She’d been young once. She remembered what it was to wait for someone who hadn’t decided yet whether to come back.

At a quarter to twelve he packed his books and picked up both cups. The coffee hadn’t been touched. He carried it out.

She never knew what had happened. She only knew that the boy who’d booked a room for two had sat in it alone for nine mornings, and had never once changed the booking. And she knew that on the tenth morning the door at the top of the stairs went at eight sixteen, and his head came up, and the girl walked in with her shoulder against the door and three books too many, and stood there in the doorway looking at him, and he looked at her, and Mrs. Cai went and found something urgent to do in the stacks.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time Mrs. Cai retired, they weren’t students. They’d graduated and got jobs and married, and had become the sort of adults who only came to a library when they needed something in particular. He still came in now and then, to collect a journal, or to return a book his wife had forgotten to renew.

Her last day was the last Friday in November. She’d expected flowers, perhaps a cake, a few words from the dean. Instead, when she logged in at half past seven, the booking screen said something it had never said before.

Study Room 4B — Reserved: Mrs. Cai — 08:00–12:00.

She checked the date. Friday. She checked the name again. She was still staring at it when a voice said, “Good morning.”

Wang Yu Chen stood at the desk. Beside him was his wife, in an enormous jumper, with her glasses on top of her head. They were both holding paper bags.

“Did you book a study room for me?” said Mrs. Cai.

“Because you always made sure we had one,” said Eliana.

“I did no such thing.”

“You moved the law student’s booking to 4D,” said Eliana sweetly. “In our third year. At twelve minutes past midnight. I saw the log.”

Mrs. Cai opened her mouth and shut it again.

Yu Chen put a small thermos on the desk. “Tea. The kind you drink.”

“How do you know what tea I drink?”

“He notices things,” said Eliana, and he gave her a look, and she ignored it.

Mrs. Cai laughed, and took her keys, and went up the stairs with them to 4B. It was exactly as it had always been. On the table by the window, a yellow sticky note.

A pencil drawing of a dark blue flask with a dent in its side. And underneath, in the same round untidy hand:

For the librarian who kept our mornings safe.

“That flask,” said Mrs. Cai.

“You remember?”

“You knocked it off this table in your second year. All over the floor. Something sweet. I was mopping it up for a week.”

“It was an accident,” said Eliana. “The table was unstable.”

“She blamed me,” said Yu Chen.

“You were standing there.”

“I was holding the door.”

“Exactly,” said Eliana.

Mrs. Cai shook her head and sat down in the window chair. For the first time in twenty-seven years she had the room to herself. Yu Chen poured the tea and put it by her hand.

“Thank you, Mrs. Cai,” said Eliana.

“For what?”

“For pretending not to notice.”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” said Mrs. Cai.

“Of course you don’t.”

She picked up the sticky note. “Was it always him who booked it?”

“Always,” said Eliana.

Mrs. Cai looked at him over her glasses. “Four seconds past midnight, young man. Every time. For four years. How?”

His face didn’t change. “Good planning.”

“I’ve worked here twenty-seven years. I know how that system works.”

“Then you know I’m punctual,” said Wang Yu Chen, and she laughed until she had to put her tea down.

She’d never find out. She’d never know about the alarm at eleven fifty-eight every night for four years, or the second phone with the booking page already open. She’d never know he’d chosen 4B the first time because the girl had said, once, in passing, that she liked a room with one window. She’d never know he’d put out two chairs because he wanted her beside him, and that for four years he’d thought the best part of his morning was the moment the door opened and she came in.

She didn’t need to. She’d seen enough.

“Go on,” she said. “You’ve got things to do.”

They went. She watched them through the glass of the door. At the top of the stairs he reached for his wife’s hand, and she said something that made him look down at her with that same quiet smile, and then they were gone round the corner.

She put the yellow note inside her notebook and closed it. She’d keep it. It was a rather good story, and she was quite sure she’d been there for the beginning.

chapters.title: The Sticky Note Drawer
chapters.desc: Every note Eliana was ever too shy to say out loud, kept in order in a drawer in Yu Chen’s desk, from a smiling dumpling in her first fortnight on the hill to the one that just said “Official”. The week before the wedding, she catches him reading them.
chapters.epigraph: “Some things are nice when they’re kept.”
chapters.content:
She found the drawer because he was being suspicious, and he was bad at it.

It was the Sunday a week before the wedding. He was at his desk in the long room with the bottom drawer open, reading something with a face far too soft for a man supposedly going through his hospital rota, and when she came past the doorway he shut the drawer. A little too quickly.

She stopped. “What are you hiding?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s a suspicious answer.”

“It’s an accurate one.”

“Then why did you shut it like that?”

“Because you’re standing there,” he said, and went back to his papers.

In all the years she’d known him, Wang Yu Chen had never been any good at keeping things from her. He could hide his own feelings with terrifying discipline, but anything that had to do with her showed on him like weather. She walked round the end of his desk.

“Sweetheart,” he said. “Don’t.”

“Now I definitely will,” said Eliana, and pulled the drawer open.

The first thing she saw was a yellow sticky note with a dumpling on it. A smiling dumpling with two tiny arms and an expression of unreasonable happiness, and under it, in her own handwriting: you look hungry. eat something.

She picked it up. Under it was a cup of tea. don’t drink coffee on an empty stomach, you’re not as clever as you think. Under that, a rabbit. good luck with your exam. don’t die.

There were dozens. More than dozens. The whole drawer was full of small neat stacks, each held with a paper clip, and every note had a date on the back in his tiny careful hand. She lifted the first stack. The earliest date was June 2021. The week after a night on the front steps. She’d stuck the dumpling to his front door at six in the morning and run.

“You kept these,” she said.

“Yes.”

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

“Why are they dated?”

“So I’d know when you wrote them.”

“Obviously,” she said, and he almost smiled.

She went through them standing up. University. His hospital rotations. The first year of FENCE. Drawings, reminders, small complaints. your face is distracting. please study. I’m not talking to you and underneath, smaller: you can still hold my hand. She laughed at that one, and then turned over the next and stopped laughing.

A heart. Or a heart that had been drawn, and scribbled out, and drawn again beside the scribble, and half scribbled out again, and redrawn a third time, tiny, in the corner. Under it: I meant it.

She knew this one.

October 2023. The morning after the front step at two in the morning, after the photograph of Ev, when she’d said it first. She’d been so embarrassed in daylight that she’d spent breakfast unable to look at him, and before he went to the ward she’d slipped this into his pharmacology textbook in a hurry. She’d drawn the heart, and hated it, and crossed it out, and drawn it again, and hated that too. She’d forgotten all about it.

She turned it over. Under the date, in his handwriting, one line.

She said it.

“You wrote on it,” she said.

“On the back.”

“Why?”

He stood up. “Because I wanted to remember.”

She looked at the little scribbled hearts. She’d spent that whole day terrified he’d think she’d said it carelessly, terrified he’d ask her to say it again. She hadn’t known he’d kept the evidence. She hadn’t known he’d wanted to remember it as badly as she’d wanted to hide.

✦ ✦ ✦

The notes from after the nine days were kept on their own, folded once each, held with a black clip.

tomorrow.

She’d written it the first morning after she’d knocked on his door at two in the morning in her socks, and left it on his desk before her nine o’clock lecture, because she was afraid of saying too much, of promising things she didn’t know how to keep. One word. The next day: still tomorrow. Then tomorrow. don’t be late. Then I know you’re busy. tomorrow anyway. Every morning until his finals, under his door, on his desk, pressed into his hand on the stairs. She’d thought of them as a joke. A way of saying she was still there without having to explain why she’d been afraid to come back.

He’d kept every one. On the back of the first, he’d written: She came back.

She sat down in his chair.

“You kept all of them,” she said. “Even the ones that only said tomorrow.”

“Especially those.” He crouched beside the chair. “I didn’t know if you’d go again. I knew you were trying. I knew you were coming back in the ways you could. But I didn’t know how long it would be before you could say all of it.” He touched the edge of the paper. “These helped.”

She leaned down and kissed his forehead, and his cheek, and the corner of his mouth.

“I chose you,” she said.

“I know,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rest made her laugh. buy milk. you left your book at my house. you look like this when you’re tired under a drawing of a furious cat. I miss you. don’t make it weird on a rabbit holding a heart. A small building with a crooked sign: your company. your rules. your annoying landlord. The one from his first morning at City, which she’d written while he was in the shower: you don’t have to be brilliant today. just come home. He’d kept that one in his wallet for months; she’d seen it there.

“You kept that too.”

“Especially that.”

One from the week after the bottle. please stop getting stitches. I am running out of patience. And one that wasn’t a sticky note at all, but the back of a shopping receipt, because she hadn’t been able to find a pad at seven in the morning after the porch. yes.

“Do you know how many there are?” she said.

“One hundred and eighty-six.”

“You counted?”

“Once.”

“When?”

“A while ago.”

She laughed so hard she had to put her face in her hands.

“One hundred and eighty-seven,” he added, “if you count the one in your drawer.”

She looked up. “What?”

He pointed down the long room, to her desk.

She went and opened the top drawer. In her pen tray, under a packet of black biros, was a yellow note in his writing. Two stick people holding hands. I’m still here. On the back, last week’s date.

“That’s cheating,” she said. “You hid it in my drawer.”

“You found it.”

“Because you told me.”

He smiled. She tried to look annoyed and didn’t manage.

✦ ✦ ✦

The wedding had become a problem. Not the wedding. The vows.

He’d written six drafts. She knew because she’d found them in the wastepaper basket that morning, six sheets each folded in half, each with something crossed out. She’d read the first line of the top one before he caught her.

“Don’t.”

“What’s wrong with this one?”

“Too long.”

“This one?”

“Too short.”

The third was too sentimental. The fourth too formal. The fifth he just took out of her hand. “I don’t like it.”

“Yu Chen. You’ve written six drafts and you don’t like any of them. You’re marrying me. You’re not submitting a thesis.”

“I want to get it right.”

She put the drafts down and took his hand. “You already know what you want to say.”

“It isn’t enough.”

“How do you know?”

“Because I’ve got six versions,” he said, and she laughed, and before he could stop her she folded all six together and pushed them into the back pocket of her jeans.

“What are you doing?”

“Keeping them. I want to read them after we’re married. And you’re not allowed to write a seventh.”

“That’s unreasonable.”

“You’re marrying me. You knew what you were getting.” She stood on her toes and kissed him. “Just tell me what you want to promise.”

He thought about it, properly, the way he did.

“I’ll come out,” he said. “Every night.”

She smiled. “That’s enough.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon she sat at her desk drawing on a fresh sheet of paper, and he sat at his across the long room, angled just so, pretending to read.

She drew the two gardens. The persimmon. The old wall, and the new gate cut through it. The stone path. Two small figures walking through the gate, one in a dress, one in a suit, holding hands, with a string of little lights over their heads. A tiny rabbit in the corner, because there was always a rabbit.

“What are you drawing?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s suspicious.”

“You’re suspicious.”

He got up and came round the end of the long desk and leaned over her shoulder. “Is that us?”

“Two strangers.”

“Familiar strangers.”

She went on drawing. He reached down and took the pencil out of her fingers, and put it on the desk, and took her glasses off her face and folded them and put them beside it.

“I’m drawing.”

“I know,” he said, and leaned down over the desk and kissed her, in the middle of the sentence, with one hand flat on the paper beside the two little figures.

She made a surprised sound and then laughed against his mouth. When he drew back she took the front of his shirt and pulled him down again and kissed him first, and his smile went into the kiss and disappeared there, and for a while there was nothing in the long room but the quiet, and the pencil rolling slowly across the paper, and the two of them bent over a desk they’d shared since the summer.

“Can I see it?” he said eventually.

She held it up. Two figures. One gate. One persimmon. A row of lights.

He looked at it. “You drew the gate open.”

“Of course. We’re not going to shut it.”

He took the drawing to his desk and opened the bottom drawer, and laid it on top of the stack, beside the yellow note from her twenty-third birthday that said Official.

“You’re filing it?”

“With the others.”

“It isn’t a sticky note.”

“It’s from you,” he said.

She considered that, and nodded. “Fair. How many now?”

“One hundred and eighty-eight.”

“You counted again.”

“Yes.”

“You’re ridiculous.”

“Your ridiculous husband,” he said.

“Not yet.”

“One week.”

She put her arms round his waist and her cheek against his chest.

“Do you want me to show you all of them?” he said.

“No,” she said. “I like that you’ve got them. Some things are nice when they’re kept.” She looked at the drawer. “I think I was trying to tell you things before I knew how to say them.”

“I know.”

“Sometimes I still do.”

“I know,” he said. “Keep doing it.”

In the bottom drawer of his desk there were a hundred and eighty-eight pieces of evidence that they’d already got here. A smiling dumpling. A heart scribbled out and drawn again. A run of tomorrows. One word on the back of a receipt. And a drawing of two people walking through an open gate.

“Tomorrow,” she said.

“Tomorrow,” said Yu Chen.

chapters.title: A Background Check on Her Best Friend’s Boyfriend
chapters.desc: When her best friend says, in four words, that she’s seeing Geum Sung Jae, who runs the Iron Dogs in the grey market behind the old dockyard, Eliana does what a good friend does: a thorough, unasked-for background check, three times, overnight. She finds nothing she can prove, which annoys her more than anything else could.
chapters.epigraph: “Because the first two times I didn’t find anything.”
chapters.content:
Eliana considered herself a good friend. She remembered birthdays. She kept emergency biscuits in her desk. She knew which lecturers Si-Wei despised and which brand of tea could get her to a meeting before nine. She was also good at finding things people didn’t want found.

Which was why, when four words arrived at twenty-two minutes to midnight on a Tuesday in January, she stopped working immediately.

Si-Wei: I’m seeing someone.

Eliana: ???

Eliana: WHO

Eliana: since when

Eliana: why am I finding out by text

The dots appeared. Vanished. Appeared.

Si-Wei: Don’t make a big deal.

That was not a reassuring sentence.

Eliana: i’m making a big deal. name

Si-Wei: Geum Sung Jae.

Eliana: ok. what does he do

Si-Wei: He runs a crew. The Iron Dogs.

Eliana read it twice. She knew the name. Everybody on campus who’d ever bought anything from the market behind the old dockyard knew the name. She turned her head slowly towards the stairs of Yu Chen’s house, where Yu Chen was asleep, or supposed to be.

Eliana: define crew

Si-Wei: Eliana.

Eliana: define

Si-Wei: They keep order in the grey market. It isn’t what you’re imagining.

That was somehow worse.

Eliana: i’m going to need you to elaborate

Si-Wei: Tomorrow. Go to bed.

Eliana put the phone face down on the long kitchen table and opened her laptop.

“All right,” she said to nobody.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four minutes to midnight she had three windows open. At fourteen minutes past, she’d established that Geum Sung Jae existed and wasn’t an alias. Twenty-seven. Born in Busan, in the dock district, son of a sailor who’d lost his licence. In the city since nineteen. At half past twelve she had a company registered in his name, a warehouse lease behind the old dockyard, and a photograph of him outside it in a black coat, leaning on a car he couldn’t have afforded legally at twenty-seven, looking at the camera as if it owed him money.

By one o’clock she was annoyed. Not because she’d found something terrible. Because she hadn’t found anything she could put her finger on.

No convictions. Two arrests, both dropped. A string of complaints that went nowhere because nobody would sign them. And a pattern so clear she could have drawn it on a whiteboard: every man who’d ever been hurt in that market had been hurting someone first. Loan sharks. A landlord who’d put a family on the street in a typhoon. A man who ran a gambling room and let schoolboys in. In September, three of a loan shark’s men in Harbourside’s fracture clinic on the same night with their hands broken, all of them telling the doctors they’d fallen down stairs. The same night, she noticed, Si-Wei had come into the canteen the next morning with a bruise on her wrist she’d said was a door.

She sat back.

“Who are you,” she said to the screen.

“Sweetheart?”

She jumped. He was in the kitchen doorway in a T-shirt and sleep trousers, hair on end, with the look he got when he found her awake at an unreasonable hour: concern and resignation in equal parts. He looked at the clock, at the laptop, at the empty glass beside her.

“Why are you working?”

“I’m not.”

“You’re running a background check.”

She turned round. “How do you know?”

“You’ve got three windows open, your shoulders are up by your ears, and you haven’t noticed me standing here for a minute.”

“Si-Wei’s seeing someone,” she said.

His face softened. “That’s good.”

“He runs the Iron Dogs.”

He paused. “All right.”

“All right?”

“What would you like me to say?”

“Something.”

“Something,” said Yu Chen, and she glared at him, and he came and put his hand on the back of her chair. “Tell me what you’ve found.”

She told him. The company, the warehouse, the arrests that went nowhere, the hands in the fracture clinic, the bruise on Si-Wei’s wrist.

“So he hurts people,” she said.

“People who were hurting people first, from what you’ve just told me.”

“That doesn’t make it fine.”

“No,” he agreed. “It doesn’t make him a danger to Si-Wei either.”

“I don’t know that.”

“Neither do I,” said Yu Chen. “Come to bed.”

“Ten minutes.”

He kissed the top of her head, put a glass of water by her hand and a blanket round her shoulders, and went back upstairs. She’d promised ten minutes. She’d lied.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven minutes past two she found a photograph. Geum Sung Jae outside the warehouse with a man whose name was in an old customs report about restricted goods coming in through the north freight yard. She leaned close. There. Finally.

She followed the man. He’d worked for a haulier who’d once moved crates for a distributor who’d once rented a unit from a company that had once shared an accountant with one of Sung Jae’s.

Four steps removed. Possibly five. It was nothing.

“Come on,” she said.

“You’re arguing with the computer.”

He was in the doorway again. This time he had a pillow under his arm.

“Why have you got a pillow?”

“Because apparently my girlfriend isn’t coming back to bed.”

She pointed at the screen and explained. He listened without interrupting.

“That isn’t enough to say he’s done anything,” he said when she’d finished.

“I know.”

“Then why are you annoyed?”

“Because I want to know she’s safe.” Her voice cracked a little on it. “She’s my best friend. She doesn’t tell me things until they’ve already happened.”

“Maybe she wanted to be sure before she told you.”

“That isn’t better.”

“No,” he admitted. “I suppose it isn’t.”

“One more check,” she said, turning back.

“That was your second.”

“This is the third.”

He shut his eyes. “Of course it is.”

At twenty-four minutes to three he stopped the chair. Not in any figurative sense: he put one hand on the desk and the other on the back of her chair, which she’d been spinning a quarter-turn left and right while she thought, and brought it to a complete halt facing him.

“What?”

“Bed.”

“I’m nearly finished.”

“You said that forty minutes ago. You’ve looked at the same records three times. You haven’t found anything new. You’re tired, and you don’t know what you’re looking for any more.”

“You’re taking his side.”

“I’m taking yours.”

“You’re defending him.”

“I’m saying you can’t decide about a person from things you can’t prove,” he said, “and that Si-Wei’s going to tell you herself when she’s ready, and that you’ve never once made her talk before she wanted to, and she’s never once made you. Don’t start now.” He leaned down. “And I’m asking you to come to bed.”

“I just need to—“

He kissed her, in the middle of the sentence. Not long. Long enough to stop the sentence and soften her face and make her forget what she’d been going to say.

“That was manipulative,” she said, when he let her go.

“Yes.”

“You’re not supposed to admit it.”

“I’ve learned from experience,” said Yu Chen, and reached past her and saved her work and shut the laptop.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were halfway up the stairs when her phone buzzed.

“Don’t,” he said.

“It’s Si-Wei.”

Si-Wei: Are you awake?

Eliana: yes

Si-Wei: I knew it. You’ve been checking him.

She stopped on the step. how do you know

Si-Wei: Because I know you. Also because I put an alert on his company names in November and you’ve set it off eleven times since midnight.

Yu Chen, reading over her shoulder, made a small noise that might have been a laugh.

Si-Wei: I checked him already. Before. Obviously. I went through everything you’re going through, and then I went down to the market and asked people. The widows’ fund. The old man at the noodle stall. The woman whose landlord he threw down the stairs. Then I asked him. He told me all of it, including the parts I hadn’t found.

Si-Wei: He’s not stupid and he’s not safe. He knows exactly what he is. He doesn’t pretend otherwise. He’s careful about which side of the line he stands on, and when he isn’t, it’s because someone’s on the floor who deserves to be. I’ve made my own assessment.

Si-Wei: And before you ask, yes, I know what I’m doing.

Eliana’s throat went tight.

Eliana: you’re still my best friend

Si-Wei: Unfortunately.

Then one more.

Si-Wei: Also I checked Yu Chen. The week after I met you.

Eliana stood still on the stairs and turned the screen round.

He read it. His face didn’t change. His eyes narrowed a fraction.

Eliana: you WHAT

Si-Wei: He passed.

Si-Wei: Barely.

Eliana laughed so hard she had to hold the banister. Yu Chen closed his eyes.

“Of course she did,” he said.

“You didn’t know?”

“I knew she didn’t trust me.”

“That’s different.”

“Not much.”

Si-Wei: I had to make sure you weren’t with a man who’d make your life smaller. He was annoyingly decent. It made the report difficult to write.

Eliana: I’m still asking him questions. tomorrow. in person

Si-Wei: I expected nothing less.

Eliana: and I want details

Si-Wei: I know. Go to bed, Lin.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seventeen minutes past three he carried her the rest of the way.

It wasn’t strictly necessary. She was perfectly able to walk, and had been walking, until she stopped at the top of the stairs to explain that Si-Wei’s assessment was still incomplete because a grey-market operation could have layers that no public record would ever show.
