He listened. Then he bent and put one arm under her knees and the other behind her back and lifted her.

“Yu Chen. I can walk.”

“I know.”

“Then put me down.”

“No,” he said, and carried her into his room and put her down on the bed and pulled the duvet over her legs.

“You’re pleased with yourself.”

“A little.”

She held out her hand and he sat down beside her.

“Do you think she’s making a mistake?” she said.

He thought about it. “I don’t know. I don’t know enough about him. But I think she knows what she’s doing. And I think she deserves to be the one who tells you about him.”

“What if he hurts her?”

“Then you’ll be there.”

“What if she doesn’t tell me?”

“Then you remind her she can,” he said, and kissed her forehead. “You don’t have to solve every possible problem before morning.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Not really,” she said, and pulled him down beside her, and put her cheek on his chest.

“You passed, apparently,” she murmured after a while.

“Apparently.”

“Barely.”

“Yes.”

“Do you know why?”

“Because I was going out with her best friend.”

“Because you were suspiciously quiet,” said Eliana.

“I was trying not to frighten you,” he said, and she laughed against his T-shirt, and was asleep before he’d finished saying goodnight.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve minutes past nine the next morning Si-Wei came into the café by the north gate with two coffees, sat down opposite her, and looked at the folded sheet of paper by Eliana’s elbow.

“How many?”

“Twenty-seven questions.”

“Eliana.”

“Twenty-eight. I added one on the bus.”

“You’re insane.”

“You’re seeing the man who runs the Iron Dogs.”

“He’s taking me to Busan for New Year,” said Si-Wei, and pushed a coffee across. “To meet his mother. She sells fish on the dock. I’m terrified.” She looked up. “Ask your questions. But first tell me why you checked him three times.”

Eliana thought about it, and answered with complete sincerity.

“Because the first two times I didn’t find anything.”

Si-Wei stared at her. Then she burst out laughing, and Eliana, who’d spent half the night deciding whether her best friend’s boyfriend was dangerous, laughed too, and unfolded the paper.

chapters.title: The Security Flaw Rematch
chapters.desc: Four years after He Si-Mei fixed her mistake and sent a bill, Eliana finally gets her in the same room: a legal contest on the thirty-second floor of Ren Hao’s firm, with signed rules and Professor Szeto keeping score. Eleven hours later the board says draw. Neither of them believes it.
chapters.epigraph: “It’ll be there when you’ve beaten her.”
chapters.content:
The email arrived at three minutes past eight on a Saturday in July, with the subject line A Matter of Professional Pride.

Eliana read the first paragraph and sat back. Across the breakfast table Yu Chen looked up from his tea.

“What?”

She turned the laptop round. He read it, and then looked at her over the top of it.

“Who’s He Si-Mei?”

“You know who He Si-Mei is.”

“I know you’ve mentioned her.”

“How often?”

He considered. “Enough that I know she’s difficult.”

“She isn’t difficult,” said Eliana. “She’s insufferable.”

The email was from Ren Hao, who was proposing, in his usual enthusiastic fashion, a contest between two independent security professionals. Legally authorised. Signed scope. An isolated test environment built by his own firm. Eliana Lin of FENCE, and He Si-Mei, who four years ago had found a flaw in a system Eliana had designed for her brother’s people, fixed it without being asked, and sent the bill.

Eliana had paid the invoice. She’d kept the report. She’d never forgotten the two words in the middle of it, typed in a plain font without any capitals at all: avoidable oversight.

She’d been nineteen. She was twenty-three now. She had a company, a building above a dumpling shop, three people who worked for her, and clients who paid her to find problems before people like He Si-Mei did.

She read the email again and smiled. He knew the smile. It was the one she wore just before she became unreasonable.

“You’re going to accept,” he said.

“Obviously.”

“Read the rules first.”

“You’re supposed to support me. Tell me I’m going to win.”

He drank his tea. “You’re going to do your best.”

“You’re sleeping on the sofa.”

“Good luck, sweetheart,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ren Hao’s boardroom was on the thirty-second floor, with the harbour laid out under the windows like something he’d paid for. Two workstations had been set up at opposite ends of a long table, each wired to its own sealed environment. There were printed rules, signed authorisations, a list of what was allowed and a longer list of what wasn’t. No live systems. No outside help.

Professor Szeto had agreed to keep score. Eliana suspected she’d agreed because she’d once given Eliana ninety-four and the word Show-off, and wanted to see what she’d made of it. By a quarter to nine she already looked as if she regretted it.

“Eleven hours!” Ren Hao announced, throwing his arms wide. “Two brilliant professionals! One room! Completely legal! This is going to be wonderful.”

“It’s going to be long,” said Professor Szeto.

“That’s why I’ve ordered lunch.”

“That isn’t what I meant.”

Eliana had come in a white shirt and dark trousers with her laptop bag over her shoulder and a pair of black over-ear headphones round her neck. Pair seven. The wire had been mended twice since the last time she’d worn them for anything that mattered, and there was still a small pale scratch on the left ear cup where she’d thrown them across a room four years ago, the night the invoice came. She’d thought about bringing a newer pair. It had seemed disrespectful to the history of the matter.

He Si-Mei was already there. Black suit, hair tied back, an oversized pair of headphones of her own on the table, and a plain ring on her left hand that hadn’t been there in any photograph Eliana had seen. She looked up.

“Lin.”

“He Si-Mei.”

“Four years.”

“I know.” Eliana put her bag down. “Still sending invoices?”

The corner of He Si-Mei’s mouth moved. “Only when they’re earned.”

“Good. I brought my wallet.”

Professor Szeto shut her eyes. Ren Hao laughed out loud.

✦ ✦ ✦

They began at nine.

Eliana worked fast. She always had. She saw patterns in things that looked unconnected, and moved between them before she’d finished explaining to herself why. He Si-Mei worked the other way. She’d sit for twenty minutes looking at something Eliana had dismissed in two, then make one small change and find a hole in it. By ten they had one each. Neither of them smiled.

At half past ten Yu Chen came in, between the end of a night shift and the sleep he should have been having, with his hospital card still clipped to his shirt and a paper carrier in one hand. Eliana saw him through the glass wall before he reached the door, and sat up a little straighter, and pretended she hadn’t.

He put a cup of tea beside her keyboard, and turned the handle towards her. Then he walked the length of the table and put a second cup beside He Si-Mei.

She looked up. “Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

Eliana stared at the second cup. “You brought her tea?”

“She might want tea.”

He Si-Mei looked at the tea, and then at Eliana. “He’s polite.”

“He’s mine,” said Eliana.

“I can see that.”

Yu Chen bent down by her chair. “Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Food.”

He waited.

“A sandwich,” she said, and he touched her shoulder and went, and Professor Szeto wrote something in her notebook that was not part of the score.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two o’clock it was four-all, and Eliana was enjoying herself. They were both good. That was the irritating part. Then she noticed something in the corner of a finding He Si-Mei had just logged, and went back to her own notes, and found that two of the problems she’d marked separately in the morning were the same problem seen from two sides, and that between them they opened a third.

“Oh,” she said.

Professor Szeto looked up. “What?”

“Two more. And one changes what the other one means.”

Professor Szeto came round the table and read the evidence, and read the score sheet, and read the evidence again, and put her head in her hands.

“Is that good?” said Ren Hao.

“Not for my afternoon.”

He Si-Mei turned in her chair. “What did you find?”

“Wouldn’t you like to know?”

He Si-Mei looked at her, and turned back to her screen. “Well done.”

Eliana had expected an argument. A challenge. She’d have known what to do with either of those. Instead He Si-Mei simply accepted it and went on working, and that was worse, and by four o’clock it was six-all and He Si-Mei had challenged the classification of Eliana’s next find. Not whether it existed. What it was called. They both explained. Both were right, in different ways. The point was held for review.

“That’s ridiculous,” said Eliana.

“It’s reasonable,” said Professor Szeto.

“It isn’t.”

“Then tell me why.”

She did. Professor Szeto listened, and turned to He Si-Mei, and listened to her, and closed her notebook. “I need five minutes.”

Eliana didn’t wait for them. She took her phone and walked out of the boardroom and along the corridor and through the fire door at the end, and sat down on the concrete stairs between the thirty-second floor and the thirty-first, and put her face in her hands.

She’d been nineteen. She’d built that system in a month for people who’d trusted her with their lives, and someone she’d never met had walked through it, and politely closed the door behind her, and sent a bill. Four years of being careful had gone into this morning. She’d checked the scope three times. She hadn’t made the same mistake. And she still wasn’t winning.

The fire door opened above her and shut again. She knew the footsteps.

“Professor Szeto texted me,” said Yu Chen. “She said you’d gone for a walk and might need one with somebody else.”

“I’m fine.”

“I know.” He came down and sat on the step above hers, so that his knees were either side of her shoulders. “Come here.”

“I’m losing.”

“You’re drawing.”

“That’s losing slowly.”

He put one hand on top of her head, the way he had when she was fifteen and furious about something, and turned her face, gently and without any argument at all, towards the narrow window in the stairwell wall. Through it, between two towers, there was a slice of the harbour, with a ferry crawling across it and the afternoon light flat on the water.

“Look.”

“It’s the harbour.”

“It’s still there,” said Yu Chen. “It was there when she sent the invoice. It’ll be there when you’ve beaten her. And you came up here on your own feet four years later and sat down across a table from her and found something she didn’t. Whatever the board says.”

She looked at the ferry until it was gone behind the second tower.

“You’re annoying,” she said.

“I know. Drink your tea. It’s gone cold, but drink it.”

She stood up. At the fire door she turned round and came back down two steps and kissed him, hard, with her hands on either side of his face, and went back in before he’d finished standing up.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past five she was ahead by one. She checked everything again. Clean. She’d done it properly. At six He Si-Mei submitted her last finding, and Professor Szeto compared it with Eliana’s held point from four o’clock, and there was a silence long enough for Ren Hao to stand up.

“Well?”

Professor Szeto took off her glasses. “Seven-seven.”

“What?”

“A draw.”

“No,” said Eliana.

“Yes,” said He Si-Mei.

“After eleven hours?”

“After eleven hours,” said Professor Szeto.

Eliana sat back. He Si-Mei sat back. They looked at each other down the length of the table, and said, at exactly the same moment, “Rematch.”

Ren Hao laughed until he had to hold the back of a chair.

They finished the report at eight. Every finding written up, checked, classified, signed. Eliana signed her name harder than she needed to. He Si-Mei signed hers and looked across.

“You’ve improved.”

“Thank you.”

“You’re careful now.”

“I learned.” Eliana hesitated, and then said it, because it was true. “You were right. Four years ago.”

“The one you paid for?”

“Yes.”

“I know,” said He Si-Mei, and smiled, properly, for the first time all day. “Next time I’ll win.”

“No, you won’t.”

“Seven-seven, Lin.”

“Temporary.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was waiting in the car park under the building, leaning on the driver’s door of his old grey car and reading something on his phone. Eliana came out of the lift and saw him, and walked, and then halfway across the concrete she started running.

He looked up. “Sweetheart—“

She jumped. He caught her, because he always caught her, with both arms round her and one step back to take the weight, and she wrapped her arms round his neck.

“Seven-seven!”

“Is that good?”

“No. It’s a draw. She should have lost.” She leaned back far enough to see his face, and then didn’t bother looking any more and kissed him, hard enough to put his back against the car. He was smiling against her mouth. He kept on smiling until she’d stopped.

“Eleven hours,” she said, with her forehead on his.

“I know.”

“Did you sleep?”

“Some. Did you eat?”

“Don’t.”

“Did you?”

“Food.”

He laughed, and put her down, and opened her door.

Her phone buzzed in the car before they’d left the car park. An email, from an address she’d had in her contacts for four years under the name INVOICE (DO NOT PAY).

He Si-Mei: Rematch. Date to be agreed. Fee: none.

Eliana read it twice. Then she put the phone face down on her knee and looked out of the window at the dark side of the harbour, smiling, and didn’t reply until they were home.

chapters.title: Neither of Them Can Cook
chapters.desc: Two clever people who live on instant noodles and whatever Auntie Tsoi leaves decide to make dumplings from scratch for the whole family’s Sunday lunch. By eleven o’clock they have a plan, a spreadsheet and something that has to be hidden in the oven and later buried in the garden.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re clever people. You can learn to fold a dumpling.”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past eight on the last Sunday in October, Eliana made a decision that would later require sixty professionally made dumplings, one telephone call and a small burial.

She was going to host Sunday lunch.

It wasn’t an unreasonable decision. Ah Sim had gone on Friday to stay with her sister for a week, and the Lin kitchen next door was shut, and Sunday lunch had never been missed since Elowen was a girl. Auntie Tsoi had the day off and had gone to a temple fair with three women from her old street, leaving enough soup in the fridge for a household. Eliana didn’t want soup out of the fridge. She wanted to make something with her own hands and put it on the table in the house that was now theirs, and watch her family eat it.

“Let’s make dumplings,” she said, while Yu Chen was waiting for the kettle.

“Today?”

“For lunch.”

“For how many?”

She counted on her fingers. “Elowen and Zhao. Raiden and Jinx. Ev and Jun Hyuk, they’re back for a week. Baba. Us.”

“Nine.”

“About sixty dumplings.”

“All right,” said Yu Chen.

She loved how easily he agreed with her. She didn’t understand yet that he’d agreed because he assumed she knew how to make dumplings. Neither of them did.

✦ ✦ ✦

By a quarter to nine they had a plan. He’d found three recipes and laid them side by side. She’d built a spreadsheet with columns for ingredients, quantities, timings and contingencies, and a row at the bottom headed Risk.

He divided the work: he’d do the filling, she’d do the dough, they’d fold together. It was a good plan. At sixteen minutes past nine she found out that dough was less cooperative than a spreadsheet.

“Why is it sticking?”

He looked over from the chopping board. “More flour.”

“I put more flour in.”

“More again.”

“How much more?”

He came and looked into the bowl, and picked up a little between his fingers. It stretched, and hung, and fell off.

“Is it meant to do that?”

“I don’t think so.”

“You’re supposed to be good at instructions.”

“I am.” He read the recipe. “It might be the water. Too warm.”

“You told me warm water.”

“I thought warm meant warm.”

She put her hand flat in the bowl. “What do you call this?”

He touched it. “Quite warm.”

She started again. The second bowl looked like wallpaper paste.

The filling was worse. He’d chopped the cabbage fine and the chives finer, and mixed them with minced chicken and ginger and spring onion and soy and sesame oil, measured to the gram. It looked beautiful, which made her suspicious. She tasted a little from the end of a spoon.

“Interesting,” she said.

“Good?”

“Interesting.”

He tasted it and reached, without a word, for the soy.

“How much is that?”

He stopped pouring. They looked at the bottle and then at the bowl and understood together that the filling had become a problem.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past ten the kitchen looked as if a sack of flour had gone off in it. Two bowls of failed dough. One of filling that would have made a fisherman thirsty. He came up behind her and put his arms round her waist.

“How are you feeling?”

“Concentrating.”

“On what?”

“Whether I can still cancel lunch.”

He laughed into her hair. “We can still fold.”

“You believe in us?”

“Even after this.”

The first dumpling was finished at twelve minutes to eleven. It looked like a small lumpy pillow. She held it up for him to admire, and he admired it, and its bottom split and the filling fell out onto the board.

“Too much,” he said, and showed her how much was right.

“That isn’t a dumpling,” she said. “That’s a suggestion.”

Her second looked like an envelope, her third like a flower that had given up. By his eighth he’d developed a technique that involved pressing the edges together with the face he used for closing a wound in a child’s forehead, and the eighth was perfect.

She stared at it. “Why is yours perfect?”

“I followed the instructions.”

“I followed the instructions.”

“Perhaps creatively,” said Yu Chen, and she pinched his waist and he caught her hand and kissed the flour off her knuckles.

At six minutes past eleven they had twelve dumplings, of which five would stand up on their own. The first batch went in the steamer. At the six-minute mark she lifted the lid to look and he put it back down without comment. When the timer went they opened it on two that had fused into one, one that had burst, and one that had become a pale soft object of no known kind.

He picked one up. It sagged over his chopsticks like a tired sock.

“Fry the next lot,” he said. “They might hold.”

They didn’t. At eleven forty-seven the kitchen filled with smoke. At eleven forty-eight the alarm went off. At eleven forty-nine her phone lit up.

FENCE HOME: Smoke detected, kitchen.

FENCE HOME: Movement, kitchen.

She looked up at the little white camera she’d put in the corner of the ceiling herself in August. It looked back.

“Don’t say it,” she said.

Yu Chen didn’t. He turned off the gas, and opened the back door, and stood under the alarm waving a tea towel until it gave up.

The dumplings in the pan were black. Not golden, not well browned. Black right through. She sat down on the kitchen stool and didn’t say anything.

She’d wanted to do something nice. Not because anybody expected it. Because this was their house now, with the porch wall gone and the gate to the lane open, and she’d wanted to bring the whole family through it and give them something she’d made.

“Sweetheart.”

“I invited everyone,” she said. “I made something that has to be buried.”

His mouth moved.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“Your face is laughing.”

He crouched in front of the stool. “We can still have lunch.”

She looked at him. Then her face changed, and she reached for her phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Auntie Au? It’s Eliana. I’m so sorry to ring on a Sunday. Have you got dumplings?” A pause. “About sixty. Whatever you’ve got. And a few dishes, if there are any.” Another pause, longer. “No. Nobody’s ill. It’s—yes. Yes, that’s what happened. Thank you. Thank you. I’ll pay double.”

She put the phone down. “She’s sending sixty, from Terrace Road. She said she knew it would come to this when I asked her for a recipe on Thursday and wrote down the wrong numbers.”

“Problem solved,” said Yu Chen, and in the end she laughed too.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came at half past twelve. Elowen and Zhao first, then Raiden and Jinx with a bag of pears, then Ev in a yellow coat with Jun Hyuk behind her carrying a cake he’d been told not to bring, and last of all Lin Jian, through the gate from the lane in his Sunday shirt, carrying nothing because he never did.

Every one of them stopped inside the door and sniffed.

“Something happened,” said Jinx.

Zhao looked at Yu Chen. Yu Chen looked back. Neither said anything.

“Where’s lunch?” said Elowen.

“Coming.”

“What is it?”

“Dumplings.”

“Homemade?”

“Originally,” said Eliana, and Raiden started laughing before he’d taken his jacket off.

Elowen looked past them. The oven door was shut. Through the glass there was something on a tray, covered in foil. She took one step towards it. Yu Chen took one step sideways, which put him between her and the oven, calm as a wall.

“Please sit down.”

“What’s in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why’s it covered?”

“Because it’s nothing,” said Yu Chen.

Elowen began to smile.

Lin Jian had been standing by the door, looking at the kitchen with the face of a man who’d raised a houseful of children and fed a great many people who’d tried to kill him. He looked at the oven. He looked at Yu Chen.

“Terrace Road,” he said.

Yu Chen paused. “Yes.”

“Good,” said Lin Jian, and went and sat at the head of the table.

Eliana stared at her father. “How do you know?”

“Because I can smell the alternative.”

Raiden nearly fell off his chair.

The dumplings came at eight minutes to one, in two big tins, carried up the lane by Auntie Au’s nephew. They were beautiful. Neat pleats, golden bottoms, a shine of oil. There were greens with garlic, and prawns nobody had asked for. Eliana put vinegar and chilli oil in the middle of the table, and gave up pretending, and sat down.

Zhao bit into one, chewed, swallowed.

“Hm,” he said.

Elowen looked at him. He took another bite.

“Hm.”

“Zhao,” said Eliana. “What does that mean?”

“That they’re good,” said Zhao, and took a third.

Jun Hyuk ate six and asked if there were more. Yu Chen put the first one on Eliana’s plate, the way he always put the first of anything on her plate, and she ate it and it was perfect and she sighed.

“At least someone in this city knows how to make a dumpling.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch Elowen offered to help clear, and Eliana said no, and Elowen went into the kitchen anyway and headed straight for the oven. Yu Chen stood up. He reached the oven at the same moment she did, and put himself in front of it again, entirely polite.

“Elowen.”

“You’re protective of that oven.”

“It’s hot.”

“It’s been off for an hour.”

“Please leave it.”

She laughed. Then she saw Eliana’s face.

“Oh, no,” she said, delighted. “Zhao! Come and see what my sister’s done!”

Within half a minute most of the family was in the kitchen. Yu Chen opened the oven, because there was no longer any point not to, and lifted the foil. Under it was a tray of burnt, burst, collapsed dumplings, laid out in rows by someone who’d once made a spreadsheet about them.

There was a silence. Raiden broke it, laughing so hard he had to lean on the counter. Jinx looked at the tray and said, “Ambitious.” Zhao looked at it for a while and said, “Hm.”

“We made them,” said Yu Chen, with one hand on Eliana’s back.

“You did the filling,” she said. “Don’t share the blame.”

“Then I deserve some of it.”

Lin Jian came to the kitchen door last, and looked at the tray, and then at his youngest daughter with flour still in her hair.

“Terrace Road,” he said. “Next time ring earlier.”

She stared at him. Then she laughed until her eyes ran.

✦ ✦ ✦

By five they’d all gone home, through the gate and down the lane. The kitchen was clean. Only the tray was left. Eliana carried it out into the garden and Yu Chen followed her with the little trowel from the shed.

“Are we really doing this?”

“You said they had to be buried.”

“I was joking.”

“Were you?”

She looked at the tray. “No.”

Under the persimmon, where the light was going gold and the last leaves were letting go one at a time, he dug a small hole and she tipped the dumplings in. They landed with a soft, unhappy sound.

“Goodbye,” said Eliana.

“Rest well,” said Yu Chen, and covered them over.

He stood up and brushed the soil off his hands, and saw a line of flour still at her hairline, and wiped it away with his thumb. Then he put two fingers under her chin and tipped her face up.

“You wanted to make something for your family,” he said. “You brought them all through the gate and they stayed till five.”

“They ate someone else’s dumplings.”

“They ate dumplings,” said Yu Chen, and kissed her, slowly, under the persimmon, with soil on his hands and flour on hers, until she’d forgotten what she’d been going to argue about.

“Next time,” she said against his mouth, “we’re ordering.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes past six Auntie Tsoi came back from the temple fair, and went straight to the kitchen with a covered tin she must have been carrying since the bus, and put it on the counter, and took the lid off. Inside were dozens of dumplings. Some boiled, some fried, every one of them folded into twelve small even pleats.

“Ah Sim rang me,” she said, before anyone could ask.

Beside the tin she put a folded piece of paper. Eliana opened it. One word, in Auntie Tsoi’s square careful hand.

Watch.

“Tomorrow morning,” said Auntie Tsoi, already washing her hands. “Both of you. Six o’clock. You’re clever people. You can learn to fold a dumpling.” She dried her hands and turned round. “And you used too much water.”

Eliana froze. Beside her, Yu Chen looked at the floor, and his shoulders began to shake.

“Don’t,” said Eliana.

He didn’t say anything at all. He just kissed her cheek, and she put the note in her pocket, where it stayed.

chapters.title: The Sisters’ Group Chat
chapters.desc: Eliana is the admin, which means she runs the sisters’ group chat with an iron hand, adds Haozhen once for a joke, adds Raiden for a worse one, and removes Raiden whenever he gets back in. Three years of a family, told one message at a time.
chapters.epigraph: “I knew you loved him. That was enough.”
chapters.content:
Elowen started the group in the summer of 2024 and called it LIN SISTERS. Elara muted it within the hour. Eliana sent seventeen stickers before dinner.

By the end of the first week Elowen had added Jinx, and then Aurelia, and then Serafina, because Aurelia said she wasn’t going to be in a group her little sister wasn’t in, and renamed it THE WIVES.

Eliana: two of us aren’t wives

Elowen: Aspirational.

Elara: I’m leaving.

Elowen: You can’t. I’m admin.

Nobody left. Eliana turned out to be the busiest member by a distance. She changed the group picture to a photograph of all six of them in Aurelia’s workshop, wearing loupes and pretending to be serious. She made rules. Anyone who said guess what had to say what within a minute. Anyone who found a good restaurant had to share it. Anyone who got engaged, married, promoted or into trouble had to tell the group before they told anyone else. Elowen objected to the last one on principle. Eliana held a poll. The result was five to one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden got in at the end of August.

Raiden: Hello ladies

Jinx: No.

Raiden: Darling. I thought we were friends.

Jinx: We’re married. That’s why I’m warning you.

Elowen: Who added him?

Raiden: Nobody. I have Jinx’s phone and the pin to it. Also I have evidence that someone in this chat climbs back over a garden wall at six in the morning

Eliana: lies

Raiden: I have photographs

Eliana: they’re not admissible

Raiden: The wall is next door to Baba’s. The garden belongs to a medical student

Elara: Who?

Eliana: nobody

Elowen removed Raiden.

He’d been a member for thirty-eight seconds. He complained about it in person the next day at Jinx’s garage, with two bags of food and the injured face of a man who’d suffered a great wrong.

“Thirty-eight seconds,” he said. “She didn’t even let me say goodbye.”

“You weren’t supposed to be there,” said Eliana from a stool by the bench.

“One day you’ll need me.”

“I’d rather ask a wall.”

“The wall would be quieter,” said Jinx, from under a motorbike, and that was the end of it until the next time.

There was always a next time. In October Elowen tried to change a notification setting, pressed the wrong thing, and made Eliana an admin. Eliana never gave it back. By Christmas she’d removed every other admin, including Elowen, and when Elowen noticed, Eliana sent a crown.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the spring of 2025 the group had its own language. A photograph of a cup of tea meant someone was waiting for something. A photograph of a ceiling meant someone was lying in bed wanting attention. A single full stop from Elowen meant she was angry. A single full stop from Elara meant she was tired. Jinx’s messages were one sentence long and ended arguments. Aurelia sent fabric, and gold, and things she thought would suit Eliana. Serafina sent voice notes eleven minutes long from the driver’s seat.

Eliana sent everything. Yu Chen’s attempts to keep a fern alive. His handwriting on her coursework. His hand on a library table, never his face. She didn’t need to show his face. They all knew. They knew how long she took to reply when she was with him, and that “going to bed early” meant next door.

In April Haozhen was given papers in his own name, for the first time in his life, and in May Eliana added him.

Eliana: welcome Haozhen

Haozhen: Hello.

Elowen: ELIANA.

Eliana: he’s marrying Serafina. he’s practically family

Serafina: You could have asked me.

Eliana: surprise

Jinx: Leave while you can.

Haozhen: Noted.

He stayed three hours. He read everything, back to the first sticker. He didn’t write another word. At nine minutes to three in the morning he left the group, and Serafina reported later that he’d laughed so much he’d had to go and sit in the car. Eliana considered the experiment a success, and never added him again.

✦ ✦ ✦

One night that same May she was lying on Yu Chen’s sofa with the phone held above her face when Elowen found her.

Elowen: Are you home?

Eliana: yes

Elowen: Which home?

Eliana: mine

Elara: Your location’s on.

Eliana: that’s a privacy violation

Jinx: You shared it.

Eliana: by accident

Serafina: How does a person accidentally share their live location?

Eliana: technology is complicated

Yu Chen was beside her, reading a journal. He glanced down.

“Your sister?”

“Yes.”

“Are you telling her where you are?”

“I’m telling her I’m at a house.”

He put the journal down, and his hand went to her waist, and she ignored it, and went on typing.

Eliana: I’m going home soon

He kissed the side of her neck. She deleted the message. Typed it again. He kissed the place under her ear, slowly, and she shut her eyes and the phone buzzed against her chin.

Elowen: Are you coming home tonight?

“You’re distracting me,” she said.

“Sorry,” said Yu Chen, who wasn’t.

She typed yes with enormous determination. He laughed against her throat, and she made a small helpless sound, and he stopped at once and lifted his head, which was somehow worse. She threw the phone onto the rug, and turned over, and kissed him first, and the group chat waited, and then gave up and went to sleep without her.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the last days of November 2025 the chat went silent in a way it never had.

A man with a knife had come up the alley behind Baba’s house after Sunday lunch, and Elara had stepped between him and their father. Yu Chen had held her arm together in the lane while Eliana cleared the neighbours away. Elara lived. She came out of City Hospital with her arm in a splint and stopped talking to anyone at all.

Elowen: Has anyone heard from Elara?

Serafina: I rang. Nothing.

Jinx: Same.

Aurelia: Is she all right?

Eliana: she’s safe. Xing Yue’s with her

Eliana couldn’t make her answer. She couldn’t make her laugh at a photograph. So that night she opened the private chat with Elara and wrote one word.

Eliana: here

No reply. She wrote it again the next night. And the next. Sometimes she sent a photograph instead. The persimmon with its last fruit. A terrible cake from the bakery by the ferry. In December, the two stray cats asleep on the step of the red door, curled into each other in the sun. She never asked a question. She never asked why. She only made sure the conversation stayed open.

Every night, for eleven weeks, one word.

The answer came on the eighteenth of February, the day after New Year, at seventeen minutes past three in the afternoon, as a voice message six minutes long, and Eliana listened to it on the sofa in the house next door with both hands over her mouth. That evening, for the first time since November, Elara wrote in the group.

Elara: Here.

Nobody made a fuss. Jinx sent a cup of tea. Serafina sent a voice note that was only breathing and then crying and then sorry, sorry, I’m driving. Elowen sent a full stop that meant, this once, nothing at all except that she’d seen it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the summer of 2026 Raiden had been removed four more times. He’d found three separate ways back in. He’d tried to persuade Jinx to make him an admin. Jinx refused. He tried Aurelia, who said she didn’t want the responsibility. He tried Serafina, who asked Haozhen what he thought, and Haozhen replied, from the other room, Noted.

In August he got back in again.

Raiden: Why am I not an admin

Jinx: Because you’re Raiden.

Elowen: You’re not a sister.

Raiden: I’m family

Serafina: You’re a family problem.

Raiden: I know something about Yu Chen. From 2022

Eliana: no you don’t

Raiden: I’ll tell you if you make me admin

Eliana removed Raiden.

She put the phone down on her desk at FENCE. Across the room Si-Wei looked up.

“Raiden?”

“He says he knows something about Yu Chen from 2022.”

Something moved in Si-Wei’s face and went away again. “Ask Yu Chen.”

“Why is everyone being suspicious?”

“Because you ask too many questions,” said Si-Wei, and went back to her spreadsheet.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the seventh of November 2026, at twenty-one minutes past two in the morning, Eliana posted a photograph of her left hand.

A thin band of warm old gold, under a porch light.

Eliana: so

Elowen: I SAW.

Elowen: I SAW FROM THE WINDOW. ZHAO SAW. BABA SAW. THE WHOLE HOUSE SAW.

Serafina: ELIANA.

Jinx: Finally.

Elara: Is that what I think it is?

Eliana: yes

Elowen: CALL ME.

Eliana: you’re forty feet away

Serafina: I need to see it in person immediately.

Eliana: it’s two in the morning

Serafina: I HAVE NEVER BEEN MORE AWAKE.

Aurelia: It’s beautiful, sweetheart. It suits you.

There was a pause. Then:

Elowen: Aurelia.

Elowen: Why are you so calm.

Aurelia: Because it’s beautiful.

Elowen: You knew.

Aurelia: I resized it.

Eliana sat up in bed so fast that Yu Chen, who’d been lying with one arm round her and his eyes shut, opened them.

“What?”

She turned the phone round. He read it. A small smile started at one corner of his mouth.

Eliana: WHEN

Aurelia: Three weeks ago. He brought it to the workshop in a handkerchief. It was his mother’s. He wanted it to fit you the first time.

Eliana: AND YOU DIDN’T TELL ME

Aurelia: He asked me not to. Nobody’s ever asked me that so politely.

Jinx: I suspected.

Elara: I didn’t know. But I thought it would be soon.

Then the phone buzzed in a way it shouldn’t have.

Raiden: Congratulations

Eliana: HOW ARE YOU HERE

Jinx: He asked me to add him. I wanted to see what would happen.

Raiden: I’ve been waiting since 2022

Eliana: what does that mean

Raiden: I was collecting Jinx’s anniversary present from Aurelia’s. The boy next door was at the counter with a little box. He asked how you’d resize an old gold ring without hurting it. Then he saw me and said, politely, please don’t

Raiden: So I didn’t. For four years. I’d like credit

Aurelia: That’s true. He came in and asked. Then he went away again and didn’t come back till October.

Eliana put the phone face down on the duvet and looked at the man beside her.

“You asked about it in 2022?”

He didn’t answer at once. “I wanted to know it could be done.”

“We weren’t even together.”

“No,” said Yu Chen. “I knew I’d want to, if you ever were. I didn’t know when.”

She looked at him for a while in the lamplight. Then she leaned down and kissed him, and the phone buzzed under the duvet and buzzed again, and neither of them did anything about it.

When she picked it up again it was eighteen minutes to three.

Raiden: I deserve credit

Eliana: you deserve removal

Serafina: I knew nothing and I’m offended.

Elara: I knew you loved him. That was enough.

Elowen: I’m crying.

Jinx: Congratulations, little sister.

Raiden: Can I come to lunch tomorrow

Eliana: no

Raiden: I kept the secret for FOUR YEARS

Eliana: goodnight

Eliana removed Raiden.

Four minutes and twelve seconds. A personal best. Yu Chen was laughing without making any sound when she put the phone on the bedside table.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

She lay down with her cheek on his chest and lifted her left hand and looked at it against the dark.

“You let everyone know before me.”

“Two people,” he said. “Raiden by accident.”

“And they all kept it.”

“Yes.”

She thought about that. The two people at the counter, four years ago, and the one who’d known and said nothing at all, for the length of a whole degree. The chat buzzed once more on the table.

“Leave it,” said Yu Chen.

“It might be important.”

“At three in the morning?”

“It could be.”

He caught her hand, the one with the ring, and kissed her knuckles one at a time.

“You’re engaged,” he said.

“Yes.”

“To me.”

She smiled into his chest, and left it. When she woke at eight there were sixty-one unread messages, and Raiden was back in, and she was still, as she had been since the autumn of 2024, the only admin.

chapters.title: A Notebook of Teas, All for Her
chapters.desc: Yu Chen keeps a notebook of teas, every one worked out for one of Eliana’s bad nights: can’t sleep, won’t eat, nine hours at a screen. It’s a love letter he’d never call one. One page near the back isn’t in his handwriting.
chapters.epigraph: “Sometimes she only needs somewhere to put her hands.”
chapters.content:
She found the notebook because he told her not to touch it, which in nearly twenty years he should have learned was the quickest way to make her touch anything.

It was a Thursday in March, and she’d come home from FENCE before six, which was so unusual that he’d looked at her twice in the hall. He went to put the kettle on. She went up to the study to find her charger, and found instead, on the corner of his desk between a pharmacology text he no longer needed and an emergency handbook he did, a small notebook in soft dark green leather, rubbed pale at the corners.

“Not that one,” he called up the stairs, as if he could see her. “Sweetheart. Leave that one.”

She opened it.

The first page had a date at the top in his neat small hand. September 2021. Under it: First day on the hill. Says she isn’t hungry. Jasmine, weak, no sugar. Drank half and said it tasted like grass. And under that, in a different pen, added later: Finished it anyway.

She smiled and turned the page.

It was a list of teas. Every one had a date, a way of making it, and a line or two about her. Some were practical. Some were so exact that she wondered whether he’d been keeping a record of her whole life.

Chamomile, cooler than you’d think. For when she’s been at the screen too long and says she isn’t tired. Don’t put it by the keyboard; she’ll forget it. Put it in her hand.

Roasted barley. For cold evenings when she says the room’s too warm and puts her hands up my sleeves. No honey.

Light oolong. For when she’s upset and wants to talk about anything except why. Don’t ask straight away. Sit down first.

She stopped turning so quickly. The dates weren’t random. They marked things.

October 2023. The night of the photograph. Ginger, honey, a lot of both. She’s shaking and says it’s the cold. It isn’t the cold. Sit on the step with her till it’s finished. Don’t let go of her hand to drink mine.

April 2025. The nine days. The writing was the same, but it pressed harder on the paper. Ginger and jujube. She isn’t sleeping. She’s eating less. Don’t ask her to explain anything; she can’t. Give it to Ah Sim at the back gate and don’t tell her to say who it’s from. She’ll know. Under it, the next day: Same tea. Ah Sim says she drank it. The next: Same. Then a line by itself. Tomorrow. And on the page after, with nothing else on it at all: She came back.

She sat down in his chair.

September 2025. The breach. The weeks she’d hardly slept, tracing the people who’d taken the family’s names and sold them. Peppermint and roasted barley, for nine hours at a screen with her eyes stinging. She’ll say ten more minutes. Don’t believe her. Don’t touch the keyboard. She’s allowed to stop. She doesn’t have to finish it tonight.

She remembered every one of those cups. She’d thought, at the time, that he was being annoyingly attentive. She hadn’t known he was writing it down. He hadn’t written down what she’d been doing, any of the code or the names. He’d written down her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came into the study with two cups and stopped when he saw what was in her hands.

“That was private,” he said.

“It’s about me.”

“It’s mine about you.”

“Page one says I drink tea like grass.”

“You said it tasted like grass. I wanted to remember which one you didn’t like.”

She held the notebook up. “How many pages?”

“Not many.”

She turned to the back to count, and found that the last pages weren’t in order. Two near the end had been written and rewritten. One was in his handwriting, darker ink, smaller, as if he’d gone over it again and again. It didn’t have a date. It had a number.

Nine. Mine. For the nights she won’t say are bad.

White tea, made gently. A little osmanthus. Not too fragrant, not too hot. She doesn’t always need to be asked what’s wrong. Sometimes she only needs somewhere to put her hands.

“Nine?” she said. “Why is it called nine?”

He put the cups down on the desk. “Because the first eight came from books, or from Auntie Tsoi, or from Ah Sim. That one’s the first I made up. I kept getting it wrong. I’ve changed it eleven times.” He looked at the page as if it might still need work. “The others are for things you’ll tell me about. Not sleeping. Working too long. Nine’s for when you won’t.”

“How do you know when I won’t?”

“You stop looking at your phone,” he said. “And you go round the house straightening things that are already straight.”

She looked at him.

“You’ve recorded my bad nights,” she said. “Since my first day at university.”

“Some of them.”

“That’s slightly concerning.”

“I know.”

“Have you ever thought about how strange this is?”

He considered it, properly. “Yes.”

“And?”

“I kept doing it.”

She laughed, and he sat down on the edge of the desk, and some of the stiffness went out of his shoulders.

✦ ✦ ✦

The page after his nine wasn’t his.

The handwriting was round and quick and leaned to the right. There was a crooked title, underlined twice.

FOR WHEN HE GETS IN THE WAY.

One cup of extremely bitter tea. No sugar. No honey. No comfort. Serve to Wang Yu Chen when he’s decided that I’ve been working too long and starts looking at me over the top of his glasses.

A small furious face.

If he complains, tell him it’s medicinal.

And underneath, smaller, in the same hand: Actually make him a normal one. He doesn’t like bitter tea.

She put her hand over her mouth. She remembered it now. The spring of 2022, sitting on his bed bored stiff while he revised for something enormous, finding a green notebook on his desk with half its pages empty and deciding, with all the wisdom of nineteen, to improve it. She’d put it back and forgotten it.

“You kept this.”

“It’s in my notebook.”

“You could have torn it out.”

“You wrote it,” said Yu Chen.

He’d left it exactly where it was, for five years, between his own pages. Every time he’d written a new tea for her, he’d turned past it.

She shut the notebook and held it against her chest.

“Make me nine.”

“Now?”

“Now.”

“You’re not having a bad night.”

“I know. I want it anyway.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He made it the way he’d made everything he’d ever made for her, without hurrying. She sat on the kitchen counter and watched. He warmed the pot and poured the water away. He measured the leaves into his palm and looked at them and took four back out. He waited for the kettle to go off the boil, and then waited a little longer, and poured, and put in the osmanthus at the last, three small gold flowers that sank and turned, and set the cup in her hands rather than down beside her.

It smelled faintly of apricots and rain. She drank. It was perfect, of course.

“Well?”

“It’s good.”

“Good,” said Yu Chen, and leaned on the counter opposite, looking pleased in the way he only let show at home.

She put the cup down. Then she reached out, took hold of the front of his shirt and pulled him across the kitchen until he was standing between her knees, and put both hands on his waist under the hem of it, where his skin was warm.

“You’re strange,” she said.

“I’ve been told.”

“You remember which teas I like. You remember the nights I don’t sleep. You even remember the nights I pretend I’m fine.”

“Sometimes.”

“Thank you,” she said.

He put his thumb along her cheekbone. She leaned up and kissed him before he could answer, and tasted osmanthus on her own mouth and his, and held on to him with her knees as well as her hands. He put one hand flat on the counter beside her hip and the other at the back of her neck, and kissed her back slowly, as if there were nowhere either of them would ever need to be. When she drew back their noses were still touching.

“You should make a new page,” she said.

“What would it say?”

She took his hand off the counter and put it against her face.

“For when she knows.”

“Knows what?”

“That she’s loved,” said Eliana. “All the time. Not only on the bad nights.”

He looked at her for a while. Then he kissed her again, harder, and lifted her off the counter.

“I can walk.”

“I know,” he said, and carried her up the stairs anyway, with her arm round his neck and her laughing into his collar.

✦ ✦ ✦

He put her on the bed and pulled the blanket over her feet. She looked towards the door.

“The notebook’s downstairs.”

He reached into his back pocket and took it out.

“You carried it up?”

“You’d have asked for it.”

He put it in her hands, and she opened it at the page called nine, and held it out to him.

“Read it.”

“Sweetheart.”

“Please.”

He sat down on the edge of the bed. He read it the way he read everything aloud, plainly, as if the words were only words.

“White tea, made gently. A little osmanthus. Not too fragrant. Not too hot.” He stopped. “She doesn’t always need to be asked what’s wrong.”

She was watching him.

“Sometimes,” he said, “she only needs somewhere to put her hands.”

He looked up. She was already reaching for him. She took his face in both her hands, and held it, and said, “Here,” and he turned his head and kissed the inside of her wrist.

Later, when he’d gone down to wash the cups, she took the pen from his bedside table and opened the notebook at the next empty page. She wrote a date at the top in her round quick hand, and underneath it a heading, underlined twice.

TEN. FOR WHEN HE KNOWS.

And under that, after some thought, nothing else, because some pages didn’t need instructions. She put it back on his side of the bed, open, and turned off the lamp, and waited to hear him find it.

chapters.title: The Monitor Wall
chapters.desc: On the night they graduate, Eliana takes Yu Chen up to her room to show him what she does all night, and he tries, once, to understand her five screens so he can help. He doesn’t. But he learns which chair, and which hour, and that turns out to be the help.
chapters.epigraph: “Which hour’s the worst?”
chapters.content:
On the night they graduated, at a quarter to eleven, Eliana took him in through the red door and up the back stairs of her father’s house in the dark.

“Shut your eyes.”

He stopped on the second step. “Why?”

“Because I’m showing you something.”

“Your father’s in the house.”

“My father’s in his study with the door shut, and Ah Sim’s asleep, and you’ve been in this house a thousand times.”

“Not since April,” said Yu Chen. “Not up these stairs.”

She looked at him in the light from the landing window. He was still in the white shirt he’d worn under his gown, with the collar open now, and he looked more nervous than he had at any point that day, including when he’d crossed the stage in the Great Hall in front of his cousin. That afternoon on the steps outside, with the whole of her family watching, she’d kissed him. Baba had seen it. He’d turned round and gone to the car without a word. Neither of them had said anything about it since.

“Shut your eyes,” she said again, more gently, and he did.

She led him past the photographs on the landing and the little table where Ah Sim kept the spare keys, along the corridor to the room at the end, and opened the door.

“All right. Open.”

He opened them and stopped.

Five screens, in a slightly uneven arc along the long desk under the window. Blue and white and a faint green, the only light in the room. A laptop underneath the middle one. Cables tied back in neat bundles. Three notebooks in a stack, the top one with a yellow sticky note on the cover that said DO NOT TRUST YOUR MEMORY AFTER 2 A.M. Nothing was untidy, only organised in a way that one person alive understood.

He’d been in this room since they were children. He’d sat on that bed and on that floor and read on that rug. He’d never been here at night, with it switched on.

“Five?” he said.

“Five.”

“Why?”

“Because I need them.” She was smiling. She was excited, which he didn’t often see when it came to her work; she’d talk about it in general if anyone asked, but she never brought anyone into it. Tonight she’d brought him here on purpose. “Come here. I’ll show you what I do all night.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She pulled her own chair in to the desk and the spare one in beside it, and he sat in the spare one, and then put both hands flat underneath his thighs.

She stared at him. “What are you doing?”

“Nothing.”

“Why are your hands there?”

“So I don’t touch anything.”

She understood, and her smile went all the way across her face. For four years he hadn’t touched her keyboard. Not once. Not when she fell asleep over it, not when she left it open in the library to go and find coffee. It was the one rule he’d made for himself without ever saying it aloud, and she’d noticed it at nineteen and never told him she had.

“You can sit like a normal person,” she said.

“I am a normal person.”

She pointed at the first screen. “That’s the fence.”

“What fence?”

“Everything. All of it. Baba’s house, Jinx’s garage, Elowen’s building, Ev’s house, the warehouses, the cars, the phones.” She pointed along the arc. “That one’s the cameras. That one’s the doors. That one’s watching for anyone making a copy of a key. That one’s my notes, because if I don’t write it down I forget what I’ve checked. And that one’s whatever’s gone wrong this week.”

“What’s gone wrong this week?”

“Nothing yet. It’s only Thursday.”

She explained it the way she’d never explained it to anyone, slowly, with the building as a picture: front door, side door, windows, cameras, the guard who might be bribed, the cleaner whose card might be borrowed, the delivery van at the back that nobody ever thought to look at. He listened properly, with his whole face. He asked a question about the van that was the right question. He asked one about the cameras that was so wrong it made her laugh out loud.

At twenty past eleven she leaned back.

“How much of that did you follow?”

He thought about it honestly. “A third.”

“That’s better than Raiden.”

“Raiden’s not a doctor.”

“Raiden would have touched the keyboard,” she said.

He took his hands out from under his legs at last and put them on his knees, which she supposed was progress. Then he looked at the five screens and at the chair, and at the window, where the lane was dark and the persimmon over the wall was a black shape against a slightly paler sky.

“Which hour’s the worst?” he said.

She’d been reaching to move a window. She stopped. Nobody had ever asked that.

“What?”

“When you’re doing this. Which hour’s the worst?”

“Three,” she said, without having to think.

“Why three?”

“Because everything slows down. Not the computers. Me. I’ve been looking at the same things for hours. I think I’ve found something and it’s nothing. Or I think there’s nothing, and then there’s one small thing in the corner that changes all of it.” She looked at the screens. “And at three I start being angry with myself.”

“Do you stop?”

“Sometimes.”

“How often?”

She looked at him. “You’re asking a lot of questions.”

He waited.

“Not often,” she said.

He didn’t say anything to that. He didn’t tell her she should, or that he worried. He looked at her chair, and the space beside it where he was sitting, and the clock in the corner of the middle screen, and she watched him file it somewhere behind his eyes, the hour and the chair and the space, as if he’d just been given something important to keep.

“Don’t look like that,” she said.

“Like what?”

“Like you’re going to take my computer away.”

“I’d never,” said Yu Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten to midnight she got up to fetch water from the bathroom, and when she came back he was in her chair. Not touching anything. Sitting bolt upright with his hands on his knees, looking at the middle screen as if it might bite.

She came round behind the chair and bent over the back of it and put her arms round his shoulders, and her hair fell down on either side of his face.

“You’re allowed to touch it.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes. Look.” She pointed past his ear. “That. That’s something I found last week.”

He tilted his head back to look up at her instead of the screen. She was upside down to him, with her glasses slipping. He was upside down to her, with that small serious line between his brows that he got when he was trying to understand something he cared about.

She kissed him like that, upside down, from behind the chair. His mouth was warm and surprised and then not surprised at all, and his hand came up off his knee and found the side of her face and held it there. When she straightened up her glasses were on the end of her nose and he was smiling in a way she’d seen perhaps three times in her life.

“That wasn’t an explanation,” he said.

“It was a reward.”

“Then I’ll ask more questions,” said Yu Chen, and she laughed, and swapped the chairs back, and showed him the thing from last week properly, and he got it, near enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

At sixteen minutes past twelve something came up on the fourth screen.

It wasn’t large. A login from somewhere it shouldn’t have been, against one of Raiden’s accounts, at a time Raiden would never have been awake to make it. She leaned in. She didn’t say anything. She didn’t notice her own face, but he did: the way it went still, and then flat, and her mouth set, and her shoulders came up towards her ears, and her eyes stopped moving between the screens and stayed on one.

He’d seen that face before. Not the one she wore when she was concentrating. The other one.

He didn’t ask what was wrong. He didn’t ask if she was all right. He got up without a word and went out.

She barely noticed. She was three windows deep when a cup appeared beside her left hand, not on the right where the mouse was, but on the left, where she’d never knock it over. White tea, made weak, nothing in it. She looked round. He was back in the spare chair with one of her old textbooks open on his knee, reading, or pretending to.

She drank some, and put it down, and went back in, and after a while her shoulders came down.

It took her until twenty to two. It was nothing in the end, or nearly nothing: a hotel’s broken system in another country, borrowing an old password of Raiden’s from a leak years ago. She locked it out and wrote it down and leaned back, and found he’d fallen asleep in the spare chair with the textbook open on his chest.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard her father before she heard anything else.

A door downstairs. Slow steps along the hall. They came to the foot of her stairs and stopped there, the way they had most nights for as long as she could remember. Sometimes he came up. Mostly he didn’t. Sometimes he asked Ah Sim in the morning whether she’d been working late. Sometimes he stood at the bottom for a minute and went back to his room, and she’d lie awake trying to decide whether she’d imagined him.

She sat still. Yu Chen woke up, with no sound at all, and looked at her, and then at the door.

“Your father?”

She nodded.

“Do you want me to go?”

“No,” she said.

They waited. Neither of them moved. At the bottom of the stairs Lin Jian stood with the light of her five screens coming down the stairwell to him, and the sound of nothing coming with it, and he must have known exactly who was in the room. He didn’t come up. He didn’t turn away either. He stood there, in the dark, as if he were keeping watch over something he didn’t know how to walk towards.

Then the steps went back along the hall, and a door shut.

She let out a breath she hadn’t known she was holding.

“He does that most nights,” she said.

Yu Chen reached across and took her hand. He didn’t tell her what it meant. He didn’t tell her that her father was trying, or that he wasn’t. He held it, and stayed, until her hand stopped being cold.

At ten to three she saved everything and turned off the first screen and the second and the fifth. She left the middle two running, because she always did.

“Finished?” he said.

“For tonight.”

He stood up and put her textbook back where it lived without having to ask, and picked up the empty cup. At the door he stopped and looked back at the chair, and the hour on the clock, and her.

“Three,” he said, as if he were writing it down.

“Three,” said Eliana.

The next night, at three, there was a knock on the window from the top of the garden wall, and a cup of tea held up to the glass.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Brought His Blanket
chapters.desc: On their first wedding anniversary Eliana comes home from a job abroad, takes his mother’s old cream blanket out of the cupboard and tells Yu Chen what she was really doing on the steps that June night in 2021, the night she finished school, when he came out and sat down beside her and she fell asleep on his arm. Or didn’t.
chapters.epigraph: “I wasn’t dreaming. I didn’t want you to go.”
chapters.content:
She came home from the airport on the afternoon of their first anniversary with her suitcase still smelling of somebody else’s country, and went straight upstairs, and began taking things out of the cupboard on the landing.

Two winter coats. A box of photographs. One of his shirts, folded with the precision of a man who’d been taught by Auntie Tsoi and then improved on her. Behind them, right at the back, wrapped in a pillowcase, the blanket.

She lifted it out. Cream, old, gone soft as a cloth, with small flowers stitched along the hem in a thread that had once been pink. One corner had been mended by hand, unevenly, by someone who didn’t sew. She knew who.

“Are you all right?” he called from the bedroom.

“Don’t come out.”

A pause. “Should I be worried?”

“Probably.”

She heard him laugh. She stood on the landing with the blanket against her chest and was eighteen again, and cold, on a stone step at two in the morning in rabbit slippers, deciding not to cry.

When he came to the door anyway, still in a white shirt with his sleeves rolled and his hair damp, he saw what she was holding and stopped.

“I thought it was at the back of the cupboard.”

“It was.”

“You went looking for it.”

“I’ve been thinking about it for a week,” said Eliana. “In a hotel with no persimmon tree. Happy anniversary.”

He came and put one hand on the blanket, and one on her face.

“Happy anniversary, sweetheart.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d booked the dinner a year ago. She’d found out three weeks earlier, looking for a receipt in his email, and discovered a confirmation dated the twenty-fifth of October, 2027. Two days after the wedding. The same small place up the hill where they’d gone the night after the porch, the same table by the window, a note asking for the same pudding.

“You booked a table a year in advance,” she’d said, holding his phone up.

“I knew I’d want to go back.”

“What if we didn’t like it any more?”

“We do.”

“What if we’d moved?”

“We haven’t.”

“What if we’d got divorced?”

He’d thought about it. “I’d have cancelled.”

She’d laughed so hard she’d had to sit down on the stairs.

They walked home afterwards through the lane, under the lit windows of her father’s house, where somebody had left the porch light on for them on purpose. He opened their half of the gate. She carried the blanket in from the chair where she’d left it on the porch, folded over her arm.

“Are you going to tell me why?” he said.

“Upstairs.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat on the end of their bed with the blanket on her knees. He took his watch off and put it on the table and sat down beside her, patient in the way he’d been patient for most of her life.

“Do you remember the night?”

“June 2021,” said Yu Chen. “The night you finished school. Your father looked at the certificate and went into his study. You came out at two o’clock and sat on your step and told me you were enjoying the scenery.”

“It was a beautiful neighbourhood.”

“There was a bin.”

“And a shrub,” she said. “Do you know how you knew I was outside?”

He thought. “I heard the front door.”

“You heard the bolt.” She looked down at the flowers on the hem. “That bolt was the loudest thing in the Walled City. Baba used to say he could hear it from the end of the lane. Everyone in our house knew to lift the door and slide it slowly, so it didn’t wake anyone.” She smoothed the blanket with both hands. “I didn’t lift it. I slammed it back as hard as I could. And then I sat on the step and counted. You were out in eleven seconds.”

He was looking at her. “You did that on purpose.”

“Your light was on.”

“Eliana.”

“I wanted somebody to come out,” she said. “Not somebody. You. I didn’t know how to knock on your door at two in the morning and say, nobody said well done and I’m sad about it. So I made a noise and waited to see if you’d hear.”

For once he had nothing to say at all.

“There’s something else,” she said, before she lost her nerve. “When I fell asleep on your arm. I wasn’t.”

He went still.

“I was nearly asleep. I was warm, and you’d stopped talking, and I didn’t want to open my eyes, because if I did you’d see I was awake, and then you’d stand up and say goodnight like a sensible person and go home.” Her face was hot. “So I kept them shut. And you looked at your phone, and I heard you think about waking me, and you didn’t. You put the blanket up round my shoulders. And then you said it.”

“Said what?”

“Congratulations, Eliana. You’re going to do well. And when you don’t, I’ll still be here.”

His face changed. She’d seen it change for her a thousand ways, and this was one she’d never seen.

“You heard that.”

“I’ve been carrying it about for seven years.” She laughed, unsteadily. “Nobody had said it. You said it to someone you thought was asleep. And at five, when Elowen came and you tried to get your arm back, I held on to your shirt. I wasn’t dreaming. I didn’t want you to go.”

He took her hand off the blanket and turned it over and held it.

“Why didn’t you ever tell me?”

“Because I was eighteen, and I didn’t know what to do with wanting someone to stay.” She looked at their two hands. “And then I was nineteen, and twenty, and it got harder, not easier. And then I was your wife, and I thought I’d tell you on a day that deserved it.”

“I’d have stayed,” he said. “Bolt or no bolt.”

“I know that now.”

“I’d have stayed till Elowen came,” said Yu Chen. “I’d have stayed till your father came. I’d have stayed till the delivery van.”

“I know.”

He put his hand to her face, the way he did when he wanted her to stop looking away.

“Close your eyes,” he said.

“Why?”

“Close them.”

She did. He kissed her left eyelid, lightly, and then her right, and she felt each one go through her like warm water. Then he kissed her mouth, slowly, without any hurry at all, and she put her hand on his cheek and kept her eyes shut a little longer than she needed to, the way she had on the step.

“Still pretending?” he murmured.

“Not tonight,” said Eliana.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood up and shook the blanket out over the bed, and smoothed it flat with both palms, the flowers along the hem lying across the white sheet like a line of small footprints. Then she turned round and began, with great concentration, to undo his shirt.

He let her. He stood with his hands at his sides and watched her face while she did it, one button at a time, and when she’d finished she pushed it off his shoulders and put her mouth to the hollow of his throat, and felt him breathe in under her lips. He undid the zip at the back of her dress himself, slowly, his knuckles running down her spine, and the dress went to the floor, and she stepped out of it and pulled him down onto the bed by the hand.

The blanket was soft under her back. It smelled of cedar from the cupboard and, faintly, of him. He knelt over her and looked at her for a while, in the lamplight, as if he still couldn’t quite believe it, and she reached up and pulled him down.

He took his time. He always did, but tonight he took longer. He kissed her collarbone and the inside of her elbow and the place under her breast where her heartbeat showed, and when his mouth closed over her nipple she arched up off the blanket and caught her fingers in his hair. His hand moved down over her stomach, and between her legs, and found her already wet, and stayed, and moved, slow and sure, until she was breathing in short broken pieces and saying his name into the pillow.

“Look at me,” he said.

She opened her eyes. He was watching her the way he had watched her all her life, with nothing hidden in it now, and she came like that, with her eyes open and his name in her mouth, holding on to his wrist so he wouldn’t stop.

When she could see again she pushed at his shoulder, and he rolled onto his back on the cream blanket, and she climbed over him and took him in her hand, and then inside her, slowly, all the way, watching his face change. His hands came to her hips. She moved, and he groaned and tipped his head back, and she leaned down until her hair fell round both their faces, the way it had fallen round his face upside down over a chair once, years ago, in a room full of screens.

“I’m here,” she said against his mouth. “I’m still here.”

He sat up and held her, one arm across her back and one hand in her hair, and they moved together like that, close, unhurried, his forehead against hers and the old blanket rucked up beneath them, until he was shaking and she was shaking and she felt him come apart inside her with her name, said low, like something he’d been saving. She held him through it and a moment later followed him over again, quieter this time, with her face in his neck.

They stayed like that, wrapped round each other in the middle of the bed, until their breathing slowed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later he pulled the blanket up over both of them, and tucked the edge round her shoulder with exactly the same small careful movement he’d used on a front step at four in the morning, seven years ago.

“Too tight,” she said.

He loosened it.

“Better?”

“Much.”

She lay with her cheek on his chest and her hand over his heart, and listened to it go back to its ordinary pace. Outside, the persimmon moved in the dark. Across the joined porch, somebody in her father’s house turned off the light they’d left on.

“I think I loved you before that night,” she said. “I only noticed on the step.”

“Don’t tell me that. I’ll be impossible.”

“You’re already impossible.”

“I know,” said Yu Chen.

“You always knew when I was pretending I didn’t need you.”

“Not always.”

“Most of the time.”

“Sometimes I only guessed,” he said, and pressed his mouth to her hair. “I was glad you let me stay.”

She lifted her head and looked at him in the dark.

“Next year,” she said, “don’t book the dinner a year ahead.”

“Why not?”

“Because I want you to ask me where I’d like to go, and then I want to watch you book it the same night.”

He laughed, low, under her hand.

“Then ask me,” he said, “what I’ll be doing next year.”

“What will you be doing next year?”

“This,” said Yu Chen, and drew the blanket up over her shoulders again, and she shut her eyes, and this time, with his arm under her head and nowhere either of them had to be by morning, she let herself fall asleep for real.

chapters.title: Before the Persimmons Were Ripe
chapters.desc: Lin Jian waited outside a dried-goods shop for six evenings before Qi Wanqing came out and laughed at him. This is how he loved her: the persimmon branch, a registry in 1987, the kitchen chair where she said no, a lemon tree, two children in one week, a girl from Plum Steps, red eggs he could never dye properly, and the hospital corridor where he lost her.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to look frightening in here”
chapters.content:
Lin Jian first saw Qi Wanqing in the autumn of 1985, through the open front of her family’s dried-goods shop, and she made him wait outside it for six evenings running.

He was eighteen. He had already learned that a man could make himself useful in the Walled City without making himself respectable. He moved goods off the piers. He knew which boats came in late, which warehouses had changed hands, and which men were best not met after dark. He was good at faces, and better at keeping his mouth shut.

She made him wait because she served everyone else first. An old woman who couldn’t decide how many mushrooms she needed. A delivery boy counting coins into her palm. On the fourth evening she saw him through the shopfront and turned her back.

He stood there anyway. Across the street Mok sat in the car with the window down, and laughed at him every night on the drive home.

On the seventh evening she came out with a cloth bag over her shoulder and a pencil behind her ear, stopped in front of him, and looked him up and down.

“You again.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t you have somewhere to be?”

“I do.”

“Then go.”

He looked at her, and she laughed. Out loud, as if he were the most ridiculous thing she had seen all week. He had been feared and obeyed and now and then flattered. Nobody had ever laughed at him. He found he liked it.

“Have you eaten?” he said.

She gave him directions to a noodle stall at the end of the street and walked off without waiting to see if he followed. He followed. Mok, watching them go round the corner, said to nobody, “Finished,” and he was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

She never made it easy. She made him wait outside shops while she bought thread and soap and rice and a hundred things he couldn’t imagine needing. She chose oranges one at a time. She stopped to talk to neighbours and left him standing under an awning with his hands in his pockets.

“You look as though you need practice,” she said, when he asked why.

“At what?”

“Waiting.”

He could have told her he’d spent half his life waiting for men to finish talking so he could decide whether to trust them. Instead he bought her a paper bag of roasted chestnuts. She took it without a word of thanks, and then gave him the warmer ones.

He didn’t tell her everything about the piers. She didn’t ask him to be a different man.

In the spring of 1986, she kissed him first.

They were under the branch that reached over the wall from the Song garden next door, and the persimmons were small and hard and green. He reached for one.

“Not yet,” she said. “It isn’t ripe.”

“It looks like a persimmon.”

“It is a persimmon. It isn’t a good one yet.” She touched the branch with her fingertips. “Leave it a few days. The fruit from this branch is sweeter if you let it be.”

He was looking at her instead of the tree, and she knew it. She stepped in and kissed him, briefly and with complete certainty, and when she drew back and he still hadn’t moved, she laughed and took his hand and did it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday the sixteenth of May, 1987, he wore his first good suit to the registry. Wanqing wore a plain dress, did her own hair, and carried no flowers. Outside on the steps Mok took their photograph: his hand at her back, her mouth open on a laugh at something he’d said a second before the shutter went.

At the dinner in the Walled City, Mok’s toast was the story of the seven evenings outside the shop. Wanqing laughed so hard she had to put her tea down, and Lin Jian didn’t interrupt, only watched her, and understood for the first time in his life that a man could be rich and still poor in every way that counted.

He was moving beyond the piers by then. Warehouses. Transport. Arguments settled without the police. The Syndicate wasn’t yet the shape it would become, but the reach was there, and he was young and ambitious and increasingly hard to refuse. That autumn he came home to the tall house with the keys to a bigger one on the hill, with a garden and a gate and twice the rooms.

Wanqing listened to all of it from the kitchen chair by the window. Then she said, “No.”

“No?”

“I don’t want it.”

“There’s a garden.”

“There’s a garden here. There’s a lane. There’s Ah Sim, who I’ve just given the key to the back gate.” She put her hands flat on the table. “Jian. I don’t need a bigger house. I need this one with you in it.”

He waited for her to change her mind, and she didn’t, and he gave the keys back. It would be thirty-seven years before anybody said no to him in that kitchen again.

That night she took his jacket off and hung it on the back of the same chair. She loosened his tie and undid his collar and looked at him as if she had all the time in the world.

“Let me see you without it,” she said.

She undressed him slowly, not because she was unsure but because she seemed to enjoy finding out that under the careful clothes and the practised stillness was a man who could forget what to do with his hands. When he reached for the lamp she caught his wrist and turned it on herself, and looked at him: his shoulders, the knife scar under his ribs, the places the world had marked. He had been measured and assessed all his life. He had never been looked at like that.

“You don’t have to look frightening in here,” she said, and put her palm against his face.

He closed his eyes. He couldn’t remember the last time he’d been allowed to. She took off her dress herself, and her slip, and pulled him down onto the bed by his open shirt, and when he touched her it was as though tenderness were a language he had only just been taught. She kissed his mouth and his throat and the scar. She guided his hand between her legs and held it there until he learned what she wanted, and he learned it, and she arched under him and said his name in a voice he would hear for the rest of his life. When he came into her she wrapped her legs round his back and kept her eyes open, watching his face, and every time he tried to hide in his own silence she drew him back with her mouth. They moved together slowly until she shook and broke against him, and he followed her with his forehead pressed to hers.

Afterwards he lay awake with her hand on his chest. He had spent years trying to become a man nobody could hurt. She had made him want to be one who could be loved.

✦ ✦ ✦

The low wall between the Lin porch and the Song porch annoyed her from the first summer. It made the two porches look as if they were arguing.

“Take it down,” she said.

“Later.”

“There are always things to do first.”

Every summer she asked, and every summer he said later, and in the end she made him fit a rail along the top instead. She liked to lean her elbows on it and talk to the neighbours.

In the autumn of 1995 Elowen was born, with a serious little face and a voice that filled the tall house. Wanqing called her Wenwen before he’d learned to hold her, and he never called her anything else. That year Wanqing put a lemon tree in a pot on the back step and an orchid on the kitchen windowsill, and her green tin tea flask began to go everywhere she went.

In April 1998 she gave him a son, Raiden, and that same week he brought home a girl two days older, in a silk blanket stitched with a heron: a king’s daughter he had been paid to make disappear. Wanqing heard him out and looked at the girl.

“We keep her,” she said. “She’s his twin.”

So the king’s daughter became Evangeline, registered as Raiden’s twin, and Wanqing dressed her in pale blue. And Raiden, for reasons Lin Jian had weighed long before either child came through the door, went north to Wanqing’s cousin, Auntie Lan, at the White Tower farm in the borderland, where nobody would look for a Lin son. Wanqing didn’t pretend it was painless. She hated his work for one whole night. She sat in the kitchen with the flask untouched beside her and said, “You brought this to our door,” and he said yes, and she said, “Don’t tell me it was necessary,” and he didn’t. In the morning she made breakfast. She never said it again.

On Monday the fourth of November, 2002, a small girl walked down Plum Steps holding two of his fingers, looking up every few steps to make sure he was still there. Wanqing was waiting at the bottom and crouched to meet her.

“This is home,” she said, and to him, “Her name was Xiaoyue. Little moon. She can be Elara.” She brushed the girl’s hair off her forehead. “Love her more than the others.”

He never told his wife what he had done to the girl’s family. Some truths were kept not because they were hard to say, but because the person who heard them would have to live differently afterwards.

✦ ✦ ✦

For every child’s first month, Wanqing boiled red eggs and made Lin Jian dye them. He was terrible at it. The shells came out patchy, and he blamed the dye.

“You can negotiate with half the city,” she told him, “and you can’t make an egg red.”

“I could find someone who can.”

“Then it wouldn’t be yours.” She made him promise, for the next one, that he’d do it himself. Not Ah Sim, not Mok. Him. “So you remember,” she said.

On Tuesday the eighteenth of February, 2003, the hospital corridor was too bright. That was what stayed with him. The light on the floor, the row of chairs, the doors that opened and closed without giving him the answer. Mok sat with Elowen asleep on his coat; she was seven. A doctor came out and spoke about time and what had been tried, and then said there was nothing more. Lin Jian must have asked something, because the doctor spoke again. The youngest had lived. He couldn’t understand why she had, and her mother hadn’t.

That spring, grief went somewhere. At the West Basin wall Mok held the chain and Lin Jian held an iron pipe, and Zuo Hanlin, whose men had burned the Qu family’s house in 2002, did not walk away. There was no justice in it and no ending. He went home with the same empty place inside him.

He bought a black suit for the funeral and wore it to every important thing afterwards. At four in the morning on a February day he boiled the first red egg alone in the dark kitchen, the orchid wilting on the sill, the green flask clean and empty on the counter.
