The colour came out uneven. He took it out anyway, and put it outside a door he couldn’t open, and stood in the corridor looking at the wood.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday the twenty-third of October, 2027, he took the photograph out of the yellowed envelope in his desk. Wanqing under the persimmon one summer before Eliana, one arm up to a branch, hair coming loose, laughing at something outside the frame. She’d been reaching for a fruit that wasn’t ripe. He had told her to wait. She’d told him she knew perfectly well when a persimmon was ready.

He turned it over and wrote on the back, She would have wanted to see you happy, and sealed it in a new cream envelope with his daughter’s name on the front.

The porch wall was gone. The rail had been kept. Someone had cut a gate in the garden wall so that the two gardens met under the persimmon, and through it the Song house was full of people and lights. Eliana was standing by the gate in her wedding dress, and when he came down the path she turned, and he couldn’t speak, because she had her mother’s way of forgetting to guard her face.

“Your mother liked this tree,” he said, and gave her the envelope. “For you. Open it later.”

Then he asked her something, for the first time in her life, and she said yes, and he walked his youngest daughter through the gate her mother had wanted, under branches heavy with fruit that wasn’t ready yet, and would be, if they let it be.

chapters.title: The First New Year With Everyone Married
chapters.desc: For the first time, all five Lin children come home for New Year with the people they married. Ah Sim rules the kitchen, the husbands weigh their red envelopes, Raiden makes a toast nobody asked for, and after the fish their father says their mother’s name.
chapters.epigraph: “At least nobody’s missing.”
chapters.content:
By nine in the morning on New Year’s Eve, Ah Sim had banned every Lin child from the kitchen of the tall house, and every husband and wife but one. Jinx was allowed to stay because she carried things and didn’t ask questions.

“Those plates go to the dining room.”

Jinx, halfway to the sitting room, looked down at the plates, turned round and went the other way without comment. Raiden appeared in the doorway behind her.

“Good morning, everyone.”

“No,” said Ah Sim.

“I haven’t done anything.”

“That’s usually how it starts. Your wife is allowed in my kitchen. You are not.”

The tall house hadn’t been this full on New Year’s Eve in years. It had been full of children once, and then full of absences, and then of careful visits where people came at different times and left before the evening got difficult. This year Baba had said that nobody was eating anywhere else. Five children. Five husbands and wives. One round table.

Elowen and Zhao came first, from the house on the hill, with three tubs of food Ah Sim had specifically told Elowen not to bring. Evangeline and Jun Hyuk came from Fig Tree Lane with a box of pastries Ah Sim received like evidence. Elara and Xing Yue came from Camphor Hill with two bags of oranges, which Ah Sim inspected and approved, and Elara looked at her husband and said, “You got approval,” and he bent and said something into her ear that made her stop smiling and elbow him.

Eliana and Yu Chen came last, through the gate in the garden wall, with a tin of tea and a bag of mandarins. Her red jumper was too big at the cuffs. He was carrying everything else.

“You’re late,” said Elowen.

“By three minutes.”

“Then we’re sorry,” said Yu Chen, and Eliana pinched his arm, and he looked down at her with a face so soft that Elowen made a small noise of disgust and went to find a vase.

From the study doorway Baba watched them all arrive. The house was full. Not of visitors. Of family.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden lasted until eleven before he tried for the roast duck.

Ah Sim caught his wrist. “That’s for dinner.”

“I’m checking the seasoning.”

“It isn’t seasoned yet.”

“I have a sensitive palate.”

“Then use it to find the door.”

He found the door, and Jinx, carrying a tray of greens past him, said he ought to stop trying, and he asked her whether Ah Sim liked him.

“She tolerates you.”

“That’s worse.”

“Much,” said Jinx, and he caught up and kissed her cheek, and her mouth moved at the corner, and from the stove Ah Sim shouted that she could see them.

The table was laid by six: steamed grouper, roast duck, braised mushrooms with greens, prawns in their shells, dumplings, long noodles, a pot of soup, and enough rice to keep an army quiet. Uncle Mok sat at Baba’s right. The rest of the table filled itself without anybody arranging it. Elowen beside Zhao. Raiden and Jinx opposite. Ev and Jun Hyuk next to Elara and Xing Yue. Eliana and Yu Chen in the last two chairs.

“Everyone’s here?” said Baba.

“Everyone,” said Elowen.

“Then eat.”

For the first few minutes nobody spoke, because they were all serving someone else. Zhao put fish on Elowen’s plate. Jun Hyuk moved the chilli out of Ev’s reach. Xing Yue picked the coriander out of Elara’s bowl without looking. Raiden reached across Jinx for a dumpling and got her chopsticks across his knuckles. Eliana took the smallest piece of duck, and Yu Chen took it off her plate and put a bigger one there instead.

“I can choose my own.”

“You were choosing the smallest.”

“Perhaps I wanted the smallest.”

“Would you like to swap?”

She thought about it. “No.”

Across the table Elowen watched them. “Do you two ever stop?”

“I think it’s a medical condition,” said Raiden.

“You’re married to Jinx,” said Eliana. “You don’t get to comment.”

“Finally,” said Jinx, “some sense.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After the first dishes were cleared Baba brought out the red envelopes. Ten. Five for his children and five for the people they’d married. He laid them on the table one at a time, the same size, the same red, and, though nobody had asked, almost certainly the same thickness.

Zhao picked his up and weighed it between two fingers. Across the table Jun Hyuk did the same. Their eyes met.

“What are you doing?” said Elowen.

“Nothing,” said Zhao.

“You’re comparing them.”

Both men put their envelopes down at the same moment, without a word. Raiden looked from one to the other with enormous interest. Xing Yue had put his by his bowl without touching it.

“Not curious?” said Elara.

“Your father gave it to us. That’s enough.”

Baba heard. His eyes rested on Xing Yue a second longer than usual. Then they moved to Yu Chen, whose envelope had already disappeared into the inside pocket of his jacket.

“Aren’t you going to look?” Eliana whispered.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s the same as yours.” He glanced up the table. “Your father isn’t careless.”

After the fish Raiden stood, because nobody had asked him to make a toast and that had never stopped him.

“Please be brief,” said Jinx, with her eyes shut.

“To Elowen and Zhao, who’ve been married longest, and make it look easy, which we all know is a lie, because Elowen is terrifying.”

“Raiden.”

“In a useful way. To Ev and Jun Hyuk, who are quiet, which is lucky, because Ev has enough opinions for two.” He turned to Elara and Xing Yue, opened his mouth, and for once ran out of words. He scratched his cheek. “He makes her talk less,” he said at last. “Nobody else ever managed it.”

A dumpling hit him on the shoulder. Elara had already gone back to her tea.

“Thank you, Raiden,” said Xing Yue, and reached for the greens.

“And to my wife—“

“Sit down.”

“—who has tolerated me for longer than any sensible person would,” said Raiden, and kissed the top of her head, and sat down, and the table laughed so hard that Uncle Mok woke up.

✦ ✦ ✦

By ten the dishes were cleared and the family had spilled between the dining room and the sitting room. The New Year programme was on too loud. Elara and Ev were on the sofa with photographs of a garden. Zhao and Jun Hyuk were discussing a hinge. Xing Yue found Uncle Mok’s glasses on top of Uncle Mok’s head.

Baba stayed at the table, and Elowen came back in with two cups of tea and sat down beside him. For a while they watched the others through the doorway. Then he put his chopsticks down.

“Qing would have liked this table.”

The room didn’t go quiet all at once. The television kept going. Raiden said something to Jinx. But Elowen heard, and turned to him. He had said things about their mother before, the garden and the eggs and what she liked. He had never once, in twenty-five years, said her name in front of his children.

Elowen’s eyes filled. Zhao, standing behind her chair, took a folded handkerchief out of his pocket and put it into her hand without a word.

“She’d have said there was too much food,” said Baba.

“And then eaten all of it,” said Elowen, laughing and crying at once, and leaned her shoulder against his, and he let her.

In the doorway Eliana had heard too. Yu Chen’s hand found hers, and nobody rushed to fill the silence. For once the family let it stay.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five to midnight Uncle Mok announced that everyone had to go outside, and Ah Sim stood at the door with a tray and made each of them take an orange before they crossed the step, because nobody left her house in the new year without something sweet. Raiden took two, and was made to put one back.

The lane was already loud. Neighbours were out with red paper bundles of firecrackers, every door was open, and the air smelled of smoke and orange peel. Baba and Uncle Mok stood by the gate. Ah Sim stood beside them with the expression of a woman who had fed half the street.

At midnight the first firecrackers went off and rolled down the lane like a train.

Raiden kissed Jinx before she could tell him not to. Elowen kissed Zhao. Ev went up on her toes to kiss Jun Hyuk. Elara caught Xing Yue by the front of his coat under a red lantern. And Eliana had already turned to Yu Chen, and he had one hand on her waist and the other in her hair before the first bang had finished.

“Happy New Year, sweetheart.”

“Happy New Year,” she said, and kissed him.

Ah Sim covered her mouth. “In the street. Honestly.”

“They’re married,” said Uncle Mok.

She watched them a little longer, and then, under her breath, she counted. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. She nodded, satisfied.

“At least nobody’s missing.”

Baba looked at the five of them under the lanterns.

“No,” he said. “Nobody’s missing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went back through the gate in the wall a little after one, and the Song house was dark except for the porch light. Eliana took her shoes off by the door. Yu Chen put the leftover mandarins on the counter, and came and took the pins out of her hair one by one.

“You heard Baba,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I’ve never heard him say her name like that.”

He drew her against him. “Maybe tonight it was easier. Everyone was there.”

“Do you think she’d have liked you?”

“Probably,” he said. “I’d have had to wait outside the shop for a week.”

She laughed, and kissed him, and took his hand and led him upstairs.

In their room she undid his shirt herself, button by button, and pushed it off his shoulders, and he lifted her red jumper over her head and kissed the smell of firecrackers off her neck. She pulled him down onto the bed and he came willingly, laughing when her hair caught on his watch, and then not laughing. He kissed her breasts and her stomach and the inside of her thigh, slowly, while the last firecrackers went off down the lane, until she had her hand in his hair and couldn’t keep still. When he came up over her she guided him into her and held him there, deep, and they moved together under the covers with the window open a crack on the cold and the smell of orange peel coming up from the kitchen, no hurry in it at all. She came with her face in his shoulder, and he followed her a moment later with her name.

Afterwards she lay with her cheek on his chest.

“Next year we’ll bring more oranges,” she said.

“How many?”

“Enough for everyone. And flowers for Ah Sim.”

“Good.”

Next door the tall house still had its lights on. Ah Sim would be making sure the kitchen was clean. Uncle Mok would be asleep in his chair. And Baba would be sitting a little while longer under the old photographs, with their mother’s name no longer locked behind his silence.

chapters.title: All Four on the Same Night
chapters.desc: Yu Chen is the emergency registrar on nights, his cousin Xing Yue is the surgeon on call, Elara brings a transfer from Harbourside, and Wei Long stands outside theatre with a prisoner. At three Eliana arrives with five boxes of noodles. At four a man comes into the department with a knife.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s why I’m choosing to.”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past eleven on a Saturday night in March, Wang Yu Chen had a drunk man in cubicle four explaining that his broken nose was a birthmark.

“You fell down three steps,” said the man’s girlfriend.

“The steps attacked me first.”

Yu Chen checked his pupils and asked him to follow a finger with his eyes. “Your nose is broken. We’ll X-ray it and make sure nothing else is.”

“Can you make it straight?”

“Not tonight.”

“Why not?”

“Because I’m not a carpenter,” said Yu Chen, and the nurse beside him turned away to the sink and stayed there.

Then a burn. Then a fall. Then a woman with abdominal pain whose husband had driven her in himself because he was sure it would be faster than an ambulance, and was wrong. By midnight Yu Chen had stopped looking at the clock. He was twenty-five, a year and a half into emergency medicine, and beginning to understand that the department kept its own time: ten minutes of something like calm, then three patients through the doors at once. A cup of tea could sit untouched for three hours. He liked the work. He liked being the one who knew what to do when everyone else was frightened. He was still learning what that weighed.

At twelve forty-eight his cousin walked in, in dark theatre scrubs under his coat, with a phone in one hand and a list in the other.

“You’re early,” said Yu Chen.

“I’m on call.”

“You’re always on call.”

“That’s how being on call works,” said Xing Yue, and took the coffee Yu Chen handed him, and drank half of it before his phone rang. He listened for some seconds without his face changing at all. “Bring him straight through.”

“Laparotomy?”

“Stab wound to the upper abdomen. Police custody. Pressure falling.” He put the cup down. “Find me a theatre.”

At the doors Yu Chen said, “Be careful.”

Xing Yue looked back. “That’s your job,” he said, and was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

The prisoner arrived at twelve minutes past one with two officers and a paramedic crew: thirty-two, a single wound under the ribs, two lines in, blood soaking through the dressing. On the trolley he tried to sit up.

“Where’s my brother?”

“You’re in hospital,” said Yu Chen, with a hand on his shoulder. “We’re looking after you.”

The man grabbed his wrist. Yu Chen didn’t pull away. After a moment the fingers loosened. Bloods, the blood bank, a scan, the anaesthetist, and then Xing Yue in the doorway reading the images on the screen without sitting down.

“Theatre,” he said.

One of the officers stepped forward. “Doctor, we need to maintain custody.”

“Then maintain it outside the sterile area. You can ask me questions when he isn’t bleeding.”

At half past one Song Wei Long came up the corridor in his overcoat and tie, three weeks from his own wedding and looking as if he hadn’t slept since Thursday, spoke to the officers, and took up a position outside the theatre doors with his hands behind his back. Yu Chen found him there ten minutes later.

“Inspector.”

“Doctor Wang.”

“You can sit down.”

“I’m fine.”

“You’ve been standing since you arrived.”

“Habit,” said Wei Long.

“Not a useful one,” said Yu Chen, and Wei Long looked at the boy he had raised from the age of eight, and sat.

A theatre nurse came out with a folder. “Dr. Wang?”

Both men stood up. She looked at them, and then at the doors behind her, where the third Dr. Wang was operating.

“Still in theatre,” she said, and went back in.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six minutes past two an ambulance came from Harbourside with a woman in her forties, a vascular injury from a road collision, worse on the journey than when she’d left. Elara stepped out behind the crew in navy scrubs with a transfer folder under her arm. She’d been on Dr. Xia’s firm since July. Yu Chen still sometimes saw, under the surgeon, the small girl from the house next door who used to sit on the back step with a book.

“How was the journey?”

“Longer than it should have been.” She gave him the folder. “I’ve spoken to your vascular team.”

She walked beside the trolley all the way to resus, telling the receiving team what they needed in the order they needed it, and when the woman looked up at her, frightened, Elara bent down.

“You’re at City now. The team here knows what’s happening. I’m staying.”

At twenty to three she found Xing Yue outside theatre between cases, talking to the anaesthetist.

“You came,” he said.

“I had a transfer.”

“Have you eaten?”

“You’re asking me that while I’m holding a folder.”

He took the folder out of her hands. She let him. When he’d gone back in, the scrub nurse leaned against the wall beside Elara and said that half the theatre had a bet on whether he’d say more than ten words to anyone tonight.

“You’ll lose,” said Elara. “He’ll talk to me.”

“That’s cheating.”

“Marriage,” said Elara, “is full of advantages.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At three Eliana came through the staff entrance in a coat over her pyjamas, hair in a loose knot, carrying two bags.

“It’s three in the morning,” said Yu Chen.

“I can read a clock.” She held the bags up. “Noodles. One for you, one for Xing Yue, one for Elara, one for your cousin.”

“And the fifth?”

“The policeman outside theatre. He looked hungry.” She straightened his collar. “Have you eaten?”

“Not properly.”

“Then you will.”

She took the boxes down to the theatre corridor herself. Elara was on the chairs with her notes on her knee, and Wei Long stood up when he saw her coming.

“For me?” he said.

“Unless you’re sharing it with the wall,” said Eliana.

He ate standing up. Elara told him he was supposed to sit, and he said that was what Yu Chen had said, and that perhaps they were all fine, and Eliana told them all they were impossible and sat down beside her sister. For a while the two of them ate without speaking, and Eliana didn’t ask anything Elara couldn’t answer.

At twenty past three a man collapsed in the waiting room, and the call came over the department: cardiac arrest, resus two. Yu Chen put down his noodles with the last mouthful still in the box.

Compressions were already going when he reached the room. Three minutes since collapse, previous heart disease, his wife outside. He took the airway and watched the monitor and the team leader and the rhythm, and the next decision, and the one after it. Time narrowed to the man on the trolley. After another cycle the rhythm changed.

“Stop compressions. Pulse check.”

He put two fingers to the man’s neck. There.

“Pulse present.”

Somebody let out a breath. Then the next part: stabilise, monitor, find out why. When he could, he went out to the wife and told her that her husband’s heart was beating again, and that he was still gravely ill, and she put both hands over her mouth and cried, and he stayed with her until a nurse could.

When he came back to the station Eliana was there. She didn’t congratulate him. She held out a cup of tea, and he took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve minutes past four the prisoner’s cousin came in through the main doors asking for him, loudly. A nurse explained that the patient was in surgery. He came closer to the desk. Yu Chen, walking back from resus, saw the nurse step backwards and the man’s hand go inside his jacket, and saw the handle of a knife before he saw anything else.

He walked into the space between the man and the nurses’ station and put one hand up.

“Stop.”

“Get out of my way.”

“Put it down. He’s in surgery. Nobody here is going to hurt him.”

“You’re lying.”

“I’m not,” said Yu Chen, in exactly the voice he used to tell people their husband was alive, and didn’t look round, and didn’t move, while behind him somebody called security.

The man took a step forward. Yu Chen didn’t step back. Then Wei Long came up the corridor from theatre, having left his noodles on a chair.

“Police. Put it down.”

The man turned, and in the turning Wei Long had his wrist, and the knife hit the floor, and security came through the doors, and it was over. Nobody was hurt. The department began to move again around the place where it had stopped.

Yu Chen looked down at his hands. They were shaking.

Wei Long came and stood in front of him. “Are you hurt?”

“No.”

Wei Long looked at the hands. Yu Chen closed them. Wei Long didn’t argue, and went to give his statement.

Eliana had seen it from the end of the corridor. She waited until it was dealt with, and then she came and took him by the wrist and led him three steps away from the desk, out of everyone’s way, and didn’t tell him he’d been brave or that he shouldn’t have done it. She just held his hands in hers and rubbed her thumbs over his knuckles until they stopped.

“You’re shaking.”

“I know.”

“That’s all right,” she said, and the calm went out of his face for a second, and he breathed out, and she held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five Xing Yue came out of theatre and took his mask off.

“Bleeding controlled. Intensive care.”

Elara closed her eyes. “Good.”

“Your patient?”

“Through the procedure.”

“Good.”

Behind him the scrub nurse said, “That was twelve words, Dr. Wang,” and went away grinning, and Xing Yue looked at his wife, who was laughing.

“What?”

“Nothing,” said Elara. He looked at the fifth box of noodles, untouched on its chair, and was told it was for the policeman, who had eaten standing up. “That’s not eating,” said Xing Yue, and took her hand. “Come and sit somewhere.”

“Are you ordering me?”

“Yes,” he said, and she let him.

By six the worst of it was over. The man from resus had gone up to the unit. The prisoner was in intensive care. The cousin was in a cell. Eliana had found a bench by the corridor window. Xing Yue sat at one end of it reading post-operative notes, with Elara asleep against his shoulder. Yu Chen came out of the department with two teas and sat on Eliana’s other side. Wei Long came back with an empty box and a bottle of water and took the chair opposite.

“Thank you for the noodles.”

“Was it enough?”

“Yes.”

“How long have you been awake?” said Xing Yue, without looking up.

“Since yesterday.”

“That’s not sensible.”

“Neither is operating till five.”

Xing Yue considered this. “Fair.”

Three of them had grown up within shouting distance of the Walled City: two boys in the Song house and a girl who had come down Plum Steps holding her father’s hand. The fourth had come south from the hills to teach the youngest how to be a doctor and had married the girl from next door instead. A surgeon, an emergency registrar, another surgeon and an inspector, on a hospital bench at dawn, nobody needing anything from any of them for a few minutes.

“Next time,” said Wei Long, “bring five.”

“That was the fifth,” said Eliana, pointing at the box on the chair beside him, and he looked at it and laughed out loud, which Yu Chen had heard perhaps twice in his life.

At a quarter to seven the light came grey through the windows. Elara was asleep. Eliana had fallen asleep against Yu Chen with her fingers curled in his sleeve. Wei Long had his arms folded and his eyes shut and would have denied it. Xing Yue looked at them all, his wife, his cousin, his cousin’s wife, the man who had raised his cousin, and said, “Unbelievable,” to nobody, and pulled Elara’s coat up over her shoulders.

At seven the day team came. Yu Chen woke Eliana by saying her name.

“Everyone survived,” she said, looking round.

“Yes.”

“Come home.” She looked at his hands, and threaded her fingers through his. “I’ll wait while you hand over.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know,” said Eliana. “That’s why I’m choosing to.”

chapters.title: The Lin Family Weekend, Part One: Arrivals
chapters.desc: Elowen and Zhao host every Lin child and every husband and wife for the Mid-Autumn weekend, in a house with an armoury and a panic room under the tulips. Raiden brings a floor plan with the rooms wrong. Zhao says one word to each husband. Eliana arrives late because she rewired the gate.
chapters.epigraph: “Because you drew it.”
chapters.content:
Eliana knew three things about the house on the hill. Her eldest sister was an excellent host. Zhao Zhendong was an excellent husband. And between them they had made a house that felt less like visiting family than walking into a building whose security had been designed by a man who didn’t entirely trust anyone who wasn’t his wife.

“There’s a camera above the stone lantern,” said Yu Chen, as the car came through the outer gate.

“Zhao did that.”

“And another on the garage.”

“Are you criticising my brother-in-law?”

“I’m admiring the work.”

“You’re a terrible liar,” she said, and he smiled and slowed down, because Jinx’s motorbike was parked across the drive at an angle with the sidecar empty, and Raiden was sitting in a garden chair beside it with his helmet in his lap like a man recovering from an expedition.

“Why is he sitting down?” said Eliana. “Jinx drove.”

“Being driven by Jinx is tiring,” said Yu Chen, and she laughed, and the weekend began.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden had brought a suitcase, a rucksack, two bags of snacks and a rolled sheet of paper he held out like military intelligence.

“You’re late.”

“We’re twenty minutes early.”

“Late compared to me,” said Raiden, and Jinx took the paper out of his hand and unrolled it.

“He’s been drawing this since Thursday.”

It was a floor plan of the house: three floors, a basement, the glass plant room, and several rooms Eliana was fairly sure had never been meant for guests, every bedroom labelled with names in his beautiful draughtsman’s capitals. Some were right. Eliana found herself and Yu Chen in a room marked 2F north: beside laundry.

“Why would we sleep beside the laundry?”

“Convenience.”

“He’s put Xing Yue in the pantry,” said Jinx, “and Jun Hyuk in the armoury.”

“He’s qualified,” said Raiden.

Zhao came down the front steps in a dark shirt with his sleeves rolled up and the expression of a man who had been watching the drive for ten minutes. He looked at Raiden’s feet.

“Shoes.”

Raiden stopped talking, took them off, and set them side by side on the bottom step. “Good morning, brother-in-law.”

“Good morning.” Zhao looked at Jinx. “Welcome.” Then at Yu Chen. “Doctor.”

“Zhao.”

That was all. Eliana had watched them talk easily enough at dinners, about the hospital and the house and whatever Raiden had last done. But there was always something in the way Zhao said Doctor that sounded like an inspection, not unfriendly, only thorough.

“Inside,” said Zhao to Raiden, and Raiden went, with his shoes in one hand and his floor plan in the other.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ev and Jun Hyuk came on foot, having taken the bus from Fig Tree Lane and walked the last stretch uphill.

“Why not a taxi?” said Eliana.

“I like to see a road first,” said Jun Hyuk.

“Before what?”

“Before I arrive somewhere.”

“He says this every time,” said Ev, and hugged her, and asked whether Raiden had started, and was told about the floor plan, and shut her eyes.

“He’s put me in the armoury,” said Jun Hyuk, without surprise.

“How do you know?”

“He asked me last week whether I preferred a room with a lock.”

Zhao came down the steps again, kissed Ev’s cheek and took her bag, and then he and Jun Hyuk looked at each other. Neither spoke. Neither offered a hand. They nodded, once each, with the calm of two men who had both done things nobody at this weekend would ever be told about, and had decided long ago that there was nothing useful to say.

“See?” murmured Raiden, at Eliana’s elbow. “That’s why I put him in the armoury.” Jinx hit his arm.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xing Yue and Elara arrived at twenty to one, Xing Yue already on the phone as he got out of the car. “No, don’t wait till Monday. Have the imaging reviewed today. Then ring me.” He hung up. It rang again.

“Welcome to the weekend,” said Elara to the sky.

“That’s four,” said Xing Yue, without looking up, and Elara said she knew, and hugged Eliana, and told her he’d promised to stop after lunch, and that he wouldn’t.

“I can hear you,” said Xing Yue.

“Good,” said Elara.

He put the phone in his pocket long enough to say “Eliana,” and then “Cousin” to Yu Chen, who said “Cousin” back. They shook hands. Yu Chen took Xing Yue’s bag without being asked and Xing Yue let him, and his phone rang again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana and Yu Chen should have been there an hour before, except that Mrs. Chiu had rung from the outer gate to say it was sticking again, and Eliana had said it would take ten minutes, and it had taken forty-five. So she came up the last of the drive with her toolbox, and Yu Chen came up behind her with both their bags.

“You’re sure it’s fixed?”

“Yes.”

“You said that twenty minutes ago.”

“Because it was. Then the sensor wasn’t talking to the panel. Then the wiring was older than both of us.”

“And then?”

“Are you interrogating me?”

“I’m interested in the gate.”

“You are not,” said Eliana, and Mrs. Chiu, waiting at the top of the steps, took both her hands.

“You fixed it, Miss Eliana?”

“It should open smoothly now.”

Mrs. Chiu looked past her at Yu Chen. “Your husband waited the whole time.”

“She was thorough,” said Yu Chen, and Mrs. Chiu laughed and said she always was.

Zhao was in the doorway. He looked at the toolbox, and the luggage, and his sister-in-law.

“You rewired my gate.”

“It was sticking.”

“Doctor,” he said to Yu Chen.

“Zhao.”

“Do you two have to greet each other like a board meeting?” said Eliana, and Zhao took the toolbox out of her hand and went in.

On the steps she caught Yu Chen’s sleeve. “Did you bring my headphones?”

“Yes.”

“My charger? My small notebook?”

“Yes. And yes.”

She smiled at him, and he smiled back, and she went in after her brother-in-law feeling, absurdly, as if she’d been given something.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was beautiful in the way only a house lived in by people with a great deal of space and strong opinions can be: a wide stair, a sitting room full of garden light, a corridor of photographs. The armoury was on the lower floor behind a door that looked like a storage cupboard, and Raiden had already found it and was examining the lock.

“Don’t,” said Jinx.

“I’m looking.”

“With your hands.”

Zhao appeared behind him. “Don’t.”

Raiden took his hand away. “Of course.”

“Why is there an armoury?” said Eliana.

“Because Zhao,” said Jinx, and that was the whole of the explanation anybody ever got.

Mrs. Chiu took them round the garden. The panic room was under the tulips, its door set into the side of a raised bed. The glass plant room stood at the far end, full of orchids and ferns and wet earth. And by the side wall, in its big glazed pot, was the lemon tree that had been their mother’s, which had lived on the back step of the tall house until Elowen married and took it with her.

Eliana went straight to it. There were small green lemons on it. She touched one.

“She says it’s doing well,” she said.

“It is,” said Yu Chen.

Just then the fortress felt like a home. Then Raiden shouted across the lawn that she was in the wrong room.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Chiu assigned the rooms at half past one with a clipboard and the authority of a woman who’d run the house longer than most of the family had been married.

“Mr. Zhao and Miss Elowen, the main bedroom. Mr. Raiden and Miss Jinx, second floor, east. Miss Evangeline and Mr. Jun Hyuk, second floor, west. Miss Elara and Dr. Wang, third floor, garden side. Miss Eliana and the other Dr. Wang, third floor, over the lemon tree.”

Raiden looked at his plan. “Three of mine are wrong.”

“Four,” said Mrs. Chiu.

“Which is the fourth?”

“Your own,” said Mrs. Chiu. “Because you drew it.”

Their room was at the end of the top corridor, with a balcony and a window right over the lemon tree. Eliana went straight to the glass.

“You always look at the garden first,” said Yu Chen behind her, and kissed her temple, and went to the bags. She watched him unzip the small one and take out her headphones first, then the case with the spare cables, then her notebook, and lay all three on the desk before he unpacked a single one of his own shirts.

“You did mine first,” she said.

“You use them.”

She crossed the room and put her arms round his waist from behind, and held on. He stopped folding.

“Thank you,” she said.

“For what?”

“Everything,” said Eliana, and her phone buzzed against his back.

Elowen: Come down. Raiden is arguing with Mrs. Chiu about the rooms.

✦ ✦ ✦

Baba came at a quarter past two with Ah Sim and Uncle Mok. A car pulled up outside, and before anyone else had noticed, Zhao was already going down the steps. Nobody had called him. He simply went.

“Mr. Lin.”

“Zhendong.”

Zhao took the bag from his hand and stood aside so that Baba could climb the steps first, and Eliana, watching from the sitting room, realised that Zhao hadn’t come down the steps for anyone else all day. Not Raiden. Not Jun Hyuk. Not Xing Yue. Not even his wife, who’d been here all along. For her father, he went down.

Uncle Mok looked round the hall. “Big house.”

“There’s an armoury,” said Raiden.

“Why?”

Raiden hesitated. “Zhao.”

Mok nodded, as if that explained everything.

Baba greeted his children one by one. Elowen kissed his cheek. Raiden hugged him and was tolerated. Ev hugged him. Elara took his hand. Eliana came last.

“Did you fix the gate?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” said Baba, and looked past her. “Yu Chen. How is the work?”

“Busy, Baba.”

“Then rest this weekend.”

Ah Sim came out of the kitchen and told everyone to wash their hands, and Raiden said finally, and was told he’d been eating snacks for two hours and could wait.

Lunch was loud, because there were too many people at the table who knew each other too well to stay quiet. Xing Yue answered a call and was told by Elara to put it away and did, for almost twelve minutes. Jun Hyuk served Ev the fish without asking, and Zhao passed him the sauce without being asked either. Yu Chen put a piece of fish on Eliana’s plate, and she said, “That’s enough,” and he stopped, and across the table Raiden said they were always doing that.

“Doing what?”

“Communicating without telling the rest of us.”

“Would you prefer we announced everything?” said Yu Chen.

Raiden considered it. “Yes, actually.”

Eliana looked round the table. Her father. Her sisters and her brother. The people they had married. Ah Sim. Uncle Mok. Children who had once lived in the same few streets, grown up and gone and built their own houses, and somehow ended up here, together, all of them. Under the table Yu Chen’s hand found hers, and she held on.

“Do you think we’ll survive the weekend?” she asked him later, in the glass room, among the orchids.

“Yes.”

“Even with Raiden?”

“We’ve survived worse,” said Yu Chen, and she laughed and took his hand and led him back towards the noise.

chapters.title: The Lin Family Weekend, Part Two: The Wives’ Kitchen, the Husbands’ Lawn
chapters.desc: The women take the kitchen and the men are sent out to make the barbecue. Inside, the wives tell each other the most romantic thing and the most frightening thing their husbands have done. Outside, five men stand round a fire, and Jun Hyuk asks what each of them would do if someone hurt his wife.
chapters.epigraph: “And then I’d stitch him afterwards.”
chapters.content:
The men were sent outside at seventeen minutes past three. Nobody voted. Mrs. Chiu put a crate of live crabs on the kitchen table, looked at the five husbands in the doorway, and said, “The women are cooking. You can make the barbecue.”

“Excellent,” said Raiden.

“You don’t know how to make a barbecue,” said Jinx.

“I know how to eat one.”

Zhao took the bag of charcoal from Mrs. Chiu. “Outside,” he said, and they went: Zhao with the charcoal, Jun Hyuk with the tongs, Xing Yue with his phone already at his ear, Yu Chen with a tray of skewers, and Raiden walking backwards across the lawn explaining to Jinx through the glass that he had been born for outdoor cooking. Jinx shut the door on him.

“They’re easier to manage at a distance,” she said.

The kitchen at the house on the hill was big enough for a restaurant, and the five of them still ended up round one table. Elowen at the counter with her sleeves rolled, running it all without seeming to. Ev opening a bottle of wine. Elara picking herbs off their stalks. Jinx taking charge of the crabs, because she wasn’t afraid of anything with claws. Eliana peeling garlic at the window that looked straight out on their mother’s lemon tree.

“Mrs. Chiu said don’t let Raiden near the sauce,” said Jinx.

“Is the wine for cooking?” said Eliana.

“Some of it,” said Ev, and poured five glasses.

“To the men,” said Elara.

“Outside,” said Jinx, and they drank, and for perhaps forty seconds there was peace.

Through the glass they watched the barbecue not happen. Raiden was holding the tongs. Zhao was looking at Raiden. Jun Hyuk was reading the back of the charcoal bag. Xing Yue was on the phone. Yu Chen was laying out every skewer in rows.

“Yu Chen will make it,” said Jinx. “Zhao will supervise. Jun Hyuk will do whatever Zhao says.”

“Xing Yue will pretend not to be interested,” said Elara, “and then fix whatever’s wrong with the grill.”

“And Raiden will burn something,” said Eliana.

“Himself,” said Jinx, and they laughed the way you can only laugh about people you know to the bone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ev put her glass down. “What’s the most romantic thing your husband’s ever done?”

Jinx stopped with a crab in her hand. Elowen looked suspicious. “Why?”

“Because we’re all married and we’re shut in a kitchen.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

“It’s an excellent reason,” said Ev, and Jinx wiped her hands on a cloth and said, fine, she’d go first.

“Two washers.”

“Two what?”

“Steel washers. From the bin in the garage. Five days before the registry, he cut them into rings.” She looked at her own hand. “The first one didn’t fit. He made it again. He said he wanted something ordinary, that we could wear every day and it wouldn’t matter if it got oil on it.” She shrugged. “He’s wearing his now. Look.”

They looked. Out on the lawn, Raiden was waving the tongs at Jun Hyuk, and on his hand a dull steel ring caught the light.

“That’s lovely,” said Ev.

“Don’t tell him I said so.”

Ev’s was next, and she didn’t need to think. “He followed my bus. Every Sunday, the six o’clock going north. I thought it was a coincidence. Then I saw his car two streets behind it, every week.” She smiled. “When I asked, he said he was going the same way.”

“Every Sunday?” said Elara.

“Apparently. He’d wait till I’d gone through my door before he drove off. I didn’t know how much he was doing until I stopped taking that bus.” She looked out at Jun Hyuk, who was watching the trees at the bottom of the lawn. “And he was on the next one.”

Elara was laying lemon slices on a plate, a careful distance apart. “A brass hook,” she said, when they turned to her. “My first morning on Dr. Xia’s firm, there was a brass hook inside my locker door with E.W. on it, and a card under it with one line from the rules we’d written, number nine.” She smiled at the lemons. “He’d remembered that I hate putting my bag on the floor. He never said he’d done it.”

“That’s so him,” said Elowen.

Eliana knew they’d ask her. She also knew she was going to go red.

“One hundred and eighty-eight sticky notes,” she said.

Jinx put the crab down. “He kept them?”

“All of them. Dated. In order. In a drawer.” She found she was smiling at the garlic. “Since the first one. A dumpling saying you look hungry, eat something. Some are just reminders to drink tea. Some I wrote when I was angry with him.”

“He kept those?”

“He said they were still mine.”

Elara reached over and squeezed her hand.

“To men who keep things,” said Jinx, lifting her glass.

“And you?” said Ev to Elowen.

Elowen had been smiling the whole time. “No.”

“Elowen.”

“He’s done a great many things,” said Elowen, and picked up a knife. “Clean the crabs.”

They laughed, and let her. But Eliana saw how long the smile stayed on her eldest sister’s face, and thought that some things were too precious to turn into kitchen talk.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next question came from Elara, lower.

“What’s the scariest thing he’s ever done?”

Nobody put a glass down. But the laughter went out of the room, and on the lawn a piece of charcoal cracked.

“The scariest thing about Jun Hyuk,” said Ev at last, carefully, “is how quiet he gets. I used to think it meant he wasn’t afraid. Now I know he’s trying not to let his fear become mine.” She turned the stem of her glass. “Once I saw how far he’d go to get me out of somewhere. He didn’t shout. He made a decision and moved. I’ve never seen anyone look so calm.”

“The shipyard,” said Elowen. “That’s all.”

Nobody pushed her.

Eliana looked out at the lawn. Yu Chen was standing by the grill talking to Zhao, one hand in his pocket. She thought about the alley behind their father’s house, the last Sunday of November, nearly three years ago, and Yu Chen coming out of the gate next door in a grey jumper and kneeling in the lane with both hands round Elara’s forearm, his face so still she hadn’t recognised it.

“He’s never once been frightening to me,” she said. “The frightening thing was how calm he was in the alley. He told me exactly what to do and I did it. Afterwards, when the ambulance had gone, his hands were shaking so badly he couldn’t hold the cup Ah Sim gave him.”

Elara, whose wrist it had been, didn’t say anything. She only put her hand on Eliana’s arm.

“Well,” said Jinx eventually, picking up another crab. “I think we’ve established they’re all slightly terrifying.”

Elara laughed first. Then the rest of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

Out on the lawn the husbands had been standing round the grill for eleven minutes. Raiden knew, because he was counting. He had tried the weather, the sidecar, the case for a second sidecar, and the question of whether the house needed a bigger grill, and nobody had responded. Zhao was arranging charcoal. Jun Hyuk was watching the tree line. Xing Yue had taken a surgical journal out of his jacket. Yu Chen was turning skewers.

“Does anyone want to talk?” said Raiden.

“We’re talking,” said Zhao.

“When?”

“Now.”

“We’re family,” said Raiden, wounded. “I’ve been making conversation for eleven minutes.”

“Then you don’t need to make it,” said Jun Hyuk, and Raiden thought about this, decided it was fair, sat down on the low wall, and lasted thirty seconds.

“Do you think they’re talking about us?”

“Probably,” said Yu Chen.

“What do you think they’re saying?”

“That you talk too much.”

Xing Yue laughed behind his journal, almost inaudibly. Raiden pointed at him. “You’ve been waiting to say that.” Xing Yue turned a page.

Then Jun Hyuk, still watching the trees, asked a question.

“Have you ever thought what you’d do if someone touched your wife?”

Raiden stopped moving. Zhao looked up. Xing Yue shut his journal. Yu Chen put the tongs down.

“Touched how?” said Zhao.

“Hurt her.”

“Then I’d hurt him,” said Raiden, and glanced at the house as though Jinx might hear. Zhao looked at him until he went on. “Fine. I’d get him away from her. Then I’d call the police. Then I’d make sure he understood.”

“Reasonable,” said Jun Hyuk.

“I’d make sure he never came near her again,” said Zhao, and didn’t explain, and didn’t need to.

“I’d get Ev somewhere safe,” said Jun Hyuk. “Then I’d deal with him.”

There was something in the word deal that made Raiden decide not to ask.

“Elara first,” said Xing Yue. “Then I’d decide what needed to happen.”

“You’re all frightening,” said Raiden. “Doctor?”

Yu Chen had his hands resting on the edge of the table.

“I’d get her away from him,” he said. “I’d make sure she was safe.” He picked the tongs up again. “And then I’d stitch him afterwards.”

The silence was a long one. Raiden turned his head slowly. Xing Yue looked up. Jun Hyuk stared. Zhao’s eyebrows moved, perhaps a millimetre.

“If he needed it,” added Yu Chen, and turned a skewer.

“That’s the worst answer,” said Raiden.

“I didn’t say I wouldn’t call the police.”

Xing Yue’s shoulders moved once. Jun Hyuk went back to the trees. Zhao went back to the charcoal.

“I have a new appreciation for you,” said Raiden. “It’s not a comfortable one.”

The grill caught fire, the actual grill, not the lawn, and Zhao had it out in a minute while Jun Hyuk moved the food. And then the glass door opened and Elara came across the grass with a plate.

“Try this.”

Xing Yue stood. “What’s in it?”

“Something Mrs. Chiu made.” She went up on her toes and kissed him, once, a hand on his cheek, as if there were nobody else on the lawn. “Too much lemon?”

He looked at the plate. Then at her. “No.”

“Good,” she said, and went back inside, and behind Xing Yue four men became extremely interested in the fire.

“What?” said Xing Yue.

“Nothing,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past four the food went out to the long table under the trees. Raiden admitted to burning one piece of bread. Eliana took a plate from Yu Chen and put a piece of fish on it and said, “Eat,” and he said, “All right,” and did.

“What did you talk about out there?” she asked.

“Raiden talked.”

“And?”

He took a drink of water. “What we’d do if someone hurt our wives.”

“What did you say?”

“That I’d get you somewhere safe.” He looked at her, perfectly grave. “Then I’d stitch him.”

She laughed so hard she had to put her glass down. He watched her do it with no expression at all, and under the table his hand found hers.

At the head of the table Baba looked round at his children and the people they had married, the quiet ones and the loud ones, the man with a steel washer on his finger and the man who followed buses and the man who fixed brass hooks and the one who kept a drawer of sticky notes, with something on his face that was nearly peace.

chapters.title: The Lin Family Weekend, Part Three: Who Knows Their Spouse Best
chapters.desc: Eliana builds a buzzer, writes a spreadsheet and makes Raiden the host. Five couples answer questions about each other with Baba as judge, and the answers reveal a year remembered for a noodle order, a tea notebook, a forty-minute search and the exact morning someone changed her mind.
chapters.epigraph: “I married you. I knew what I was getting.”
chapters.content:
Eliana had made a spreadsheet. In hindsight that was the first warning. The second was the buzzer: a small black box she had built that week, with a red button, a green button and a display that read 00, sitting in the middle of the dining table.

Raiden found it in under a minute. “What does this one do?”

“Nothing you need to know.”

“Does it explode?”

“No.”

“Then why can’t I press it?”

“Because I built it.”

“She usually has a reason,” said Yu Chen, pouring tea, and Raiden pressed the red button, and a loud electronic blare went round the room, and Jinx took the buzzer off him.

“Then who’s the host?” said Raiden.

Nobody volunteered. Eliana looked at him, and he sat up so straight his chair creaked.

“Me?”

“Unfortunately.”

She plugged her laptop into the television. WHO KNOWS THEIR SPOUSE BEST? came up in large letters, and under it the rules. One point for every right answer. Answers on cards. No changing a card once it’s collected. Raiden is the host. Baba is the judge.

“Why am I the judge?” said Baba.

“Because you’re impartial.”

Raiden made a noise. Baba looked at him. Raiden had never looked so happy to be supervised.

Five couples at the table: Elowen and Zhao at one end, Raiden and Jinx beside them, Ev and Jun Hyuk opposite, Elara and Xing Yue with his phone face down by his cup, Eliana and Yu Chen in the middle. Baba at the head with the score sheet. Mrs. Chiu put down a plate of mooncakes, looked at the buzzer, asked whether it was necessary, was told yes, and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

Question one: What does your spouse order at the noodle stall?

Eliana wrote: Dry noodles, less oil, extra greens. Soup on the side if he’s come straight off a shift. Says he doesn’t want chilli. Wants a little. Beside her, Yu Chen was already folding his card.

Raiden read Zhao’s first. “Elowen: fish-ball noodles, thin, no coriander, extra spring onion.” He stopped. “Changed from thick to thin in the summer of 2021, when she said the thick ones were too heavy for lunch.”

Elowen turned to her husband. “That was when.”

“Yes,” said Zhao.

“You remember the year?” said Raiden.

“She changed her order,” said Zhao, as if there could be no other reason to remember anything.

Yu Chen’s card said: Brisket noodles, thin, less oil, extra greens, no coriander. Afterwards, white tea, made weak.

“That’s not part of the order,” said Eliana.

“You always want tea afterwards.”

“Not always.”

“After noodles.”

She considered. “Usually.”

Jun Hyuk got Ev’s right. Raiden had written spicy seafood for Jinx.

“Wrong,” said Jinx. “I don’t order seafood.”

“You did last time.”

“Once.”

“You said you liked it.”

“I said it was acceptable,” said Jinx, and Raiden looked at the card and then at the table and said, “She changes it to keep me alert,” and Eliana laughed so hard she dropped her pen. Baba wrote a nought.

“I appeal,” said Raiden.

“Denied,” said Baba.

✦ ✦ ✦

Question two: How does your spouse take their tea after a bad night?

Eliana had put this one in on purpose.

Xing Yue’s card for Elara gave the tea, the temperature, the steeping time in seconds, and a note that strong tea gave her headaches when she was tired. “You wrote the temperature,” said Raiden.

“She doesn’t like it too hot,” said Xing Yue, mildly puzzled. “Is that unusual?”

Then Raiden picked up Yu Chen’s card and read it out. “White tea with osmanthus, made weak. Warm, not hot. No sugar. If she says she doesn’t want it, leave it beside her anyway and don’t mention it. If the night was bad, make it weaker.”

He put the card down. “Why is there a procedure for when she refuses?”

“Because sometimes she refuses,” said Yu Chen.

The table erupted. “YOU HAVE A SYSTEM.”

“It’s tea.”

“It’s an operational protocol.”

“He has a notebook,” said Eliana.

Every head at the table turned. Yu Chen closed his eyes.

“Eliana.”

“Sorry, sweetheart.”

“You aren’t.”

“No,” said Eliana.

Raiden demanded to see the notebook, and was refused, and demanded again, and was refused again, and Baba gave Xing Yue and Elara one point and Eliana and Yu Chen two.

“Why two?”

“Because he answered correctly,” said Baba.

“So did Xing Yue!”

“Then he has one,” said Baba, and Raiden looked at the score sheet and said the judge was not impartial, and the judge looked at him, and he sat down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Question three: What’s the first thing your spouse does when they get home?

Elowen took off her earrings and checked the door was locked. Ev put her bag down, washed her hands, and asked whether Jun Hyuk had eaten. Elara took her shoes off and went straight to the fridge, because she always came home starving. Eliana took her shoes off, looked for Yu Chen, and asked whether he’d eaten.

“Not always,” she said.

“When I’m home,” said Yu Chen, and she thought about it and gave him that.

Raiden opened his own card and read it in silence before he read it aloud. “Jinx comes home and checks whether I’ve done something stupid.”

“Correct,” said Jinx.

“That isn’t the first thing you do.”

“It is.”

“You just assume.”

“Because you usually have,” said Jinx, and Baba gave them their first point, and Raiden punched the air.

✦ ✦ ✦

Question four: What would your spouse do if you went missing for an hour?

This time the wives wrote, and their husbands had to say whether it was right.

Ev’s card said: He’d already know where I was. Jun Hyuk read it. “Correct.”

“How?” said Raiden.

“Forty minutes,” said Jun Hyuk.

Ev turned. “Forty?”

“Usually. It depends where you are.”

“That’s not comforting,” said Raiden.

“It wasn’t meant to be,” said Jun Hyuk.

Elowen’s: He’d know before the hour. “Correct,” said Zhao. “And you don’t go anywhere for an hour without telling me.”

“Not any more,” said Elowen, and that was the whole conversation.

Jinx’s: He’d fall off something looking for me.

“Why would I fall off something?”

“You fell off the garden wall. You fell off the garage roof. You fell out of the tree at your father’s.”

Raiden opened his mouth, and shut it.

Elara’s: He’d ring me. Then the hospital. Then the places I go. He’d go silent. Then he’d find me. Xing Yue didn’t deny a word of it.

Eliana’s said only: He wouldn’t wait an hour.

“Correct,” said Yu Chen. “She tells me when her plans change. If she didn’t, I’d know something was wrong before then.”

“Know how?”

“I’d know,” said Yu Chen.

“You’re all terrifying,” said Raiden to the men at large. Zhao drank his tea. Jun Hyuk said nothing. Xing Yue turned his phone over. Under the table Eliana found Yu Chen’s hand, and held it.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were questions after that about birthdays and favourite meals and the one thing each of them always forgot to take out of the house. Jinx remembered that Raiden had been frightened of thunder as a boy, and when he said he wasn’t any more, said, “You still move closer when it rains,” and he had no answer. Elara knew Xing Yue’s breakfast and that he never put his phone on silent. Xing Yue knew which side of the bed she chose when she was upset. Yu Chen knew which of Eliana’s notebooks she was using this month and that she always left the last mouthful when she was full. Raiden got Jinx’s coffee wrong and her favourite food wrong and her birthday right.

“Why does everybody know so much?” he said.

“Because we pay attention,” said Jinx, and patted his hand.

Then the last question came up on the screen, and the room went quiet.

What’s one thing your spouse changed their mind about because of you?

Jun Hyuk’s card: That asking for help isn’t failing. Ev’s face went soft. “She used to try to do everything herself,” said Jun Hyuk. “Not everything,” said Ev. “Most things,” said Jun Hyuk, and she let him have it.

Xing Yue’s: That she can ask for what she wants without explaining why she deserves it. Elara didn’t move. Then she smiled, and her eyes were wet.

Jinx’s: That some things can be mended instead of replaced. “Because of the rings?” said Raiden. “Because of you,” said Jinx, and for once he didn’t make a joke.

Yu Chen’s: That forever isn’t something she has to be afraid of. Eliana looked at him, and he didn’t look away. She thought of the porch at two in the morning and the word she’d finally said without being frightened of it.

“Correct,” she said.

Zhao’s: That she doesn’t have to carry everything alone. “That’s it?” said Raiden.

“She changed her mind on Thursday the twentieth of May, 2021,” said Zhao. “The night before, she told me she didn’t need any help. The next morning she rang and said she’d changed her mind.”

Elowen looked down at her hands. Then she found his under the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

The final scores came up on Eliana’s spreadsheet. Elara and Xing Yue, eighteen: champions of wit, all of it hers. Ev and Jun Hyuk, seventeen, for accuracy. Elowen and Zhao, sixteen: perfect memory, no commentary. Eliana and Yu Chen, sixteen: the notebook incident. Raiden and Jinx, nine.

“Nine?” said Raiden.

“We had fun.”

“Nine?”

“I married you,” said Jinx. “I knew what I was getting.”

He looked deeply moved. “That’s romantic.”

Baba stood up and took a small wooden box from under his chair, and the table went quiet, because nobody had known there was a prize. He put it in front of Elara and Xing Yue. Inside was a silver frame, and in the frame an old photograph of five children on the back step of the tall house under the persimmon branch: Elowen at the back trying to look serious, Raiden with something that might have been a toy sword, Ev laughing, Elara with her hands in her lap, and Eliana, tiny, leaning against her eldest sister.

“I had it framed in the spring,” said Baba. “For when you were all here.”

Elowen touched the glass. “Thank you, Baba.”

“Look at my hair,” said Raiden.

“You had terrible hair,” said Jinx.

“I was twelve.”

“Exactly.”

Then Raiden remembered the forfeit. The losing couple kisses in front of everyone. Jinx looked at Eliana. Eliana said, apologetically, that she had written it.

“One kiss,” said Jinx.

“Of course,” said Raiden, and took her face in both hands and kissed her, and then again, and then, apparently deciding the first two hadn’t been enough, a third time, until Jinx was laughing against his mouth and telling him that was plenty. Eliana checked her watch. Four minutes and twelve seconds. Zhao looked at the ceiling. Jun Hyuk took a long drink. Xing Yue turned his phone over again.

Yu Chen leaned down to Eliana. “Would you like to beat it?”

“Are you volunteering?”

“Only if you want.”

She kissed him first, briefly, warmly, and Raiden shouted that it was unfair and that it had not been four minutes, and Eliana told him he wasn’t the host any more.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, at the window, with the lemon tree dark below and the family spread across the sofas, Yu Chen put his arms round her from behind.

“Your game was a success.”

“Even with Raiden?”

“Especially with Raiden.” He kissed her temple. “You told them about the notebook.”

“How many pages is it now?”

“Enough,” said Yu Chen.

“You’re secretly romantic.”

“Secretly?”

“Not any more,” she said, and from the dining table Raiden announced that next year he was making the spreadsheet, and five women said no at once.

chapters.title: The Lin Family Weekend, Part Four: The Mall
chapters.desc: Five husbands are sent to the biggest shopping centre in the city to buy the dinner and one present each, alone, while five wives follow them with binoculars. Zhao stands in a florist’s for twenty-one minutes, Yu Chen rings Jinx about headphones, and on an escalator all five men become exactly who they are in three seconds.
chapters.epigraph: “She wants the old ones to last forever.”
chapters.content:
The plan was simple. Five husbands, five lists, the biggest shopping centre in the city on a holiday Sunday. No wives, no ringing for advice, and nobody comes home without the dinner shopping and one present each, chosen by himself.

Eliana had written the rules in a shared document, with a line at the bottom in bold: THE PRESENT MUST BE CHOSEN BY YOU. NOT BY YOUR WIFE.

“Why so strict?” Raiden had said.

“Because you’ll buy Jinx a helmet.”

“She needs a helmet.”

“She needs a present.”

“Don’t,” Jinx had said, and he’d sighed.

At half past ten on Sunday the five of them stood in the main entrance with a list each. Zhao looked prepared. Jun Hyuk looked calm. Xing Yue looked as if he had already decided which three shops he needed and in what order. Yu Chen was reading his list for the second time. Raiden looked delighted.

Behind a pillar by the information desk, five women watched them go. Eliana had a coffee. Ev had sunglasses. Elara had bought a shopping bag specifically to look inconspicuous. Jinx had no patience. Elowen had binoculars.

“Why have you got binoculars?” said Eliana.

“To observe.”

“We’re in a shopping centre.”

“Exactly,” said Elowen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao read his list once in the supermarket doorway and went straight to the vegetables as if he’d memorised the floor plan, which he probably had. At the fish counter he showed the woman his list and asked about the crabs, and chose the ones that were still moving. Then he picked up two kinds of mushroom that weren’t on the list.

“He remembered,” said Elowen, behind a stack of bottled water.

“Remembered what?”

“The ones I like.” She lowered the binoculars. “He’ll check the dates on everything before he leaves.”

He did.

Raiden reached the snack aisle and stopped. He put a bag of crisps in his basket. Then another. Then a third. He looked at his list. He looked at the crisps. He put the third bag back, and picked it up again, and moved on to the dried mango.

“There’s nothing about snacks on that list,” said Ev.

“Exactly,” said Jinx, and shut her eyes.

Jun Hyuk was done first. He didn’t look at the offers or the bakery and bought nothing that wasn’t on the list, except that at the tea shelf he stopped, put one packet in his basket, and then a second, different one.

“He knows I like the first,” said Ev, low, “and he likes the second.” She watched him walk on. “He always remembers that.”

Xing Yue had photographed his list and checked the menu with Elara before leaving, without once asking her what to buy. At the fruit he picked up a pomelo, weighed it, smelled it, put it back, and did the same with nine more before he chose three.

“He’ll be there for a while,” said Elara. “He wants the best ones.” She smiled. “I wish he spent that long choosing his own lunch.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen wasn’t in the supermarket at all. He’d gone into an electronics shop on the first floor, and Eliana stopped dead outside the window.

“He’s buying my present.”

He was standing in front of a wall of headphones. He picked a pair up, read the box, put it back. He picked up another. A shop assistant came over and showed him a third, and he listened politely and looked at the wall again.

“He won’t find mine,” said Eliana. “They stopped making them. He bought the last forty pairs in the city when they did.”

“Forty?” said Elara.

“They’re in a cupboard. He mends them when the wires go.”

“Then what’s he doing?”

“I don’t know,” said Eliana, and found that she was smiling so hard her face hurt.

Inside, the assistant was explaining the merits of a wireless pair. Yu Chen took his phone out. In Jinx’s bag, her phone buzzed.

THE DOCTOR (ELIANA’S)

She answered it with her eyes on the shop window. “You’re in the electronics shop.”

“How do you know?”

“Lucky guess. What do you want?”

“I wanted to give her something new,” he said. “Something for her ears. They don’t make her kind any more and the ones they’ve got are all wrong. Wireless. She won’t like wireless.”

“She won’t,” said Jinx. “She doesn’t want new ones, Yu Chen. She wants the old ones to last forever.”

There was a pause on the line.

“Do they sell soldering irons in there?”

Jinx laughed so loudly that Elowen had to pull her behind the pillar.

Through the window they watched him leave the headphone wall, walk to the far side of the shop where the tools were, and spend a long time with a fine-tipped iron in a proper stand, the kind Jinx used for the small work. Then he took it to the counter and asked the assistant something, and the assistant got out an engraving pen.

“He’s buying you a soldering iron,” said Jinx.

Eliana put her hand over her mouth. “That’s my husband.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The florist was on the second floor. Zhao went in at a quarter to twelve, looked at the roses, looked at the orchids, asked a question about a pot of white jasmine, and then walked over to a row of little potted citrus trees and stopped in front of a lemon branch no taller than his forearm, with three small green fruits on it.

He asked the florist something. She answered. He touched a leaf. Then he stood there.

Five minutes. Ten. Fifteen. On the escalator Elowen lowered the binoculars. At twenty minutes she sat down on the nearest bench.

“Are you all right?” said Ev.

“He’s buying me a lemon tree.”

“It’s a branch,” said Jinx.

“In a pot. Because I love Mama’s.” Elowen pressed her fingers to her lips. Through the glass Zhao was asking how much sun it needed and whether it would be happy by a kitchen window. “I can’t believe him.”

“You’re going to cry.”

“I’m not,” said Elowen, who was, and got up. “Somewhere he can’t see me.”

Xing Yue went into the bookshop at a quarter past twelve, straight to fiction, took a novel off the shelf, read the back, read the first page, sat down in an armchair and read the first chapter. Then he turned to the second.

“He’s checking it’s good enough,” said Elara, at the window. “He won’t give me a book because the cover’s pretty. He wants to know I’ll like the story first.” She watched him turn a page. “I hope he likes it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past twelve the men met at the escalators. Zhao had the lemon branch in its pot held carefully against his chest. Jun Hyuk had two neat bags. Xing Yue had the book. Yu Chen had a small paper bag. Raiden had the dinner shopping, and also four bags of crisps, the dried mango, two bars of chocolate and a drink. They started down towards the food court, and the women followed at a distance, and that was when it happened.

It took three seconds.

A man on the escalator behind Jinx, who’d been closer than any of them had noticed, put his hand on her bag. The strap came off her shoulder. She turned, and he pulled.

Three seconds later Jun Hyuk had his wrist. Raiden had the bag. Xing Yue had stepped between the man and a family coming up the other side. Yu Chen was already turned to Jinx with a hand on her arm.

Zhao hadn’t moved at all.

He was standing two steps above them, with the lemon branch in his arms, looking at the man. That was all. The man looked at Jun Hyuk’s hand on his wrist, and at Raiden with the bag, and up at Zhao. Then, with great care, he sat down on the landing at the bottom of the escalator, and stayed there.

“Are you hurt?” said Yu Chen.

“No,” said Jinx.

He looked at her wrist anyway. Jun Hyuk didn’t let go until centre security came running, and then said, “Keep the camera footage,” and the security man said yes, sir, of course, and apologised to Zhao, who hadn’t said a word. Raiden held the bag out to Jinx.

“Are you all right?”

She took it, and put her hand on his cheek. “I’m fine.”

Only then did his shoulders come down.

On the escalator above, the women looked at each other.

“Three seconds,” said Elara.

Jinx glanced up and saw them. “How long have you been there?”

“Long enough,” said Eliana.

“YOU’RE HERE!” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

They gave up hiding in the food court. The lemon branch sat on a chair of its own beside Zhao. Raiden was explaining the escalator to a security officer for the third time, although the officer had finished writing some while ago. Xing Yue was reading his book again.

Eliana sat down next to Yu Chen. “What did you buy?”

“Something for you.”

He gave her the paper bag. Inside was the iron, fine-tipped, in its stand, and on the handle, in neat engraved capitals: Y.L. For the nights I’m on shift.

“I couldn’t find your headphones,” he said.

“I know. I watched you.” She held it up to the light. “You rang Jinx.”

“She said you wanted the old ones to last forever.”

“I do.” Her voice wasn’t quite steady. “You know you don’t have to mend everything yourself.”

“I know. So now you can.”

She leaned over the table and kissed him, in the middle of the food court, over a soldering iron.

“WHAT DID HE BUY?” said Raiden.

“A soldering iron.”

Raiden stared, and then slapped the table. “THAT’S THE MOST ROMANTIC THING I’VE EVER HEARD.”

“You bought me crisps,” said Jinx.

“They’re your favourite.”

“They’re not.”

Raiden looked at the bags, and at his wife, and his face fell. “They’re not?”

“No,” said Jinx, and he pushed the whole pile across the table to her and said, “Choose,” and she laughed in spite of herself and kissed his cheek.

Elowen touched one of the leaves on the little tree. “Where will we put it?”

“By the kitchen window. It gets the morning.”

“Did you ask?”

“Yes.”

“Twenty minutes,” she said. “In the florist’s.”

“Twenty-one,” said Zhao, and she laughed and kissed him, and he took it with his usual composure, except that his hand came up and stayed at the back of her head.

Xing Yue put the novel in front of Elara. “I think you’ll like it.”

“You read the first chapter?”

“And the second.”

“Was it good?”

“Good enough to keep going.”

“Then I’ll read it,” she said, “and you’re not allowed to tell me what happens,” and he said he hadn’t finished it, so he couldn’t, and she kissed him too.

“Everybody’s kissing today,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car park Yu Chen opened the passenger door for her, and she stopped before she got in.

“Thank you for my present.”

“You’re welcome.”

“Will you teach me to use it properly? I always burn myself on yours.”

“Yes,” he said.

On the way home she sat with the paper bag on her knee and her hand in his on the gear stick, and thought about the three seconds. Jun Hyuk had moved first. Raiden had gone for what mattered. Xing Yue had stood between the trouble and strangers. Yu Chen had gone straight to the person who’d been hurt. And Zhao hadn’t needed to move at all.

“Something wrong?” said Yu Chen.

“No. Just thinking how lucky we are.”

He lifted her hand and kissed the back of it, and kept driving.

chapters.title: The Lin Family Weekend, Part Five: Lanterns on the Lawn
chapters.desc: Lanterns on the lawn, mooncakes from Auntie Au, thirteen small lanterns with thirteen names, and a nine-word speech from Baba. Raiden finally gets his photograph. Ah Sim and Uncle Mok share their mother’s green flask on the bench by the lemon tree.
chapters.epigraph: “Your mother wanted a big table. Here it is.”
chapters.content:
By the time the moon came up over the hill, the lawn had become a small village of light, and it was Raiden’s fault.

He had been put in charge of the lanterns. He’d bought too many and hung some too high, put three across the path where nobody could walk without ducking, and insisted that the biggest should hang from Mama’s lemon tree because it was the most cinematic position. Jinx had told him the lemon tree was not a film set. Now one lantern hung crooked over the grass, another was caught in the branches, and Raiden stood under it with a bamboo pole.

“Don’t pull it,” said Jinx.

“I’m encouraging it to come down.”

From the terrace Eliana watched with her chin on Yu Chen’s shoulder and his arms round her waist.

“Should we help?”

“Jinx is helping.”

“Jinx is telling him to stop.”

“That is helping,” said Yu Chen.

The garden smelled of cut grass and warm paper and the osmanthus incense Mrs. Chiu had lit by the steps. The mooncakes had come up the hill an hour before from Auntie Au, two enormous boxes and a note saying she’d made extra because the Lin family had obviously grown too big to be trusted with ordinary amounts: lotus seed, red bean, salted yolk, and a smaller box of the snowy ones Eliana liked, marked with a little drawn flower. Eliana had noticed the flower. She’d also noticed Yu Chen put that box beside her plate without a word. He did that sort of thing.

Behind them the house was full of the weekend’s evidence: shoes in the hall, a hair clip on the stairs, a pile of board games, and the score sheet from Saturday night, which Raiden wouldn’t let anybody throw away. Tomorrow everyone would go home. Tonight nobody seemed in a hurry to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Baba came down the steps a little after eight with a wooden box, and the talk on the lawn softened without stopping, to make room for him. He put the box on the table by the mooncakes. Inside were thirteen small paper lanterns, and on the base of each, in his careful hand, a name.

Raiden turned his over. Raiden. “Are these all for us?”

“Who else?”

Baba gave them out one at a time. Elowen. Zhendong. Raiden. Jia. Evangeline. Jun Hyuk. Elara. Xing Yue. Yu-er. Yu Chen. And the last three for himself, Ah Sim and Mok.

“Thirteen?” said Uncle Mok.

“Thirteen.”

“Somebody will have to count Raiden twice.”

“I heard that,” said Raiden.

“You were meant to,” said Mok.

Baba waited until they had all come in close. He looked round at them: his children, the people standing beside them, Ah Sim, who had been part of the house so long that nobody could remember a family occasion without her, and Mok, who had carried chairs and mended gates and simply appeared whenever something needed doing, for forty years.

“Your mother wanted a big table,” he said. “Here it is.”

Nine words, and nobody moved. Elowen’s hand found Zhao’s. Raiden’s grin went soft. Ev looked at the grass. Elara reached for Xing Yue’s fingers. And Eliana looked at her father, who stood with one hand on the back of a chair as if he’d said something ordinary.

For years the table had been a place where things were missing. A chair nobody used, a name nobody said, a birthday with an empty place beside it every year. Now there were too many of them to fit.

“She’d have liked tonight,” said Eliana.

His face changed, not much. “Yes,” he said. “She would.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The photograph was Raiden’s idea, and it had been since Saturday. He had tried at the arrivals, but nobody would stand still. He’d tried at lunch, but Zhao had been looking at the food and Xing Yue at his phone. He’d tried after the game, and Jinx had shut her eyes, and Elara had been laughing, and Eliana had turned to look at Yu Chen, and Baba had been looking at Elowen. Tonight he had a new plan.

“Everyone on the steps. Please.”

“That’s new,” said Jinx.

“I’m evolving.”

“Slowly.”

He arranged them. Baba in the middle, because he was the father. Ah Sim and Mok on the bottom step. Then he moved two lanterns nearer, and checked the moon, and asked Jun Hyuk to hold a third one higher, and stepped back.

“Everyone look here.”

Nobody did. Elowen was saying something to Zhao. Ev was laughing at Jun Hyuk. Elara had turned up to Xing Yue, who was looking down at her. Eliana was whispering to Yu Chen. Baba was watching his daughters. Ah Sim was telling Mok something about the snowy mooncakes.

“EVERYONE, LOOK AT THE CAMERA.”

That worked for about a second. Then Yu Chen murmured something, and Eliana laughed out loud, and every head on the steps turned to her. Raiden lowered his arms, said “Fine,” and pressed the shutter anyway.

He looked at the screen. For once, he didn’t complain. Thirteen people on the steps, and nobody looking at the camera. Every face turned to someone. Zhao looking at Elowen with the face he wore when he thought nobody could see. Ev’s hand on Jun Hyuk’s arm. Elara smiling up at Xing Yue. Jinx looking at Raiden, who was in the corner of his own picture looking triumphant. Ah Sim laughing at Mok. Baba looking at his children. And at the end, Eliana with her cheek on Yu Chen’s shoulder and her eyes shut with laughing.

“That’s it,” said Raiden, and turned the screen round.

Jinx looked. “That’s a good one.”

“Obviously.”

He sent it to the family chat.

Raiden: Finally. The perfect photograph.

Jinx: You took it by accident.

Raiden: Art is not an accident.

Elara: Keep this one.

Eliana: i want a print

Raiden: Everyone gets a print.

Jinx: No watermark.

Raiden: I WASN’T GOING TO.

Jinx: You were.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lanterns were lit, and the family spread out over the lawn with their little lights. For a while the evening belonged to all of them. Then, slowly, it began to belong to each two.

By the lemon tree Zhao held Elowen’s lantern while she straightened its handle, and she asked whether he’d do this again, the whole weekend, and he looked at the crowded steps and the lit house and said, “Whenever you want,” and she turned in his arms and put her forehead against his chest and let herself be held without having to say anything else. By the garden wall Raiden had stopped talking at last and was looking at the photograph again, and told Jinx she looked pretty in it, and when she said she was barely in it said, “I can see you. I always can,” so seriously that her answer never came, and she took him by the front of his shirt and kissed him, and he kissed her back slower, as if he’d finally remembered there was nothing to hurry for. Under the old tree at the end of the lawn Ev stopped in the middle of a sentence and told Jun Hyuk she liked having nowhere else to be, and he put their lantern down carefully on the grass and took her hand and kissed it and said then they wouldn’t go anywhere for a while. On the dark side of the steps Elara asked Xing Yue whether the book had a good ending, and he said he hadn’t finished it, and tucked her hair behind her ear and said he’d read the rest with her, and kissed her with one hand at her jaw. And by the terrace Eliana held her lantern against her chest and watched them all.

“Everyone looks happy,” she said.

“They are.”

“Are you?”

“Yes,” said Yu Chen, and kissed her forehead.

On the bench by the lemon tree, the one with a leg that had been mended twice, Ah Sim and Uncle Mok sat with two cups between them and Wanqing’s green tin flask, which Elowen had found in the cabinet that afternoon and washed and filled with the weak tea their mother used to make on evenings like this.

“Still warm,” said Mok.

“She carried it everywhere.”

“Not into the kitchen. She said the kitchen was too hot.”

“She said that so nobody would ask her to cook,” said Ah Sim, and Mok laughed, low and old and familiar. They watched the five couples moving among the lanterns. “She’d have been pleased,” said Ah Sim. “All of them. Even Raiden.”

“Especially Raiden,” said Mok, and she put her hand over his on the bench, and neither of them hurried the tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the moon was high, the family began drifting in. Baba stayed on the terrace, and Eliana stopped at the bottom of the steps.

“Baba?”

“Going up?”

“In a minute.”

She went up the steps and hugged him. It wasn’t long. It didn’t need to be. His hand rested on her back.

“Good night, Yu-er.”

“Good night.”

He looked past her at Yu Chen, waiting a step below. “Look after her.”

“I will,” said Yu Chen.

Their room was over the lemon tree, and from the bed Eliana could see the crooked lantern Raiden had hung in it, still glowing. She took off her earrings and put them on the bedside table. Yu Chen closed the door.

“You’ve looked at that photograph four times,” she said.

“It’s a good photograph.”

“Do you think we’ll do this again next year?”

“I think Raiden will have booked it before anyone can stop him.”

She laughed, and caught his hand before he could ask if she wanted to sleep, and pulled him down.

He kissed her slowly, because there was nothing tonight to be quick for, no shift in the morning, no phone, nobody calling from the next room. She pulled his shirt over his head and kissed the small old scar by his eyebrow, and he slid her nightdress up and off and kissed her throat and her breasts and the soft skin over her ribs, taking his time, until she arched under his mouth and said his name. Outside, one lantern went dark, and then another. He drew the curtain halfway and came back to her, and she guided him into her and wrapped her legs round him and held him there, deep and still, both of them breathing. Then a long creak went right across the ceiling, as if someone enormous were walking about upstairs, and she burst out laughing.

“It’s the beams,” said Yu Chen, against her shoulder. “It’s an old house.”

“It’s your sister-in-law’s dramatic house.”

“Like its owner’s sister,” said Yu Chen, perfectly innocent, and she gasped and caught his face and kissed him so he couldn’t say anything else, and began to move, and he moved with her, slow, her heels at his back, until she shook apart under him with her face in his neck and he followed her a moment after, her name low against her ear.

When the last lantern went out she was still holding his hand.

Somewhere above them the house creaked again.

“Don’t,” he said.

“I didn’t say anything.” She settled her cheek on his chest. “I like it. It sounds lived in.”

“Good night, sweetheart.”

“Good night, my Yu Chen,” she said, and the old house, full of thirteen people and the last warmth of the lanterns, creaked round them.

chapters.title: Terrible Advice From the Cousin Who Raised Him
