chapters.desc: In 2022 Wei Long tells Yu Chen to tell Eliana everything he wants, and Yu Chen doesn’t. In 2025, after the nine days, Wei Long asks him about a consular officer who sits on his desk, and gets his own advice back. Eliana hears both from the garden wall.
chapters.epigraph: “I know what happens when you don’t.”
chapters.content:
At twenty, Wang Yu Chen had learned that there were several kinds of trouble. There was the ordinary kind: an anatomy paper he hadn’t revised enough for, a simulated patient he’d read wrong, a lab coat that had gone grey in the wash. And there was his cousin.

Wei Long was twenty-seven, a detective, and the person Yu Chen had spent most of his childhood trying to impress. He was also, Yu Chen had lately discovered, far too interested in his private life.

“You’re seeing her.”

It was nearly midnight in December, in the kitchen of the old Song house. Yu Chen had a bowl of Auntie Tsoi’s soup between his hands and a textbook he wasn’t reading. Wei Long had come in off a late shift twenty minutes before with a bag of oranges and the face of a man who had already decided the conversation was going to be unpleasant.

“Who?”

“Don’t.” Wei Long sat down opposite. “The girl over the wall.”

The spoon stopped. Only for a second. Wei Long saw it, because he always saw everything.

“How long?”

“That’s not relevant.”

“You’re a medical student. You can tell when someone’s blood pressure is dropping. You must be able to tell when a question’s going to be answered.”

Yu Chen ate another spoonful of soup. “Last year.”

“Last year.” Wei Long took an orange out of the bag and began to peel it, slowly, watching him over it. “Does she know what you want?”

“She knows I love her.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

Yu Chen looked up. Wei Long went on peeling.

“Does she know you want all of it? Not this term. Not next summer. The whole thing.”

Outside a car went down the lane, and somewhere in the back of the house a pipe knocked. Yu Chen looked at his bowl.

“She doesn’t like things being made difficult,” he said at last. “She’ll say something and then take it back. She’ll ask me to stay and then tell me I don’t have to. If I ask her straight out, she says it’s fine either way.” He turned the spoon over. “I don’t want her to feel she has to give me an answer before she’s ready.”

“Then don’t ask her for one,” said Wei Long. “Tell her. Tell her what you feel, and what you want, and don’t make her guess, and don’t decide for her that she can’t stand to know. She deserves to know where she stands.”

It was the least teasing thing Wei Long had said to him in years.

“What if it changes things?”

“Things have changed. You’ve been sitting here since ten eating soup like a man waiting for a message. And ten minutes ago you smiled at your phone.”

“I didn’t.”

“From her?”

Yu Chen didn’t answer. Wei Long pointed at him with a piece of orange. Yu Chen took the piece out of his hand and ate it.

“Eat your own.”

“Tell her,” said Wei Long.

“I’ll think about it.”

“That’s an answer to a different question.”

Yu Chen picked up his spoon. There was a particular kind of stubbornness in the Wang side of the family. It didn’t shout. It sat still and waited for everyone else to get tired. Wei Long had spent most of his life trying to deal with it and had never got any good at it.

“You’ll regret it,” he said, “if you keep making her guess.”

“I know,” said Yu Chen.

He didn’t say he would.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t take the advice. Not completely; that would have been too easy. He told her he liked being with her. He told her he missed her. He waited outside her lectures and brought her dinner and remembered how she took her tea.

He didn’t tell her that he’d started measuring his days by the small things they did together. He didn’t tell her that the thought of her ever leaving made something in him go still. And he didn’t tell her that when he thought about the future he couldn’t see one she wasn’t standing in.

Sometimes, when she fell asleep on his shoulder in 4B, he’d look down at her and think about the kitchen and the oranges, and then put his jacket over her and decide there’d be another time. There was always another time, until, one night in March 2025, on her step at two in the morning, he finally said I want to marry you, three years too late and all at once, and she ran inside and bolted the door, and for nine days he found out exactly what it cost to make someone guess.

Wei Long stopped asking. Mostly. Every so often there’d be a message.

Ge: Have you told her?

Yu Chen: Told her what

Ge: I see.

Or:

Ge: Honesty is a useful quality.

Yu Chen: You should try it. You told Auntie Tsoi you were working late. You were at the cinema.

Ge: Operational discretion.

Yu Chen kept that one. He intended to use it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the spring of 2025, after the nine days, Wei Long came back to the Song house for dinner. He’d moved out the summer before and left Yu Chen the house and a list of everything that leaked, but he still came on Sundays, and he still sat in the same chair.

Auntie Tsoi had left soup on the stove. Yu Chen was eating it over his notes for an assessment. Wei Long sat across the table looking at his phone. He unlocked it, locked it, unlocked it again. On the fourth time a name came up on the screen, ISLA REN, and he turned the phone face down so fast it slid.

Yu Chen looked at the phone and then back at his notes. “Ah.”

“Don’t.”

“You’re seeing her,” said Yu Chen.

“I’m not.”

“All right.”

The silence lasted about twelve seconds.

“She’s a consular officer,” said Wei Long.

“I know.”

“She’s busy.”

“Most people are.”

“She keeps coming into my office. She says she has a question about a case, and sometimes she does, and sometimes she just sits on my desk and reads whatever I’m writing.” He looked at the window. “I’ve told her not to sit there.”

“Why?”

“It’s my desk.”

“Is she in the way?”

“Not exactly.”

“Does she move anything?”

“No.”

Yu Chen put down his spoon. “She sits on your desk?”

“Yes.”

“Let her.”

Wei Long stared at him as if he’d expected something more sophisticated from a medical degree. “That’s your advice?”

“Do you want her to stop?”

Wei Long said nothing.

“Then let her,” said Yu Chen. “Or tell her you like her there.” The corner of his mouth moved. “I was told once that honesty was important.”

Wei Long laughed, short and surprised. “You’re still holding that against me.”

“You gave me the advice.”

“And you ignored it.”

“Yes,” said Yu Chen. “That’s why I’m giving it back. I know what happens when you don’t.”

Wei Long stopped laughing. The kitchen seemed to have twenty years in it. The eight-year-old who’d followed him round this house after the funeral. The fourteen-year-old who’d waited up for him after night shifts. The boy who’d learned to cook because Wei Long was hopeless at it, and who had once sat on the floor beside him after a bad case and handed him half a packet of biscuits without a word. They’d never been any good at saying things straight. Wei Long had raised him. Somewhere along the way Yu Chen had grown into someone he could lean on.

“She’s not my girlfriend,” said Wei Long.

“All right.”

“She hasn’t said anything.”

“Neither did Eliana,” said Yu Chen, and then heard himself, and Wei Long smiled.

“Interesting, isn’t it.”

“Eat your soup.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana had heard all of it.

She was sitting on the garden wall between the two houses, where she’d come looking for him and meant to knock and then heard Wei Long’s voice through the open kitchen window and stopped. Not to eavesdrop, she would tell herself later. Not entirely. She took out her phone and opened a note and typed.

Things Wang Yu Chen says when he gives advice:

Dec 2022, to Ge: tell her the truth. she deserves to know where she stands.

Spring 2025, to Ge: she sits on your desk? let her.

She read it over and added: apparently he gives excellent advice he doesn’t follow himself.

The kitchen door opened and Yu Chen came out with two cups of tea, and stopped.

“How long have you been there?”

“Not long.” She took the cup. “Your cousin’s interesting.”

“He’s difficult.”

“He raised you.”

“Unfortunately,” said Yu Chen, and sat down beside her on the wall.

They drank their tea. After a while she said, “You gave him good advice. Both times.”

“I didn’t follow the first.”

“Why not?”

He thought about it properly, the way he did. “I thought I had more time.”

She put her hand on his wrist. “You did. In the end.”

“In the end,” he agreed, and turned his hand over so their fingers met.

“Would you have said it differently if you’d known I was listening?”

“No.”

“Good.” She leaned against his shoulder. “Thank you for telling me the truth. Even if it took you three years and a step at two in the morning.”

He looked at her, and there was nothing in his face at all except her, and she kissed him.

From the kitchen doorway Wei Long said, “Are you two going to stand out there all night?”

“Go home,” said Yu Chen.

“This was my home for twenty years.”

“Then go to your other one.”

Wei Long looked at their joined hands and smiled. “You’re welcome, by the way.”

“For what?”

“Raising you.” He went back inside. “Good night, kid.”

Eliana looked at Yu Chen. “Kid?”

“He still calls me that.”

“I like it,” said Eliana.

Later that night, in bed, she opened the note again and added one line under the rest.

they raised each other and neither of them knows how to say it.

She saved it. On the other side of the bed Yu Chen reached for her hand without opening his eyes, and she put the phone down. Some things didn’t need writing down. She was keeping the note anyway.

chapters.title: He Joins the Family Chat
chapters.desc: Eliana adds her father to Lins + Strays. After forty minutes he sends one word. Every morning at six there’s another, and the family learns to answer a man who means far more than he types, until her birthday the next year, when he sends four.
chapters.epigraph: “Breakfast at seven. Your favourite.”
chapters.content:
The family chat had been called Lins + Strays since 2023, when Eliana named it, and nobody had ever asked her what it meant. Raiden had immediately made the group picture a photograph of a stray cat outside a butcher’s. Jinx had changed it back. Raiden had changed it again. Eliana, as admin, had finally set it to a photograph of the five of them at the dinner table, which had lasted three days before Raiden replaced it with a badly cropped picture of Yu Chen asleep on a sofa. Yu Chen had never said a word about it. He had simply changed his own picture to plain white.

The chat held the five Lin children, the five people they’d married, and, depending on the week, whoever Raiden had added and Eliana had removed. It was not organised. It was extremely active.

At fourteen minutes past nine on a Monday morning in June, Eliana added one more.

Eliana added Lin Jian.

For three seconds nobody wrote anything.

Raiden: WHO

Jinx: Don’t.

Elowen: Eliana.

Eliana: good morning

Raiden: YOU ADDED BABA

Raiden: TO THIS CHAT

Jinx: Look at the name of the chat.

Raiden: WE ARE NOT CHANGING THE NAME. HE’S A STRAY TOO.

Yu Chen: Good morning, Baba.

Then nothing. For forty minutes the chat, which had never in its life been quiet for forty minutes, was quiet. At six minutes to ten, after what was obviously long and careful thought, Baba sent his first message.

Lin Jian: Eaten?

The first to answer was Yu Chen.

Yu Chen: Yes, Baba. Have you?

Lin Jian: Good.

Eliana looked up from her phone at her husband across the breakfast table. “You’re quick.”

“He asked.”

“He asked everyone.”

“Then he might be waiting,” said Yu Chen, and drank his tea.

Raiden: Yes. Two eggs, toast, noodles and a bun.

Lin Jian: Why

Raiden: WHY WHAT

Jinx: He means why so much.

Lin Jian: Too much.

Raiden: IT’S A HOLIDAY

Lin Jian: Monday.

Raiden: EXACTLY

Eliana laughed so hard she spilled her tea, and Yu Chen, mopping it, said that her father had a point.

✦ ✦ ✦

Baba learned to text in stages. At first his messages read like instructions to a department. Home? Rain. Dinner. Late? The family took some days to understand that none of them were statements. When he sent Rain, he meant: is it raining where you are, have you got an umbrella, does someone need fetching. When he sent Dinner, he meant: have you eaten, what are you having, shall I send something. He didn’t see why everyone couldn’t simply tell.

Lin Jian: Rain.

Elowen: Yes, it’s raining here.

Lin Jian: Umbrella?

Elowen: Yes.

Lin Jian: Good.

Zhao: Hm.

Lin Jian: Hm.

Elowen screenshotted it and sent it to Ev on its own. Elowen: Look. They’re the same person.

By the second week there was a routine. Every morning at six o’clock Baba sent one word. Not at one minute past, not at one minute to. Six. And the word was almost always different.

On Tuesday it was Awake? and Zhao answered Hm, and Baba answered Hm, and Elowen sent the screenshot to the whole chat with I can’t. On Wednesday it was Cold? and Ev said a little, she had her jacket, and Baba said Wear more, and Raiden said I AM FINE, and Baba said Not asking you, and Jinx said HA. On Thursday it was Home? and Elara and Xing Yue both said yes, and Elara asked whether he was home too, and after a long pause he said Yes, and she said Good, as if she were the parent. On Friday it was Busy? and Yu Chen said he was on a late shift but free now, and Baba said Eat first. At two the next morning, when Yu Chen came off that shift and checked his phone in the hospital car park, there was a second message under it, sent at eleven, which nobody else in the chat had seen because it had been sent to him alone. Lin Jian: Raining. Drive slowly. He sat in the car and read it three times before he started the engine, and never told anyone, not even Eliana, who found out anyway, because she always did.

On Saturday it was Sleep?

Jinx: Yes.

Raiden: No.

Lin Jian: Why

Raiden: I WAS WAITING FOR JINX

Jinx: I was asleep.

Lin Jian: Let her sleep.

Raiden: BUT

Lin Jian: Sleep.

Raiden: GOOD NIGHT

On Sunday it was Together? and Eliana said yes, everyone was coming to lunch, and Raiden said he’d bring dessert, and Baba said Buy less, and Raiden said he hadn’t bought it yet, and Baba said Hm.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hardest part was learning how to answer him. His messages were short, but they carried far more than they said. Home? meant he wanted to know everyone had got in safe. Cold? meant someone might need a coat. Eaten? meant he wanted to know the people he loved had looked after themselves, which he’d never once in his life said out loud and didn’t know how to.

So the family began to answer him in his own language, and Zhao was by far the best at it.

Lin Jian: Dinner?

Zhao: Hm.

Lin Jian: Good.

Elowen: I think they’ve developed their own language.

Raiden: I THINK THEY’RE HIDING SOMETHING

Jinx: They’re talking about dinner.

Raiden: HOW DO YOU KNOW

Jinx: I was there.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first photograph he ever sent was of a pot of soup. No words with it.

Eliana knew the bowl beside the pot before she knew the soup. Pale blue, with a chip near the rim. It was one of her mother’s, and it had lived at the back of the cupboard in the tall house for as long as she could remember. Then she knew the soup: chicken with lotus root and peanuts and red dates, the one Ah Sim used to make for her when she was small and couldn’t sleep, from a recipe in her mother’s handwriting that had been kept in a drawer by the stove.

Eliana: did you make soup?

Lin Jian: Yes.

Eliana: which one?

Lin Jian: Yours.

Eliana: mine?

Lin Jian: Your mother wrote it down. Ah Sim made it for you. You liked it.

She looked at the photograph. Somewhere in her memory there was a kitchen table, her feet not reaching the floor, Ah Sim blowing on a spoon. She hadn’t known her father had ever been in the doorway.

Yu Chen: Looks good, Baba.

Lin Jian: Come and eat.

Yu Chen reached across the table and touched her hand. “We can go now.”

She nodded, and because she didn’t want it to become too serious, typed:

Eliana: save me a bowl

Lin Jian: Yes.

Lin Jian: Come early.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of the year he was part of the chat as if he’d always been there. Six o’clock, every morning. Sometimes a photograph. He learned to send voice messages and used the function twice. The first was eleven seconds long and consisted of a kettle, a cupboard door, and Baba saying, “The weather is good today.” The second was three seconds. “Raiden. Stop sending stickers.” Raiden sent five more. Baba didn’t reply, and didn’t leave.

When Eliana rang one evening to ask if he wanted to learn video calls, he said yes. He didn’t understand why everyone laughed when the camera showed the ceiling, or why Raiden kept saying, “Baba, we can see the light fitting.” But he tried again. And again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday the eighteenth of February, 2029, Eliana woke to her phone buzzing under the pillow at six in the morning, and opened the chat with one eye.

Not one word this time. Four.

Lin Jian: Happy birthday, Yu-er.

She read it twice. Beside her Yu Chen lifted his head.

“Sweetheart?”

He had said it to her at the grave for three years now. He’d said it at breakfast. But he had never written it down, for anyone to see, in front of everyone. She turned the screen to Yu Chen, and he read it, and his face went soft.

“Happy birthday,” he said.

She was smiling, and her eyes were already wet.

Eliana: thank you baba

Eliana: I’ll come for breakfast

Lin Jian: Good.

Lin Jian: Eat first.

She laughed through it, and Yu Chen pulled her in against him.

Raiden: HAPPY BIRTHDAY YU-ER!!!

Jinx: It’s six in the morning.

Raiden: IT’S HER BIRTHDAY

Elowen: Happy birthday, little one.

Evangeline: Happy birthday, Eliana.

Elara: Happy birthday. See you at breakfast.

Zhao: Happy birthday.

Jun Hyuk: Happy birthday.

Xing Yue: Happy birthday.

Yu Chen: Happy birthday, sweetheart. Come back to sleep for ten minutes.

Lin Jian: Good.

She pressed the phone against her chest. For years her father had left a red egg at her door and stood at the foot of her stairs, and learned, slowly and badly, to come closer without making her do all the work. Now he sent her one word every morning at six, and once a year, apparently, four.

“Do you think he’ll ever learn full stops?” she said.

“Probably.”

“Stickers?”

“No,” said Yu Chen, and kissed her forehead. “Happy birthday, my love.”

The phone buzzed once more.

Lin Jian: Breakfast at seven. Your favourite.

Eliana: I’ll be there

She didn’t need to ask what he was making. He remembered.

chapters.title: Ah Sim’s Gate
chapters.desc: The red door in the back wall of the Lin house, told by the woman who has kept its key since Qi Wanqing gave it to her in 1987: a girl from Plum Steps, a boy with a map on his arm, a daughter-in-law told to sit down, a step scrubbed clean, and a girl who always preferred the wall.
chapters.epigraph: “Sometimes it’s the only way they know how to come home.”
chapters.content:
The gate was red before anybody thought of calling it mine.

It’s a small door in the back wall of the Lin house, away from the front steps and the lane where visitors announce themselves. When I first held its key, in 1987, the paint was new and the hinges were new and the step was clean. Madam Qi Wanqing gave me that key in the kitchen, standing by the chair she had just refused a bigger house from. She put it in my palm and closed my fingers round it.

“This one is yours.”

“Madam, the gate belongs to the house.”

“Then you can look after the house,” she said.

That was how I came to have a key to the back gate before her husband did. He found out a week later, looked at the key in my hand and then at his wife, and she only smiled. I didn’t ask why she chose me. I had been in service long enough to know that some things are better received than questioned.

I learned the gate’s habits. It sticks a little in the rain. It complains if you shut it too quickly. You have to lift the latch before the key will turn, and if you know how, you can open it without waking anyone in the house. I learned who came through it, and who needed it opened before they knocked. And I learned that a gate doesn’t only keep people out. Sometimes it’s the only way they know how to come home.

✦ ✦ ✦

In November 2002 Madam brought the little girl from Plum Steps through it, holding the child’s hand on one side and her husband’s on the other, and said, “This is Ah Sim. She knows where everything is.” The girl looked at me as if she wanted that to be true. I gave her a bowl of rice with an egg in it, and she ate every grain, and that was Elara.

In February 2003 Madam went out through the front door to the hospital, and did not come home through any of them.

I kept the key. Nobody asked me to give it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the spring of 2008 a boy came up the alley that nobody in the house had seen since he was a few days old.

I’d been told, like everyone, that the Lin son had been sickly since birth and lived in the country with a cousin. I was in the kitchen when I saw him through the window: ten years old, thin, in a woman’s coat too big for him, walking up the alley with a map drawn in biro on the inside of his arm, carrying himself with the stubborn straightness of a child who has come a long way on his own and intends to pretend it was nothing.

I stood with a cloth in my hands and didn’t know whether to call anyone. Then Master Lin came past me without a word, and lifted the latch, and opened the gate himself. He didn’t shout. He didn’t ask where the boy had been or how he’d got there. He sat down on the step.

“You’re home,” he said.

That was all. The boy stopped and looked at his father. Then he came through.

I made sure there was food. That was my part. In a house somebody has to know when to speak, and somebody has to know when to put a bowl on the table. The gate stayed open until Raiden was inside.

✦ ✦ ✦

On a Sunday at the end of January 2024 a young woman knocked on it.

I knew who she was. Everyone in the house knew by then that Raiden had been married for more than two years to a girl who fixed motorbikes in Tai Hing, and that nobody had been told. She had the look of a person who’d come to see somebody and hadn’t yet decided whether she’d admit she needed anything. I’d seen that look on daughters and husbands and on people who’d spent too long trying to manage everything by themselves.

“Come in,” I said.

She came in. Master Lin was in the kitchen. He offered her his lawyer, for some trouble she was in, and she said no, and the kitchen went still. I was at the stove. I remember that I didn’t turn round.

“Nobody has said no to me in my own kitchen since 1987,” said Master Lin, and I knew whose no he meant, and so did he. “Sit down. Eat. You’re my daughter-in-law.”

She sat. I put a bowl in front of her. When she left, I opened the gate again, and she thanked me, and I told her not to thank anybody for sitting down. She smiled. The gate shut behind her, and after that she came through it whenever she liked.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was one girl who hardly used it.

Eliana preferred the wall. The garden isn’t as quiet as she believed, and the old wall between our house and the Song house has opinions about people who cross it without using a proper entrance. Sometimes I heard her before I saw her. Sometimes I’d look out at six in the morning and find her coming down the persimmon on our side with her slippers in her hand, with the confidence of someone who had decided long ago that a little difficulty wasn’t going to stop her.

I didn’t ask where she’d been. I knew. The boy next door was usually involved.

Wang Yu Chen came through the gate often enough that I stopped thinking of him as a visitor. The boy from the Song house. Polite. Quiet. He had a habit of arriving at exactly the right time, and of looking at the wall when she was late.

I fed him. Of course I fed him. A boy who comes into a house shouldn’t have to wait for someone to remember he might be hungry.

Sometimes they came in together. Sometimes she came first and he followed. Sometimes they sat at the kitchen table, and I put something down between them without asking what they were doing. I knew they were growing up. I knew the way they looked at each other was changing, years before either of them said a word to anyone. You learn things, cooking for a family long enough. You learn who leaves the last piece for whom. Whose tea goes cold because they’re talking. Whose footsteps make somebody else look up.

She wasn’t good at saying what she wanted. He wasn’t good at saying what he felt. But he kept coming back, and she kept finding her way to him, wall or no wall. And when her father told me in April 2025 that the boy wasn’t to come round any more, I went on feeding him through the gate anyway, and Master Lin knew, and said nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Sunday of November 2025 there was a knife in the alley outside the gate.

I won’t pretend a thing like that becomes ordinary because you’ve lived a long time, or because you’ve seen people frightened before. It doesn’t. Elara’s blood was on my step. The house was full of people that night, and all of them were at the hospital or on the telephone, and the next morning at six I went out alone with a bucket of hot water and a brush.

I didn’t ask anyone to do it for me. I scrubbed until the stone was clean. Then I rinsed the brush, and stood and looked at the red door shut behind me.

I’d been given its key in 1987, before he had his. I’d opened it for a child from Plum Steps and a boy with a map on his arm and a girl with oil under her nails. I’d watched Eliana climb the wall instead, and watched the boy next door wait. That morning I wanted the step clean. Not because stone forgets. Because the people who come through that gate shouldn’t have to look down and remember.

When I’d finished, I put the key back in my apron pocket where it belongs.

✦ ✦ ✦

By 2028 the gate had become part of the house in a way nobody thinks about. People come through it without asking. They know to lift the latch. They know how far to push before the hinge complains, and where to leave their shoes, and which way to go round if the kitchen’s busy. There are husbands now, and wives, and more voices at the table than there have ever been. People who once stood on the other side of the wall come through carrying food and presents and books, and things they bought because they thought somebody might like them.

Master Lin still comes in the back way sometimes. He’s learned, slowly, that a house can be entered without making everybody stand up. Eliana still comes and goes, through the gate they cut in the garden wall for her wedding as often as through mine. The boy next door still looks for her. Some habits aren’t worth breaking.

I keep the key. People ask why, when everyone knows how to open it. I’ve never had a good answer. Perhaps because Madam gave it to me. Perhaps because my hand knows its shape without looking. Perhaps because a key is a small thing to keep, when you’ve been trusted with a whole house.

One night this autumn I sat by the back door and listened to them all in the garden. Raiden too loud. Jinx telling him to stop. Somebody laughing. Eliana’s voice, and then the boy’s. I didn’t need to see them to know where they were.

I went into the kitchen. There was food left. There is always food left. I covered the bowls and put them away and checked the back door. The red gate was closed, but not locked. I touched the key in my pocket.

For forty-one years I have opened that door for the people who needed it. I’ve opened it for children and for grown men and women, for people who came with maps and with worries and with no explanation at all. And I’ve learned when not to shut it too quickly. A person might need a moment on the step. A person might need somebody to sit down beside them. A person might need to be told, without being asked to explain anything, that they’re home.

I turned off the kitchen light. Behind me the red door stood where it always has. I kept the key.

chapters.title: Every Eighteenth of February
chapters.desc: Twenty-five dawns at Qi Wanqing’s grave, one each year from the first after she died to Eliana’s twenty-fifth birthday: who came, who didn’t, what their father said and didn’t say, and the red egg left at Eliana’s door every year by someone she never saw.
chapters.epigraph: “The day was hers, too.”
chapters.content:
2004. The first time Lin Jian went back to the cemetery at dawn, Elowen was eight and old enough to know her mother wasn’t coming home, and Evangeline was five and asked why everybody had to wear black. Elara, four, slept on Ah Sim’s shoulder. Eliana was one year old that morning and understood none of it, not the white flowers or the bowed heads or why her father stood so still in front of the stone. He didn’t say happy birthday. That night, after the relatives had gone, a red egg appeared on the floor outside her bedroom door. Nobody explained it. Nobody asked.

2005. Elowen carried the flowers in both hands and kept the stems together all the way up the hill. Eliana, two, followed her sisters along the path until her legs gave out, then held her arms up to Ah Sim. Lin Jian stood at the stone and never once looked down at the smallest of them. That evening the egg was on her step again, bright against the grey boards. She found it before breakfast and tried to roll it down the corridor.

2006. Eliana stood at the back in a red cardigan too warm for the day and asked why they were there, and nobody answered quickly enough, and the question went away on its own. At home the egg was waiting. She ate it with rice and asked Ah Sim whether red eggs tasted different from ordinary ones, and Ah Sim said only that this one was made with love, and didn’t say by whom.

2007. Eliana had learned that the eighteenth was a day when the house went quiet: no running in the corridor, no asking for sweets, no pulling at her father’s sleeve while he looked at the photograph on the stairs. At the grave she stood a step behind Elowen, who had begun to arrange the flowers without being told. Lin Jian said nothing to his youngest, though she looked up at him the whole time with the patience of a child waiting to be included. That night she saved half the egg for the morning.

2008. White flowers. He stood alone after the others had stepped back, and Eliana, five, started towards him, and Ah Sim caught her hand. That spring a boy she had never met would walk up the alley with a map drawn on his arm, and their father would open the back gate himself and say You’re home, and she would be told he was her brother, who had been ill in the country. But on the eighteenth there were still only four of them on the hill. That night the egg came with a paper napkin folded under it, so the shell wouldn’t stain the floor. She kept the napkin for months.

2009. Raiden came up the hill for the first time, ten years old, and stood next to Ev, the twin everyone had told him he had, and stared at a name on a stone that he had never once heard said. Eliana had picked one flower herself on the way, and stepped forward to lay it with the others. Lin Jian moved aside without looking at her. The flower landed crooked. Nobody straightened it. That night she ate the whole egg, yolk and all, though she didn’t like the yolk.

2010. It rained. The caretaker offered Lin Jian shelter and he refused it and said he’d wait a little longer, and Eliana waited too, though nobody had asked her to, until her shoes were soaked through. At home the egg was wrapped in a twist of red paper. She carried it to the kitchen and asked Ah Sim to warm it, and Ah Sim did, though it didn’t need warming.

2011. Eliana was beginning to understand that the grave wasn’t simply a place where they remembered someone. It was where her father became a man she couldn’t reach. At home he asked the others about school and meals and lessons. On the hill he belonged to somebody else entirely. She stood behind the others with her hands folded in front of her coat. That night she took the egg up to her room. She never saw who left it.

2012. Raiden complained that the flowers were uneven and then fixed them himself. Eliana had a drawing from school in her pocket, five children holding hands under a tree, which she wanted to leave on the stone and couldn’t make herself walk forward with. It went home with her. That evening she put it in the drawer with the napkins, under the egg.

2013. She was ten, and had noticed that her birthday wasn’t like other children’s. No candles at breakfast. No singing. The cemetery came first. Lin Jian told the stone about the girls’ schools, and the house, and the weather, and didn’t mention the date. In the car home Elowen whispered happy birthday, and Eliana said it didn’t matter. That night she peeled the egg so carefully that the shell came off in one piece.

2014. Raiden had a school match and their father said he needn’t miss it. Eliana followed the others up the hill in new shoes that rubbed her heels raw. She didn’t say anything. At the stone Lin Jian said Elowen was doing well, and Raiden was more responsible, and Elara had been busy, and Ev’s orchids had flowered, and didn’t say the name of the girl standing behind him. On the way down Elowen saw the blood on the back of Eliana’s sock and made the driver stop. The egg was on the step. She ate it standing up.

2015. She was tall enough now to stand level with Elowen and still stood a step behind her, a habit nobody had taught her and nobody asked her to break. Eliana looked at the date cut into the stone, which was also her birthday, and wondered whether her mother had known it would be. She didn’t ask. That night she put the egg beside the photograph in her drawer.

2016. Her father looked tired. She had a birthday card for her mother in her pocket, but the words in it felt childish now, and it stayed there. That night the egg had a tiny crack near the top. She didn’t throw it away until morning.

2017. She was fourteen, and old enough to understand that a man could love someone who was gone and still not know how to love the child who had stayed. She didn’t have the words for it yet. She only knew that on the eighteenth of February her father looked through her like a window, and on the other days of the month he sometimes remembered to ask whether she’d eaten. At home she held the egg for a while and didn’t eat it until Ah Sim brought up her dinner.

2018. Elowen had begun bringing flowers of her own, never the brightest, the stems always trimmed. Elara came straight from a lecture in her first year of medicine, with her notes still under her arm. Eliana had stopped bringing things. When Lin Jian turned to go, he didn’t notice that his youngest hadn’t moved. Elowen did, and waited for her. That night Eliana cut the egg in half and put one half in the fridge.

2019. There was a cake in the kitchen when they got back, and nobody sang, because she’d asked Ah Sim not to make a fuss. At the grave her father had talked for nearly an hour about his children and the house and the persimmon, and hadn’t said the name of the one whose birthday it was. The egg went into the drawer with the napkins and the drawing and the card. She had no idea why she kept them.

2020. Fewer people again. Zhao, who had married Elowen at a registry a month later in March, wasn’t there yet. Eliana stood at the edge of the path, seventeen, nearly grown, and expert at not being noticed. That evening she looked at the egg on her step a long while before she picked it up, and for the first time wondered whether her father knew she always found it. Whether he knew she kept them. Whether he knew she had never once taken it for an ordinary egg.

2021. Her eighteenth. Zhao came, and stood at the back, and their father nodded to him. It was her last February at school; in the summer she’d finish and go up the hill to the university, where the boy next door had somehow also decided to go. The visit was short. At midnight her phone lit up with a message from the window across the garden. Yu Chen: happy birthday. look outside. On the wall between the two gardens, in the frost, he had left a cup of honey lemon with a saucer over it to keep it warm, and the egg was waiting at her door when she came back in.

2022. Friday. She found the egg on her step at dawn and, for the first time in her life, took it outside. Yu Chen was sitting on his own step with two cups, as if he’d known. She sat beside him on the other side of the little wall and cracked the egg and gave him half, and he didn’t ask where it had come from, and she didn’t say. Later he took her to the planetarium, and under the turning ceiling he called her Yu-er for the first time, and she thought the day had always felt like a room with one light missing, and that someone had just found the switch.

2023. Saturday. Only Ah Sim and Raiden knew there was anyone in her life, and Zhao, who said nothing, so the boy next door didn’t come. He was on his step when the family car came back, with a flask and a cup, and she sat with him for ten minutes in her black coat and didn’t need to say anything. That night the egg was at her door, and she carried it over the garden wall, and they ate it on his floor.

2024. Sunday. The family was bigger. Elara came with her husband, Xing Yue, who had married her at a registry the August before and stood a respectful step behind her with his hands clasped. Jinx came for the first time, in a borrowed black jacket. Lin Jian told the stone about two weddings. Yu Chen still wasn’t allowed to be anyone, officially; he waited at the cemetery gate in his old grey car, and when the family had gone down she walked back up the path and sat beside him for a while, and their sleeves touched.

2025. Tuesday, and she was twenty-two, and in five weeks the boy next door would say on her step at two in the morning that he wanted to marry her, and she would run. But not yet. Ev came with Jun Hyuk, who had married her under the fig tree at Christmas. Yu Chen waited at the gate again. The egg was at her door that night, and she carried it next door and put it on his kitchen table between them, and he didn’t ask her to eat it.

2026. Wednesday. She was living next door now, and before dawn she waited behind her own front door in the Song house and caught her father on the step, a red egg in his hand. It was always me, he said. At the grave Elara didn’t come; she hadn’t spoken to anyone since the knife. Yu Chen stood beside Eliana in the open, for the first time. Their father looked at the stone, and then, after twenty-three years, he turned to his youngest daughter and said, “Happy birthday, Yu-er,” and that he was sorry. It didn’t undo anything. But he had looked at her. She held the egg in both hands at home, and cried before she could peel it.

2027. Thursday, three months after the porch and the ring. Elara was back, her wrist healed, with Xing Yue. Her father’s eyes went to the ring on her finger, and he said happy birthday again, more easily, and didn’t leave early. That night the egg was on her step, and they ate it at their own kitchen table, among the wedding plans.

2028. Friday, her twenty-fifth. All of them came: Elowen and Zhao, Raiden and Jinx, Ev and Jun Hyuk, Elara and Xing Yue, Ah Sim and Uncle Mok, and Yu Chen at her side. There were two red eggs on her step that morning. One from her father, perfect. One from her husband, lopsided, unevenly coloured, which he gave her with the gravity of a man handing over something precious, and her father looked at it and said nothing unkind. At the stone he wished her happy birthday as if it had never been hard, asked about FENCE, and what came next, and spoke to her as if her life were something he wanted to know about. She didn’t stand a step behind anyone. The day was hers, too.

extras.title: Since Summer
extras.line: The night she tells him what she does. He already knew. She reads his phone while he washes her bowl.

extras.title: Lin Yu
extras.line: A blanket on a wet wall, a red egg, a sky with her other name on it, and someone who says hi inside her config.
